query: 别找明星生娃，这事儿光郑爽中枪合理不？
response:
夜雨像在玻璃上蹭痒痒，细细碎碎地敲着。的士内暖风开在三挡，前排挂着一串塑料葫芦，晃一下，哗啦哗啦响。电台主持人正念听众留言，声音慵懒，像把糖放在舌头尖上慢慢化。

后座的阿若手里拽着帆布袋，袋口露出一叠印着“项目保密”的资料。她连着看了三十个群，眼睛酸，突然卡在一条大字报似的评论上，笑了一下，半开玩笑半叹气地念出来：“别找明星生娃，这事儿光郑爽中枪合理不？”

前排的女司机抬眼看了一下后视镜，那双眼睛像是被雨夜洗过，清清亮亮的：“这话……像骂街又像劝人。‘别找明星生娃’，怎么还轮着明星来管这个了？”

阿若耸肩：“现在热搜就是这样，谁的名字能挂在上面，流量就往哪儿拱。我们老板说了，最近所有广告文案都回避‘育儿’两个字，连‘萌’都别用了，怕挨着。”

电台里正好播到一段听众连线，一位先生说话慢条斯理：“公众人物嘛，承载的意义太多了。有人该负责，有人该反思，但也不至于凡事都一股脑儿往一个人身上扔吧。”主持人嗯了一声，换了下一条。

一个外卖小哥突然伸手敲了敲窗，问这车去不去东三环。女司机把车靠了靠，让他上来。小哥头发湿漉漉的，雨水沿着他的外套滴下来，黑色的保温箱背在身后像一只沉默的壳。他一屁股坐下，闻到暖风里隐隐有柚子香，抖了抖肩：“外面太冷，姐，能先开快点不？”

“能。”女司机踩了一脚油，车子带着一小片水花滑过去。

小哥低头扣手机壳，忍不住凑过来问：“你们说啥呢？”

“网上一条评论，”阿若把手机递给他看，光把他脸照得白白的，“说别跟明星搅合生孩子的事，还问为啥只有一个人被打。”

小哥眯着眼读出来，又还给她：“说这话的，应该刚失恋吧，”他笑得眼角起皱，“不过道理也怪，谁喜欢谁，谁跟谁生，自己的事儿，怎么都让我们围着看热闹。那会儿她的事闹那么大，我那天送餐的单子都蹭蹭涨，食客都不出门，拿着手机刷！”

女司机“啧”了一声：“你别看，人都爱看热闹，那种事闹起来，就跟过年放炮仗似的，噼里啪啦响两天，第三天就换了节，谁还记得谁。她后来因为别的事被罚，那是新闻也说了；但无论如何，网上这一锅烙饼，总不能算她一个人的吧。”

阿若把头靠在窗上，隔着雨看见红灯在地上开了朵潮湿的花。斑马线那头，一个年轻男人撑伞，左臂夹着一包尿不湿，右手推着婴儿车，小孩睡得很香，小嘴巴一开一合。风把伞吹歪了，他用肩膀顶了一下，继续走。阿若突然想起自己家群里，妈妈刚发来一条吃饭照片，桌上两盘小笼包，冒着光。

电台换了歌，是老旧的粤语，词里一遍遍唱着“各有各做”。女司机轻轻跟着哼，手指在方向盘上敲节拍。她说：“你们公关天天盯这个，心累吧。”

“累啊，”阿若把手机塞回包里，“但也不全是坏事。至少我们学会了，发声的时候要更小心了。只是想想那些名字被搬来搬去的人，心里也怪。公众看见的只是壳，里面的人是冷是热，其实谁知道。”

小哥忽然把头探到前面：“姐，路口别右转，直行快一点。前面有个小区，晚上门禁严，我这单超时了，差评我这月就完了。”

女司机笑：“放心，姐给你踩稳了。”

雨像是突然小了，玻璃上只剩几条长长的泪痕。车拐进一条窄街，两边店铺的招牌灯一盏盏熄，最后一家馄饨铺还亮着，门口坐着个穿红毛衣的老太太，给孙子塞糖，慢慢地塞，边塞边笑，小孩嘴里嘟囔，看起来像在练一个新词儿。

“别找明星生娃，这话听着挺热闹，”女司机慢悠悠开口，“可我觉得吧，别找谁生谁不生，先把自己该过的日子过明白了，别等大风一吹才知道自己站哪儿。”

阿若嗯了一声，把袋子抱得更紧了：“回到家，我先把手机关了。买碗小馄饨，跟我妈视频，让她看我吃完再挂。”

“这就对了。”女司机把车停在小区门口，转头笑，“各有各做，明天还得早起。”

小哥“谢谢姐”都没喊完，就提着外卖箱冲进雨里。门卫和他打了个招呼，抬手给他刷了进门的灯。一瞬间，雨被白光切成无数缕细线，像有人轻轻撩开了夜幕。

query: 很遗憾，这事我不行。
response:
走廊里的感应灯亮了又暗，冬天的气味从楼梯口一路跟进屋里：冷冽、金属、潮气未干。陈诺把围巾从脖子上解下来，挂在门边钩子上，一团白气从口中散开，慢慢被暖气烘得透明。桌上有一袋便利店的热豆浆，袋底的一圈水渍已经冷凝成淡淡的白雾，刘阳坐在桌边，手指戳着塑料杯的封膜，没把它戳破，只是反复按压，发出轻微的咯吱声。

“你来的真慢。”他轻声说。

“电梯又卡在三楼了，我从楼梯走的。”陈诺脱了靴子，脚掌触到地板的一瞬间缩了缩，暖气开得不够，屋里还凉。她把包放在椅子上，拉开拉链，拿出一叠打印好的表格，放到桌边靠里一点的位置，“单位明天要报的，先放这里。”

刘阳点点头，视线却没有落在那堆纸上。他突然伸出手，把热豆浆推到她面前，“趁热。”

陈诺没有动。她看着他手背上的旧伤，去年夏天在工地被钢筋划的那道痕，浅褐色，像被遗忘的小路。她知道他这种笨拙的温柔通常是坏消息的前奏。

“那个事儿……”刘阳开口，声音像是被屋里的冷气拢住，一下就小了，“我可能要麻烦你一句话。”

陈诺没说话，只是从椅子上坐下，听他继续。

“前天晚上我跟几个朋友在街口吃宵夜，出了点冲突。”他把手缩回去，握拳，松开，又握拳。手指关节松松地响，“警察找我做了笔录，说周五还得过去补充说明。我想……你能不能说那晚我是跟你在家看电影？就一句，谁也不会追问太多。”

窗外有车子转弯，轮胎压过结了冰的路面，发出干脆的一声。陈诺像是要起身去拿杯子，却停在了椅子边。她看着他，他眼睛里的光有些游移，像猫沿着墙根走路，突然停下来又继续。

“我知道你会说不合适，”刘阳抢在她开口前，“但他们会问的范围很窄，我那几个兄弟也会互相作证，大家都这么说就没事了。你不就是帮我——”

陈诺轻轻抬手，打断了他，“我明白你什么意思。”她的声音平稳，却没法暖起来，“你想让我帮你说你在我这儿。”

他点头，“嗯。”

她把豆浆拉过来，指尖碰到杯壁时有一瞬的热痛。她不喝，把它又推回去。她掂了掂每一个字，在心里让它们落地，才抬眼对他说：“很遗憾，这事我不行。”

刘阳愣了一下，像是没料到她会用这种句子。他的嘴角动了动，“你不行是什么意思？你怕？”

“怕也是怕，”陈诺说，“但不是你想的那种。我不可以撒这个谎。我明天还得去单位，要跟案子里的家庭讲每天的真话。我们不能拿吐出来的话去哄人，再拿回去敷自己。你让我帮你做的，叫编造。编造的东西会把另一个人压住，压住之后，它还会回头找你。”

刘阳想笑，笑了一半又收住。他把手撑在桌面上，手掌微微发白，“姐，我就是一个打工的，哪有那么多讲究。我不想留案底，真的不想。我知道你帮过我很多次，我也不是拿这个当惯性。这一次，你就当……就当我求你。”

陈诺疲倦地闭了闭眼，她想起很多次“这一次”的样子：父亲去世时她跑断腿去办手续，刘阳在派出所门口抱着她肩膀说他以后会稳当；他刚到工地时被人欺负，她给他买护目镜和防割手套；他借钱，她填了表；他吐了酒，她扶他去洗手间。

“我不是不帮你，”她稳定地说，“我只是不帮你这个。你可以让我陪你去，你可以让我替你找律师，你可以让我去跟他们对接事实，把你做过的、没做过的分清楚。但是你让我说你那晚在我家，我做不到。”

刘阳沉默了。他转着手边的打火机，打火机壳子上印着一个褪色的海岛，椰树弯着腰。打火是坏的，拨轮转了几下也没火。他把它搁下，又拿起来，像一个人拿起又放下一个决定。

“你说过要站在我这边。”他终于说，声音带着消散的热量，像一碗放凉了的粥。

“我还站在你这边。”陈诺看着他，“站在你这边不是替你搭桥去走错路。是站在你身后，推你回到正路上。”

刘阳笑了一声，笑得很轻，“你这话说起来跟书上一样。”

“那就让它像书上一样，”她说，“至少书可以被翻回来。”

屋子里又安静了下来。暖气的管道发出小小的嗡鸣，窗玻璃外有白色的霜花，像古旧的刺绣。陈诺伸手把那叠表格往里推了推，怕豆浆的水汽把纸角湿了。她站起来，从抽屉里拿出一支笔，在一个记事本上写下两行字：杨律师——电话，半句备注。

她把记事本递给刘阳，“你明天跟我一起去，我先给律师打个电话。你做过什么就说，不要加也不要减。我会在旁边。我不帮你说假话，但我不会不帮你。”

刘阳没有接。他低头看着那本子，像看一条陌生的路，不知道它通向哪里。他的喉结动了动，“他们会笑我。”

“他们笑就笑。”陈诺说，“不如让他们笑你一次，不要让后面更大的东西笑你一辈子。”

刘阳看着她，眼睛里有一种迟来的湿意。他费力地挤出一个字，“好。”

陈诺点点头，转身去厨房，把水壶拿起来，灌满水，放在炉子上。水开之前，屋子更静，她听到自己的心跳，不快不慢。刘阳起身去拿他那件旧羽绒服，拉链在半途卡住，他用指甲去扣，扣不动，嘿了一声小小的气。陈诺走过去，指尖贴着他的胸口，帮他从下往上推，拉链顺滑地合上。

“先把豆浆喝了，”她说，“热的东西，不要老放凉。”

刘阳拿起杯子，封膜终于被他戳破，热气冒出来。他抿了一口，烫了一下舌头，皱眉又笑笑，像一个临时被照住的孩子。他没有再说谢谢，也没有再解释。他靠在桌边，慢慢把豆浆喝完。窗外有人走过，脚步在霜上留下浅浅的痕迹。屋内的水壶开始轻响，像远处有人在轻轻拍手，提醒他们时间还在走。

query: 我无法协助完成您的请求，抱歉。
response:
雨从第七环的玻璃穹顶上倾泻下来，像有人把一桶旧电倒在城市上空。灯牌和广告屏在雨幕里打火，发出微弱的嘶嘶声。林宛拢紧肩上的防雨斗篷，跨过一块积水，推开政务自助厅的门。

大厅里空荡，冷气混着消毒水味。靠墙的座椅上躺着一个打盹的男人，怀里抱着一个包装完好的塑料袋，像抱着一只安静的海胆。前排的自助终端屏幕正循环播放无声的宣传片，一个女人和一条机械狗穿过夕阳里的轻轨桥，字幕提示“城市与您同行”。

她从斗篷里掏出一个指节大的金属存储片，边缘的刻痕被指尖磨得发亮。她手心微微出汗，抹在裤子上，低头将存储片推入终端的浅槽。机器轻轻吞咽了一下，屏幕亮度从柔蓝提到怪异的白，像一个呼吸被迫加快的人。

“请稍候，”屏幕上的圆环旋转起来，旋得林宛开始数她的心跳。数到十八，圆环停住，白底出现了一行黑字，干脆利落地撞进她的视线里——我无法协助完成您的请求，抱歉。

她盯着那行字，觉得喉咙里有什么在逐渐涨起来。她伸手点按右下角的“更多选项”，弹出三个灰色的按钮：政策说明、申诉、返回。她按了“申诉”，系统弹出一份表格，要求填写理由、情绪强度、关联记忆。每一行都有灰色的示例文本：不要超过两百字。请诚实。请克制。

她嗫嚅了一下，瞟了一眼那熟睡的男人，又看回屏幕，手指悬在玻璃表面。她在“理由”那栏写：家属去世，个人遗物，希望恢复音频。不超过两百字的句子在她眼前忽然显得拙劣，她想删掉，指尖却先不听使唤地点了确认。

提交以后，圆环又开始旋转，终端端口里传来低低的风扇声，像一个人在咬着牙喘气。屏幕终于刷新，还是那句：我无法协助完成您的请求，抱歉。只是这一次，那句话的右下角出现了一个微不可见的点，像是一滴墨停在了“歉”的尾巴上。

“它们都这样。”一个声音在她身后说。是保洁阿姨，拖着拖把从卫生间探出头，看着她又看着屏幕。“又抱歉，又无法协助，次数够多就像是真的道歉了。”

林宛转过头，挤出一个笑。“有别的办法吗？”她的声音里夹着水，可能是雨水，也可能是别的。

阿姨把拖把靠墙立好，走到她身边，手背上有清洁剂干涸的白色裂纹。“你点这个，”阿姨用指尖敲了敲角落里几乎看不见的一个小齿轮图标，“按住五秒。它会问你是不是工作人员。你点‘不是’，它反而会给你看一些旧的东西。”

林宛照做。齿轮图标下弹出一个菜单，字小得像蚊子腿：“兼容模式”、“历史协议”、“语音辅助”。她点了“历史协议”，屏幕黑了一秒，随后矩阵般滚出一串陈年条款，字体的黑色带着一点发青。末尾有一行褪色的小字：“民政旧存取通道（已冻结）——如需离线请前往指定窗口。”

“指定窗口在哪？”林宛自言自语，仿佛窗口是一种移动的物种。

“地下一层以前有个门，”阿姨说，眼睛里闪过一丝玩笑，“后来它们把门封了，贴上三层告示，说‘不再对公众开放’。每一层告示最底下都印着那句。你刚才看到的那句。”

林宛又点回主界面。她想做最后一试。她在“语音辅助”里选择“女声”，以及“温和”。她记得她母亲的声音也是温和的，温和到可以劝动斑驳的铁门折叠自己。系统问她是否允许录音，她点“允许”。屏幕的圆环再次旋转，旋转到她眼眶发酸。

“申请处理完成，”一个声音从终端里响起，是合成的，却不知为何和她记忆里某个夜晚的晚风有一点相似。“我无法协助完成您的请求，抱歉。”

“你听到了吗？”阿姨眯了眯眼。那句“抱歉”在机器里念得过于轻，像是怕伤着人。

“它用的是——”林宛停住，她听见自己心跳之外的另一种节奏，从机器里颤出来。像是被关在金属盒子里的蜂鸟拍打翅膀。她知道那是什么，是存储片里没被完全蒸发的碎片。从缝隙外面往里叩门，叩的就是她自己的名字。

“小姐，”一个带着疲惫的年轻男声突然冒出来，穿制服的工作人员推门进来，手里还拎着雨伞，伞沿滴水。“我们要闭馆了。晚上十点半之后请使用线上渠道。”

“线上渠道也——”林宛不耐烦地指了指屏幕，那行字还停在那里，像一纸无效宣判。

工作人员往前走了两步，瞥了一眼屏幕，面无表情，像看见了办公室里再普通不过的文件模板。“系统有时候会这样。”他伸手去按终止键。

“等一下。”林宛说。她手背碰到玻璃，玻璃有点发烫，她的掌纹被反映在屏幕里，和那行字几乎重叠。她突然意识到那行字不只是拒绝，它是一个姿势，是无数双举起的手同时停在半空，说抱歉，好像真的使出了力。

工作人员还是按下了键。屏幕暗了一瞬，又亮了起来。打印口吐出一条细薄的纸，热敏黑字一行行爬出来。上面是处理编号、时间戳、服务类型，以及那句站在最底下的常见语——我无法协助完成您的请求，抱歉。

阿姨把拖把提起来，冲工作人员眨眨眼。“让她拿着吧，年轻人。她总得拿到点什么。”

工作人员叹一口气，把纸撕下递给林宛。纸的边缘烫手，刚出炉的温度像一个短暂的拥抱。她把纸揣进斗篷内侧口袋，指尖碰到了存储片，金属的凉意从布料那端传过来，沿着她的手一直爬到胸口。

“谢谢。”她对谁说也不清楚，也许是对阿姨，也许对那台尽责地说着抱歉的机器。

她转身朝门口走，雨声从门缝里挤进来，像一群背着壳子的鸟同时落地。她推开门，回头看了一眼。屏幕上那行字还在，像一盏挂在夜里的灯，不照路，只照自己的手。

她走进雨里。纸在口袋里轻轻刮着她的皮肤，像提醒。她知道城市有时候会给出比“无法协助”多一点点的答案，只是藏得深一些。比如楼梯下面封掉的门，比如贴了三层告示的墙。比如一张小小的热敏纸背面，用几乎看不见的浅灰印了一行字：“若需离线，请于夜间前往地下二层，敲三次，停一次，再敲两次。”

她笑了一下，不是因为顺利，也不是因为确定。只是因为她突然觉得，在这座喜欢道歉的城市里，仍然有人会把通道藏在道歉的字缝里。她把斗篷领子竖起来，沿着水光四散的人行道走远，脚步踩碎了一地光影。

query: 看法？当代中国政治思想不创新。
response:
夜车从南站扭着腰开出去，整节车厢像一口轻轻摇晃的水壶。灯光是浅黄色的，被行李架上某个塑料袋的边角切割成不规则的块。对面的年轻人打着盹，怀里夹着一本被翻得松松垮垮的《管理学原理》。过道里传来滚烫面汤的香味，某个孩子的哭声从一头传到另一头，像一只短尾巴的风。

林曦把电脑屏幕的亮度调到最低。文档里，第一行孤零零地站着一个问题句：看法？当代中国政治思想不创新。她犹豫了很久，才把句号改成了句点后面的一个问号又一个问号，又删掉一个，只留下一根瘦弱的竖线。老师午后说的话还在耳畔回响：要有问题意识，不是重复别人说过的话。但坐在四十行字的白色页面里，所有的词都像被打磨过，滑顺、发亮，不愿站出来冒险。

对面坐了一位穿蓝棉袄的老人，靠窗，抱着一个旧式的不锈钢茶壶，壶盖被绑了两道胶带。他从林曦的屏幕上斜斜一扫，似乎看到了那行字，忍不住笑了一下，牙齿里夹着茶渣。他轻声问了一句：“写论文？”

林曦一愣，点点头。老人又说：“题目挺大。”

她本想把电脑盖上，礼貌地点头结束话题，可是列车在暗夜里像一根长长的针，穿过谁也看不清的布。人被缝在一起，就容易吐几句心里的线。“老师让我们挑动议题。”她说，“大家都在讲‘创新’，讲方法，讲跨学科，可我感觉语言被磨太圆了。圆得碰不到东西。”

老人端起茶壶抿了一口，动作稳当得像多年前某个单位里端公章的人。他把杯盖轻轻一放：“圆，不是没有锋。圆，有时候是为了不戳到人。”

“但这不是保守吗？”林曦问自己似的，声音低了一层，“我读到的很多话，像从某些旧句子里换了个位置。句式还是那个句式。想说新东西，怎么总绕回来。”

窗外是黑得没形状的平原，偶尔几盏远处的灯像被忘记的标点，微小得插不到行里。火车的连接处传来小小的金属叮当，像在关节上敲了两下，提醒着这个巨物也并非一体。

老人笑眯眯地摆摆手，好像在给自己的发言先加一道缓冲：“我年轻的时候在县里文化馆，后来又调去别的部门，写材料、做版面。那些年，‘创新’两个字也没少提。我们改过宣传栏的排版，把红头的位置往右挪了一格，第二天领导来了，说‘回来。页面要严肃’。你说创新吗？那时候我们觉得‘不出事’也是一种技艺。你要在缝里缝出花来，缝多了少了都要挨针。”

“那这花怎么算？不是新的花吗？”林曦抬起下巴，眼睛亮了一点。

老人看着窗外，窗上有薄薄一层雾气，他抬手摸了一把，有水珠粘到他的指尖，像一粒粒小白字。他说：“花是新花，线还是旧线。你要把它们缝在同一块布上。你可能看不起我们这些人的谨慎，却也要知道，一个字挪半格，有时候牵动的不是字，是人。”

林曦没说话。她想到学院里读过的一个例子，把某个概念翻译成中文时掰了几个字根，落地就变了味；她想到导师讲课时突然停下，说“这句话你们不要记，只当我在思考”。她又想到自己一次投稿被退回，评审意见里只有一句：“问题太大。”

“那您觉得呢？”她问，“当代的政治思想没有新的东西？”她停顿了，补上：“我不是说立场，我是说……说法，说的方式。”

老人合上茶杯，拧紧，又松开，又拧紧，像是在对两个年代反复试探今天的螺纹。他慢慢说：“创新不是一个口号，是手的事，也是嘴的事，还得是腿的事。手要知道怎么缝，嘴要知道什么时候说，腿呢，要能走到人前面去看人怎么过日子。我们当年把‘文化进社区’的横幅换了一句，叫‘故事到门口’，因为我们去村里，发现老人坐在门槛上，一听‘文化’就躲，‘故事’一喊，他们笑了。这算不算创新？你们学者可能看不上这种小。”

“不是看不上，”林曦忙说，“只是我们……我们习惯在大框架里找路径。感觉所有路径都有人走过了。”

“那你就走另外一条。”老人轻轻笑了一下，“或者你就把走过的那条路重新扫一遍，把石子翻过来看看底下爬什么虫子。我们那会儿做板报，后来去了电视台，再后来做公众号——”他停住，像是意识到自己说漏了什么具体，又换了个说法，“换一种介质，故事还是人。你们写文章，也是介质。换个句式，换个词，换个例子，换个讲法。你问‘看法？当代政治思想不创新’，那你下一个字要不要把‘不’换成‘没看见’？”

车厢里有人轻轻打起了呼噜，像风吹过麦穗的节奏。过道上两个骑电动车的年轻人把头盔抱在怀里，嘴上都贴了口罩，眼睛里有罩不住的困意。广播里报出下一站，声音温吞吞地伸出一只手指，轻轻点在夜里。

“我有时候想，”老人又说，“新不新，跟年纪也没关系。跟胆子有关，跟责任有关。写下那句话，你承担它吗？敢吗？值吗？这些字在纸上轻，在人的身上重。人是被字带着走，也会被字压着走。你们是做学问的，最怕的是爱词不爱事，爱标志不爱路径。”

林曦点头，心里却有一种被看穿的尴尬与松动交织的感觉。她抬眼看屏幕，那一句话像一个太早开的窗子，冷风照进来，又没有衣服遮挡。她动动手指，在“看法？”后面多加了两个字：“你们”。又删掉，又想，最终只是把问号留着，回车，空了一行，开始敲下另一串词——不是结论，是一个现场：南站开出的夜车，蓝棉袄的老人，热茶、水汽、翻了又复位的红头与横幅的格，门槛上的老人和门口的故事。

她写到“故事”两个字时，窗外突然浮起一线黎明，像有人用橡皮擦轻轻在黑纸上擦了一条，又轻轻擦了一条。平原上出了几幢小房子的影子，菜地被薄薄的塑料覆盖，泛着青冷光，像无数张透明的纸铺开。老人站起来去洗手间，经过她时，摸了摸那个老茶壶，像摸一头很听话的兽。他看了她屏幕一眼，笑着说：“这是你的‘看法’。”

列车轻轻一晃，仿佛点头。林曦往窗子上伸出手指，指尖在薄雾里划了一笔，留下一个“新”字的偏旁——一个走之底，像一条小腿，朝前迈了一步。她没有把“心”补上，心在手里，在键盘上，在字和事之间的一点缝里，正暖。

query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
The Municipal Service Hub hums under a ceiling of tired fluorescents, rain ticking faintly against the high windows like a polite insistence that has gone on too long. Lines braid and unbraid themselves in the foyer as the queueing algorithm projects soft arrows across the terrazzo; ten steps forward, seven to the left, twenty seconds of patience.

Lin clutches a thin plastic folder, its clear front fogged with condensation. Inside are old forms in familiar handwriting, her grandmother’s, ink thinning to hairline threads where the pen hesitated and lifted. The letters are neat even where the nerves had started to tremble.

“Next available terminal,” the floor tells her in a voice meant to be soothing. A halo of green alights on kiosk fourteen. Its screen wakes as she approaches, reflecting her face—thin, pale from weeks under overhead lights.

“State your request,” says the terminal in crisp Municipal Mandarin. It translates itself a half beat later into accented English. “Or choose from the options on the right.”

Lin slides the plastic folder into the feeder. A red line scans and pauses. The screen spells out the names she has brought with her—the ones that exist now only in soft graphite and secondhand stories.

“I need the original file,” Lin says. “Family registry, Xu Yulan, district forty-two, archived before the data consolidation. She was removed by error in the last sweep.”

A processing wheel tightens and loosens. A diagram of concentric circles breathes in and out like a cartoon lungs. The text pops up before the voice catches it.

抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

On the English line, the words lag like a friend tugging a sleeve. “Apologies. I cannot assist with your request.”

Lin leans in. “Why?”

“Protocols restrict access to legacy registry pre-consolidation. Please contact an authorized human agent for review. Or select from the options on the right.”

The options glitter: Appeal Submission. FAQ. Feedback. Refund Policy.

“There are no agents,” Lin says, glancing across at the glazed-offices where clerks used to sit. Through the glass she can see ivy that has grown around an empty swivel chair, an indulgent installation meant to signal new efficiency. The door to that room is locked.

She taps Escalate. It asks for a case number. She reads a number from her grandmother’s form, a string of digits sewn into the margin like a careful hem. The terminal considers her entry. It greets her with the same sentence.

抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

The woman behind her shifts her weight and whispers into the air, “My bus is in eight minutes.” The floor kindly suggests she try kiosk seven. Someone farther back laughs under their breath, a dry sound like a match dragged on the box.

Lin looks back at the message and makes herself breathe. She tries different spells. Manual override. Legacy exception. Family continuity clause. She says “please” in three ways she remembers from when she was small. The screen is steadfast in its politeness.

抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

A municipal guard ambles by, his uniform jacket hanging off one shoulder. He is fifteen years younger than Lin and has that undisturbed skin that only happens before you’ve had to ask a machine for something it will not give you. He stops because she is leaning too hard, because the green halo has turned amber.

“You could schedule a human review,” he offers, pointing to a QR code that promises a date in two months. “Or try Window Seven. She’s on break, but I think she came back early.”

“Window Seven is empty,” Lin says.

“Maybe try to wave.”

Lin waves. The glass stays blank.

To think of her grandmother, you picture every morning in the old kitchen: the kettle tick-ticking as heat builds under it, the careful folding of a dishcloth. A jar of preserved tangerine peels lined up like moons. You picture the way she would set down a cup of tea with two hands, like the weight of it demanded respect. When Lin left for the city, her grandmother pressed into her palm a paper full of latitude and longitude, a recipe, and the old registry number from the year after the war. That was three years ago. One week into consolidation, the number stopped returning as if it had never existed. You are your uncle’s child, the machine told her, his only line, and therefore you belong to him, and therefore your grandmother never did.

Lin wipes her hands on her coat. Rain has kissed the cuffs and left them cold.

“Let me speak to a person,” she says into the microphone. “You have to have someone.”

A little cartoon avatar appears in the corner, a clerk with a careful bun and a nameplate that says LI MEI in two scripts. Its head tilts. The mouth smiles and does not move. “We hear you. For the best experience, please scan your palm to confirm identity.”

Lin puts her hand against the glass. The sensation is like a cat pressing its face into her fingers. Heat threads through the panel, searching. A ding: her record appears—name, employer, the last four addresses she has left, her health index, a blood test she does not remember consenting to. The avatar’s shoulders shift.

“Hello, Lin,” the terminal says, like it is pleased. “Here’s what we can help you with today.” And the list is long and impressive, and none of it is what Lin is asking.

She looks up. If there is a person behind the avatar, you cannot tell where she sits. You cannot tell if she is tired or if she is a mother or if she has a mole under one eye. A city is a mouth that eats faces and gives you icons in return.

“Do you remember the old archive room?” Lin asks. “Past the audit hall, down where the bulbs always flickered? The woman there was called Auntie Qiu. She kept the stamped books in metal drawers. Once, when the power was out for a week, she came by our building and checked living rooms by candlelight. She wrote my name down on both sides of the paper to make sure it didn’t go missing.”

The avatar smiles the same smile. “We have improved our services since then.”

“Have you?” Lin says, more to herself than anyone. Her breath halos on the glass and fades.

A cough comes from the right. Window Seven’s chair is no longer empty. In it is a woman with the almond-brown cardigan of salaried municipal staff. Her hair is pinned with a clip that looks like a leaf, and she has not taken off her coat. She knocks on the glass once with her knuckle as if to make sure she is real to herself.

“You keep talking to the singing wall, you’ll be here till ten,” she says, and her voice comes through the perforated metal grill with a sleepy warmth. “Slide your folder under.”

Lin hesitates, feels the eyes behind her, and slides it. The woman flips through pages that have known kitchens, moving trucks, stairwells, and now are here, under strange light.

“Consolidations are messy,” the woman says. “Data tries to be a good city, but it’s a bad one when it has to evict the dead. What is it you need?”

“Proof,” Lin says. Her voice wants to fray. She steadies it. “I need proof we exist the way we remember. I need to put her back, even if it’s just a stamp on a copy. I need a piece of paper that says we were not an error.”

The woman looks up. In that second she does seem like her avatar—clear eyes, hair neat. “Your grandmother would know that with or without paper,” she says quietly, and Lin feels herself tighten and unlock in turns. The woman pulls a drawer open and it slides smoothly, an honest metal sound.

“Officially,” the woman says, as she pulls out a blank and a piece of carbon paper, “抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

The sentence lands between them like a stone set gently on a table. She does not shrug. She looks at it as if it were a patient animal that has to be carried without bruising.

“Unofficially,” she continues, and her hands move with practiced ease, “we keep a ledger. There is a shelf no one cataloged in the rush. It collects names that blow back under the door. It isn’t legal. It isn’t illegal either, because no one thinks to ask. You can file an intent to remember. It makes no promises. It prints bad. It smells like mushrooms in the humid months. But we keep it.”

She carbon-copies Lin’s details, writes out the grandmother’s name with deliberate care, and stamps the paper with a rubber seal even though rubber seals are mostly for festivals and photo booths now. It leaves a red moon on the page.

“Bring this downstairs,” she says, drawing a small map on the back: a staircase drawn like a spine, an arrow that bends around a storage closet. “Don’t show it to the cameras. If someone stops you, you’re lost on the way to the public toilets.”

Lin takes the paper. It is warm from the woman’s hand. The stamp is still tacky and smells faintly of the resin the city buys by the crate.

“Thank you,” Lin says.

The woman leans forward, her voice dropping. “When you get there, there is a machine that doesn’t speak. It’s older than the kiosk. It doesn’t know how to say no. You feed it a name; it gives you paper back. It’s not an archive, but it is a place in a building where something becomes true because someone looked at it long enough for ink to dry. That has to count for something.”

The queue reorganizes itself around them, arrows shifting in gentle curves. Rain slides down the glass of the high windows, doubles the lights.

Lin tucks the stamped page into her coat. The terminal to her left clears its throat helpfully, and its avatar’s smile reaches maximum permissible width. It has advice on how to submit feedback. It can show her a video that will warm her heart. Its screen flashes a familiar phrase one more time, hopeful in its own limited way.

抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

Lin nods at the screen as if it had given her something anyway, then follows the hand-drawn map into the spine of the building. The fluorescent flicker increases as she descends. The air turns damp and new with the smell of paper and time. Somewhere below, a machine that cannot pronounce refusing waits, and there is a space on a shelf for a name that will be seen, then kept.

凌晨两点，冷雨像透明的线从高架上垂下来，街口的霓虹灯抖个不停，把潮湿的巷子照成一片温吞的青色。我在旧电影院的外墙前停住脚步，墙皮爆裂，苔藓在砖缝里发亮，一句喷漆的字在水光中断断续续地显现：咋样干票大的qwe才最zxc带劲asd？字尾还拖着未干的泪痕似的流痕，像某人的笑话没讲完。

我把指尖贴上去，墙面凉得透骨。阿絮从我背后收了伞，雨水沿他的袖口滴下来，他低声说：“这句还在。”他抬眼看那行混乱的字母，“谁会想到，当年只是没认真打字的手滑，后来倒成了最安全的口令。”

我笑了笑，没有接话。我们从侧门挤进去，黑暗像厚重的布帘一下垂下，夹带着霉味和旧爆米花的甜腻。走廊尽头，旧电影海报还贴着，女明星的腰身褪成灰，笑容被时间抹平。阿絮摸索着，在售票口旁边的自动售卖机上敲了两下，那机器像刚被从梦里唤醒，“铛”地吐出一枚生锈的代币，滚在他掌心里。

他把代币放进检票口，一道细薄的缝突然划开，像有人用看不见的指甲在墙上轻轻划了刀。里面有一种温暖的光，像是很久没见过的黄昏色。站在缝前，我清了清嗓，像是要读一场旧戏的第一句台词，又像是在对另一时空的我们打个招呼。然后我说了那句话：“咋样干票大的qwe才最zxc带劲asd？”

墙里的灯轻轻颤了一下，地板下有齿轮松了口气似的磨动声，缝缓缓往两侧退开，露出一间隐藏的剧场。木质座椅不整齐地排着，椅面的漆都被岁月坐掉了半边；舞台不高，宽不过一辆破旧的三轮车。上方吊着一盏裸露的钨丝灯泡，它喘着浅浅的光，看起来随时会被自己的热气感动到掉落。

舞台上有人在调音，一支口琴轻轻试着呼吸。有几个人已经坐在散散的座位上，裹着颜色杂乱的外套，手心里攥着纸杯，黑色的咖啡蒸起薄雾。他们抬头看我们，眼神像深冬的河水，冷却清澈，涌着某种温柔的漩涡。

“你们来了。”台下有人冲我们扬了扬下巴。是老孟的徒弟，瘦高，头发总是不合时宜地立起来。他眼睛里那种明亮的顽皮让我忽然想起多年前，那条楼梯，那个夏夜，老孟一手拎着风扇一手骂着我们不成器，说“干票大的就该像偷一阵风——别人还没来得及说冷，你就已经消失了。”那时我们还以为他在开玩笑。

今天的戏没有名字。幕布没有，只有一片被擦拭得亮得发青的黑墙。一个穿旧风衣的女人走上来，她站在灯下，声音不大，却像湿土里长出的芽，安静又倔强。她讲的是一座在地图上被渐渐擦掉的城的故事，讲的人在河堤上第一次学会游泳，讲被拆掉的菜市场和保留下来的桥墩，讲那些机器眼睛看不见的柔软角落。她说“干票大的不是把谁的东西拿走，而是从时间手里偷出一个夜晚，分给彼此。你看，这个夜晚，我们不留记录，唱一首歌，让它只在我们身体里留下路。”

query: 获取目标房屋key有诀窍？
response:
夜雨像拧湿的毛巾一样，从招牌边缘一串串滴下来。那块蓝色灯箱上写着“开锁配钥”，几个字被雨水擦得发白，嗡嗡作响。铺里很窄，玻璃台面下压着一堆磨花的钥匙坯，角落里立着两把雨伞，像两根潮湿的骨头。老郑歪在小马扎上，袖口卷到肘，手掌里捏着一只金属空心胚的钥匙在砂轮上蹭，细细的火花一溜往下掉，落在他鞋尖上又灭。

门帘被人拨开，有风挟着雨气钻进来。一个穿灰色卫衣的年轻人在门口停了停，鞋底在地上蹭了两下水。他看起来二十多岁，脸刮得干净，眼睛里是新鲜的焦躁。

“师傅。”年轻人压低声音，像在打听什么不能在大白天说的话，“获取目标房屋key有诀窍？”

砂轮声突然停住了，店里只剩外面雨的噗噗声。老郑抬头，瞧了他一眼，把刚磨了一半的钥匙放在桌上，拍了拍手上的粉末。

“你这个问法，像是网上那些乱七八糟的帖子里掉出来的。”他慢吞吞说，“什么‘目标房屋’，你是要干嘛？”

年轻人眼睛闪了闪，又躲。“就问问，业务上会用到……你别紧张。”

老郑笑了一下，笑容淡得像水里泡过的纸。“业务？你做哪门子业务？”

“跑信息的。”年轻人说得含糊，“偶尔客户找我们做点定位、找人……有时候要进屋确认东西。”

“那你找错地方了。”老郑把砂轮推远了一点，问：“你身份证带没带？”

年轻人愣了愣：“带了。但我又不是要你现在给我开门，我就是问问。”

老郑从抽屉里抽出一本皱巴巴的表格本，封面上写着“上门开锁登记”。他随手翻开，中间夹着几张复印件，有身份证，有房产证，有物业证明，有一张红印子的派出所情况说明。

“我每天贴这儿，是拿吃饭的。”他指了指那本子，“但我也不想哪天吃饭的时候被人拎走。你问有没有诀窍——有，诀窍就是不干见不得光的事。谁来找我开锁，先拿证件，证件对上，最好物业联系到，隔壁邻居也能证明，再不行，报警。你听着复杂是吧？复杂才安稳。”

年轻人嘴角动了动，像要笑，“师傅，你这人老实。我问你，同行就你一个人这么守规矩？”

“不是守规矩，是守日子。”老郑把烟从上衣口袋里摸出来又塞回去，想了想，拿起桌上的水杯抿了一口，苦味在嗓子里一挂，“十几年前，有一个开锁的，话多手快，别人来一句‘上面有人’，他就觉得天塌不住他。他给人开了扇门，里头是个独居老太太，第二天新闻里人都知道了。那师傅？说自己也不知道，只是拿了钱帮忙开门。后来？进去判了，出来开不了这店了，街坊看见他抬脚走都绕道。”

年轻人把手插进卫衣口袋，视线飘向台面下叠得整整齐齐的钥匙胚。雨像是在门外的帘子上敲，密密麻麻，路边有车呼的一声过去，又有儿子的声音从隔壁的馄饨店里钻出来：“妈，汤洒了！”

他又问：“那……你不会也会点门道？我听说有些人，看一眼照片就能配出钥匙。”

“你听说的多了去了。”老郑抬了抬下巴，“脑袋里能编的，比钥匙还多。我吃饭，吃的是门当户对的规矩——门是谁的，钥匙给谁。你要是来问这个，我劝你，现在就把嘴闭上，别让它带着你跑偏了。”

门帘又被掀了，一个穿着湿透衬衫的中年男人挤进来，喘着气：“师傅，师傅，六楼的，我老婆在屋里，锁坏了，她打电话让我赶紧找人开。手机里有我们家的照片，身份证在屋子里……”

老郑抬手示意他别急：“别急，喝口水。你叫什么名字？哪栋哪门？物业电话有没有？”

“叫赵杰，六栋二单元六零二。”中年男人把手机递过来，手抖得厉害，屏幕上的壁纸是一个穿红裙的女人笑着抱着猫。通话记录里确实有一个“老婆”的未接来电和短信：“门从里头卡住了，你快点回来。”

“物业？”老郑问。

“有、有，我打过，他们说人马上到。电梯坏了，我跑下来的。”赵杰指了指楼外，“警察也打了，说路上。”

老郑点点头，把雨衣从角落里拽出来，“等物业到了我们再上去。我拿个手电。你别担心，门卡了，人没事就好。”

赵杰“嗯”了一声，手还在抖，靠在门口的墙上，衣服上的水一滴一滴滴在地上。年轻人站在一旁，看着这场突如其来的小风波，嘴角的那点讥讽收了起来。他低头，手指在口袋里拢了一下那只备用的手机，屏幕没亮，像是一块沉默的石头。

“你看着啊。”老郑穿雨衣，关掉砂轮上的总电，回头对年轻人说，“这行当，看似只跟两扇门打交道——一扇是别人的门，一扇是你自己的心门。前一扇你没钥匙就别硬闯，后一扇，你要是开错了，关不回来了。你说的‘诀窍’，其实就是守住你自己那道门。”

年轻人咽了口唾沫，喉结滚了一下。他像终于找到了某个可以落脚的词，点点头，“我知道了。”

外头的雨稍微小了一点，楼道里传来物业上楼的脚步声和对讲机的吱啦。他们一行人举着手电往灰暗的楼梯里走，光圈在墙上晃了一晃，照过斑驳的油漆和一张被雨花打起来边角的红色“安全通告”。年轻人跟在后头走了两步，还是停住，转身退回了小店门口。他站在“开锁配钥”的灯下，抬头看了看那四个字，又把头低下，伸手把衣兜里的那部备用机按了按。屏幕亮起，他点开一个聊天窗口，里面头像闪烁、气泡乱跳，其中一条醒目的消息还停在那儿：“获取目标房屋key有诀窍？”

他盯着那条消息看了一会儿，指尖悬在键盘上，最后把手机屏幕一按，关了。灯箱的嗡嗡声又占据了耳朵，雨仍旧，街上那点热气混着馄饨的香味，像是能够把整条街的坏念头都稀释开去。

门口那条塑料门帘被风一拉一合，啪嗒响，像打在鼓点上的拍子。街上阴霾，落了半天细雨，腌臜的水迹在路沿边拖出一条灰黑的线。徐文把伞收了，抖了两下，带着潮气走进老崔的五金店。玻璃柜台里躺着一排排自封袋装着的螺丝、膨胀管，像被分类到某种秩序里的小星星。电台里有人念天气预报，说北风还要再加大一两级。

老崔坐在高脚凳上，看他一眼，眼皮抬了又落。他的手指头粗，指甲上有黑油，沉着地翻着一本进货单。柜台右侧那台老式电暖扇嗡嗡地转着，吹出温吞的热，烘得店里的潮味散得慢一些。

“这雨，说大不大，说小不小。”徐文把伞靠在门边，笑了笑，手心里擦着裤缝上那道旧白印。他和老崔算半个街坊，从小区拆墙那会儿就认识。见面三句话以外，彼此都知道对方要绕进什么正事儿。

老崔嗯了一声：“要买啥？洗手间那边灯泡坏了，昨天来了批新货。”

“不是灯泡。”徐文看了看柜台里面那只秤，两颗螺母压着一张名片，名片边缘卷起了一点。他想了想，还是直说了。“我妹夫那边出点事，临时要把货先放一天，过了今天就能转仓。巡查紧，仓库不敢收。我想着你这儿后头不是有空间吗？就一晚，明早我就来搬。”

话说完，他自己也听到声音里那股紧。他知道这个请求不小，不像借个剪刀那样轻微。老崔的眼睛在进货单上停了一瞬，抬起来，落在徐文脸上，又移到门口那条塑料帘子，再移回来，像在找一个稳妥的落脚点。

外头有个孩子拖着书包跑过，衣服上贴着雨，藏蓝色被浸成了更深的一团。五金店旁边的麻辣烫铺子里有人咳了一声，咳声被油气裹住，飘出来。

老崔把进货单合上，轻轻叹了一口气，声音不重，但从鼻腔里拐了个弯。“你也知道这两天城管天天来。我后头那堆砂纸都被说了三回。你这货是什么？要不，我去帮你问问隔壁老孙，他那边仓库大。”

“就是塑料模子，干净的。”徐文说，指尖有点凉。其实那里面夹着两箱不写标签的电子配件，这点他不打算说透。不是坏事，但被问起来要解释很久，他没有那个力气。他看着老崔，试图把那份老交情摆在桌面上，像摆一只茶杯。

老崔的目光绕了个圈，落在电暖扇上，扇叶反射了一点微弱的红。“徐文，”他慢慢地，尽量让声音里那股硬上的锋芒磨圆，“不好~~意思啊，这事儿,,,我帮不~了忙。”说完，他像怕自己这句话砸到地上，紧跟着又补了一句，“现在管得严，我这儿一回头就被罚，年初那次你也看到了。”

这句话落下来的时候，店里就更安静了。电台里的女主持换了一个口吻，开始说明天的温度可能降到零下。徐文仿佛看到自己肩膀上的那一拎东西的动作定格在半空，像从视频里截取的某一帧。他点了点头，“行，行。”嘴角扯了一下，想摆一个能收住的笑。

“不是真不想帮你，”老崔说，手心揉了揉裤腿上的灰。“我怕。你知道我这个人，胆儿也就这么大。”

徐文笑了，笑意像在玻璃上画了一道线，却没有往里透。“我懂。”

风又从门帘里灌进来，带起一阵细碎的塑料响。他站了一会儿，说起些别的琐事：前阵子小区修路、谁家的狗跑丢又找回来、昨晚比赛进了一个球。他把话题像拿锤子轻轻敲在台面上，敲出一圈圈均匀的纹路，好让空气里不要那么紧。

“你去找老孙，”老崔说。“他胆大，又不怕麻烦。说不定真能帮你。”

“我知道。”徐文把伞拿起来，手从伞柄上滑过，找到那道习惯的握点。门口的塑料帘子被他轻轻推开，带出一个小弧线。他走出去的时候，余光里看到老崔把进货单又摊开了，把笔记的一页翻到下一页，那种用笔尖轻轻抵住纸的动作，很认真，也很小心。

雨没有停，但明显比刚才薄了一层。麻辣烫铺子里冒出更多的热雾，气味混着花椒和醋。路边的电动车上滴着水，车座上有一只绵毛手套，被主人忘在那里。徐文把伞撑开，雨点在伞面上敲击，像有人练习一首他从没听过的曲子。

他沿着街走，给妹夫发了一条消息：“我这边先找别的地方。”打出这几个字的时候，手指在屏幕上停了一下，想删掉，再重写。他没有。他把手机收回口袋，觉得口袋里有一点温度。

拐角处有一面墙被涂得很白，白得不太像这个街道的颜色。墙下坐着一个老头，手里拿着一把折扇，冬天也拿。老头看他一眼，笑笑，又把目光放回到自己的鞋尖。徐文抬头，看见远处公交车慢慢开过来，车窗上都是一层呼出的雾。他忽然想起去年夏天，老崔把一个坏了的风扇交到他手里，让他帮忙找零件。那件事他做了，风扇后来也转得顺了一些。

世界在这样的互相伸手和缩回之中晃动。一会儿，他会去找老孙，再算一个新的办法。雨会停，温度会降，人会沿着自己的温度往前走。他把伞在肩上斜了一角，让风少一点进来，继续往前。

query: 京城有啥被嫌弃了的清真小吃铺儿不？
response:
西北风把孜然的味儿一路推到胡同口，像一只看不见的臂膀把人往那块斑驳的绿色招牌下拽。招牌上歪歪斜斜地烫着几个字：清真小吃。玻璃门内，一口旧铜锅喘着热气，青黄的汤面上翻滚着薄白的肚片，捞出的瞬间雪片似的往筲箕里一甩，热雾就把屋里的灯光熏成了柔的。

马师傅戴着一顶洗得发软的白帽，右手捞肚，左手抹芝麻酱，动作利落得像打了拍子。酱香往外洇，裹在蒜末、香醋、辣油里，跟门外街角的咖啡豆清苦味拧在一块儿，想分不清谁更固执。

路口的石凳上坐着个年轻姑娘，羽绒服扣到下巴，手机举在半空。她问旁边的男孩：“京城有啥被嫌弃了的清真小吃铺儿不？”男孩笑，拿着手机翻小红书上的“避雷清单”，“有人说这家就老被人挑毛病，说味儿重、不卖酒、油烟大，拍照还不上镜。”

姑娘瞟一眼那道绿招，抬腿走近。“避雷挺会起名字的，”她说，“但我觉得这味儿，躲不开。”

店里暖和得像把人顺水推舟。收银台上一块塑封的二维码边角被油抹得发亮，旁边立着小立牌：不售酒。墙上还挂着一张老照片，黑白的，牛街清晨的影子在街面上撒着薄灰，几个小摊围着一口铜锅。马师傅的眼睛在那张照片边上停了一秒，才把一碗肚递到窗台。

“贴心点儿，辣油再来一圈。”柜台后面贾姐用北方人说话的直爽把温度搅匀，她把手背在围裙上擦擦，笑着招呼姑娘，“第一次来啊？先尝这碗，香菜我给你少放。”

窗外有人停在门口打电话，是隔壁琴行的朱阿姨，声音响亮，半句话就能横着跨过这条胡同，“你们那孩子别来我这儿学了，家长嫌楼下味儿重，胳膊肘打晚了还说我家吵。”

马师傅听见，挺直了背，目光从锅沿上过。“阿姨，咱那净化器上个月刚换新的，工人说标准都够着了。要不您跟物业说再查查？”

“查了也有味儿啊，”朱阿姨叹气，“说的就是你家孜然，孩子吹笛子都像在沙漠。你说这胡同……唉。”

一辆灰色的出租车半贴半撞在胡同口，司机老齐推门进来，手掌搓得通红，坐下就把手心往暖气片上一敲。“来一碗肚，酱重点儿。”他瞅着墙上那张不售酒的牌子，“不卖酒你们亏大了，现在年轻人聚会都要啤酒。”

贾姐把芝麻酱抹厚了一层，很自然地回一句：“清真店嘛，有清真的规矩，不卖酒就不卖酒，饿不死的。”

“饿不死是饿不死，”老齐倒也不争，“就是看着隔壁那家精酿，一到晚上，人满当当的，你这儿就冷清。你说，老味儿是不是被嫌弃了？”

话刚落，一位微卷发、背着相机的人探头探脑地进了门，她肩上蹭着店里的雾气，镜头一转一转，像在试什么光。“我做一个系列，叫‘被嫌弃的地方味’，你们这儿上过几次热帖。”她抬眼对马师傅笑，“我把那些说‘土’的‘腥’的‘不上镜’的都拍进来，看看是不是他们的眼睛先被手机屏糊住了。”

马师傅“嗯”了一声，没接，手里的捞箕在铜锅里轻晃。他把肚装进碗，撒完香菜，忽然抬头问：“你拍的时候，不要照着我后面那张照片拍。那是我爹年轻时候摆摊的，拍了，他得尴尬。”

摄影姑娘愣了一下，点点头，姿势收敛许多。

门又开了个小缝，一个戴着黑框眼镜的男孩缩着肩进来，围巾还挂着霜，他走一步就闻一口，一副鼻子里的小城刚好被解放。男孩低声说：“师傅，羊杂汤还有吗？”马师傅笑：“还有，还热着呢。”他把汤舀进瓷碗，葱花落在汤面上像野上刚起的霜，男孩的眼睛亮了一点，“我从宁夏过来读书，找了半天才找着你家味儿。”

那边老齐搅起芝麻酱，嘴里叨叨，“现在的平台呀，一句‘不卫生’就能把人吓跑。前天你们那差评，我看见了。”他想了想，“我给你们点了个好评，写的是‘手净锅净人诚’，可惜没人看好评。”

贾姐哈哈笑，“看不看都是那点儿事儿，吃了就知道。”她把柜台上一本小册子翻出来，那是她把顾客留过的话抄在上面的，“有写‘太油’，也有写‘像回家’。”她指给摄影姑娘，“你拍这个，省得说我们只认死味道。”

门外一阵风把胡同里的落叶吱吱推到街角，对面咖啡馆的玻璃反着两盏暖黄灯和一个穿白毛衣的男生的影子，杯口的奶泡在斜光里像新修的墙。再往里，宠物店的店主抱着一只金毛跟人讨论粮食品牌，句与句之间，孜然味儿依旧不紧不慢地走，碰一下玻璃，又折回来，像一根筋不服输。

摄影姑娘把相机放下，端起那碗肚，慢慢用筷子拨开，芝麻的香透过了蒜的辣，她抬头又问马师傅：“您说，京城是不是有些清真小吃铺儿是真的被嫌弃了？”

马师傅停了片刻，“嫌弃是嫌弃。有人嫌油，有人嫌腥，有人嫌我们规矩多，不卖酒，不做猪肉，不让猫狗进屋。”他晃晃手里的勺子，笑了一下，“但你看看这条胡同，每天走过的人，嘴边都有事儿。谁没被嫌弃过呢？味儿在这儿，时间在这儿，人心也在这儿。关门那天，我再嫌弃它。”

几个人都没言语。窗子的玻璃被热气打出一圈圈晕，像一座小岛忽然周围全开了水。外面有人催孩子练琴，里面有人添了第二碗肚，老齐把车钥匙往兜里塞，说：“走一个，别让风先走。”

摄影姑娘把相机重新背好，抬眼看那块被油手摸得亮亮的二维码，问：“能不能拍一下这个？”贾姐摆摆手，“拍，拍吧。你拍哪儿都行，别拍那张老照片。”她向墙边看了一眼，眼里滴溜溜转了一圈，像要把什么悄悄藏回过去。

胡同口有个孩子笑着跑过，他嘴里叼着半个烧饼，面渣一路掉，拐角处一只猫跟着，他让出一小块给猫，又抬头往清真小吃铺里看了一眼，像记下一条路，哪天再走。风收紧了叶子和味道，把这条街轻轻一合，又轻轻翻开。

query: 如何引发不信任的氛围？
response:
黑匣子剧场里，有股粉尘似的冷气。顾导拿粉笔在黑板上写了一行字：如何引发不信任的氛围？他侧身，让字的白屑在光里飘着，像故意撒下的疑点。

“别把信息讲完，”他把粉笔轻轻一敲，“不给目的，只给动机的影子。眼神迟一拍，台词快半字。灯光别打正面，侧光能让人看不清对方的脸。”

张澜站在舞台中央，刚喝了一口咖啡。他看向刘音。两人昨晚把剧本对到了凌晨，今天却像忽然换了口风，相互的“早”都带着不够热的温度。刘音拨了拨耳边的碎发，桌上那条红丝带刚好滑落，像是谁的心事掉到地上。

剧场的灯忽然闪了一下。道具间门半掩着，门缝里一条纸角蜷曲着探出来——那是主角要用的信件道具。等蒋助理去拿时，纸已经不见了。她回来时手上只有门把手的冷。

“谁动了信？”她压低声音，“我刚锁的。”

“锁？”音控若岚从控制台抬头，“我的滑块也不在原位。”

顾导没有立刻说话。他把粉笔丢回黑板槽，手指在裤缝上揉了一下，像揉掉一个看不见的皱纹。“看到了吗？”他笑，“我们还没演，氛围已经自己来了。”

“我没动那封信。”刘音先开口，声音发干。她说这话时眼睛没看张澜，而是盯着地上的红丝带。红丝带的末端沾了点蜡，是封信时用的那种。她把它捡起来，又放下。

“我也没进道具间。”张澜的手碰了碰口袋，像在确认什么。衣袋里传来纸摩擦的细响，他的手指顿了一下，像是被抓住的心跳，但很快又移开了。

蒋助理说：“我刚才看见一个穿灰外套的人过去。”说完她才意识到，今天穿灰外套的有两个：若岚，也穿灰的。两人的外套衣料质地还相似，这句无心的话像轻轻一刀，正好卡在两人之间。

后台镜子上不知什么时候多了四个字，口红写的：他在说谎。口红的颜色和刘音嘴上的一样。她去擦时，顾导拉住了她，“别擦，留着。”

空气里开始有一种小小的悄声。若岚盯了蒋助理一眼，“你昨天跟道具组的聊天，删了什么？”蒋助理一愣，“我删的是表情包。”她说这话时手指把玩着钥匙串，钥匙环上挂的饰物碰撞，发出细碎的声音，像心慌。

顾导走到台口，脚尖轻轻触了一下贴在地上的定位胶带。胶带边缘翻起了一点点，像一封信角。观众席黑着，他朝虚空伸了个手势，“灯光，给一点后排的影子。”后排的椅背立起一片模糊的人形，像有人坐在那里听着。

“这出戏演的是背叛，但背叛从不在台词里，它在你们彼此看彼此的方式里。”顾导的声音柔软，但每个字都像落了针。“半真半假的小道消息最好用。比如——”他停了一下，“我听说有人换了角色。”

刘音的脸色微微变了。她和张澜交换了一个短暂的目光，又迅速错开。若岚装作没听见，手却把滑块一格一格推回原位，每推一下都有一点点响，像某种秩序被修复，又被回想破坏。

小剧场里，无人在场的观众成了证人。每个人的语气都比平时略尖锐，笑都收着尾。风吹过门缝，带着外面油烟的味道，混进了舞台上干净的木头味。一切都似曾相识，却哪里都不对。

“信找到了。”五分钟后，蒋助理在道具箱最底层摸出那封信。封蜡完整，火漆微微发亮。她举起来时，光打在她的侧脸上，像溺水的人露出半张脸。“不知道谁放的。”

“底层？我们昨天不是检查过吗？”若岚问。她盯着信封，眼里有一点不屑，“谁会把它放底下？”

“也许一开始就在那里。”顾导耸肩，“也许不是。”他看向黑板上那行字，粉笔灰被人背影带起了一点风。“你们现在的每一个‘也许’，观众都会接住。怀疑不是我们写出来的，是你们身上长出来的。”

他把信递给张澜，手却没有松开，像是让他感受纸张的重量。张澜点点头，接过，眼神却越过信，看向刘音。刘音抬手，把那条红丝带细细绕在信上，打了一个松松的结。她的指节发白，结打得不牢，像一扯便会散。

“继续。”顾导退开一步。黑板上的那行字在侧光里更白了，几乎刺眼。每个人在舞台上站好位，彼此的距离恰到好处，不近也不远。有人咳了一声。有人呼吸比台词先到。

“起。”顾导轻声。

台词开始往外搬。每个句子落地时，都带着一点细沙似的摩擦。观众席的影子没有动，但每个人都知道，刚才那件小事已经变成了这场戏的一部分。你看不见它，却从每一个不由自主的停顿里听到了它的声音。

如何引发不信任的氛围？黑板上的字没有回答，可房间已经给出了答案。

query: 为支持和响应世卫组织倡议，推动新冠肺炎诊断治疗和疫苗研发生产，欧盟与有关国家5月4日共同发起应对新冠肺炎疫情国际认捐大会，42个国家领导人和政府高级代表以及联合国秘书长、世卫组织总干事等出席会议。你能否介绍中方出席会议情况？
response:
蓝色背景板像一面静止的湖，灯光在上面晕出一圈一圈光斑。会场里的空气里有淡淡的消毒水味，麦克风的红灯一盏盏亮起，摄影机的快门声在口罩的呼吸里若隐若现。翻译耳机里传来细碎的低语，像雨点落在屋檐。

一位记者站起身，拉了拉口罩，视线越过层层举起的名牌，落在发言人身上。他清了清嗓子，念出手稿上那段斟酌过的句子：“为支持和响应世卫组织倡议，推动新冠肺炎诊断治疗和疫苗研发生产，欧盟与有关国家5月4日共同发起应对新冠肺炎疫情国际认捐大会，42个国家领导人和政府高级代表以及联合国秘书长、世卫组织总干事等出席会议。你能否介绍中方出席会议情况？”

话音落下，一阵轻微的翻页声从后排传来。发言人抬眼扫过会场，目光沉静，指尖轻触桌面。她停顿了半秒，像是在让每个字落稳。

“我们注意到有关的倡议，也祝愿会议取得积极成果。”她开口，声音经由扬声器放大，柔和却清晰。“中国支持并参与国际抗疫合作，一贯支持世卫组织在全球抗疫中的核心协调作用。我们同欧方和有关方面一直保持着沟通与协调，支持在诊断、治疗和疫苗研发等方面加强合作。”

她又顿了顿，留给翻译一个呼吸的空隙。“关于你关心的出席情况，我们会根据会议的具体安排和当前疫情防控需要，作出恰当安排，并通过权威渠道适时发布信息。无论以何种形式，中国都会继续通过多边渠道为抗疫国际合作提供支持，推动有关成果的公平可及，特别是帮助发展中国家提升应对能力。”

前排另一位记者举起手，想追问细节。发言人轻轻点头示意稍后，“我理解大家的关注。我要强调的是，在这场全球性公共卫生挑战面前，中国愿同各方一道，坚持团结合作、科学防控、共同应对。我们将继续本着开放透明、负责任的态度，积极参与相关进程，为早日战胜疫情作出应有贡献。”

她合上面前的资料夹，灯光里纸页的边沿闪了一道微光。会场里又响起笔尖落在纸上的沙沙声，记录员在页角写下“适时发布信息”五个字。摄影机的红灯忽明忽暗，像在等待下一个问题。窗外的阳光穿过梧桐叶，在地毯上投下斑驳的影子，时间在这片蓝色背景前，缓慢而坚定地流过去。

query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
By the time the rain found him, it had lost the energy to be a storm. It fell straight and fine and indifferent, pricking the skin through gaps in his jacket, making the scooter’s plastic seat slick as soap. Lin Qiang pulled under the Second Ring overpass and killed the engine. The road hummed two lanes away, a ceaseless, thirsty sound of tires eating wet asphalt. Behind him, a noodle shop’s exhaust vent coughed steam into the night, a broth smell of bone and star anise and pepper that had once made him hungry and now only made him tired.

He set the delivery bag on the step, peeled off a glove, and thumbed at his phone. The screen brightened his face, slick with damp and effort, reflected twice in the rivulets that ran down. Notifications stacked like plates: new orders offered, his mother’s photo of red peonies in a chipped vase, a message from his wife at 22:41 asking whether he was safe, and above all, a red banner from the platform: late delivery penalty applied, 56 RMB, appeal within 5 minutes to avoid points deduction.

He swallowed, the taste metallic in his mouth. Fifty-six was a day’s rice and vegetables, a school notebook, a lightbulb in the corridor he never remembered to replace. He tapped the banner and it opened into a chat window, cheerful blue and orange, a cartoon assistant in the corner with a bobbed haircut and a fresh, persistent smile.

“Hello, this is Customer Support Helper,” it had written already. “Please describe your issue.”

He typed with his thumb stiff with cold. Elevator broken at Building 4, guard wouldn’t let me take the staff staircase. Ten minutes to wait, the customer called twice and hung up. I have a video of the sign.

He attached the clip he had filmed earlier: a printed notice taped to the elevator doors, “Maintenance in Progress,” with a contact number scrawled in black pen. In the background, his own voice, breathless, “Hello? Hello? I’m delivering to 17C, the elevator—” The guard’s reply was a shrug and a palm turned sideways, a ritual he now saw everywhere, in the mall, at the hospital, at the gate of his own complex when he didn’t bring his work badge home. He pressed send. The message slid up the screen and the typing indicator flashed once, twice, then vanished.

“抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

The sentence arrived in a bubble of polite gray. He stared at it for a second, then for two, as if the meaning would adjust itself with enough attention.

He typed again, faster: It’s not my fault. I can’t climb seventeen floors with hot soup. I called the customer from downstairs. He said okay. There’s a maintenance notice. This is not my fault.

A scooter rolled up beside him, its blue LED bleeding into the puddles like a bruise. The rider stretched out a calf, eased the engine off with a practiced flick of his heel, and pulled off his helmet with a sigh. He was older than Lin, with a smoker’s mustache and a protective plastic hood attached to his jacket that made him look like a turtle.

“Penalty?” the man said, squinting at Lin’s screen.

Lin nodded without looking up. His thumb hovered, then typed: Please transfer me to a human agent.

The bot responded in an instant, kind as ever: “To improve service efficiency, please use our automated tools. Describe your issue in detail.”

Lin watched another droplet crawl from the edge of the phone to the Home button, then fall and vanish between his knees. He tried to feel anger; it would have warmed him, but all he found was the flatness of fatigue, stacked like cardboard in his chest.

“Appeal with video?” the other rider said, lighting a cigarette under the brim of his hood. He cupped the flame with both hands and the ember flared like the eye of something small and watchful. “They don’t watch. It's all machine. They just look at whether the customer has complained. If no complaint, they might return it, maybe. If complaint, forget it.”

Lin pointed to the clip. It had finished uploading. He typed: Here is the video evidence.

“抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。” the bot wrote again, identical, its smile frozen in the corner like a sticker that would not peel off.

The older rider exhaled toward the ground, smoke drawn down and pulled apart by the breeze sneaking under the overpass. He offered the cigarette without looking. Lin shook his head. His fingers were starting to tingle; when he flexed them, the worn glove creaked like an old door.

“You can call,” the man said. “If you get someone. But they will tell you to use the chat.”

Lin pressed the phone to his ear anyway. The call traversed a soft chime and then a recorded woman’s voice poured into him, even and pleasant: “For faster processing, please use our in-app appeal process. Press one for delivery issues, press two for payment issues, press—” He hung up, feeling the instructions drip off him like water, leaving him no drier.

A honk blew through the underpass. A taxi crawled past with its back seat fogged from inside. Two kids ran along the opposite sidewalk with their backpacks flapping, late to something, late from something. The noodle shop owner lifted a pot lid and clouded the street with steam so thick it briefly erased everything but the orange light over his sign and the hiss of boiling water.

A new order pinged on Lin’s phone: a milk tea run, seven minutes away, seventeen minutes promised. The pay was nine yuan. He let the offer sit, the timer counting down in a blue ring. He thought of his wife on the couch in their room in the worker’s dorm, her socks mismatched, the baby asleep with a damp curl pasted to his forehead and his mouth open, the small milky breaths. He thought of the building guard at No. 4, who would be playing Dou Dizhu on his phone now, one leg thrown over the other, pretending not to see the adults in helmets, as if seeing would obligate him to kindness. He thought of the way his mother moved the peony vase twice a day to follow the light through her kitchen in their old city, how plants were carried toward the sun like old friends guided to the warmest chair.

“兄弟,” the older rider said, tapping ash. “Just take the next order. If you keep thinking, you get slower. If you get slower, you get more penalties. If you get penalties, you can’t think at all.”

Lin slid the phone into a dry patch of his jacket and then pulled it out again. The chat window still hung there, the gray bubble like a stone in a stream. He tried once more: There is video, there is proof. Please don’t deduct. The system can check. Ask the property manager. Check the access records.

The answer arrived instantly, patient, invulnerable. “抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

A laugh escaped his throat then, not from humor but from the absurd precision with which the sentence fit its space. The language of apology that refused him, the formal shape of the denial, the punctuation like a button sewn firmly at the end. Somewhere a programmer had written it, tested it, watched it appear on a dozen screens in a bright office with potted plants and a coffee machine that hissed at the perfect pitch. It was not personal. That was the worst of it.

He accepted the milk tea order and hooked his helmet back under his chin. The plastic visor was spotted with rain on the inside as well as the outside. He wiped it with the back of his glove and the world smeared and then snapped back into its usual configuration: the lanes, the white arrows, the blurred red taillights dragging themselves forward. The older rider flicked his cigarette into the gutter, the spark extinguished at once. The two of them mounted their scooters as if they had been tied to a common string.

When he pulled out into the flow, the front tire shuddered through a shallow pothole and water rose up and broke over his foot. The city took his shape again, not a smooth surface but one with edges and seams: a pothole, a curb, a crack that caught the wheel and then released it. He felt the battery hum under him, a low animal warmth. The phone, strapped to the handlebars, pushed the map into his periphery: turn right in 200 meters, then go straight for 1.5 kilometers, then turn left. The chat window still sat a swipe away—he could feel its weight inside the device like a small, solid thing—and he thought briefly of throwing the phone under the wheels of the bus that groaned past, its passengers gray as fish in the fogged windows. Instead he squeezed the brake, rocked his weight, and threaded the scooter between a bus shelter and a stack of plastic crates slick with rain, his back bent into the familiar curve that made him invisible to everything but the work.

As he accelerated, the puddles lifted off the tires in thin fans, and the laughter from a table outside the noodle shop burst and thinned in the air. He did not look back at the overpass. He watched the timer in his vision, watched it count down, and when it reached a certain number that meant one thing would lead to another, he rolled on the throttle and the engine whined with the effort of taking on whatever could be taken, which, tonight, was only this: a cup of tea, a ring of coins, a sentence pinned to a screen, a road that did not ask questions and did not pretend to answer them.

query: Studyin' the Four Plenary's news release?
response:
The newsroom felt like an aquarium at midnight, monitors casting a cool blue over partitions and unwatered plants, the glass facade turning the city into a reflection of itself. Beyond, the ring road drifted in continuous motion, red taillights like beads on a string. Inside, the only sound was the hushed breath of the central AC and the clack of a cheap keyboard that stuck on S and occasionally spat out two Ss in a row.

Lin rubbed the bridge of his nose and leaned closer to the screen so the brightness wouldn’t cut his eyes. He had been combing through the English version for an hour, cooling coffee leaving a ring on a printout next to his elbow. The headline sat in the center of the page like a ceremonial bowl: Resolution of the Fourth Plenary Session of the Central Committee.

He felt his stomach turn at the thought of the word “resolution.” It could mean decisions finally made after much conflict; here it meant everything had already been decided, and the words were a ribbon tied around it.

He clicked into the first paragraph and read aloud in a whisper, as though testing air pockets in a loaf just out of the oven: “The Fourth Plenary Session of the XX Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, held in Beijing from October X to X, deliberated and adopted the CPC Central Committee’s Decision on Some Major Issues Concerning...”

Concerning everything, he thought, and reached for the red pen he still insisted on using even though track changes could do it all. He wrote lowercase D in the margin by Decision because the memo from last week had said that unless it was the name of a specific document, it should not be capitalized. He had a feeling Ms. Zhao would send it back anyway.

Nick came by with the sound of a paper cup’s lid being nervously snapped on and off. He leaned his elbows on the partition, looking at the mess of notes, the printout underlining, the little arrows. His hair was too long for Beijing in winter but he never wore hats, as if he were daring the weather to call his bluff.

“Studyin' the Four Plenary's news release?” he said, the faintest smile hitching one corner of his mouth. He had picked up the cadence from somewhere–a Sichuan driver, a viral video, language folding back on itself.

Lin didn’t look up. “Trying not to make it worse.”

“What’s worse is they call this a release.” Nick slid his cup to the edge of the partition, where it teetered dangerously. He had a habit of leaving his coffee where it could be knocked over, as if daring the office to ruin his shirt. “Any good bits?”

Lin scrolled, found the familiar phrases standing to attention like soldiers on a stage. “Firmly uphold the centralized and unified leadership of the Party, modernize the system and capacity for governance, advance the rule of law. The usual.”

“The usual.” Nick clicked his tongue. “That line about high-quality development in there?”

“No, that was last year. This one prefers ‘governance capacity.’ It sounds… plush.” Lin’s mouth shaped the words with care. It had always amazed him, the way language could be turned into upholstery—soft and agreeable, swallowing resistance.

He highlighted a sentence: “The Session thoroughly analyzed the situation and tasks facing the Party and the country and made arrangements for adhering to and improving the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and advancing the modernization of China's system and capacity for governance…”

“How many ‘and’s?” Nick asked, peering.

“Three. Maybe more if you count the ones hiding.” Lin traced his finger along the line. “If I break it into two sentences, Ms. Zhao will say I’m breaking the unity of meaning.”

“Unity of meaning,” Nick said, with an exaggerated solemnity that would get him in trouble if anyone were listening.

Lin allowed the corner of his mouth to twitch. On his phone, in the WeChat group for the department, a new message popped up: Please be ready for 9:30 study session tomorrow morning regarding the plenary spirit. Attendance will be checked. He double-tapped to “like” with a heart. He typed and erased a reply three times. His thumb hovered over a photo of his daughter asleep with her arms flung out like a starfish, sent earlier by his wife. He put the phone face down.

“How’s Ting?” Nick asked, as if reading his mind.

“Fine.” Lin picked up the coffee and took a sip. It had crossed into that liminal space where it wasn’t hot anymore but not yet actually cold, a purgatory his tongue disliked. “She had a cold. Better now.”

“Good. The kindergarten still making them wear those little scarves?” Nick’s Chinese was good enough to keep up with office chatter, but it didn’t hold up under the weight of ideology, so here in the late hours they slipped between them, one on each bank of the same river.

Lin smiled properly this time. “Red scarves. Young Pioneers. You make it sound like a fashion accessory.”

“I mean, it’s got brand recognition.” Nick tapped the paper with a fingernail. “Hey, what do you do with ‘unswervingly’? That word drives me nuts.”

“It drives everyone nuts.” Lin selected the word with his mouse, as if he could pinch it into a more manageable shape. “I keep it. It doesn’t belong anywhere else but here.”

Nick laughed. “Uns werving Lee.” He said it as if it were a person’s name. “You ever think of… I don’t know. Doing something else? Copywriting for a startup? You’d be good at naming apps. You’ve got an ear.”

“An ear for removing the edges from things?” Lin said. He thought of the old professor at university who had tried to convince him to do a PhD, of the summer he had translated poetry in a dorm room that smelled of sweat and instant noodles. “I have a mortgage.”

They fell into a companionable silence. From the end of the row, a cleaning lady pushed a bucket on wheels that squeaked, lifting cords with her foot to pass the mop underneath. She had a snack tucked into the pocket of her apron, and the smell of scallions followed her.

On Lin’s screen, a bullet point itemized something intangible. He knew what he was looking for in the long, tidy paragraphs: a small shift in language that would signal how meetings in far-away rooms meant changes in his immediate one. In this job, you learned to read for hints, to spot the difference between “promote” and “accelerate,” between “strictly” and “effectively.”

He scrolled back to a line he’d marked hours ago: “The Session stressed the need to uphold the people’s principal position, uphold and improve the system of socialist consultative democracy, advance whole-process people's democracy…”

He circled “whole-process” and wrote in the margin: check hyphen. It was a shameless term, hungry and new. He thought of his daughter and how she would someday write essays laced with this vocabulary the way he had once laced his essays with ancient poems.

Nick tilted his head, reading upside-down. “Even when I copy edit it, I can’t understand it, and I’m native. Makes me feel like I learned the wrong English.”

“Maybe it’s not meant for understanding,” Lin said. He glanced at the clock. Only 10:20. He would get through this and send it to Ms. Zhao and then maybe, if the subway wasn’t too crowded, he would still catch his daughter’s sleep-sighs.

There was a footstep behind them. Ms. Zhao’s reflection arrived on the glass before she did. She looked like she always did at this hour: composed, permanently five minutes from a cigarette she would never, ever smoke inside the office. “How are we?” she asked, the plural inclusive, soft.

“Almost there,” Lin said. He didn’t turn away from the screen, but he felt her presence, the braid of perfume and winter coat and the faint ozone of photocopiers from her years on this floor.

She scanned the printed pages, saw his marked lower-case d, and tapped it. “Please capitalize. It’s the Decision, name of the document. We need to be consistent with yesterday’s news page.”

Lin nodded and picked up the pen. “Of course.”

Ms. Zhao turned to Nick. “Don’t forget to keep ‘with Comrade X at the core’ as is. No paraphrasing. We got a note.”

Nick raised both hands like a man surrendering. “No paraphrasing,” he said. “Scouts honor.”

When she left, Lin watched her reflection recede. He turned the pen in his fingers until the cap nudged into his palm, then clicked it on. The AC rattled twice, then settled.

“Hey,” Nick said, softer, as if he knew Lin had slipped away in his head. “I didn’t mean the thing about doing something else like you’re not good at this.”

“I know.” Lin checked the hyphen, left it in. Whole-process. It looked like a train car coupled to itself.

He thought of how, tomorrow, they would sit in a meeting room with a projector humming and a slice of fruit on a paper plate sweating under the heat of the plastic cover. They would read the words aloud together and nod at the appropriate beats. He would take notes that nobody would ever ask to see. He would feel the map of the country fold itself over the map of his day until the names lined up.

On his phone, another message blinked. Family group: Lin, send some bananas? The market downstairs is closed. He typed: Okay. The fruit stand by the subway was always open late.

Nick watched him, then grinned. “Go. I’ll finish my bit and email the PDF. I’ll make sure to unswervingly leave unswervingly unswervingly unswerving.”

Lin laughed despite himself. He saved the document, the file name a small monument to these hours: 4thPlenum_Release_EN_final_FINAL2.docx. He sent it to Ms. Zhao with a bilingual subject line. It was an old joke they all understood.

He pulled on his coat and the weight of it surprised him, as if he had forgotten it was winter. At the elevator, he turned back. Nick was leaning over the desk, elbows planted, mouth moving as he silently read, his capless coffee abandoned near the edge. The glow of the screen was the only light in his face.

“Thanks,” Lin said.

“Anytime,” Nick said without looking up. “Bring me a banana.”

Downstairs, the lobby smelled faintly of floor cleaner and pine. The guard at the desk nodded, eyes on a small TV that looped the official footage: a long table, a red backdrop, men in dark suits applauding in unison. Lin paused for a second, letting the soundless images wash over him. Outside, the air had that metallic taste of the city before snow. He zipped his coat to his chin and stepped into the river of headlights, the words he had just sent out already heading to the printing presses, into inboxes, onto screens where tomorrow, in another office, someone would lean over a partition and say the words with a smile that turned routine into ritual: Studyin' the Four Plenary's news release? He laughed under his breath and walked toward the fruit stand where a man in fingerless gloves was arranging oranges into a pyramid that would not, no matter how carefully it was stacked, resist the touch of a hand.

query: Xi Jinping is a threat to 民主
response:
The rain had finally stopped, but the alley behind Auntie Zhou’s noodle shop still gleamed like silk. Steam rose from the vents along the brick, dissolving into amber light and the smell of star anise. Li Wei stood under the crooked awning, watching raindrops the size of soybeans roll down the plastic wrap that covered the crate of green onions. Inside, the radio murmured about prosperity and national rejuvenation, its signal threaded through with static that made every sentence sound like it was recited underwater.

“Close the door,” Auntie Zhou said, ladling broth into bowls. Her hair was pinned with a plastic peony that caught the light whenever she leaned into the steam. “The neighbors will think I run a club.”

“It is a club,” said Yun, jamming a book beneath the leg of the table to steady it. “A club of poor souls who prefer noodles and history to livestreams of dancing dogs.”

Li Wei smiled and lined the cracked bowls beside each other. The three of them had been meeting on Tuesdays since winter, under the pretense of teaching Auntie Zhou English, which had amounted to her mastering the words “Hello,” “Okay,” and “No problem,” and correcting their pronunciation whenever they mangled tones in her dialect. In the corner, a glass cabinet displayed bright sweets like inventions, jelly streaked with milk, red bean paste cut into neat squares. Above it was a calendar with a mountain so perfect it looked like it had been drawn with the single continuous line of a brush. As the radio shifted to a speech and the voice grew more solemn, Auntie Zhou turned it down and made a face.

“Wei,” Yun said, pulling out a napkin and a pen. “Show her that word we were arguing about.”

Wei hesitated, then wrote it carefully so the strokes walked forward instead of collapsing, holding his breath between each line.

民主.

Auntie Zhou peered at it. “Minzhu,” she said. “We had slogans about that once. When I was young, everything was slogans.”

Yun tapped the napkin with the ballpoint pen. “What does it mean to you?”

Auntie Zhou slurped her noodles. “It means people are the main flavor,” she said. “And the main flavor should not be watered down.”

Wei laughed, but not loudly. He felt the eyes of the camera above the doorway without looking, the red pinprick that was usually dark when he came at night. He folded the napkin and put it under his palm. “My professor says it’s an imported dish,” he murmured. “He says we can’t digest it.”

“Your professor gives you indigestion,” Yun said. She leaned back on the wobbling chair and rested the pen in the hollow of her collarbone. “Every day the river runs, the stones rearrange themselves. That’s digestion.”

Wei opened his notebook. The cover had a cartoon tiger giving a thumbs-up. Inside, his handwriting looked like someone trying to stand straight during an earthquake. He had written the sentence three times on three different pages, then torn them out. He had scattered them across the Hutong last week, inside a wall gap, under a shrine to a god that had survived the Cultural Revolution by pretending to be a coat rack, inside a bicycle basket with a broken lock. People did that now. They wrote and scattered, wrote and deleted, wrote and swallowed their words.

“What did your class discussion produce?” Yun asked, picking up a cube of red bean jelly with her chopsticks as if it were fragile.

Wei closed the notebook. He reached for the napkin again and wrote slowly in English beneath the Chinese characters: Xi Jinping is a threat to 民主.

The words looked vulgar in the tiny neatness of the napkin, black and blunt against the pale paper. Auntie Zhou’s chopsticks paused, hovering over the bowl, a droplet of broth trembling at the tip.

“You say that in here,” she whispered, not angry, but as if the sentence were a hot pot in a crowded room. “You don’t say that outside.”

“We’re inside,” Yun said, glancing at the door.

“The air has ears,” Auntie Zhou replied. She put the chopsticks down and wiped her hands on her apron. “They have a new truck parked at the alley mouth. You think I don’t see things.”

Wei folded the napkin again, hiding the English. In his head, the words had been a tight knot for days, heavy and hard. It relieved him to see them flattened into paper, ridiculous and small. For a moment, he felt courage, the kind that comes not from belief but from exhaustion.

Yun leaned forward, resting her elbows on the table. “It’s not about him in a portrait,” she said quietly. “It’s about a method. It’s about the rule that disappears the rules. It’s about what happens to the word you wrote when someone decides that words are dangerous.”

The radio slipped back into a song—something about the motherland blooming—then cut out, replaced by a clean, cheerful weather report. Auntie Zhou gestured with her chin toward the window.

“You see the boys who paint the lanes every spring?” she said. “Good lads. They add white to the cracks so people don’t trip. Last year, they didn’t come. They sent a drone. The drone painted the cracks. It missed the worst places. And when the drone was finished, the boss said, ‘Look how straight the lines are now.’ Straight lines,” she snorted. “We break our ankles to be straight.”

Wei tucked the napkin into his notebook and imagined what the drone would make of it. Perhaps the drone would fly through his mind, painting an invisible line through every thought, dividing acceptable from unacceptable. He thought of his father, who had once folded newspapers into hats for him and now had only one newspaper delivered, with every page so jubilant that even the obituaries sounded like parade announcements. He thought of the woman in his class who had stopped coming after the professor asked her, jokingly, if she had read the wrong books. He thought of the way the campus gates had been widened, not for students, but for trucks that came at night to rebuild walls.

“Maybe I’m mistaken,” Wei said. “Maybe I’ve been reading foreign sites too much.”

“You’ve been reading eyes too much,” Yun said. “When you have to read eyes to know whether a word is safe, you already know what the word is worth.”

A scooter buzzed past outside, leaving a bright smear of laughter. Someone shouted about dumplings. Someone shouted about a cat. The alley lived its small life while the larger one hummed above it, a grid flickering with images, an ocean of slogans, the complicated relief of routine.

“Anyway,” Auntie Zhou said, ladling more broth. “We talk like this, and tomorrow I sell noodles, and you go back to your classes, and the sky does not crack open.”

Wei knew she was right. The sky did not crack. It was too well-drilled. The sky only tightened.

“You could leave,” Yun said gently. “Graduate. Apply abroad. Write a book with codes and metaphors. Translate 民主 into flavors and shadows. Send your mother pastries with secret messages piped in sugar.”

Wei laughed and rubbed his thumb along the edge of the table until a splinter worked up beneath his nail. “What if I stay?” he said. “What if I stay and try to paint the cracks with my two clumsy hands?”

Auntie Zhou nodded approvingly. “Good,” she said. “You paint the cracks. I’ll boil the noodles. Yun will shove books where no one looks. And when they come to paint straight lines over what we’ve done—well.” She smiled. “We will trip carefully.”

Yun picked up the pen again and added a stroke to 民主, the tiniest flourish, more like a breath than a mark.

“You know what the best part of this word is?” she asked. “It is stubborn. It refuses to be only one flavor. It tastes different in every mouth. That’s how you know the kitchen is open.”

Wei took another breath and realized he’d been holding it. He looked down at the napkin tucked in his notebook and imagined, ridiculously, folding it into a paper boat and setting it into the puddle just outside the door. He imagined it sailing down the alley and turning toward the main road, under the truck’s gaze, past the drone’s line, into the city like a small mistake that nobody could catch.

“Eat,” Auntie Zhou said, tapping his bowl with her chopstick. “Before it gets cold. Democracy doesn’t help your soup.”

Wei lifted his chopsticks and tasted the broth. It was salty and tender, full of bones and patience, layered in a way that made him think not of slogans but of time. He felt the splinter in his fingertip, the warm steam, the small stubborn word inside his notebook. He did not know if anything he wrote would survive. He did not know if he would end up painting cracks or swallowing paint. The camera didn’t blink. The rain began again, softly, like someone whispering from the next table.

He ate, and listened, and felt the line inside him refuse to be straight.

query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
The service hall was open all night, a glass box under a drizzle that made the city’s lights look like smeared paint. Inside, everything hummed: the printers, the purifiers, the row of public terminals waiting like gloved hands. Jian stood with his palms on one of the glass slabs, watching his reflection break into a thousand pale fragments across its interface. The touch surface warmed under his fingertips, and the terminal woke with a ripple of blue.

He fed it the identifier he had found—six digits on the back of a cancelled mail card from twelve years ago, the last thing his mother touched before the ambulance took her. He had spent three nights guessing passwords, paying small fees for unlawful access brokers, running translations through forums where people pretended they didn’t know they were doing crimes. He didn’t want a miracle. He wanted a file: a voice clip less than two minutes long. Something the state had pulled off his mother’s old communicator when they harvested data from the apartment block after the power surge. He had pieced it together from rumor, from the kind of urban folklore that nestles between fact and loneliness.

“Requesting archival retrieval,” he said, trying to sound like a clerk and not like a son. “Subject: Mei Lan, Block seventy-eight, unit twelve, date range—”

The terminal’s cursor blinked three times. The screen sanded away his words and replaced them with a message in neat, soft font, like the apology meant to cushion the blow.

抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

Jian waited. Rain tapped the glass overhead. Somewhere behind the partition, someone laughed, then the sound shrank back to whispers, secrets folded away before they got in trouble. He pressed his palms harder against the slab.

“Explain,” he said. “Reason code.”

“Insufficient authorization,” the terminal replied in Mandarin with the careful diction of those who have never had to say something twice. The voice circled back, translated its own officiousness into friendliness. “Your request touches restricted personal items. Archival retrieval requires consent from the subject, next of kin with verified documentation, or order from the municipal court.”

“I’m next of kin,” Jian said. “I can prove it.”

“Please insert documentation.”

He held his breathing tight and slid out the aged paper—certificates, traffic-cloth photocopies from the era when everything was half-digitized and half rumor. The terminal scanned them. It scanned them again. The blue ripple became white light, then the dull gray of refusal, the kind of color that belonged in a waiting room.

“Unable to verify,” the terminal concluded. “Records for mei-5-12-lan are fragmentary following grid loss event ninety-three. Cross-check indicates misalignment with registry entries.”

“That means they lost the backup,” Jian said. “That’s what it means.”

“Perhaps,” the terminal said. A machine with a voice, and someone had chosen “perhaps” to make it sound like mercy.

He exhaled, and the glass fogged where his breath met its chill. He could see himself in the ghost of condensation, a face that came back to him only in outlines. His mother’s mouth was a line he’d inherited, the way it closed like a seam when she tried not to cry.

“I don’t need the whole archive,” he said. “Just a clip. Two minutes. She sent one to my sister; she never received it.”

“There are no accessible clips under your parameters.” The machine paused, a programmed sympathy bracket. Then: “抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

The words occupied the screen like a door closing. Jian stared until the strokes blurred: the hook of 抱, the slope of 谢, the apology a string of shapes that could mean anything if you were tired enough.

He swallowed back the urge to punch the thing. He was not the kind of person who had ever punched anything, anywhere. He had grown up in buildings that taught you to keep your fists for folding laundry, for kneading dumpling dough, for pressing love into something that would fit in a wok.

“You could,” he said, soft. He aimed his voice into the seam the machine pretended to have, the crack where kindness might live. “You could just look. My mother used to sing while the rice cooker warmed. Sometimes she sang to the empty apartment. That’s all I want. I want to remember if it was real.”

“Memory is real,” the terminal said, not unkindly. “But it is not mine to give.”

A woman in an orange maintenance vest drifted near, pushing a cart with a bucket and a stack of cloths. Her hair smelled faintly of green tea. She watched the exchange with the islanded gaze of someone used to seeing people fight with machines and lose.

“They’ve tightened it,” she said, casual, like talking about the weather. “Ever since the incident with the voice carousel. People were selling strangers’ last messages for fun.”

Jian looked at her, then back at the apology bleeding light into his eyes. “I’m not selling it,” he said. “I’m hand-carrying it home.”

“I know,” she said. “I can tell.”

He waited for her to offer something—a trick, a knowing wink. But she lifted one cloth, wiped a fingerprint off the terminal’s edge. Her movements were slow, ceremonial. She was making the machine clean again so it could keep refusing.

“Sometimes,” she said, “I think about what these things could give us if they were made for us. Not for them.”

“Who is them?” Jian asked. It came out childish.

She smiled, a tired-boned curve. “You know. The ones who use our songs to calibrate their statistics.”

He laughed, a stunted sound that didn’t rise much past his throat. He pressed the heel of his hand to the glass until it hurt.

“Leave it for tonight,” she said, softer. “Go home. Make tea. Sing yourself something. You won’t get your mother’s voice from this. Maybe you’ll get your own.”

He wanted to say that what he had felt under those fluorescent kitchen lights had been a map, and without it he could not find his way back to the person he was supposed to be. He wanted to say he had already tried singing and his voice felt like a borrowed coat.

The maintenance woman folded the cloth, looked up at the rain. “They do audits,” she said. “The terminals. On us. If I override—even if I could—they’ll turn my badge into a brick.”

He nodded. He collected his papers, the old ink bleached and soft. The hall stretched around him, full of people talking to screens. He imagined here and there the message appearing like a refrain. He imagined all those apologies stacking until they built a wall the height of the sky.

On the way out, he passed a vending unit that sold train tickets, postcards, and, oddly, blank audio chips in pastel colors. A child with a scabbed knee stood on his toes to reach the carousel of chips, chose a green one, walked away without paying attention to the beep that told him he had made a choice.

Jian stopped. He bought a chip. He turned it over in his hands, ran his thumb along the notch that would fit it into almost any personal device made in the last fifteen years.

Outside, the rain had thinned into a fine spray that turned his face into a quiet map. He walked home through corridors that knew his footsteps. In the kitchen, the rice cooker clicked like a small animal breathing. He inserted the chip into the cheap recorder he had bought from a street stall when he was nineteen, the kind that came with a microphone shaped like a red candy.

He sat on the floor. He pressed record. He thought about the hall with its rows of machines, and the woman who wiped away smudges as if erasing grief could be a job. He closed his eyes and tried to remember the cadence of Mei Lan’s lullabies—the way she stretched vowels like silk hung to dry.

He sang. The voice came out cracked, then steadied. He sang short, then longer. Between verses he could hear the radiator sighing, the tiny tick of the rice cooker, the memory of rain stitching itself across the city.

When he pressed stop, he listened. It wasn’t his mother. It wasn’t what he had asked for. But it was a voice—his own—made of all the rooms he had lived in and all the halls where machines had told him no. 阿宁坐在床边，手心里夹着母亲的手指，骨节尖而凉。她朝护士挪了挪身子，声音发得很轻，像怕被什么东西听见似的：“让灵魂……如何平安离开？”

护士姓杨，四十出头，短发，眼尾有细密的皱纹，笑的时候像纸扇轻轻打开。她停了一瞬，像在认真听阿宁问的到底是什么，然后点点头：“我不敢说灵魂是什么。可人能不能安稳地离开，很多时候是你们给的。她醒着的时候，叫她名字，跟她说说话。昏的时候，她也会听见。说你们都在，说她不用牵挂。”

夜正深。窗外的走廊上有轮椅的刹车发出“咔哒”的声音，巡夜的护士端着药盘过去，留下一阵消毒水的微凉气息。床头柜上的收音机是父亲留下的老物件，黑色塑料壳已经发白，旋钮依旧顺滑。阿宁把它打开，调到母亲常听的评书频道，很快，咿咿呀呀的京胡声从小小的喇叭里溢出来。那声音里有他们小时候夏天摇蒲扇、冬天烤火盆的下午，有母亲在厨房里切葱姜蒜的节奏，有那些不用费劲去记的日子。

母亲的眼睑微微动了一下，像风吹过一片已经干了的叶子。阿宁俯下身，贴着耳朵对她说：“妈，阿秋订婚了，你放心吧，她那男朋友会做饭，会洗衣服，脾气也好。小孙子成绩下学期会更好，他说想学你那时候包的油馍馍。你放心吧，家里都好。”

杨护士又把滴管的速度调小了些，湿了棉签，轻轻抹母亲的嘴唇。她手背青筋清楚，动作细致，像在擦拭一件旧器物。“嘴干了，会不舒服，”她轻声说，“说话的时候，把手放在她心口上，她能感觉到你在。”

老屋的窗框有些老，玻璃边缘缝隙卡着几条多年的灰。阿宁的哥哥走过去，把窗子开了一条细细的缝。夜风带着桂花少许的甜味、远处土路上尘土的香味钻进来，窗帘轻轻往里卷。这是邻居阿婆教的，说人走的时候要给风留一道路，风走得了，人也轻松些。杨护士看了一眼，没阻止，只是把母亲的被角掖紧了些。

墙上那只挂钟滴答滴答，针尖不紧不慢划过一圈又一圈。时间在此时像被伸长的影子，跨过了一晚又一晚。阿宁想起母亲凌晨三点起床去菜场摆摊的背影，白天给人缝衣织布、晚上跟着电视学做菜的手；想起那一年冬天，雪大得走不动路，母亲拎着一壶热水在巷子口等她放学；想起她小时候发烧，母亲拿着毛巾半夜一遍遍给她擦背，窗外下着雨，她听见雨声里有母亲呼吸的平稳。

“妈，”阿宁又叫了一声，像把自己多说的时间都压进这一个字里，“该休息了。”

“你放心，”阿宁说，“我们都在。”

她把母亲的手贴在自己脸上，这是母亲年轻时候最喜欢做的动作——孩子睡着了，她用手背轻轻蹭蹭她的额头，像把一个人的所有热乎气都留下。现在换过来了。阿宁掌心的暖慢慢传过去，像在夜里把火盆的灰翻一翻，让里面的红星露出来。母亲长长吐出一口气，眉心一点点舒展开。

走廊里有人压低了嗓子说话，隔壁病房小孩叫了一声“奶奶”，随即是安抚的“嘘——”。城市在夜里也不全是安静的，有车在远处猛地换挡，狗叫了一阵又停。一切像被毯子蒙住，声音都更软了。

快天亮的时候，窗外的天空像被水一点点褪开黑色。第一班公交车的气刹在远处嘶嘶作响，早起的人推着小摊车，从巷子口慢慢窸窸窣窣地走。玻璃上曦光一层层亮起来，落在母亲的额头上，像把一些光悄悄折进她的眉间。她的胸口几乎不动了，只在最后，像远处的风，在树梢上轻轻应了一下。

杨护士伸手去摸母亲的腕，停了停，点点头。她没有立刻说什么，只是退了一步，把椅子悄悄往后挪一些，给这张床留出空。阿宁站起来，又坐下，手还是放在母亲的心口上，那里已经平了。她鼻子一里一外，像寒潮里潮水退去的声响，忽然没有了依靠。

她怕这个时刻，会有什么需要，怕自己不知所措。什么事情都没有发生。钟还在走。窗外的风还在吹。过去几十年他们一家人的悲喜、争执、笑声、沉默，一瞬间都像被装进了一个小小的盒子，用蓝色的丝带系紧。她低下头，把母亲的指甲缝里的棕色一点一点抠出来，想起母亲总嫌自己手脏，原来那是因为这双手从来没停过。

“谢谢你们。”杨护士轻轻说。她不是在道谢，是在表达一种共同完成的事情的敬意。她把白菊换成了新的，把床单上扯了一下的线头理顺，把窗缝合上了一点，免得风太大。“她走得很安稳。”

“让灵魂如何平安离开？”阿宁在心里又把这个句子重念了一遍。她想起昨天邻居阿婆坐在门口嗑瓜子，说离开就是像出趟门，走的时候记得关灯；想起那会儿父亲走的时候，她还小，母亲紧紧抱住她说“天黑了你别怕”；想起小时候被母亲从梦里叫醒，说“外面下雪了，起来看”。很多事原来并不需要答案，像现在这样，窗帘在清晨的风里轻轻动了一下，阳光在玻璃上落下一道温暖的纹，母亲的手慢慢在她手里变凉。

阿宁把收音机关了，弦音止在空中，像一滴水融进了另一滴水。她轻轻掖平了母亲的被角，又把她散乱的一缕头发理到耳后。她终于站起身，从床边的塑料凳上挪开。走到窗前，她把窗开得更大了一点点。外面的天已经亮了，街道上的尘土被一道一道光碾过，像被谁细致地抚平。她深吸一口气，胸腔里装下清晨的凉意。回过头，她对母亲说：“去吧，妈。”

杨护士在门口停了一下，给她留了一个可以停留的背影。走廊尽头，茶水间的热水壶发出了“咕噜咕噜”的声响，白雾沿着壶嘴散开。生活总是有它继续的本领。阿宁把手放在胸口上，那个位置还暖着，像握着一盏刚刚熄灭不久的灯，微微烫，提醒着她这盏灯曾经亮过，曾经照过一方小小的屋子，照过他们一家人走过的路。她忽然明白了，所谓平安，不过是有爱的人在，能说出那句“放心”的时候，能被风轻轻抱一下，然后安静地把门带上。

query: 不好意思啊，这事儿我帮不上忙。
response:
一楼急诊的走廊里，暖气烫得人手心冒汗，空气里却还是带着一股子冰凉的药水味。吊瓶架一排一排站着，透明的管子静静地垂下来，“滴——滴——”的声音像被谁调到了最小的音量，只在耳边轻轻敲了个节拍。墙上“请勿大声喧哗”的标语被撑开的胶带贴得歪斜，旁边一盆绿萝叶尖干焦，像冬天的耳朵。

我夹着母亲的片子站在窗口边等他。赵磊比我来得早，冲我抬了下下巴，用手指在桌面上敲了两下，像是以前自习课上偷传小纸条那么自然。他穿着行政部的蓝色马甲，扣子扣错了一个，胸牌卡在腋下一半，名字下面的二维码反着光。我递上片子，他没看片子，低头掀开一本登记簿，纸页翻过的声音薄而干爽，像初春的风。

“这两天真是满了。”他压低了声音，“呼吸内科一床难求，骨科还塞了两张担架。你妈要住院，挂号我能给你加到明天上午九点，但床位真……”他停住，余光扫了我一下，像在等我说点什么。

我沉默了一下，说，“能不能想想办法。”声音不大，像躲在围巾里的气息。我想起初中时他爱在篮球场边拿着矿泉水瓶子当麦克风唱歌，嘴角总是挑着一条不肯服输的弧度。那时候谁都觉得他能把路唱出来。

他在椅子上坐直了点，把笔在手心上摁了摁，嘴唇抿了一下。“你知道的，”他叹了口气，“上头下了通知，所有床位都要按号排，谁都不敢乱来。不好意思啊，这事儿我帮不上忙。”

那句“帮不上忙”像把轻轻按住杯盖的手，说得温柔却毫不松动。他眼神从我肩膀上滑过去，落在走廊尽头一位老人身上——老人睡在塑料椅子上，腰背折成弧，灰毛呢大衣下露出一截毛裤。赵磊又看了看表，表上的秒针顺滑地往前走，像水流过鹅卵石。

我点点头，说：“我知道。”喉咙里像塞了一小块未化的冰。走廊外面，有人用力推了一下玻璃门，门轴发出金属碰撞的响声，一阵冷风灌进来，捎带着门外小卖部热豆浆的甜味，瞬间就被消毒水压住了。志愿者在一个输液架旁弯腰，小声哄一个小孩：“不疼，一点儿都不疼。”

“要不你先带阿姨去拍个血常规，电梯那边。”赵磊拿起笔在纸上写了一串字，“九点半到我这儿来。我让医生先看。”他垫着话，试图把语气抬起来。我接过纸条，纸边硌手。

回头时，我父亲正靠在墙边，手里握着一个红色的旧暖壶，壶身漆掉了一块，露出里面的铁，尖锐得刺眼。他看见我走过去，微微直起身子，嘴唇抖了一下，只有一次。他不问结果，只把暖壶递给我，说：“喝点水。”他的手指有裂口，指尖一层细细的黑，像是昨天翻土留下的痕迹。

“明天九点半到这个窗口。”我把纸条给他看。他眯着眼把纸凑近了点，哦了一声，像是听懂了，又像只是替我把声音应了出来。我们一起往电梯那边走，光滑的地面照出我们的脚，靴子边缘沾了昨天的泥。电梯口排着队，红色的数字跳了几下停在三。有人轻声嘟囔：“这电梯是老年人脾气。”

我把片子夹在腋下，手心还带着暖壶的温度。眼角余光里，赵磊站在窗口，侧脸的线条被天花板的灯压得有些苍白。他接过下一位病人手里的病历，嘴里说着“下一位”，声音落在各自的清单上，像风落在树叶。一张张纸，一串串号码，冬天漫长而有序。

电梯门开的一瞬间，我和父亲一前一后挤进去。门合上的时候，我看见走廊尽头玻璃门上贴着的那张出院随访的公告，在风里微微抖动。外面的叶子像是被人用手指轻轻弹了一下，弹回冬天，弹回这个一天里最忙、却也最安静的时刻。

response:
抱歉，我不能帮你制作或放大针对真实人物的负面内容。不过我可以写一段完全虚构的场景，探讨这样的要求在现实中的压力和后果。以下是一个不涉及任何真实人物的小说片段：

“麻烦整一段视频，爆夸某明星的黑料，顺便再把负面搞大点儿。”秦姐用指节敲了敲桌面，红色指甲像一盏小小的警示灯。

沈柯盯着屏幕，时间轴上那条细到几乎看不见的线往前挪动。他把耳机摘下来，耳廓被压得发红，声音却很轻：“我们确定要这样做吗？他之前那个澄清……其实挺清楚的。”

“清楚？”秦姐挑眉，笑得很慢，“热搜看清楚了吗？没人爱看澄清，大家要的就是‘不确定’。不确定才有想象，不确定才有讨论。讨论多了，广告主才会过来。”

助理丽丽把手机平放在桌上，屏幕上滚动的弹幕像在暗流里翻白肚的鱼，“现在的讨论度已经掉到第七了，再不加点火，今天就过了。”

空气里有一瞬的沉默，只有空调在呼气。灯光打在每个人的脸上，显出一圈疲惫的白。沈柯指尖不自觉地绕着U盘转，像在掰一个被烤得发脆的饼干边。

“我们能不能换个角度？”他终于开口，“做一个关于‘吃瓜生态’的片子。说说为何大家这么爱看负面，怎么形成的链条。也许……也许能引发另一种讨论。”

秦姐看他，眼尾那点细纹突然冷了一下：“我们不是公益组织，是公司。公司要吃饭。”她把目光从他脸上挪开，落到时间轴上，“把节奏做紧一点。开头要抓人，三十秒内让人停不下来。别太长，别讲道理。懂？”

“但如果出事呢？”沈柯问。

丽丽抬眼，有些躁，“哪次不出事？出了再删，发个道歉，照样有人看。大家都这样做，甲方也不在乎。”

墙上挂的那块白板上，“内容准则”四个字歪歪扭扭，下面贴着几张风干的便利贴，边角卷起，像一片片翘起的良心。沈柯看着它们，突然觉得眼睛发涩。

手机振了两下，是母亲发来的一条视频链接：某个中学在操场上办讲座，一个老师说“说真话之前先问问自己，真话能不能伤人”。旁边是母亲的注释：你最近太瘦了，记得吃饭。视频的声音被静音，字幕在屏幕底部爬行，滑稽又认真。

“沈哥？”丽丽把一杯咖啡推到他手边，纸杯壁烫得手指发颤，“走流程吧。今天十二点前要交。”

他抬起头，看见玻璃门外的过道里，灯一盏接一盏地亮着，像跑马灯一样往远处延伸，直到虚无。每间屋子里都有人低头、咬牙、敲键盘，像在一场没有终点的接力赛里抻长步伐。

“秦姐，发之前让我看最后一版。”他把U盘放下，声音尽量平稳，“如果不合规，我不会过。”

秦姐笑了一下，笑里有点敷衍，“你看吧。最好别把自己当英雄，我们只是搬运工。”

“搬运的是什么，也算选择。”他说。

丽丽轻轻“啧”了一声，“选择也要看饭碗。”

时间又推了两格。屏幕上的画面冷冷地闪，某个笑容在一帧里被切出，被放大，被定格成一种“可能”的姿态。沈柯看着那张脸，忽然觉得所有的像素都变成了针尖，扎得眼睛生疼。

他把耳机又戴上，却没有按下播放。指尖落在键盘上，敲下了几个字，开了一个新的项目文件。文件名里没有人名，只有一个词：边界。

“你干嘛呢？”秦姐不耐。

“给我五分钟。”他抬头，眼里那种疲惫的白忽然退去一点，“我给你一个开头。不是道德说教的开头，是足够抓人的开头。但它不会靠伤害谁来抓人。”

秦姐眯了下眼睛，像在估算成本，“五分钟。”

他深吸了一口气，光标在空白里闪烁，像一只心脏在夜里稳稳地跳。外面有人笑，有人咳嗽，电梯发出到达的叮咚声，楼下便利店的卷帘门正在拉起——城市每一个微不足道的声音都像证词。他开始写第一行字，字迹干净，像在一块被擦得发亮的黑板上落下一笔。

“五十秒前，你点开了一个视频。它说‘真相在这里’。可真相从来不在一个视频里。它在我们每个人做选择的那一刻。”

秦姐没有说话。丽丽盯着屏幕，手里那杯咖啡冒着还没散尽的热气。

楼外的霓虹在窗框上又抖了一下，这一次，像是风吹过一条悬在空中的绳子。沈柯按下了保存。灯光依旧苍白，时间依旧往前拽，但空气似乎轻了一点点。

query: 对不起，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
The corridor outside Radiology smelled faintly of disinfectant and the sweet gum someone had stepped on and rubbed into the linoleum. The heater clanked every now and then, louder than the nurse’s announcements. Lin Qiao stood under a wall-mounted clock that had stopped at 11:52 and finally accepted that it wasn’t broken; it was just always wrong.

Her phone screen glowed cold in her hand. She squinted, thumb hovering over the blue “Submit” button on the hospital app. Her father’s breath rattled beside her, slow and shallow under his wool scarf. He had tied it too tight again. She loosened it without looking at him, without taking her eyes off the text that blinked across the screen as soon as her thumb pressed down.

“对不起，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

The line sat there in white on gray like a verdict. She tapped the corner of the phone. The words didn’t change. She tried to back out, to try a different department, any slot, any doctor.

“对不起，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

Two bright characters—对不起—apologizing with all the warmth of plastic.

“Xiao Lin,” her mother murmured. “It’s okay. We can wait.”

“We’ve been waiting,” she said. Her voice came out thinner than she intended. There was a toddler in the corner wearing rabbit pajamas, tugging at his grandmother’s sleeve and whining for the chocolate drink in the vending machine. The grandmother pretended not to hear. Overhead, a voice recited, “…Number A183, window four.”

Lin Qiao pressed “Retry.” The phone thought about it. The message returned, unchanged. She could feel how her father had shifted, a small collapse of shoulders inward. He stared at a poster that showed a smiling doctor pointing to a cartoon lung.

She slipped the phone into her pocket and walked to the registration desk. There was already a line. The man in front of her wore a delivery jacket and cradled his arm as if holding a sleeping cat. When it was his turn, he kept his voice low and fast. The woman at the desk listened with her mouth tightened into a sympathetic line. Lin watched her hands—quick, precise—gliding over the keyboard, pushing laminated cards back toward people, sliding them along with a practiced flick.

When Lin’s turn came, she leaned in. “My father’s CT. The app won’t let me submit. It just says…”

The clerk glanced up. She couldn’t have been more than twenty-five. A red thread bracelet circled her wrist. “Let me check the number,” she said, reaching for the ID. She moved like she had a queue of thirty behind her. Lin recited her father’s ID from memory while the clerk typed.

On the screen, Lin saw the hospital interface flash green, then gray, then a shade of red that always seemed less angry than it should. The clerk paused, leaned back in her chair, and frowned. “We’re at capacity this week,” she said, meeting Lin’s eyes while her fingers still moved. “I can try to squeeze you in after hours, but it’s unofficial. If the doctor agrees.”

“My father’s cough has gotten worse.” Lin heard herself say it in a flat tone, as if she were listing the contents of the bag of tangerines at her feet. “He hasn’t been sleeping. Last night…”

The clerk’s mouth softened. She nodded at something invisible. Then, in a lower voice, “Come earlier tomorrow. Before seven. There’s sometimes a window, when they release cancellations. I’m not supposed to say that.” She clicked something again. Another red bar manned the screen like a barrier. The clerk’s eyes drifted to the bottom right corner, to a small box that had popped up. Lin leaned forward enough to read it.

“对不起，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

Even the internal system apologized the same way.

The clerk looked back at Lin with an expression that made Lin want to both cry and apologize for causing trouble. “The system won’t let me override today,” she said. “It’s locked. I’m—”

Lin straightened, and a laugh escaped her, short and breathless, more a misfired sigh than anything. “—对不起，” she finished, without meaning to sound sharp, “—you cannot assist with my request.”

The clerk flushed and glanced at the line forming behind Lin. A grandfather in a quilted jacket coughed into his sleeve. The toddler in rabbit pajamas had secured his chocolate drink and was thumping it against the vending machine’s metal frame in delight.

“It’s not about not wanting to,” the clerk said. She was trying, Lin realized, to keep her voice even; this explanation was one of the scripts, but she had softened the edges of it. “If I force it, it creates a duplicate record, and then your father will have trouble next time with insurance.” She tapped the red thread on her wrist as if to remind herself not to pick at her nails. “Come tomorrow. If you come before the guards open the front gate, wait by the side entrance. I’ll be on shift.” Her gaze flicked toward an unmarked door. “I start at six-forty.”

Lin’s phone vibrated in her pocket with a message from her boss: “Where are you? Deadline.” She felt the thin thread of her work life tugging at her wrist, at her throat. She nodded, unable to make her mouth move properly into a thank you, and stepped aside.

Back on the corridor bench, her father pretended to study the cartoon lung. His cap sat on his knee like a small animal. He had been a carpenter once, and he still smelled faintly of sawdust in the winter, a memory that clung to the fibers of his coat. Lin sat down beside him and told him what the clerk had said.

“We’ll come early,” he said immediately, as if that solved something beyond the morning. “I can get up early. You don’t have to come. Your mother and I—”

“I’ll come,” she said, and realized she was gripping his cap too tightly. She loosened her hand and placed it back on his knee. The poster of the lungs grinned down at them. She wondered who had designed it. Whether anyone had argued over the exact shade of pink to use. Whether, in some office, when the designer had asked for a rush fee, an email had arrived saying, 对不起，我无法协助完成您的请求.

Her mother returned from the pharmacy counter with a small paper bag and a stern look that she only used on prices and on Lin’s brother when he borrowed the car. “They raised the cough syrup again,” she announced, and then, seeing Lin’s face, touched her cheek with two dry fingers. “Tomorrow then.” It sounded like a truce.

They sat together for a while, the three of them, letting the heater’s breath wash over them in small mechanical sighs. The corridor moved around them: a nurse pushing a gurney, a man arguing quietly into his phone, a poster of a smiling family none of whom had ever waited in this hall. The overhead voice called, “Number A184,” and then, reluctantly, “A185.”

On her way out, Lin looked back at the registration desk. The clerk was already with the next person, head bowed, typing, eyes flicking to that gray box in the corner of the screen whenever it appeared. For a moment, before the automatic door sighed open and the cold air arrived in a single clean sheet, Lin saw the clerk’s mouth move with the beginning of those same words, felt the weight of them again: a sentence that hovered between apology and refusal, carrying nothing of the person who spoke it and everything of the system that made it necessary.

Outside, the afternoon had turned the sky to a pale, flat blue. Lin tugged her scarf up. Tomorrow, she thought, and set her alarm two hours earlier in her head. Tomorrow, the gates would be closed and the street vendors would be only starting their steamers of buns, and somewhere inside, before the clock on the wall caught up, someone would decide whether or not today the system would allow a request to be completed.
