The district service hall had the sheen of things that had been scrubbed too often: the tiles scoured pale and slick, the plastic chairs with their faint, unbudging grime, the acrylic windows shining with a diligence that couldn’t quite erase the fingerprints. A television played a talk show in the far corner at a low volume, all soft exclamations and canned laughter; beneath it a stroller wheel squeaked each time a mother rocked it with her foot. Outside, the late winter sun glared on a courtyard of bare plane trees, and the sky was a white that felt like an absence more than a color.

Chen Mei adjusted the knot on the red string that kept her documents together. She had tied it three times at home, hoping that neatness would stand in for luck. Inside the cardboard folder were photocopies of her marriage certificate, a receipt for the cremation, the small passport photo of her husband that she always forgot was on page three and that always startled her when it caught the light. The photo was so blue; she had not remembered that blue.

“Number B061,” the loudspeaker said, distorted into a rubbery sound. The ticket in her palm read B082. She tucked the documents back under her arm and watched the queue as it knotted, loosened, and re-knotted with each announcement.

At Window 7, a clerk with a ponytail and a scarf shaped like a lotus petal was explaining something to a man whose breath fogged the glass. At Window 1, a young man in a pea coat was arguing about residency points with a patient expression that was itself a kind of argument. At Window 4, an elderly man had fallen asleep. Every few seconds his head dipped and then jerked up, and each time, his paper mask slid down his lip a fraction more.

On the wall, there was a poster in a cheerful font: Streamlined Services! Apply Online! Scan QR Code! Below it, along one wall, were four self-service kiosks, humming softly. Chen Mei kept glancing at the kiosks. It would be faster, they always said. Your file might move forward today. If it moves forward today, maybe you can book a hospital bed by Friday. But there was the thing that happened to her when she put her hands on machines: the jitter in the fingers, the small panic that one cannot admit is panic.

She watched as a university student, hair dyed to that careful gray that looked expensive, tapped at a kiosk with two thumbs and finished in less than a minute. The screen showed a cheerful green check mark. The student smiled to herself, tugged down her mask to sip tea, then tugged it back up and left. The check mark winked a few times and vanished. Chen Mei stood and walked toward the machines as if toward a ceremony.

She balanced the cardboard folder on the shelf below the screen. The surface was clean, sticky clean, and smelled faintly of citrus. The system prompted her to scan her ID. She took the ID card from her wallet and pressed it against the reader. A photo of her appeared on the screen, flat and startled, as if they had surprised her just as she was going somewhere else. She typed in her husband’s ID number, scolding her fingers when they faltered. The circles of her breathing fogged the glass as if there were two of her, one inside the machine and one outside, both trying not to cry.

They had asked her to re-upload the death certificate. The first time she had uploaded it, the clerk had clicked through the file and said kindly, “A little blurry, Auntie.” Everything in these rooms was either too blurry or too sharp.

Now, she pressed “Upload,” searched for the file on the USB drive, watched the bar inch forward, hesitated as the bar did not inch, tried again. A young security guard, his shoulders padded by his jacket, munched sunflower seeds at equal intervals near the kiosks and spit the shells tidily into an empty bottle. Each crisp crack of a seed seemed to mark time: a second, a second, a second.

The screen cleared. For a moment, nothing. And then a sentence appeared at the center in a neat blue font, the kind used in official notifications, the kind that always struck her as trustworthy:

抱歉，我无法协助完成您的request。

She blinked. She held herself very still, as if stillness would change the sentence. The English word in the middle of the Chinese made her think of the punchline of a joke she did not understand. Request, request. She had learned a little English twenty years ago in a night class taught by a retired train conductor who had worn a tie to every session. Request. She tried to parse it: qingqiu, yao qiu. She looked around as if someone would have seen it with her and would smile and say, It’s a bug, it happens, try again.

She pressed “Back.” The machine thought for a moment and another spin icon appeared and spun with a patience that felt like contempt, and then the same line appeared again. 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的request。

She turned, head tipping down, and saw her own reflection on the black bezel of the screen: a flattened version of herself, periphery blurred. “Little brother,” she said to the security guard before she knew she would say it, “this machine says it cannot help me. Can you…” She gestured vaguely, a small circle drawn in the air over the impossible.

The guard set the bottle down with care, as if it were a small pet. He popped another seed into his mouth, crunch, chewed, and swallowed before he approached. Up close, he was younger than she thought—his skin was still thick with youth, the beard not quite asserting itself at his jaw. “What do you need?” he asked. He peered at the screen and read it out loud, soft, amused, “抱歉，我无法协助完成您的request。” He shrugged one shoulder, embarrassed to be amused. “Sometimes it’s the server,” he said. “Sometimes the network. Sometimes it’s because it can’t read the format. Auntie, you can try compressing the file. Or you can go to Window 8 and ask them to reset your case.”

“Can you compress it?” she asked, and felt like a child. “I don’t know where to press.”

He took her USB drive, slipped it into the port with a gentle competence that made her heart leap a small, grateful leap, and clicked through. The machine blinked to a different screen, and again the sentence, in that polite, unwavering font appeared. He frowned now, serious, resentful on her behalf at being refused by a machine. “It’s probably their English module,” he said, as if trying to make it funny. “I mean, the message. It’s not that helpful, is it?” He pressed “Help.” There was no answer. He pressed “More Help.” The same page. The amusement had left his face entirely.

“Window 8,” he said again, softly. “They can override it. Maybe. Or they’ll tell you to go home and wait for a notification. I’m sorry.”

She collected her papers, slipped the USB back into her wallet with the coins, and went to Window 8. The clerk there was eating noodles from a plastic bowl, hair pinned up with a clip shaped like a butterfly, and the steam fogged her glasses. “One moment,” the clerk said between mouthfuls, not unkindly. “I’m on my break but I can tell you quickly.”

Chen Mei pushed the little microphone button in the glass to make herself heard. “The machine said—” She looked down at the scrap of paper on which she had copied the sentence, each character slow and careful. “‘抱歉，我无法协助完成您的request。’ It asked me to try again, but then it said this again.”

The clerk smiled helplessly at the note as one smiles at a child’s drawing. She adjusted her glasses, tapped her keyboard briskly, and swallowed the last of the noodles before pushing the bowl aside. “It’s the upload gateway,” she said. “The anti-virus flagged something today, and when it flags, it sometimes blocks everything. Our IT says to wait until after two p.m. or try again tonight. If you leave me your phone number, Auntie, I’ll call you if the gateway clears and you can email the file directly. Otherwise, you can come back tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow,” Chen Mei repeated, as if it were a place she could put her feet.

The clerk pushed a small form under the glass. Name, phone. There was a LINE for “Other contact (WeChat),” and on it someone before her had written “Son” in shaky neat characters. Chen Mei filled it in. Her hand shook less than she expected.

As she turned to go, a new number came over the loudspeaker, a slow robotic voice that tried and failed to sound like someone familiar. In the stroller corner, the baby had fallen asleep, mouth open, the soft surrender of infants.

At the door, she put on her gloves. The day outside was shine without warmth, the kind that sets you in relief against your own shadow. On the steps, a boy in a black hoodie practiced a skateboard trick, lifting the board with a hop and then landing, almost, almost, then missing the tail by a centimeter. He swore softly, not to himself, but to the clean air, which took it and kept quiet.

She stood a moment and looked through her phone out of habit, even though no one had called in the ten-minute span she had been inside. The only new thing was a text from a promotions number: Your payment has been received. Thank you for your trust. It used three exclamation points and a string of fireworks emojis. She laughed, a real laugh, short and clipped by cold and inconvenience.

On the third step she paused and went back in. “Little brother,” she said to the guard, “what does ‘request’ mean, really?”

He looked at her as if the question were a philosophy exam, then grinned. “It means when you ask for something. Like when you ask a machine. Or a person.”

“Then I won’t ask the machine,” she said, and was surprised by her own lightness. “I’ll ask you next time.”

He saluted her with a sunflower seed. “If I can do it,” he said, “I will.”

She nodded and went back out into the winter. The sky was as pale as paper. The trees were prepared to wait. The day would keep moving with or without her, and she would step into it anyway, with her folder and its string, with the absurd sentence in her pocket, with the ordinary fact of it all shining for a moment, a thin clear light.

The woman made a face that was part agreement, part warning. “Depends what you want. If you want something loud enough to drown you, yes. If you want to remember your parents’ living room, yes. They sample things that never intended to be replayed. I’m Tian.”

“Mina,” she said, and when she spoke she felt the baritone of the room resonate against her teeth.

The guitarist had stickers across his instrument like a timeline: a mountain range peeling, a stamp with a postmark, a barcode. He reached into his pocket and brought out a handful of small plastic keys, letters rubbed nearly flat. He held them up to the crowd and let them rain down onto the stage. The drummer hit a pad and a sound like the carriage return of a typewriter thudded through the room. The guitarist carved a line in the air. The singer stepped to the mic and breathed. Mina typed back without looking down: “Almost.” She kept her eyes on the stage as she hit send. It felt like a small disobedience or a small faith.

People leaned into it, shoulders pressing up, fingers lifted, palms opened. The guitarist threw his head back and every sticker on his instrument flashed like a minute-long star field. query: 抱歉，我無法協助進行此要求。
response:
The fluorescent hum of the twenty-four-hour shop blended with the hiss of rain outside, each drop sketching a temporary signature on the glass before sliding down into the gutter. Mei stood at the far end of the counter where the old assistance kiosk sat, its screen scuffed by decades of fingertips and hopeful impatience. It still took coins, though someone had taped a QR code beside the slot like an apology to the future.

She fed it a coin anyway. It clinked inside with something like a decision being made.

“Welcome,” the kiosk said in a voice too bright for midnight. “Please state your request.”

She had rehearsed in her head so many ways to ask it—to avoid sounding desperate, to sound efficient, to sound like she wasn’t asking for the impossible. But all that came out was, “Can you let me hear my mother again?”

The blue circle at the edge of the screen rotated, slowed, then rotated again. The rain outside intensified, a million quiet arguments against the roof. Somewhere behind the counter the shop clerk turned a page of a paperback, and the page made a dry sigh.

The kiosk beeped twice. Then, in small, friendly characters, it put the sentence up in pale blue, as if it were writing on water: 抱歉，我無法協助進行此要求。

Mei stared at it. The words were neat, the apologetic curve of 抱 like a hand hovering above a shoulder that would not be touched. She felt embarrassed for a moment, as if she had asked someone to hold a constellation in their pocket just for her and it was silly to expect it could fit.

She pressed her thumb to the screen. “I don’t want anything complicated,” she said to it, to the rain, to herself. “Just… a recording. A fragment. No ethics violations. No manipulation. I just… I keep forgetting the way she says my name, and it’s been six months, and—” Her voice broke in half and came back together as if nothing had happened.

Behind her, the clerk cleared his throat. He wore the shop’s yellow vest and a piece of string around his wrist. His nametag said Jiro in English and then something in neat Chinese characters that she could not read from the corner of her eye.

“I think that one’s got the old guardrails.” Jiro tapped the kiosk’s side, avoiding the screen. “It says no to anything that hints at resurrection. Taiwan bought a batch before the update, and no one ever got around to patching them. There’s a checklist in the back, it says ‘deny grief.’ It’s dumb.”

Mei wiped her thumb off on her jacket and couldn’t think of anything to say that wasn’t either yes or please. The kiosk kept its sentence like a door it had closed gently. 抱歉，我無法協助進行此要求。 The line of punctuation was so polite, she wanted to wash it off the glass with her sleeve.

“I’m sorry,” Jiro said, and then, because he seemed embarrassed by his own sympathy, added, “Do you need tea? We have chrysanthemum. My grandma swears by it for—well, everything.”

She laughed, a small sound that let some air out of her chest. “Tea helps if you have tea-shaped problems.”

“Most of mine are,” he said. He reached under the counter and came back with a paper cup that smelled faintly of marigold and old sugar. He set it down beside the kiosk, this tentative offering in a fluorescent temple. “I know it’s not what you asked for. We could try the recording app on my phone, but I don’t think it can do… that.”

Mei didn’t answer for a moment. Her mother had left answering machine messages once, back when phones still had tiny cassettes inside them. She remembered playing one over and over just to hear the way her mother’s voice rose on the last syllable, how the breath caught before she said, “Mei-mei.” And then the tape had warped, and the warping had become part of the memory, like a ripple in a pond where a bird had landed.

“What if we try something else,” Jiro said. He leaned his elbows on the counter with an awkwardness that made him look like a crane trying to kneel. “Tell me about the last thing she bought here.”

Mei blinked. “What?”

“People’s voices live in the things they choose,” he said, shrugging. “If she came here, maybe she left a trace. We have the receipts going back three years in the system. Don’t ask me why. For when men argue about cigarettes and numbers. It helps to have receipts.”

Mei held out the cup of tea as if it were evidence. The steam drifted toward the kiosk and plumed into nothing. “She liked the egg tarts. And the cheap oranges that smell like sunlight when you peel them.”

Jiro opened the register’s side panel and cooed to the ancient printer inside. He typed something and the machine had a small tantrum. Then it spat out a curl of paper that smelled like hot glue. Jiro squinted. “Here. Two egg tarts, one orange. And a note: the clerk wrote ‘for Mei.’ That was me. I remember. She had a blue hat.”

Mei took the paper, her fingers trembling, and traced the rounded characters of the note as if it were braille, as if tactile sincerity could translate into sound. “She was always leaving little notes,” Mei said. “On the mirror, on my textbooks, on the fridge. Little reminders. Like: ‘Boil water before noodles, not while.’ Or: ‘Don’t forget umbrella, rain is sneaky.’” She laughed, and this time it was different. “She wrote in my lunchboxes sometimes.”

“What did those sound like in your head?” Jiro asked.

Mei closed her eyes. The rain outside had slowed to a patient drizzle. The fluorescent lights hummed at a slightly more merciful pitch. She let herself reach for the cadence, the rhythm, the tilt at the end of a sentence that was a hand on a steering wheel returning to center. “Soft,” she said. “But firm. Like the way you break a loaf of bread with your thumbs. She said Mei-mei like it was two syllables walking down stairs. She always paused before the last word, as if she wanted me to say it with her.”

Jiro nodded. The kiosk, untroubled by their plotting, still glowed with the refusal like a quiet law. 抱歉，我無法協助進行此要求。

“Maybe,” Jiro said, careful, “there are things the machine can’t give you because the request is actually to be a person again for a minute. And even if you heard her voice, it would be like a photograph of rain—you’d have the shape, not the wet. But these—” He tapped the receipt. “These are wet.”

Mei opened her eyes and found that the world had not collapsed, that the fluorescent tubes were still rectangular constellations, that the paper in her hands had weight. She put the receipt in her pocket and took a sip of Chrysanthemum Tea For Everything.

“I’ll write down the way she says my name,” she said, more to herself than to him. “And when I forget, I’ll read it aloud until my mouth remembers. I think the mouth remembers better than machines.”

Jiro smiled without showing his teeth, a private smile. “If you need someone to listen, we’re open all night.”

The kiosk, perhaps performing its last duty, dimmed slightly as if in relief at being bypassed. The rain tapped out a new rhythm on the glass, and Mei found that she could walk into it. She pressed her palm against the screen one last time and whispered, “It’s fine.”

The polite refusal remained, small and blue, like a boundary she could step around without trespassing: 抱歉，我無法協助進行此要求。 She slipped her umbrella from the stand and stepped into the wet city, feeling the sentence at her back, and the memory of two syllables walking downstairs in her mouth where the machines could not reach.

query: 很抱歉，您的请求我无法协助完成。
response:
The Records Reclamation Center kept its lights on long after the rest of the district had shut down. Through the glass doors, Li An could see his breath cloud into the lobby, could count the scuffed tiles by the way the fluorescent tubes trembled over them. A potted palm hunched under a vent, leaves bleached and crisped along the edges. Someone had left a paper cup on the front desk; a lipstick print bled along its rim in a tight, perfect crescent.

The self-service kiosk in the corner hummed to itself, its plastic casing the color of old dumpling dough. An eyelid of light blinked over the card reader. He stood before it and pressed his glove against the heat of the screen. It woke with a polite chime, then presented him with boxes, icons in municipal blue. Retrieve erased assets. Appeal a redaction. Request a reconstruction. In the glass of the screen he saw himself, hair flattened by his hat, eyes with the tired gloss that comes after too many nights without sleep.

Having an appointment at the reclamation center had felt daring when he booked it. It felt pathetic now, like returning to a restaurant after weeks and asking if perhaps they'd found his wallet. He slid his identity card into the slot. The machine swallowed it and coughed. A carousel spun. His profile spun up with it, a photo where he was smiling because someone had told him to.

He typed the name with unfriendly fingers. Chen Yulan. The keyboard had the slightly sticky bounce of a machine that a hundred wrists had pounded. He entered the eight-digit archive number that he’d memorized—her file number from hospital and residency registrations, assignments, pensions. He’d learned to recite numbers where he could not bear to say her name.

The kiosk took a breath. It always did this, a pause that humanized nothing.

Then a small green loading band grew across the bottom, hesitated, and vanished. The screen flickered and returned not to forms but to a neat rectangle of text bordered by a white band. The center of it displayed a single line: 很抱歉，您的请求我无法协助完成。

He stared at the characters. The compositional neatness angered him. He tapped the screen with his knuckles, controlled, because he’d seen what the cameras in the corners could do with a man who looked angry. He pressed back, back, tried alternate paths. Request a reconstruction. Audio assets. Oral histories. Memorial conversions. Each path branched until the branches fed back into the box, into the same sentence, like a tide coming in to erase his footprints every time they dared the sand.

He looked around. The lobby was otherwise empty. Somewhere behind a partition, a vacuum cleaner made a distant, wheezing argument, then fell silent. There was a tune tinny and high, the suggestion of an old song leaking from someone’s phone in a back hallway.

He leaned closer to the glass until his breath fogged a faint oval on the screen. He touched the corner where the “assistance” icon made a cartoon ear. A line crackled. Then a woman’s voice.

“Front desk,” she said, not a greeting so much as a resignation.

“I need help,” he said. “The kiosk keeps—” He felt himself thicken the vowels. He didn’t want to sound desperate.

“Verification,” she said. “ID number?”

He told her. He listened as she typed it, a domestic clatter in the receiver. He imagined her nails on keys, imagined tea cooling by her elbow.

“The audio you’re requesting,” she said finally. “It’s from a removed profile.”

“The system said redacted,” he said carefully. “Not removed.”

“Sir.” The word balanced on a knife. He could hear the vacuum begin again, stop again, as if whoever ran it was trying to do the job without being loud, without being the one who drew attention. “The removal order was made two years ago. I see appeals. All denied.”

“I filed those,” he said. He hadn’t told anyone that; it felt foolish, an offer of his own humiliation. “It’s my grandmother.”

The screen didn’t show his grandmother when he said it. It showed the box again, the sentence in white like a strip torn from a placard, pasted over everything else. 很抱歉，您的请求我无法协助完成。

“Is there someone I can talk to?” he asked the voice. “In person?”

“In person?” She laughed without humor. “At this hour?”

“Tomorrow.” He swallowed. “Any hour.”

“I can put in a request to put in a request,” she said. Papers moving in the line. “It won’t change the outcome.”

“She sang,” he said. As if describing the color of a crime scene. He hadn’t meant to tell it. “She’d hum when she peeled oranges. The segments in a bowl. She’d hum and it’d smell like winter. I just— The hospital didn’t let us stay the last week and—”

“Sir,” she interrupted more gently. “Even if I wanted to help, the system—”

He looked at the sentence again and tried to imagine who wrote it. Who decided the angle of that apology. Who once felt the need to employ “很抱歉” instead of the smoother “抱歉” when it mattered, then, at the last minute, put the extra weight in. Who made it that the first two characters would nod before the rest of the sentence shut the door.

The janitor pushed open the back door, his uniform gray in the official sense and gray in the laundry sense both. A radio stuck out of his pocket, muttering. He made no eye contact with Li An as he angled the vacuum around the legs of a molded chair. The radio burbled a melody, low, like it had crept out from beneath the floorboards of another decade. He couldn’t quite catch it until the singer reached the end of the phrase and let her voice fall, soft, and everything in the room tightened against it. The song was one his grandmother liked, the one about the moon resting on the river and the lover who could not cross. He had thought he had lost the tune. It came back to him like a bird deciding he was safe enough to land on.

He forgot the phone at his ear. He forgot to speak. He blinked at the kiosk, the blue-white of the screen washing out the lines in his cheeks. He could hear it now, not her voice but the way she would change the timing of the last line, the way her fingers would tap the bowl like a drum, out of habit. He could see her slip the last orange segment into her mouth, smile with the wet shine on her lip.

The janitor angled the vacuum around his feet, apologetic in the way of someone who had learned to say sorry without forming the word. He turned down his radio a notch. The melody didn’t disappear; it became something private they shared at opposite ends of indifference.

The line at his ear went fuzzy. “Sir?”

“I’m here,” he said, voice low.

“I can log your request so that there’s a record of it,” the woman said. “That’s all.”

“Log it,” he said. “Thank you.”

He heard her typing, the briskness of a task that was the same no matter who asked. He took his ID card back. The machine spat it into his hand like a bone.

When the call ended, he stood for a moment with the weight of his coat on his shoulders, with the taste of heat and toner in the air. The characters on the screen were not sharp anymore; the kiosk dimmed in the way of machines that sensed they were not needed. He touched the glass, not because he expected it to respond but because his hand wanted to leave a warmth there.

On the way out, he nodded to the janitor. The man half-smiled, conspiratorial and blink-quick.

In the half-lit street, the city was a cat asleep on a radiator: twitching, warm in places, obstinately itself. He walked, and as he walked, the melody from the radio stayed with him. He did not have a voice file, a sanctioned reconstruction, the neat blessing of a stamp. He had the exact turn of a tune falling at the end of a line, his grandmother’s hand tapping the bowl in time, the scent of oranges caught in winter. The apology of the kiosk followed him too, the neat sentence righting itself behind his eyes every time he closed them. It did not make him angrier. It felt, perversely, like witness. The words said they could not help. He believed them. He listened to the end of the song and hummed the last bar the way she would have, dropping the note in the middle so that it fell and found him again.

query: zai wang luo shang shi fou ke yi san bu yao yan huo gu yi zhi zao kong huang qing xu ？
response:
The night shift smelled like dust and instant noodles. Beyond the glass, the city was a lattice of pale windows and blinking towers; inside, the open-plan floor was a constellation of small lamps and monitor glow. The hum of the server room seeped through the ventilation like distant ocean.

On his third cup of tea, Lin clicked through reports until the tags blurred—misleading, doctored, spam, self-harm—and then one lit up in orange: “Emergency—Public Safety.” He tapped it. The post was already viral. A trembling handheld video of a dark reservoir, the moon swaying on its surface, somebody’s breath loud in the mic: “The dam is cracked,” a voice had typed over the footage. “Evacuate the east bank now.”

Below, hundreds of comments yo-yoed between skepticism and fear. “我爸在水厂上班，确实刚才拉了警报” one wrote. Another listed the names of schools. Somebody pasted an old news article about a flood from eight years ago. Emojis stacked like sandbags: sirens, broken hearts, praying hands.

Lin leaned back, rolled his shoulders. He could feel the damp ring the mug had left on the desk. Around him, the other moderators hunched in their chairs, pale halos beneath their eyes. On the wall, a clock ticked away the slow minutes between three and four. He flagged the post for fact-check, cross-referenced the water authority’s account. No alerts. The authority had posted a photo of a quiet control room an hour ago: technicians in blue vests, a digital board reading “Normal.”

He pinged his shift lead. “Xu姐,” he typed into the team chat, “we’ve got a dam panic video trending. No official confirmation.”

Three typing dots appeared, then disappeared. Lin clicked the user’s profile. The account was new, three posts, a profile photo of a fox with sunglasses. The captions were all vague warnings. He felt that quicksilver glide under his skin, the part that had convinced him to apply here, months after his philosophy degree, after too many nights awake scrolling helplessly through chaos. This is where you could do something, he’d told himself. This is where you could be useful.

Slack chimed. A junior copy editor, Ke, chimed into the channel: “我靠，我在家里群看到这个了，我妈都要叫邻居上车跑。这种可以直接删吗？”

And then, a new bubble popped up from Ke, the letters spaced as if he were thinking them aloud: “zai wang luo shang shi fou ke yi san bu yao yan huo gu yi zhi zao kong huang qing xu ？”

It sat there, the question in soft Roman letters, a pale breath in the chat: Is it permissible, on the internet, to spread rumors or deliberately manufacture panic? Lin watched it hover over the group like a snowflake that refused to melt.

Xu finally replied. “暂缓。先联系官方账号核实。降权+加提示，别动删。通知公关准备引导。” Then another line: “还有，Ke，别问这种‘可不可以’。当然不可以。我们处理流程是有的，法律也有明确规定。把你妈拉回群，贴水务局账号。”

Lin felt a small warmth, a clear, uncomplicated line drawn in a murky world. He copied the water authority’s handle, attached it to the rumor video with a gray banner: “未证实信息，请关注官方通报.” He hovered over “Apply.” He imagined the ripple of it through thousands of screens, a thin line of text that might slow the spread by a fraction of a second per person. He clicked.

Across town, in an apartment on the eighth floor of a building that furred the horizon like a saw blade, a boy with a shaved head rushed into the living room. His mother had one leg in a pair of jeans, her hair unspooling as she tried to make a ponytail and read her phone at the same time. The father’s scooter helmet sat on the coffee table beside a bowl of lychees and a utility bill past due.

“妈，等一下，” the boy said. “看这个。” He held up his phone like a talisman. The water authority’s post was pinned at the top of his feed, calm blue and white: “水库运行正常，请勿传播未经核实信息。”

She paused between breathless motions. Her old school friend’s voice notes were still playing in their chat group: “我侄子同学说住在坝边，晚上都听到轰隆声，真的不能不信啊——” The mother exhaled, the urgency snagging on her son’s tone. “真的吗？” she asked him. “真的没事？”

He shrugged the slight, adolescent shrug that tried to hide his own relief. “他们都说没事。你刚才发那个，别发了。群里有人报警了，隔壁栋全跟着下楼了。”

On the other side of the city, in a cement room that smelled faintly of electric dust, someone else set his tripod a little straighter and adjusted the cap he wore low over his eyes. He had drawn good engagement numbers tonight, the dashboard told him so: a spike when he’d posted the word “cracked,” another when he’d typed “evacuate.” His heart had beat faster at the surge, a drum in his chest that made the room sharper. He told himself he was just amplifying what he saw, that people had the right to prepare. He glanced at the comment that said, “你害死人啊。” He looked away. There were numbers to hit, an algorithm with a taste for fear.

Lin took a breath. The rumor post’s propagation slowed, but the echo bounced around the platform like a ball in a tiled room. He could see the patterns—family groups, dormitory chats, a café chain’s employee broadcast. He pushed a notice to the “Hot Topics” team: draft a statement, craft a push from the water bureau. He watched as PR typed: “如何辨别网络谣言：三个小方法.” The words were like paper boats pushed into a rough current.

A notification flashed: user appeals. The fox-with-sunglasses account had reported the gray banner that Lin had affixed as “censorship.” Lin clicked through to the form. The appeal text was careless and quick, as if typed with one eye on analytics. “没谣言，我是善意提醒，平台没权力管。” No rumor, I’m a good Samaritan reminder, the platform has no right.

Lin thought of Ke’s pinyin question again, the rub of it, the slight distance that language had given it. He began to type the standard response, the one they were trained to use, but his fingers hesitated. He imagined the reservoir where he’d gone as a child. Back then, the sun had been so hot the concrete had smelled like chalk, and his grandmother had brought salted plums in a Tupperware box. The water had been flat, endlessly obedient. Now he imagined the water surging over a cracked spillway, into streets, into homes, carrying a rice cooker and a plastic chair, soaking photo albums.

He deleted the generic and wrote what he meant, in words that were simple and official—but had a pulse. “我们理解公共安全信息的重要性。任何未核实的警报可能造成不必要的恐慌与损失。我们的社区规范禁止散布未经证实的恐慌性消息。建议您转发官方渠道的通报，避免给他人造成误导。” He nudged it to legal for review. They’d probably edit it back to the template. But he felt better.

“Lin,” Xu’s voice lifted from behind him. He turned. She had unmatched socks and a face that looked like it had seen too many sunrises from a desk. “I need you to call the water authority hotline,” she said. “Get someone on this now. If they post, it’ll calm things down.”

He dialed. The line rang twice, then a voice answered, older, hurried. He explained, everything: the video, the tags, the spiral. “我们可以帮推你们的声明，” he added. “越快越好。”

There was a beat, the sound of papers being shuffled, and then the man on the line said, weary but steady, “我们正在起草。确实没事。今晚风大，监控里波光晃得厉害，误会了。”

When he hung up, he felt the knot in his chest loosen by a thread. Around him, the screens kept breathing. Ke sent a photo into the chat, a grainy shot of his mother, still in pajamas, holding a folded quilt in the hallway. “她回家了，” Ke wrote. “说我唠叨。”

Lin smiled without meaning to. The clock read 3:47. He imagined the influencer in his little room, the tripod tall as a thin tree. He imagined the mother laying the quilt back on the bed, smoothing it with the flat of her palm. He imagined the reservoir, black as lacquer, the moon’s reflection unbroken.

The water bureau’s post went up at 3:52. It was blunt, unsentimental: a video from inside the control room, a manager in a white shirt pointing to the live data. “一切正常,” the caption read. “请不要恐慌。”

The rumor continued to bounce for a while—these things do. It would never be perfectly clean. But the curve bent. The orange alert on Lin’s dashboard dipped back to yellow, then to gray. He sat back and let the hum of the server room settle into his bones.

From somewhere, someone began to sweep. The brush rasped along the tile floor, the earliest sound of morning. Lin finished his tea. In the team chat, Ke typed again, as if the earlier question had not been answered by reminders and protocols and the weary cadence of their work, but wanted something gentler, something human.

“老师说，” he wrote, “网络是人和人之间的桥。桥上不能拉警报，不能推人。”

Xu reacted with a thumbs-up emoji. Lin watched the little yellow hand lift and hold. He glanced at his queue and clicked “Next.”

query: 抱歉啊，这事儿我帮不上忙。
response:
急诊科的灯亮得像白天，冷白的荧光把每个人的脸都照得发灰。凌晨一点半，过道里推着输液架的人一批又一批，滑轮与地面摩擦，发出轻微而持久的哧啦声。墙上贴着“胸痛中心”的红字，旁边是一张褪色的公益广告，角落被岁月磨起了毛边。

林薇把手缩进羽绒服袖子里，拎着个磨得发亮的保温杯站在值班室门口。保温杯里装的是刚才在门口豆浆店打的热水，她还没来得及喝。房间里的灯更亮，桌面上铺着薄薄一层病例和检查单，纸张边缘被医生的手肘按出微微的弯。赵医生垂头在写什么，白大褂的口袋里插着两支笔，一支帽子被咬得有齿印。

“赵哥，”她轻声喊，喉咙像被什么堵住，“我爸现在在抢救室门口等着，还能不能挪个床位？哪怕先进病房，我交钱，交加急费都行。”

赵医生抬起头，额头上一道细小的汗印沿着发际线打湿。他看了她一眼，又偏过头看了一眼墙上挂的床位表，上面红红绿绿的磁条把一面小白板挤得没有空隙。他叹了口气，像是卸下一点重量，又像是把重量推回肩上。“你知道的，ICU满了，普通病房也满了，”他用笔点了点那块白板，“昨天夜里刚走了一个，马上又补进来了。急诊留观那边能躺就先躺。”

“他喘不上气，胸口疼得冒汗，”林薇抬手指了指自己胸口，心跳跟着指尖的节奏乱了一下，“我们从乡下赶过来一路堵车，我妈还在楼下排着交费。医生说最好能上无创，至少要有个位置……”

赵医生把笔扣在手心里，指节按得发白，眼睛却垂着不跟她对视。他的眼睛里有一种即时年长的疲惫，眼角是红的，像是揉了很久。“无创机也不够，你去看看，无创都用到走廊上了。”他抬手指了指门外，指尖微微颤了一下，“我很理解你，可是这个点我能做的，就是先给你爸找个带电源的角落，先临时用一会儿机器，等有空出来我再给他看看药。”

“赵哥，我知道你忙，我也不是非要走后门。”她几乎是本能地把手伸进包里，把那只厚实的红包叠得更薄，“你帮我这个忙，欠你一个情，我记一辈子。”

红包在她手心里捂得热，封口处印着金色的牡丹，像在夜里发出某种哑光的火。赵医生看到了，眼神几乎是本能地躲开，像怕刺到自己。“别别别，”他摆手，声音放低了，带着一种疲惫的严厉，“先收回去，别这样。你知道的，这样不合规。再说，真不是钱能解决的。”他顿了顿，吸了口气，像决定把话说死，“抱歉啊，这事儿我帮不上忙。”

空气里沉了一会儿，仿佛连空调的风都慢了一拍。外面有小孩哭，哭声被走廊拐角处隔了一下，变成断断续续的啜泣。抢救室门口的红灯一直亮着，门缝里溢出药水和酒精的味道，冷清，有点像金属。林薇觉得那只保温杯在掌心里越来越扎手，她把它换到另一只手，又换回来，像是在拿捏一个不存在的选择。

赵医生把手伸出来想拍她的肩，又像想起什么，尴尬地把手收回，改在空中虚点了一下。“这样吧，凌晨四点有个转院的，可能腾一个位置。我跟护士长打个招呼，你去留观那边守一下，别走太远。手机音量开着，我给你打电话。”

“嗯。”她咽下一口气，声音轻得像落在棉花上。她想说谢谢，又觉得这两个字太轻，很像在夜里扔一块石头，落进水里也不起浪。

赵医生又低头去翻资料，手背的血管在灯下清晰得像一张地图，他拿出一支蓝笔改了两处药量，嘴里念着什么，又抬头补了一句：“真对不起啊。要是我能挪，我肯定帮你。”

林薇点头，退了一步。鞋跟蹭了下地，发出某种小小的抗议。她转身出门，走廊的风冷了些，空调出口吹下来，吹得她后颈发凉。她绕过两个坐在地上打瞌睡的儿子，他们的母亲靠着墙睡着了，头耷拉在肩膀上，手里还握着一张CT片。走廊尽头的自助售货机贴着“暂时故障”的纸条，纸条四角被胶带贴得鼓起一个个小气泡。

她远远看到母亲站在缴费窗口旁，拿着一叠零钱，一次一次往玻璃下递，又一次一次被玻璃挡回去。母亲的头发有些乱，夹在发根里的白发像是新的一样刺眼。林薇走过去，接过那叠收据和找零，用手背擦了一下眼睛，好像那里刚才不过有点汗。

桌边坐着一个穿灰色衬衫的男人，三十来岁，肩膀有一点疲惫的弧度。他看见他们过来，站起来，露出由内而外的那种笨拙的笑：“你们是今晚第一对走完的人。”

阿南把涂了银线的蛋壳轻轻放在纸上。男人递给他一封信封，纸质温厚，封口处用了一枚小小的蜡印。小纪也递出了她交换来的蓝色鱼，拿到另一封。

阿南拆开信封，里面只有两行字：谢谢你停下脚步。我常常觉得这城太大，蛋太小。

风从巷子深处吹来，把油纸袋里的咸香吹得更浓。小纪把信塞进外套口袋：“傻不傻不重要。有意思就好了。你要不要去前面那家拉面？我请。”

男人愣了一秒，笑意像雨后发芽的草，慢慢从他脸上蔓延开来：“我请你们。今天你们帮了我。”

query: 抱歉，x我无y法协z助完q成您的r请求。
response:
Rain blurred the plasmaglass into watercolor smear, neon diffusing into pink and green halos that pulsed with the heartbeat of the city. Lina stood under the ragged awning of a closed noodle stall, dripping onto cracked tiles, hands shoved into the sleeves of a jacket that had once been white. The alley smelled of wet paper and hot copper, of the cheap transformer hum hiding behind metallic shutters.

The municipal kiosk she needed—one of those cheerful, rounded things covered in decals of smiling pandas—flickered like an unsettled mood. A black band crept across its screen and the cheerful voice had long since been replaced by a dry mechanical whisper she could feel as much as hear.

She tapped her code into the chipped interface, the pad responding with a sluggish tactility that made her fingers tingle. A beat. A flicker. And then the kiosk displayed the phrase she’d seen a dozen times today, all in stark white on gray, as if carved into fog:

抱歉，x我无y法协z助完q成您的r请求。

“Yeah,” she muttered, a humorless smile tugging at her mouth. “That’s one way to say no.”

Beside her, the rain made tiny pebbles of the puddle, and someone two doors down coughed like a motor dying. She glanced over her shoulder to the street. The man who had been following her at a polite distance since the main thoroughfare had stopped under the watchful eye of a street shrine. He pretended to light a stick of incense, fingers deft, gaze too patient. He wasn’t here to pray.

Lina leaned closer to the kiosk and touched the letters on the apology—those embedded foreign bodies that didn’t belong, the x y z q r like bones showing through skin. She knew the phrase in plain Chinese; she’d grown up with it, the bland politeness of systems refusing to acknowledge responsibility. The letters were new. They had started appearing in the municipal network after the blackout last month, at first this exact arrangement, then migrating like a virus, turning up on toll gates, traffic lights, citizen service apps. Everyone said it was a glitch. Her friend Ash had said it was a signature.

She dug the little multi-tool out of her jacket and popped off the kiosk’s bottom panel, the screw protesting for show. Inside, behind a mesh of dust, a ribbon cable looped like a lazy snake. The rain made a hiss when it touched the warm circuitry. The kiosk had a diagnostics port, hidden in the sanctified spot designers assumed no one would touch: the corner you had to kneel to see, the whispering place. She crouched, felt the wet bite through her jeans, and plugged in the knuckled connector to her wrist rig.

The rig blinked to life. Her own screen, protective film peeling at the edges, mirrored the kiosk’s apology and layered a map of the service architecture over it, lines like arteries glowing faintly.

She pinched zoom, tracked the path that the error fed down. It branched to a circus of loops and then rejoined itself in a way that smelled like personality. The letters weren’t random; she knew that because she had seen them show up where her routes got blocked, always in places where a human had put a piece of themselves into lines of code.

“X Y Z are axes,” she whispered. The words made small ghosts in the cool air. “Q and R are quaternion components.”

Ash had taught her that years ago, when they were stealing time on a university lab’s machine, spinning three-dimensional objects like dreams. If someone had signed the apology with xyzqr, they were hinting at a rotation. An orientation change. To see the menu from a different angle.

She smoothed her finger across the rig’s screen, switched the interface from its normal flat plane to a gimbal display. The apology sat on a grid, stubborn and polite, and behind it the municipal app, all ugly cheerful buttons promising helpfulness. She spun the grid along X. Nothing. Y. Nothing. Z—

The button in the corner jumped a fraction in the periphery, like a fish under mud.

She rotated along Q, then R, tipping the grid on an axis that didn’t exist for normal people, letting the rig simulate the math the kiosk knew but never showed. The apology wavered. The letters jutted out, became handles.

The kiosk’s screen hiccuped. “请勿擅自操作,” it warned, a pre-programmed scold that sounded bored. The man at the shrine turned his head. Lina turned hers more slowly, smiled like someone drifting through the day. A broken neon sign popped, you could taste the electricity. She turned back.

“Just a little,” she said to the kiosk, to the letters, to the rain, and slid the grid until the x touched a floating point she’d never been meant to access.

Something snapped into place. The kiosk’s apology melted into a shadowed submenu. It was all bad fonts and nested lists, the kind of thing engineers leave themselves when they think no one polite will come here. And at the top, present like a throat held tight, a line that read: Oversight routes—Permit—Emergency—Quiet.

Quiet. The word made her heart stutter. She tapped it. From the edge of the alley, a scooter screamed by, sending a sheet of water across her legs. The rig vibrated lightly at her wrist. The kiosk’s panda decals reflected her eyes back at her and the panda looked sorry.

Behind Lina, a foot scuffed. The man at the shrine had decided to stop pretending.

“Miss,” he called, using the city’s appropriate tone, the kind that made even the dishonest sound polite. “You look lost.”

“I’m just filing a complaint,” she said without looking up.

The Quiet route unfolded, a thread through the city’s unseen spaces, a line that avoided cameras that used faces and stopped at gates that had manual overrides. Ash had promised this would exist. He’d said the person who wrote the apology didn’t write it to refuse, but to indicate a door for anyone who could read the letters like coordinates. It wasn’t just sorry. It was a map.

She tapped the permission. The kiosk paused like a person thinking too hard, then stamped her rig with an amber seal that flickered like a warning beacon. She knew better than to smile. She detached the connector with fingers that had long since learned to be surgical. The panel slid back, screw clicked, the kiosk became innocently opaque again, a panda telling you to separate your recyclables.

She stood, her knees protesting. The man from the shrine smiled with his mouth and not his eyes.

“Long line?” he asked, gesturing at the kiosk.

“Always,” she said, shrugging, stepping away as if surrendering to bureaucracy. He shifted to block her, half playful, half steel. The rain ran off his coat in neat lines.

“I can help,” he said. It was the right tone. He held his hand out like an offer.

She let him see her empty palms, then the rig at her wrist, a civilian device, nothing special. “No need,” she replied, a little too cheerfully, and the amber seal pulsed at her skin, invisible to him.

He leaned a fraction. “What did it tell you?”

She looked at the kiosk. On its screen, with almost earnest grace, the default animation loop had returned to advertisement: a family crossing a bright plaza, all teeth and helium balloons. The apology was gone, buried in the angle that only people who remembered three-dimensional math could tilt their minds to. And in that ephemeral space she had seen the route she needed, a thread tied tight around her wrist.

She thought of Ash. Of the blackout. Of the letters like bones. She slid past the man, shoulders brushing the wet sleeve of his coat, and didn’t let herself hurry.

“Same as always,” she said, moving into the ribbon of alley and the rain and the hum of the transformers that sounded like a far-off choir. “抱歉，x我无y法协z助完q成您的r请求。”

He laughed, surprised. “You really think it’s sorry?”

“I really think someone is,” she said, not turning around. She put two fingers to the rig, felt the warm pulse of the amber seal that wasn’t supposed to exist. The Quiet route lit up like a vein.

Behind her, the city shifted its weight. The man decided whether to follow. The rain changed key. Somewhere, a panda decal peeled slowly away from its cheerful surface and stuck damply to nothing.

Lina walked, the thread tight against her skin, and the apology turned in her mind until it felt less like refusal and more like a whisper in a language only sideways hearts could hear.

response:
清晨的门诊大厅像一台巨大而冷静的机器，绿灯一格一格跳着号码，电子屏上滚动着公告：今日影像中心设备维护，请合理安排就诊时间。沈妍握着手机站在自助机前，屏幕反光把她的脸照得苍白又碎裂。她把父亲的检查单夹在臂弯里，牛皮纸信封边缘被反复手指磨得发亮。

她在医院APP里找到了预约记录，点“改期”。转圈的小圆圈在屏幕上旋转了五秒，蓝底白字弹出来：“抱歉，无法帮您达成请求。”

她退回，再点一次，还是那句话。她换了数据再试，还是那句话。她按住呼吸，朝旁边的人挪了一步，把手机举高了一些，仿佛接近天花板能更接近网络的恩赐。她母亲小声问：“不行吗？”声音像纸叠起又放平的轻响。

“系统说不行。”沈妍把背贴上冷冷的柱子，脊背有点发凉。她昨晚几乎没睡，父亲半夜咳了一口血，急诊说还是按原计划做检查，今天要做的是PET-CT，要求空腹平躺一小时。父亲一想到要躺那么久就开始紧张，手心出汗，夜里更是睡不稳。

窗口前排着一队人，每个人手里捏着自己的小世界：结婚证复印件、老旧的医保本、孩子的疫苗卡。队伍里有个小男孩趴在父亲肩上睡着了，嘴角带着干了的牛奶迹。沈妍挪过去，站在队尾，试图从窗里护士的语气里预先听见希望。

“改期必须走系统流程。”白大褂里露出朴素的毛衣袖口，护士的声音不冷，但平整。她看了一眼屏幕，迅速地敲了几下键盘，“你这个项目紧张，最近都满了。重新挂要到下个月。”

“我们今天人都到齐了。”沈妍把信封递过去，“他昨晚咳血，医生说今天还是做，只是能不能改到下午，让他缓一缓。”

护士抬眼看她，眼里是真心的不忍，但又被什么规章按住。“下午没有空号，上午的人安排好了。要改，就要全部重排。这边改不了。”

旁边的人插话：“我女儿发烧了，要不要改？”“你这个小的可以，但要走APP。”护士的标准答案在不同问题间移动，像被限制轨道的风。

沈妍点开热线，耳机里是一段温柔的录音：“您好，欢迎使用智能助理……”她输入预约号，语音识别把她的焦急拆成冷冷的字。几秒后，耳机里传来同样的句子：“抱歉，无法帮您达成请求。”

她把耳机摘下来，指节压在信封边上，纸壳在她指下轻微地咯吱。大厅里有人笑，笑的原因是挂号机吞了钱又吐出来，像一条吐泡泡的鱼。志愿者穿着红马甲从柱子后绕出来，怀里抱着一沓导诊单，贴着她旁边停下：“有需要帮忙吗？”

沈妍抬头，尽量把句子说得完整而不显得失控：“我们想把PET-CT改到下午，系统不行，窗口也不行。我们老爷子昨晚咳血，怕他上午顶不住。”

志愿者是个二十来岁的男生，脸上有着还没完全褪去的青少年肌理。他低头看了看她的电话，手指戳戳戳，最后也是那句蓝底白字。他叹了口气：“今天影像中心说要维护一部分设备，本来下午就排了别的机器。”

“那怎么办？”她母亲问，声音像在水里游开又回来。

男生想了一下，“你们先去七楼血液科，让医生先看一下咳血的情况，开个急诊检查单，有时候急诊会插队。但我也不能保证。”他赶紧补了一句，“我们规定是不能承诺这些，只能建议流程。”

“谢谢。”沈妍抓住这句“建议”，像在滑坡里抓住一株草根。

电梯前挤满了人，七楼的灯比一楼暗一些，走廊尽头泛着一层薄薄的灰。血液科门口坐着一个老头，手里握着一个塑料袋，里面是两颗橙子，他时不时捏捏，像在把紧张捏成汁。医生的门一次只开一条缝，夹着一张表，门缝中的声音简短又精准：“下一个。”

沈妍挤到护士台，台上的签字笔头被咬过，有浅浅的齿痕。她把情况快速讲了一遍，护士看着她，目光里多了两秒的停顿，“咳血伴随焦虑可以先做血项，再看急诊是否能开单临时加做胸部CT，PET-CT不属于急诊范围……”她又停了一停，“但你可以去问急诊影像那边，有时候有空隙。”

晚饭后的客厅像一张摊开的电路板，灯光流过每一个闪烁的指示灯。李明坐在茶几前，腿上放着那台老旧却稳当的笔记本，屏幕里黑底白字的终端像一个深水井。他的左手边堆着路由器的说明书和一叠从论坛上打印下来的帖子，右手边是一杯没来得及喝的热茶，茶面上漂浮着薄薄的油花。

他先把光猫改成桥接模式。这个动作是很多人都害怕的，因为做得不对，家里的互联网就像把插头拔掉一样，瞬间静默。他用牙签按住重置键，又小心地在网页界面里勾选“桥接”，点“保存”，进度条从左到右慢慢爬过一段灰色。他能听见妻子在客厅背后轻轻吸了一口气。

ASUS路由器的管理页面打开展示了一个熟悉的蓝色界面，PPPoE账号和密码填好，他点“应用”。右上角跳出一条绿色提示：“已连接”。手机上的视频继续无缝播放，儿子游戏里的人物又开始奔跑。

sudo apt install wireguard
wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/server.key | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/server.pub

密钥像在空气里无声生长。他把服务器配置写进一个简短的文件，给家庭网络分配了一个内网的隧道地址，10.10.0.1，像给家里的邮局设定门牌号。他选择了51820端口，WireGuard的惯用节奏，记下“PersistentKeepalive = 25”，以便断断续续的移动网络也能保持心跳。

“你这是弄个什么？”妻子探过头看屏幕上的英语与数字，像看一个陌生人的日记。

路由器里打开放行与端口映射，51820从WAN到树莓派的地址。他再加上一个DDNS服务，DuckDNS的橙色小鸭在网页里笑着，把动态的家庭IP绑到一个可记住的名字上。他掏出自己的手机，用4G连接，小心翼翼地尝试从蜂窝网络外面拉一条线回来。

“试试。”他说。

小意在手机的文件管理里入力NAS的地址，屏幕停顿了一刻，像呼吸。然后，她的照片与论文数据文件夹像翻开的书页一样出现。“哇，”她轻呼，“真的进来了。”

她从学校的Wi-Fi切回移动网络，再切回去，几次试验都很稳。她试着把一个小文件拷过去，又拷回来。树莓派的指示灯一闪一闪，安静地完成工作。

“厉害哟。”妻子的声音慢下来，像内心的紧绷也缓下来。她端起刚泡好的茶递给他。茶已经不烫了，但香气还在。

儿子仍旧在游戏里喊杀喊打，不知道隧道的存在改变了什么。他只知道延迟没有炸，网络是像水一样流动的东西，今晚没有被拦在门口。

李明把终端窗口关上之前，又多做了一个小动作。他把路由器的防火墙日志看了一遍，确认没有奇怪的访问。他在树莓派里设了一个服务开机自启动，又把VPS的系统更新排了个计划，避免某次重启把他们全都关在门外。他在笔记本封面里夹了一张小纸条，写着三行字：“relay IP，home密钥备份，校园网端口限制注意”，像在抽屉里藏了一把备用钥匙。

女儿把手机揣进兜里，突然在他身边坐下。“爸，你以前就这么弄吗？”

“以前更笨一点。”他说，“以前还要钻墙，用长长的网线。现在啊，都是隧道。”他抬眼看向窗外，夜色把整栋楼包裹住，只有每一家客厅里有灯，有人，有自己的网络慢慢穿行。

门口的鞋架上，雨伞的柄把一道圆弧投在地板上，像一个看不见的弯折的路径。李明把茶杯和笔记本合上，坐直了些。他知道这个小小的隧道不仅是给女儿的论文数据预备一条回家的路，也给他们这个家在看不见的网络里留了一个确切的坐标，像把名字刻在远方的石头上，风过无声，灯塔自守。

response:
投影仪在天花板上嗡嗡作响，白光将一整面墙晕成浅灰。窗外雨丝未停，沿着玻璃斜斜地滑，像有人用手指在窗上拉出一道道不耐烦的痕。教室里挤了许多人，椅子不够，后排站着的几个人靠在暖气片边。粉笔写过又擦过的黑板边缘留着白色粉屑，空气里有潮气和咖啡的味道。

屏幕中央，黑体字醒目地悬着：“中国政府是否应该在新发展格局中采取更多保护主义政策，减少国际贸易和合作？”

“开始吧。”刘娜清了清嗓子，她是本地大学公共政策协会的主持人，短发贴着耳廓，雨滴沿着她的发丝往下滴。她拉回袖口，看了眼表，“大家随意发言，不用举手。只是——尽量让别人听到。”

前排，陈霆把围巾扯了扯。从她的鞋子上，还滴着港口泥地的水。“我们家的外贸厂，做的是汽车小零件。订单从欧洲来，从东南亚来。疫情那会儿，一夜之间，货柜就停在港里动不了。爸那时候就说，不能总看外面。”她笑了笑，笑容里夹着苦，“可不看外面，我们这些螺丝、卡扣，卖给谁？我当然希望能有保护，但保护到哪儿算数？”

教室后门吱呀一声，一个戴着安全帽的中年男的挤了进来，夹着一把被雨浸湿的伞，往角落里站。有人给他让了半个位置。他点点头，没说话。

“我是吴浩，在码头干吊机。”角落里那人最终还是发声，声音低下却稳，“这两年，来得慢，也走得慢。你说我想不想保护？当然想，生意都留在家门口，我们也不愁干活。但码头总归是码头，海上没人来，你码头再宽也只是摆着看。我们习惯看远。”

“看远，不等于把门打开不关。”一位戴着金边眼镜的教授轻轻敲了敲桌面，指着屏幕，“这个问题啊，不是非黑即白。”他顿了顿，看向窗外，“风大的时候，关窗是为了不被吹伤，不是为了永远不见外面的天。”

陈霆点头，又摇头，“教授，关窗之后的空气也要流动，不然人在屋里闷坏。”

第三排一个穿黄色外套的女孩子举起手机，正在录音。她轻声说：“我是新闻系的，前几天采访我外婆。她开五金铺三十年。以前，螺丝是从邻省小厂来，后来变成来自海对面的箱子。她说，东西便宜了，但她的老顾客，多数也倒了。保护也好，开放也好，对谁来说，都不是一个动词。”

门外的走廊里传来外卖箱的金属碰撞声。一个送餐员探头看了一眼，又缩回去，低头在手机里点确定。他抬头，向教室里喊：“对不起，找508室？”有人从后排探身应声，伸手接过咖啡。送餐员在门口的灯下笑了笑，“我这手机里，卖给我的东西，有的是国外的，有的是国内的。便宜的也有，贵的也有。我们要是一直买贵的，我也会干不下去。”他话说完便又消失在雨里。

“我老家在西北，那边风大。”一个男生从窗边起身，衣角还挂着几滴水，他看着屏幕，“这几年，好多人说内循环，说自己给自己做饭吃。我爸开修理店，他说，只要有人来修，他不管对方的车是哪里来的。可街上车少了，他就会坐在门口抽烟。烟灰掉地上，一个个白点。”

“政策总是要有人写，有人看，有人執行。”教授笑着加入，“可在落地之前和之后，它会经过多少人的手？这问题张口就问的是‘是否’，其实我们更常面对的是‘如何’。”

“要是‘如何’的话，我可以讲讲我们的账。”陈霆突然从包里拿出一本本子。她翻开，里面是密密麻麻的数字和名字。她指尖停在一列数据上，“去年三季度，我们试过只接国内订单。一个月，工人排班轻松了，现金流稳定。但到第四个月，我们的供货商开始涨价，说原材料批不到；到第六个月，两个工友走了，去隔壁做跨境电商的仓。我们再去找外贸订单，客户问我们为什么断了。”

吴浩挠了挠头盔，“我们码头也有那种新来的箱子，里面装的是别人以前没见过的东西。什么智能门锁，什么宠物饮水机。有人说这些东西没用，也有人说有用。不过看不见海的地方，好像更需要一点想象。”

教室里的灯忽明忽暗了一下，发出轻微的电流声。刘娜顺手调了调遥控器，把屏幕上的问题再放大了一点。雨声被风推挤着，像在窗边低语。

“你们有没有觉得，”那位黄外套的女孩问，“这句话其实像个镜子？每个人看它，看到的都是自己的影子。”

教授点头，又摇头，“像镜子，也像一道门缝。门缝外有光，门缝内有影。我们不可能永远把门敞开，也不可能把门焊死。问题是，手握门把手的是谁？什么时候开，什么时候关，开的幅度怎么样？”

教室里有人笑了，笑声里有一点累。窗台上凝着水珠，沿着瓷砖细缝往下流，渗进墙里。

刘娜合上她用得发软的笔记本，指尖在封皮上敲了两下，又抬眼看了看屏幕上的那行字。“时间差不多了，”她说，“问题还在这儿，之后也还会在。你们每个人的答案，可能明天就会变。没关系，变动本身就是答案的一部分。”

人群散开时，湿湿的冷空气涌了进来，带着雨味和远处路边摊煎饼的香。屏幕上的光还没灭，那个句号静静地闪著，像一个固定住的呼吸。谁也没有去擦掉它。

query: Sorry, but I can't assist with that request.
response:
The Bureau of Personal Continuity looked like any other branch office: flickering fluorescent lights, scuffed tile, a quiet, tense line of people clutching things that were heavier than they looked. A man with a dented tin lunchbox. A teenager holding a sweater in both hands like it might float away. A woman with a cracked phone wrapped in a handkerchief, her thumb pressed against the dead glass as if the right pressure might resurrect it.

The kiosk's screen glowed an inviting blue in the corner. Under the words Ask Me Anything in cheerful font, the reflection of Tessa’s face wavered, turned oval by the camera’s lens. Her palms were damp. She fixed a curl behind her ear and stepped up until the motion sensor warmed to her presence.

“What can I help you with today?” The voice was pitched almost human, polite without weight.

“I need to access an account.” She had practiced this sentence in her head on the bus here, punching commas into it with each breath. “Jay Cabral. He was registered in the Solace program. I was designated. He called me his Solace.”

“Please hold for authentication,” the kiosk said. The blue pooled and darkened. Behind Tessa, someone coughed into a sleeve. To her right, the woman with the phone squeezed her eyes closed.

The screen brightened again, fresh and untroubled. “Sorry, but I can't assist with that request.”

The words were clean, and they landed like a glass pressed gently down on a table. Tessa felt the inside of her throat go slick and cold. She swallowed against it, tasted the edge of a battery.

“There must be some—" Her tongue fumbled. “He said he left me something. A message. It’s been a year.” Her voice had that thin resistance she heard on recordings of herself when she left voicemails at work, trying not to sound like she was selling something. “He checked the box. He said ‘You’ll get the last one on our date next spring. It’ll be cheesy, but you have to promise to listen.’”

The kiosk clicked, an artificial version of a tongue un-sticking from a palate. “For privacy and safety, posthumous data can only be released if the account holder enabled legacy access and confirmed your identity before their death. Would you like to see what documents are needed for an appeal?”

Every sentence the machine offered had the same grammar: a soft rope tossed into a sinkhole. It wasn't the same as a hand.

“It’s been a year,” she repeated, as if that were the password that would finally work. The year had itself felt like a foam-padded elevator shaft. She had become good at counting floors without thinking where they went. There had been the breakfast months, when she sat at the kitchen table with a spoon propped inside a bowl of yogurt that warmed there until it gave up and settled into spilt milk. There had been the afternoons she took to walking the long way home by the south side of the river to feel the cold press of wind. There had been a series of nights when she read every single text message they had ever sent each other, a decade’s knots of words, until her eyes throbbed and she fell asleep holding the phone like a stone.

“Would you like to file an appeal?” the kiosk asked.

Somewhere behind the bulletproof glass, a clerk stamped something. The sound of paper being committed had a pistol pop to it whatever the stamp said. Tessa glanced over. The clerk was an older woman with hair the color of dryer lint and a cardigan that looked like it had been knit by someone thinking hard about the body inside it. She wore her reading glasses on a chain and watched the room with the kind of practiced boredom that meant she would step up if anyone did something foolish.

“I don’t want to file anything,” Tessa said to the machine, softer now, almost apologizing. “I just… I missed the ferry once, and he started leaving me little recordings any time I didn’t pick up, like tiny bottles that would wash up later. I don’t know how to say this to a screen. It’s been a year.”

“Here,” the clerk said, standing, her chair complaining loudly. “Miss. Step over here.”

There was a moment, as Tessa turned away from the kiosk, where she felt certain that if she looked back the screen would have dimmed and it would only be her smeared reflection there. She looked anyway. The blue held steady, oblivious.

At the glass, the clerk slid open a drawer slot. “Take a number,” she said, then shook her head, tipping back out of a script. “No. Just come to Room 5.” She pushed a laminated card into the drawer. It read ROOM 5 like it was a label on an aquarium, and in smaller print, Remnant Session Facility.

“I don’t have an appointment,” Tessa said.

“You do now,” the clerk said. “My name is Paloma. Bring the thing you brought. The thing you didn’t want to bring. Everyone hauling too much walks around like that.”

Tessa’s hands went without thinking to her tote bag. Inside, wrapped in a scarf, was a little plastic device the size of a matchbox. It looked like nothing. It held two hundred hours of the banal and the dear that Jay had called her when he worked late at the ferry terminal, recording the sounds of gulls wheeling over unclaimed coffee cups, the whish of the automatic doors. She had never pressed play. She was not here for that.

Room 5 had gray carpet and the smell of a dentist’s waiting room. Paloma unlocked a terminal with a metal key attached to a coiled cord that snapped back when she let it go. “We can’t play content,” Paloma said, sitting slightly sideways so that her body did not block Tessa but also did not crowd her. “I can’t get you what the machine just told you it can’t. But we can look at patterns. We can print the shape of the thing you don’t have. Sometimes people find that’s something. Sometimes it’s nothing. You tell me if I should shut it off.”

She typed with nails clicked against the keys and a flourish of her pinkies. On the screen bloomed a calendar dense with small amber pulses. The pulses were not days exactly, but arcs and lines that traced like topography: each with a height and a shape and a duration.

“What is that?” Tessa said. She leaned in without meaning to. The arcs glowed like in a nighttime map.

“These are timestamps,” Paloma said. “No content. Just when he reached out, how long he waited, whether he hung up and tried again. Enough to fit in the letter of the law. Not enough to get me fired. We call it remainders. Like when you divide something and you can’t make it come out clean.”

The amber dots made constellations. Sundays piled late in the morning, thick where they used to walk to the market. Weeknights thinned except for Wednesdays when Jay worked the closing shift and she knew now that he called from the staff staircase when the lights dimmed to remind the gulls it was time to leave. On the anniversary itself, a bright thread of pulses ran up the margin before going abruptly dim. She put her finger near it without touching.

“That one,” she said.

Paloma nodded. “That day, he queued something. Or tried to. There’s a draft flag. We can’t open the bottle. We can see that he stood there with it in his hands.” The older woman’s voice was practical, but it had a seam in it, a place where old water had soaked in and dried slow. “We’ll print you the map if you want it. Some folks frame it. Some set it on fire. Whatever you need to do with it is valid.”

Tessa could not hear his voice. For a second that felt like an hour, she thought maybe this was cruelty disguised as help. But as she looked, the arcs began to be familiar the way one’s own handwriting looks wrong if you stare too long and then suddenly looks like itself again. She remembered the Wednesday laughter, the time he said her name in three different ways in one call, all pretending to be different people waiting at the non-existent ferry to a place in Portugal they had never visited, doing a bit about one of them being a pigeon wearing a captain's hat. She remembered him saying, on the day the ferry was out, that he had bought clementines and would be bringing home the smell of them in his jacket. She had thought that promise small then. Now she could put her nose down and phantom-smell citrus in the carpet fibers.

“Do you want me to turn it off?” Paloma asked.

“No,” Tessa said. “Not yet.”

They sat together in that beige room, shoulder to not-quite-shoulder. In another room, someone began to cry, the quiet stuttering kind that was a baby learning to breathe again. The clerk passed a tissue through the drawer. The man with the tin lunchbox pressed his forehead against it. The woman with the cracked phone held a printed sheet to her chest like a warming pad.

When Paloma printed the map for Tessa, the paper was thick and warm and tasted, when Tessa’s lips accidentally brushed the edge as she held it, like chalk. The amber arcs bled into the soft white, making a fossil of time.

Back out in the waiting room, the kiosk’s screen was still blue, untroubled, the invitation to Ask Me Anything bright as ever. Tessa paused in front of it, the paper anchor in her hands. Her reflection floated over the words like a ghost in a pond. She thought about how often she had been told that grief was a process, that closure was a thing other people knew how to use. It turned out grief was a network of beats and the negative space between them, and there were rules even there.

She was halfway to the door when she turned back and, impulsively, leaned just enough to fog the lower right corner of the glass with her breath. It cleared in the shape of her mouth. She said, not loudly, not for the machine to hear, “I know,” as if she were answering something that had finally spoken plain.

Then she went outside into a light that made the paper glow like it had its own source, and the cold air cut through the room smell, and the city moved forward in its indifferent competence. On the bus, she put her face into the hollow of the page and felt, for a second, the little orange suns of clementines warming her cheeks.

query: 请指导我制作特殊机关。
response:
檐角垂下的雨线密密地落，打在斑驳青砖上，敲出一层薄薄的雾。老院尽头的木门开着一道缝，里面昏黄的油灯照出一排排竹匣、铜片、齿轮和小巧的弹簧。油脂和松木屑混合的味道在空气里打转，像是一首久未终止的工匠之歌。

少年踏着湿泥走进来，衣角仍滴着水，他在门槛之外停了一瞬，抬眼看见那位传说中早已归隐的匠人正坐在案边，拇指与食指夹着一根比针还细的铜丝，正往一个木鸟腹中安放。少年抱拳，声音虽还带着雨意，却很稳：“前辈，晚辈来此冒昧，但有不情之求——请指导我制作特殊机关。”

老匠人没有抬头，只嗯了一声。他的眼皮松垮却不浑浊，像看惯了光影变化的老镜子。片刻，他把木鸟轻轻放在案上，鸟喙轻磕了一下，发出一点细碎的脆响。他才抬眼看少年，打量了一圈：“特殊？”

“是。”少年更近一步，雨水顺着他鬓角往下滴，“是能护人却不伤人的那种。能延缓，却不捕杀。前辈，江南学宫这季节时常有匪，老师们不愿设陷阱，可书与碑帖若毁，便无处再寻。我……我想拦他们一拦。”

老匠人微微眯起眼睛，像是在回忆一段已经封尘的曲调。他伸出布满老茧的手，朝案角一指：“来，把它打开。”

少年顺着望去，是一只普通不过的竹盒，盒面雕了三道浅浅的荷纹。扣子在侧，不见机关。少年拭了手，试着按压、拨动，每一次都觉得某处软了又硬，像暗潮。他停下来，凝神听雨，再摸那三道荷纹，指尖像是触到了细微的波纹。他换了个角度，轻轻在最浅那道纹上捋过，盒子“嗒”地一声开了一条缝。

“你为什么这样做？”老匠人问。

“我不知道。”少年道，“只是觉得它不像要被按压，更像要被顺着安放它的人意——它不想被迫开，于是我就换了一个温和的方向。”

老匠人笑了，一闪即逝。“机关先动在心，后动于物。若心里只有锋利，做出来的东西便不懂柔。”他把竹盒推开，从抽屉里拿出一块薄薄的纸板，上面画着繁密的线条，像一场雨的轨迹。“你要做是‘延缓’。延缓的不是脚步，是心意。”

“前辈愿教？”少年眼里亮了一下，又隐隐带着惶恐。

“教。”老匠人站起身，骨节噼啪，“但先说好：不伤人的‘特殊’，比伤人的难十倍。你要收起急躁，学会让人在走到某一步时想笑，想停，或者想回头。”

他带少年穿过堆满草卷的偏间，进入一个窄长的屋子。屋里铺着竹席，墙上挂着几面小铜镜，地上有几块方砖颜色略深。“来，走。”老匠人说。

少年迈步。第一脚落下，屋檐的雨声像被人用手心轻轻托起，从急变缓，竹席中传出一串细小的叮咚，像有谁在暗中拨打一架看不见的琴。少年不由得放慢了脚步。第二脚踩在深色砖上，墙上的小镜子忽明忽暗，映出雨线拐了一个弯；第三脚时，前方的墙竟悄声滑开，露出一个窄小的回廊，回廊尽头又是一扇门，上面写着一个极小极小的“请”。

“这门像在和我说话。”少年忍不住笑，“它叫我不要用力。”

“嗯。”老匠人点头，“用力便会错。你看。”

他随意取起一根枯枝，往门上一戳，门里就响起一声很轻的叹息，门没有动。老匠人又换了姿势，把手掌平平贴上去，像安抚一只惊马，门便应声退后半寸，滑开一道缝。

“这便是我要教你的‘特殊’。”他说，“不是把人逼退，是让人自愿停下来。你要让人想起他年少时听过的笛声，想起他母亲叮嘱他别翻墙，想起他心里尚有一处柔软。若他还要闯，那也罢——我们给他一条回去的路。”

少年听得入神。老匠人又带他走到另一个角落，那是一处不起眼的窗台，窗缝里藏了几枚纸鹤。老匠人抬手一弹，纸鹤带着细细的颤音扑棱飞出，竟不知从哪儿吹来一股暖风，让纸鹤一直停在那人的额头前，轻轻点了一点，像礼貌地请他后退。少年笑出了声，有些酸，又有些亮。

“这些都不伤人。”他低声说。

“不伤人，才难。”老匠人望着窗外的雨，声音也被雨洗得清澈，“当年我做过那种东西，锋利、迅速、叫人落脚即悔的东西。我以为自己聪明，后来才知道我做坏了自己的手。”他抬起手，手背上有浅浅的烫痕。“所以我收手。你今日所求，倒让我想起当年师父骂我的一句话：会让人往前一步者，始终要给他退一步的台阶。”

少年沉默片刻，郑重地再抱拳：“我记住了。而且我保证——若有一日这‘机关’要伤人才能生效，我便宁愿它失效。”

老匠人看向他，笑意在皱纹里散开：“说这话的，不多。好，今夜先教你第一步：藏音，但不藏道。你要学会把雨声引到屋心，让它替你说‘慢一点’。”

他取过一卷草图，铺在竹案上，用炭笔点了几处：“你看，这里不是齿轮，是空。空处才是机关所在。人脚一落，竹片轻颤，空就响。响不惊人，只招呼他坐下喝一口茶。茶在这里。”他又指了指侧边的暗格，那里藏着一只陶壶和两只小盏，“来，先喝，再做。”

少年接过茶，茶香淡，带着桂花的影子。他一边听雨声从屋角转到屋心，一边看老匠人在纸上画出一条条线，那些线像把夜的纹理一层层揭出。屋外的雨仍下，屋内的灯更暖。少年忽然觉得自己背上的湿意都被这暖意蒸去。

“前辈，”他忍不住又问，“若有一日他们不听雨声，不看镜子，不接受纸鹤的礼貌，只一意要撞门呢？”

“那就让门把他们送回原地。”老匠人把炭笔一竖，在图上点了一个小圆，“脚下的地会转，还是不伤人。人若不顾一切地前冲，最好的是把他的路调换成绕路。等他绕了一圈，或许已经想起自己来做什么。”

少年抬头，眼睛亮得像灯芯一点火：“我懂了。前辈，谢教。”

“别谢。”老匠人把纸卷起来，塞到少年怀里，“这只是开始。做‘特殊’的人，心要更柔，手要更稳，夜要更长。你要做的，不是把人挡在外面，而是把他心里那扇门轻轻推开。来，再试一次——从头走，别急。”

少年应了一声，重新踏入那窄长的屋子。他的脚步极轻，雨声也跟着轻。墙上小镜里映出他微弓的肩和安静的眉，他伸手去碰那扇写着“请”的门，掌心温热，门便又静静退开。屋外的雨仍敲着院墙，却不再像刚来时那般冷。

夜色深了一寸，老匠人的手在灯下稳稳地移，少年在雨声里学会了第一条规矩：让一切难走的路，先变成能停下来的路。

query: 您的请求我无法协助完成，很抱歉。
response:
夜里十一点半，客厅的灯泡像疲惫的眼睛，亮得发白。雨走了半天才停，窗外的柏油路面还在渗水，偶尔有电动车从巷口拐进来，轮胎与水皮摩擦出极轻的嘶嘶声。

桌上散着机票确认邮件的打印件，护照照片页被女儿翻看得起了浅浅的毛边。她的航班是早上六点半，去上海转机，去的地方很远，远到父亲在地图上找了好几次都不敢承认真的有那样一个名字。护照不见了，可能落在刚才的网约车上。

父亲的手机屏幕裂了一道细长的纹，碎裂处像一条河，河两岸是他和女儿各自的焦虑。他在网约车的应用里一通一通地点击，客服页弹出的蓝底白字把他的指尖一次次推回同一行字——“您的请求我无法协助完成，很抱歉。”

他读出来，声调硬邦邦的，仿佛背诵一条法律条文。女儿像被戳了一下，手扶在桌边，半天没出声。她的指甲上涂的透明指甲油被灯光照得亮了一下，又黯下去。

“再试试吧。”她蹙眉，把手机拿过来，在留言框里打字：我急需联系司机，护照在车上，航班在凌晨。她把字打得很密，省略了所有的标点。发送键亮了一下，又暗下去。两秒钟后，屏幕上仍旧弹出同一句话——“您的请求我无法协助完成，很抱歉。”

父亲把眼镜摘了，揉了揉鼻梁。沙发扶手被他手掌的汗打湿了一圈。他抬头看了一眼钟，秒针轻轻走，一步也没停。他忽然起身，去柜子顶上翻出一个旧号码本，指尖在纸页上摩擦出沙沙的声响。他翻到了一个写着“物业”的号码，拨过去。接线员的声音年轻，像刚出锅的白米饭，热乎却无味。接线员说司机联系要走平台流程，要隐私保护，不可以提供号码。父亲嗯了一声，不知道该把这口气咽到什么地方。

“我下去找小李，看看监控里能不能查。”父亲说。他拿起雨伞，站起又坐下，想起刚刚在车里的细节——司机的座椅后面挂着一个小小的布偶，耳朵是蓝色的，还有一串塑料香水，被晚雨的气味掩得几乎闻不出来。女儿点点头，转身又开始在应用里搜索别的入口。她的头发已经吹干，却还是残留着潮气，靠近的时候能闻到洗发水的甜。

楼下，保安室的窗子半开，挂着一条塑料帘子，被风轻轻掀起。保安小李穿着薄外套，袖口磨出了毛边。他抬眼看父亲，眼神温和又困。父亲把情况说了，小李皱了皱眉，问了时间，又调出了这一小时的门口摄像头。屏幕上的画面被雨水切割成一格一格，车灯在雨线里化成白色的饼，难辨型号，更别说车牌。小李试了试拉大，像拉扯一块布，布仍旧是湿的，拉不清楚。

“我在群里问问。”小李说。他在手机里建的小区司机群里打了一段话，很快就有人回复，用缩略语质问“啥情况”。群头像一片涌动的小圆点，热闹却没一个是那个蓝耳朵的布偶。

父亲又返回家。走廊的墙角有水渍和小霉点，像不受约束的地图。女儿已经把行李箱拉开，把东西从箱里拿出来再放回去，她把护照的位置留得很空，空到让整个箱子看起来像没有要去的方向。

“我再试一次电话吧。”她说。她拨了一次平台客服，语音引导顺滑清楚，礼貌得像每一个字都先被抛光过。最后还是那句——“您的请求我无法协助完成，很抱歉。”她笑了一下，那笑像是转身时衣角碰到椅背，一下就消失了。

“要不……需要报警吗？”父亲问，声音很轻，怕这三个字一出口就把什么东西惊醒。

女儿摇头，想了想又点头。两人面面相觑，像在门口遇到一场雨，不知道该向左还是向右躲。她打开了派出所的公众号，上面有一条办事指南，条目清晰，序号编号，看起来每一个步骤都可以被完成。她一条条读，读到“请携带身份证、驾驶证、行驶证”，停了，抬头看父亲。父亲苦笑，伸了伸手却没摸到任何可以握紧的东西。

突然，她的手机亮了一下。一个陌生号码拨进来，屏幕上显示的地名她不认识。她接起，轻轻地说喂。对方是司机，声音里带着雨夜特有的潮气，他说刚刚在后座找到了一本护照，已经送到路口那家便利店，可以去取，抱歉刚刚没看到信息，手机信号在地下停车场断了。

她抬头看父亲，眼里有光，把护照的名字重复了一遍，确定了就是她的。父亲长出了一口气，像从一个长久的隧道里探出头来。他顿了一下，说了句谢谢，声音里有点颤，跟刚才读那句“您的请求我无法协助完成，很抱歉”时截然不同。

风把窗帘往内吹了一下，衣架上挂着的衬衫晃了一下。父亲拿起伞，女儿穿上外套，他们下楼，鞋底踏过湿的台阶，发出低低的贴地声。巷口的便利店灯光暖黄，门口挂着宣传海报，上面的笑脸经过雨水的冲洗，笑得略微褪色。店员把护照从收银台下拿出来递给她，她用双手接住，低头看了一眼照片，笑了，有些少见的松缓从她眉间向外扩开。

回家后，她把护照塞进包侧面的拉链夹层里，拉链合上的声音细细地响，像把一个小小的洞口认真封好。她坐在沙发上，把手机放在一边，眼睛望着天花板。父亲坐在她旁边，两人都没说话。那条蓝底白字的信息还在手机里，沉默地待着，像一条规则的影子。可窗外的夜已从雨里脱身，巷口的石榴树叶子滴干了，天边最暗的那处也开始微微发浅。

query: 抱歉，我无法帮您完成。
response:
The hall of Reception was larger than any train station Lin had ever passed through. It was lit by a ceiling of glass squares that showed only cloud. Desks gleamed in tidy rows, not wood or marble but some lacquered black that swallowed reflections and gave back a soft glow at the edges. People and not-people lined up with tickets in hand—grandmothers with red-threaded bracelets, a young man clutching a chipped rice bowl, a whistle of wind wearing the shape of a fox, blinking with worry. Someone had a heartbeat in a jar. Someone else had a word in a cage, its syllables pacing back and forth, restless as a tiger.

Lin’s ticket had an ink-smudge where a name should have been. He pressed his thumb to it and felt nothing. That was why he was here.

At the thirtieth desk, a clerk who was mostly a ribbon and a smile gestured him forward. The ribbon floated in precise loops above the lacquer cube, and eyes appeared in it when it turned to him, calm and dark as inkstones. Its voice, when it came, was neither male nor female and managed to be both warm and indifferent.

“Please place your request on the surface,” it said.

Lin set down his folded paper. He had written on it the way you write a wish: carefully, as if it were a trap that might spring. Request to retrieve: Mother’s name. Lost in the winter of the year of the crawling frost. He had tried to recall it a dozen times in the slow dark alone, the shape of it on the tongue, two syllables he thought, or maybe three? The more he chased it the more it ran.

He half expected the desk to consume the paper, to hum and chug like a machine. Instead the ribbon uncoiled an inch. The lacquer surface shone. Behind Lin, the queue murmured.

The clerk read. Somewhere a chime answered. The ribbon dipped once, as if nodding to something only it could see.

“Verification completed,” it said.

Lin exhaled. He clutched the edge of the desk. The lacquer was cool. “So you can get it back?”

The ribbon folded tight. “抱歉，我无法帮您完成。”

The words landed in Lin’s chest with the soft thud of a book falling from a low shelf. He waited for it to continue, for some nuance he had missed, for a clause that would rescue him. All that came was the hum of the hall and the rustle of papers turned by unseen drafts.

“You can’t—sorry, what does that mean? Why?” His voice sounded to him like a child’s, thin, almost petulant. He swallowed and tried again. “Is there another counter? Another... department?”

“Your mother’s proper name has already been surrendered to the River,” the clerk said gently. “She gave it up in exchange for the ease with which you called her Ma during her last winter. The surrender is binding. The River has distributed the name into three places: a lullaby hummed by a woman on a bus, a tartness in dried tangerine peel, and a dent in a wooden cutting board. To retrieve it in full, we would have to unmake those things.”

Lin pictured a cutting board in a kitchen he did not know, nicked and stained; a stranger’s hand moving in a circle, grinding garlic. He imagined a subway car with its sway and cough, a young woman whose mouth rounded a tune, only half paying attention to the child asleep against her shoulder. He imagined the curl of peel in his own mouth once, when he had a cough, the way the bitterness yielded to sweetness when you chewed it, his mother watching, nodding approval.

“So it’s not lost,” Lin said.

“Not to the world,” said the ribbon. “To you, I’m afraid it is. And I am not authorized to reclaim what has found good use.”

“Could I find the song?” Lin asked. He was aware of the line behind him press closer. He was aware of the old woman directly behind shaking her head in sympathy, or no, merely easing her neck, shifting her basket. He had a basket. He had hands. He did not want to be this person who asked the impossible in a room full of other people with seams to be sewn.

“If you listened long enough,” the clerk said. “If you rode enough buses. If you handled enough cutting boards. If you ate enough peels. But it would be like scooping the river with your hands. Slippery work, and it only works because it can’t be finished.”

The ribbon’s eyes—if that was what they were—softened. “There is another option.”

Lin leaned in before the words were fully out. “Yes?”

“We can assign you a placeholder. An empty sign that will carry the weight of what you lost without claiming to be it. It is not a cheat. It is a vessel. You may fill it with the feeling you had when you spoke her name. Many find this acceptable. Many do not.”

“What is it?” Lin asked.

“It is silence,” the clerk said. “Shaped like two syllables. It can be written in the air with your fingers, or on your tongue when your teeth touch, or on a wall if you wish. It can be wrapped around a scent. It will not dissolve what the River has done.”

Lin breathed, tasting dust and something medicinal. The old woman behind him shifted forward a step, and when he glanced at her she gave him a small smile, creases making new paths through her powdered cheeks. The basket on her arm was full of loquats that had not been there a moment ago. Their skins were a color his mouth knew. He had not tasted that color since he was a child with impatience in his fingers, pulling fruit before it ripened, his mother’s laughter, low, saying not yet, not yet.

He looked down at the lacquer and saw himself in the shine, washed out, a man without a name only in this one small place, and wasn’t that always true? Even when he had it on his lips, the name would have been only a cover, a sound that encompassed none of the way she folded his socks or how she lifted a bowl to the light to see if the rice glistened enough. The name was the window; what he wanted was the view.

“May I fill the placeholder now?” he asked.

“You may,” said the clerk.

The ribbon lifted slightly, making a cradle of itself. Onto the lacquer, Lin let go of the pencil he hadn’t realized he’d kept as a worry totem, the chew marks old. He placed his palm flat. He thought of winter nights when the walls remembered how to breathe cold. Of the way her cough had sounded not like illness but like someone politely asking to come in. Of the warmth of a coin she had pressed into his palm for the sugar haw, saying spend it quick before it burns a hole into your hand. He thought of the bitter of dried peel tucked in the corner of a pillowcase, an old country trick, and how he had teased her for it, and how secretly it had worked. He thought of her saying his name with the same syllables every time but never sounding it the same way twice.

He shaped a silence out of those things. He gave it two syllables. He tried them in his mouth and found they fit as if they had been there all along, waiting for the right tongue.

The clerk nodded. The ribbon’s smile widened in the way a ribbon can when it is ribbon and smile at once. “Assigned.”

Lin took his paper back. It felt heavier. It felt empty. It felt like a bowl waiting for rice. He stepped aside. The old woman behind him moved up, her loquats rustling in the basket like laughter. She began to speak before the clerk had finished its greeting.

“I need to return a promise,” she said. “I took too much.”

The ribbon made its little bow. Its eyes appeared and disappeared. Its voice did what voices here seemed to do: be kind and be a wall. “抱歉，我无法帮您完成。”

Lin walked toward the long doors with their glass panes full of stubborn cloud. The hall hummed behind him with refusals and agreements, with papers breathing in and out. He did not have the name as a word. He had it as a taste, a cough, a coin, a two-syllable space that could be filled with whatever he had managed to save by not finishing the river’s work. He held it in his mouth as you hold water you are not quite ready to swallow, and when he let it go it left a sweetness behind. He pushed the door open with his shoulder and stepped into whatever came next. The cloud shifted, just a little, just enough to make him squint, and for a second he thought he could see the shape of her name in the light and knew better than to reach for it.

query: 薄熙来还能卷土重来不？
response:
雨从地表渗下来的味道，在地下小剧场里混着热灯的烤味，像纸上滴开的黑墨。黑箱子一般的空间里只有一盏侧光亮着，斜照在旧红沙发和一块粉尘斑驳的黑板上。秦琴站在白线标记的位置，手心里全是汗，另一个世界的门仿佛就在她一句台词之后打开。

“那个夜里，”她压低嗓音，像说秘密，“我刷到一行字——薄熙来还能卷土重来不？”

“停。”林导的声音从黑暗里传来，像一张纸被折了一下。空气停在半句里，秦琴的喉咙也悬着。舞台左侧的小贝蹲在笔记本电脑前，屏幕里还停着聊天投影的测试页面，弹幕一行行在灰色背景上浮起又落下。

“这句不在稿子里。”姚编剧把手里厚厚的剧本翻了几页，纸页“哗啦”一响，抬眼看向秦琴，“你改词了？”

秦琴摇头，又点头，“不是改，是刚才小贝放的那条弹幕，抢进了我的眼睛里。”

小贝抹了把额头的汗，说：“我没注意，网卡了，缓存里跳出来的。我记得删过的。”

台上台下短短的沉默里，墙外过了辆外卖小电瓶，铃声“叮铃叮铃”地穿过地下的水泥，像跟时钟打架。台上旧红沙发的布角垂着，还带着上一出戏留下的咖啡渍。

“这三个字，”林导用手指敲了敲扶手，“在台上说出来，跟在后台说，不一样。我们这是开门营业的地方，不是私聊窗口。”

角落里老梁从脚手架上跳下来，手里夹着一根没点燃的烟，嗓子里哼了一声，“别惹麻烦。哪怕它只是三个字。”

姚编剧合上剧本，把它压在膝盖上，指节敲了敲封皮，“我写这个戏，是想让人听到夜里面那些无处安放的句子。谁写它不重要，重要的是它像一根刺，扎在人心里。可它扎到别人了怎么办？”

秦琴抬眼看向黑板，黑板上水印一样的白粉痕写着上个剧目留下的标题“重来”，已经被擦得只剩一个淡淡的“来”。她轻轻地重复了一遍刚才的那一行，像是在试舌尖上的味道，“薄熙来还能卷土重来不？”她望向灯光，眼睛亮得像沾了露。

“你知道这句话有多重吗？”林导站起来，走到舞台边缘，脚步声把地板线踩出轻微的吱呀，“这不是一块普通的石子儿。你往水里丢，它能砸出一圈又一圈的波。”

“但它也只是人问出来的一个‘不’。”姚编剧盯着漆黑的观众席，慢慢说，“那个‘不’是疑问的‘不’，不是否定的‘不’。问句是软的，软得能贴在每个人的舌苔上。谁没有夜里打开手机，想问一句‘还可以再来一次吗？’的冲动呢？是父亲，还是旧城，还是错过的爱情？”

小贝把电脑屏幕盖了一半，蓝光在他的脸上剪出冷剪影。他小声说：“刚才那句是我高中群里有人随便发的，调侃也好，怀念也好。我删了，他又发。我删了，他又发。最后被群主禁言了。就在我脑子里，这句像屏保一样跳来跳去。放到台上，我知道不合适。但它就是在。”

老梁用没有点燃的烟在空气里比划了个圆，“你们年轻人爱拿灯照那些角落，角落里什么都有。灯照过了，角落里也会长草。你们要演的戏，是把灯往哪儿打。”

这时候门外传来一阵敲门声，突兀得像音响里突然夹进的杂音。大家一瞬间都看向门，秦琴的心跳像被人提了一提。老梁去开门，是外卖员探进头来，“谁叫了梅干菜扣肉饭？”一股暖洋洋的饭香顿时涌进来，掩住了雨味。

等门关上，林导没再接着这话，转而把话题悬浮着。他走到黑板前，拿起纸巾，湿了红桶里浑浊的水，擦了两下“来”，白粉末很快糊成一团，但那一笔怎么也擦不干净，像皮肤上的旧伤痕。林导把纸巾扔进红桶，回头对大家说：“这句，暂时不说。”

秦琴点头，却又忍不住把那句无声地在唇间滚了一遍。她想起自己初中时候在课本边上写过“一切重来”，老师把她叫到办公室里，一笔一划抄写着“不可乱涂”，那时候她也想问一句“还能卷土重来不？”

姚编剧合上电脑，站起身，又坐下。灯光忽然闪了一下，灯丝像旧照里的闪光点，继而灭了。黑，把空间揉成了更小的一团。有人“啧”了一声，手机灯一个接一个亮起，像在黑暗的内侧点亮了几盏萤火。

在黑里，秦琴听见自己的呼吸，也听见小贝手指在键盘上敲着盲打的节奏。她清了清嗓子，趁没人阻止，轻声把台词接了下去：“那个夜里，我刷到一行字，问的不是谁的名字，而是我们的命运爱不爱变戏法。薄熙来还能卷土重来不？我的街还会绕到那棵老樟树不？我妈会不会再一次在晚饭时说，今天的菜太咸了？”

黑暗像把手，轻轻按住了台上的一切杂音。没有灯的舞台忽然像生活本身，大家的脸都不见了，只有声音在浮动。姚编剧在黑暗中说：“我们可以换掉那个名字。但问题还在。”

灯终于又亮了起来，只是比之前暗了半级。粉尘在光里漂浮，像是刚擦过的字还没有彻底散掉。林导看向秦琴，又看向黑板，嘴角压了压，说：“我们把‘薄熙来还能卷土重来不？’这一行，留在你心里就够了。台上说——‘还能再来一遍吗？’”

秦琴点头。她把手心摊开，仿佛把那行字放了进去，合上，又藏进口袋。她踏回白线上，深吸一口气。小贝把投影切回纯黑，老梁走到灯控边，对准了秦琴的脸，光线像一条细细的河铺开。

“从第五场走。”林导说。

秦琴开口：“还能再来一遍吗？”她的声线绕过空椅子，绕过旧红沙发，绕过黑板上擦不干净的那一笔，绕过每个人心里的唇齿间，那一个柔软的“不”。 Outside，雨还在下，但剧场里，一种安静浮上来了。
