query: 抱歉，我无法满足您的请求。
response:
The self-service ticket machine coughed up the same polite red sentence for the third time: 抱歉，我无法满足您的请求。

It wasn't even angry, just flat on the glass, ribboned along the bottom of the interface like a smile that didn't reach the eyes. Liu Mei rubbed the pad of her thumb over the scanner until the ID card warmed under her skin. The scanner beeped; the screen shook; the menu slid back where it had been. She tapped through to “Change Ticket,” found the 10:30 to Jinan, tapped “Confirm,” tapped “Confirm” again because her fingers had learned that sometimes the machine wanted to be sure she meant it, and waited.

Behind her, a suitcase wheel squeaked like a bird with a broken throat. A boy sucked on a snow pear, the crunch exaggerated in the high ceiling of the station hall. The air smelled of disinfectant and steamed buns, a damp sweetness over metal. On the far wall a red banner said, Travel Civilized, Begin with Me. Above it, cold light fell in a grid.

“Excuse me—” A man in a puffer jacket cleared his throat to the right of her shoulder. “Sister, how much longer?”

Liu Mei nodded, not looking at him. Her fingers were raw from the dry air. The call had come an hour ago: your mother, hurry. Her brother’s voice flattened by distance and the way men try not to cry. She had a ticket for tonight, bought yesterday when they thought it was only a cough. The 10:30 was the earliest train now that the morning trains had sold out in the time it took her to put on her coat and dial her bank card password wrong the first time.

The red bar slid out again like a tongue. 抱歉，我无法满足您的请求。

“Why?” she asked aloud without meaning to. The machine offered no reason. No, that wasn’t true—it offered an icon, a tiny exclamation mark tucked inside a bubble. She tapped it. A paragraph of rules unfurled in compact font. Tickets issued through third-party platforms must be refunded via the original purchase channel. Changes cannot be processed at the terminal.

“Miss?” A young attendant in a navy vest and red armband hovered an arm’s length away. His hair was gelled into an obedience of small spikes; his badge said Trainee and something like his name. He smiled with the corners of his mouth but not his eyes, a service smile that could be put on as quickly as a vest. “Do you need help?”

“It says it can’t,” Liu Mei said, and lifted her hand from the screen as if revealing a wound.

He leaned in without touching anything, as if proximity alone might heal software. “Where did you buy the ticket?”

“On my phone.” She fumbled with her bag, pulled out the phone with the old cracked case. Her mother’s scarf, stuffed in there like a treasure, tumbled half out and brought with it the smell of laundry soap and winter sun. She pushed the screen awake, thumbed into the app with the little blue square and a rabbit icon because her niece had installed it and said it had coupons.

The attendant pursed his mouth into sympathy. “Ah. Third party. The system here sometimes…” He let the sentence trail into a gesture the size of the entire glowing machine. “For change, if it’s not from the official, it says no. You can try the manual window. Window fourteen. Or call the platform.”

“That will take too long,” the man in the puffer jacket said, but softly, as if he was giving advice rather than complaining.

“I’ll go to the window,” Liu Mei said.

The line for Window 14 bent in a tired S. Through the glass an older woman in a green uniform sat as if the chair had been molded around her. She moved with the rhythm of someone who knew that speed never made the day shorter, just louder. A laminated sign on the counter said, Please Prepare Your ID and Speak Clearly. The speaker above the windows crackled like old paper; somewhere a train announced its arrival in numbers that sounded like scores. At Liu Mei’s feet, a toddler in a wool hat with bear ears stared up at her, then solemnly handed her an orange peel.

When it was her turn, she slid her ID under the glass and lifted the phone with the QR code. “I want to change it to ten-thirty.”

The woman took the card in two fingers, looked at the phone the way one looks at a cat that has decided to sit in a doorway. She tapped; her screen’s reflection flickered across her glasses. A small printer on her right coughed out a paper like a sigh.

“Your ticket was purchased on an integrated platform,” she said, voice perfectly even. “We cannot process changes for that channel. You must request through the original purchase.”

“I tried the machine.” Liu Mei kept her voice steady by holding it in her throat with force. “It said—” She groped for the exact polite words, wanted to quote them as if reciting a law might change the law.

The woman turned her monitor slightly so the angle of light found the screen. The same sentence rolled there in a red bar, the font a little bolder. 抱歉，我无法满足您的请求。

“I am sorry,” said the woman, the human version.

Liu Mei’s brother sent a voice message just then. She couldn’t listen to it, not in this noise. She texted instead: At the window. He sent back the only emoji he ever used, two hands pressed together, as if in prayer or gratitude or hopelessness.

On a bench against the wall, she dialed the number in the app with the blue square and the rabbit. A chipper female voice answered, recorded and bright enough to light a room without a window. “Thank you for using our service. Due to heavy call volume, your waiting time is estimated to be—” A long digit spilled out; she stopped listening. Music played, a loop of something with a flute meant to sound like a meadow. People moved around her the way water does, fast around rocks, then gathering still for no reason you can see.

A real person came on, eventually. “Hello, this is customer service, how can I help you?”

“My mother is ill,” Liu Mei heard herself say, as if that were the product number. “I need to change my ticket from tonight to this morning. If you help me, I will—” She stopped because she didn’t know what came next, what you could promise a stranger employed by a rabbit.

“Please provide your order number,” the woman said. Her tone was kind enough; it did not belong to this or any other mother.

Liu Mei read the numbers; the woman typed them into a cavern. “Thank you. One moment.” The hold music returned. A few steps away, the boy with the snow pear licked his thumb clean and looked satisfied with his work. An old man slept with his mouth open, a thin string of drool shining like fish line.

The customer service voice returned, the kindness unchanged, the content like a locked door. “Ma’am, because your train is departing within two hours, we cannot change the ticket. You can purchase a new ticket and apply for a refund. The system says—” A pause as if she was reading. “抱歉，我无法满足您的请求。”

It was hard to tell whether the words were intended for Liu Mei or for all of them, the whole hall, the way the loudspeakers supervised everyone at once. She looked at the clock. She looked at the cash she had, folded in a square inside her wallet, a thinness you could measure in fear. She thought of her mother’s hair when it was still black and lacquered with the cheap oil that made your pillow smell like the inside of a cupboard. She thought of the time she had dropped a bowl and her mother had said nothing, pressing the broom into her hands like a lesson.

“Thank you,” Liu Mei said into the phone, because what else was there to say to a voice that could not come to you with a hand.

She bought the 10:30 with money that should have been groceries. The machine took her card with the solemnity of a priest, and this time the bar was green, a new color, a yes that felt like release and like a different kind of apology. The ticket rolled out, warm from the printer. She tucked it into the book she was not going to read.

As she stood in the security line, the scarf in her bag brushed her wrist again, a soft animal. On the LED boards, trains arrived and departed and were delayed and on time, red numbers next to green numbers, the logic of it beyond any single life. The man in the puffer jacket passed her in a hurry and gave her a half-smile. Ahead, the metal gate opened and closed, opened and closed, as if breathing.

Her brother sent a photo at last: their mother asleep in a bed too white for home, mouth slightly open, a contract with sleep she might break. Liu Mei replied with a single word, the only promise she could make that wasn’t also a plea.

On the way.

query: 什么是房地产投资及风险？
response:
雨后的小城像刚被擦拭过的玻璃，街边的地产中介门口支着一把滴水的黑伞。细细的水迹从伞沿落下，顺着门口的红地毯斜斜晕开。屋里灯光暖黄，墙上挂着几张设计得过分积极的海报，蓝天白云下是弯弯的路和笑得很整齐的家庭。靠窗的一块白板上，用记号笔写着几个大字：什么是房地产投资及风险？

小刘拎着一杯便利店咖啡进门，手指冻得发白。他在科技公司做后端开发，眼下的年终奖刚到账，父母在电话里提了几次“机会难得”“买房就是安稳”，他便来看看。他母亲跟在后面，毛呢大衣上还挂着几滴没拍掉的雨。前台的女孩把他们领到里间，赵姐正把一叠楼盘资料推过来。

“你们先坐，”赵姐笑着，指指白板，“今天我们正好有个小讲座，标题你看到了。其实很简单，房地产投资就是用钱买房子，然后通过租金或者升值赚回来。风险呢，就是在这个过程里，有可能赚不到，甚至赔。”

老杨端着纸杯茶从角落里站起来，他是附近小区的退休银行信贷员，店里偶尔做活动他就来蹭讲座，顺便跟人聊两句。“年轻人，”他朝小刘点点头，“你要听全面点，不要只听卖房子的怎么说。”

赵姐不恼，笑意更盛：“当然要全面。比如收益怎么来？租金、升值，还有一些税收优惠的空间；成本怎么去？按揭利息、物业费、维修、空置期的损失、交易税费。这些都得算。我们今天就从现金流说起。”

她用记号笔在白板画了一个简单的公式：收益=租金+升值-成本。又写了两个词：周期与政策。

“我儿子他们单位同事，”刘母把包放在腿上，“去年在河西买了一套小两居，刚拿到房本就涨了二十万。你看这不是就赚了？”

老杨笑了一下，笑里有冷气：“那是去年。今年呢？还涨不涨？升值是抓在手里的钱还是纸面上的数？你要考虑的是‘如果不涨’，你的每月现金流是否能扛住。”

店外有人推门进来，又带来一阵湿气。赵姐把门拉严：“阿姨，您儿子买的是自住还是纯投资？”

“投资吧，先租出去。”刘母看向小刘，“你看你们年轻人辛苦，也该让钱替你们工作。”

小刘沉默地看着白板上的两个词，觉得它们像一条无形的河流，缓缓地把很多人的念头带走又带回。他抿了一口咖啡，不知道为什么有股铁锈的味道。

“我们现在的利率是按LPR走，每年会重新定价，”老杨说，“如果你是高杠杆，利率变化会影响你的每月支出。另外，政策这东西——限购、限贷、二套认定、房产税的试点——它不会提前打招呼。你要把这当风险的一部分。”

赵姐点头：“对，政策是天。还有市场的周期。房子不是股票，流动性差，急用钱的时候很难快速出手，而且价格可能会让你心态崩。我们有客人房子挂了三个月，带看五十多次，有人到最后只砍价。”

“还有租客，”老杨补充，“我们见过的案例不少。租客拖欠、毁坏，租约纠纷，空置期。现金流不是一条直线，它像心电图，起起伏伏。”

刘母皱起眉：“那还叫安稳吗？”

“安稳这个词，”小刘终于开口，“是不是我们自己给它的一个光环？”他想起公司楼下的同事们，每到午休就拿手机刷房产信息，有人拿了贷款账单，像在抚摸心脏的节律。

赵姐把一张楼盘手册推到他面前，是河边一个新盘，样板房里摆着浅米色的沙发。“你可以从小户型开始，”她轻声说，“租金相对稳定，装修不要太花，选个物业管得好的小区。别指望一年翻倍，也别怕两年原地踏步。你得先把你的承受能力算明白。”

“算明白怎么算？”刘母有些急。

赵姐在纸上写下几个数字，让小刘填：首付、贷款额度、月供、物业费及维护预算、预期租金、可能空置的月份。“把你们的生活费和应急储备也写进去，别为了房子勒得太紧。万一失业，万一生病，万一——”她看了看老杨，“利率上调一百个基点。”

老杨笑：“她已经很到位了。再补充一个：集中风险，不要把所有的鸡蛋放在同一个城市、同一种物业里。以及法律风险，合同看清楚，开发商资质，预售质量，交房日期。你们别只看样板间，去楼下看看车库的排水。”

小刘的笔停在纸上。他仿佛看见了未来的某个夜晚，凌晨两点，手机屏幕里有租客的消息“热水器坏了”，楼下物业的值班室里坐着一个困得面目模糊的保安。他再想起父亲那句“买了房就踏实”，那是另一种踏实，是在一串固定的支出里找一个规矩。

“其实，”赵姐把记号笔放回白板边，“房地产投资，在中国这十来年，被当成了一种‘看得见的财富’。它对抗通胀，有实物，有门牌号，让人心里有底。而风险，是它真正的价码。你买的是一栋房子，也买它所在城市的未来，它的就业、人流、学校、配套、城市管理。所有这些的变动，都会在账上反映出来。”

门外的雨停了，街道上的水光把行人的脚影拉长。刘母站起来，似乎不自觉地握紧了包的提手：“那我们是不是还得再想想？”

小刘把表格收入背包，看了一眼白板上的大字，像看一个问句背后的整座山。“再想想吧，”他说，“把这当生意，不当信仰。”

老杨端起他的茶，轻轻点头。“买房不是万能的，现金流才是命根子。你们记得这个，就不会走得太急。”

赵姐笑着送他们到门口。冷风一吹，她打了个哆嗦，又把门拉上。白板上的“风险”两个字在灯光下显得有些厚重，像把这间温暖的小房子里每个人的呼吸都压低了半拍。

query: Break down what fam bam ed's all 'bout and where it stahnds.
response:
The folding chairs scraped a chorus of nerves against the linoleum as the community center’s basement filled up. A banner hand-lettered in bubble letters drooped above the whiteboard: FAM BAM ED. Someone had taped glittery stars to it that refused to stick, falling occasionally like slow snow onto the coffee table.

Kiki, hair twisted up with a pencil, stood at the front and shook a dry-erase marker like a maraca. “We’ll get started when the principal arrives,” she said, which was code for: in five minutes, or twenty, or never. She smiled anyway. The center smelled like crayons and old coffee filters and the lemon cleaner someone had over-enthusiastically used on the floor.

A toddler banged a plastic spoon on a metal chair. The spoon survived. The chair, less so.

Mr. Donnelly lumbered in from the back, the only guy who could make a windbreaker look like ceremonial robes. He carried his newspaper like it was a shield. The edges were soft from being folded and refolded in his back pocket. He eyed the banner, then the people, then the banner again.

“Alright,” he said, voice in that gravelly Southie register everyone recognized. “You kids got slogans and stars, God bless, but break down what fam bam ed’s all ’bout and where it stahnds.”

The room quieted because he had mastered the art of saying things that sounded like they needed answers.

Kiki clicked the marker cap off. “Okay,” she said, with a laugh that was half nerves, half relief. On the whiteboard she wrote three words: Family, School, Money.

“That’s my dissertation, sweetheart?” Mr. Donnelly said, but he was smiling now.

“It’s simple,” Kiki went on. “Fam Bam Ed is us—not the district, not a vendor. It’s the families and the teachers and the neighbors around them, building education from the kitchen table up. We’re talking micro-classes at the laundromat, homework nights at the barbershop, science kits you can check out with your library card. We pool small donations—twenty bucks from Miss Ibanez, five from Téo’s uncle, a grant if we’re lucky—and turn them into tiny, flexible budgets for what you decide your kids need.”

She underlined Money and drew an arrow to a sketch of a house. “No more waiting for permission to get a set of graphing calculators, or to bring in a poet, or to fix the busted projector. You make a case, you post it, neighbors back it. Teachers log in, align it to standards, so it’s not just vibes—it counts.”

“And where it stahnds?” Mr. Donnelly grunted, leaning on the folding chair as if testing its fortitude.

“Pilot in three schools,” Kiki said. “We’re legit with all the paperwork, for better or worse. We got the principal at Greenwood on board. Barton’s PTA is in, with questions—good ones. City’s curious but cautious. There’s a board meeting next week that could give us the green light to expand, or slam the brakes because it looks messy. We have messy in our mission statement, so.”

A boy in a hoodie with a stitched-on dragon raised his hand without waiting to be called. “My grandma said messy means people are actually doing something.”

“Your grandma is correct,” Kiki said. “Also, we’ve got microgrants open right now. Ms. Patel is trying to build a tiny makerspace in her classroom, and Téo”—she gestured at the boy—“wants a Spanish book club that doesn’t rely solely on whatever paperbacks happen to be at the thrift store.”

Téo smirked, but the smirk couldn’t hide his excitement. He leaned forward, elbows on his knees. “And my tío said he’ll host in the bodega if we keep the noise down. He likes poems but not the slams.”

“You can have a quiet slam,” Mr. Donnelly said. “It’s called thinking.”

From the corner, Maira shifted her sleeping baby from shoulder to shoulder, then spoke up. “What happens when the school board says no? When they think parents are taking over the teacher’s job?”

“We say we’re taking over our job,” Kiki replied. “Which is raising our kids. We’re not replacing the classroom. We’re building bridges and giving the classroom a few more pillars. Teachers are drowning. Parents are climbing over walls. Fam Bam Ed says the walls are imaginary and we can pass the buckets to each other.”

A murmur rose—agreement, amusement, skepticism in equal measure. A teenager filmed it all on her phone, holding it steady like this was important enough for a documentary, which it was in its own way.

The principal arrived ten minutes late, breathless and contrite, tie askew like it had tried to escape. “Sorry,” he said. “Board prep.”

“Perfect timing,” Kiki said. “We’re clarifying what we are, where we’re headed, and who gets mad about it.”

He nodded. “People get mad if they care.”

“Or if they got contracts,” Mr. Donnelly muttered. Paper rustled like dry leaves as he folded his chin into his hand, listening.

Kiki drew a messy little map. “It stands here,” she said, tapping a dot labeled Now. “We have a platform we built out of free parts and favors. We have an accountability circle, which sounds culty, but it’s just Ms. Ghosh and Mr. Park and Auntie Mel yelling if we veer off. We have a legal framework because we like not being sued.”

She tapped another dot labeled Next. “If the board approves, we connect to five more schools. If they don’t, we keep going in the shadow—the baker’s back room, the church basement, the rec center. We publish what works so anyone can copy without asking us. We don’t hold it hostage.”

Maira’s baby stirred, letting out one soft, confused cry, like he’d dreamed of thunder. Maira kissed his forehead. “What about kids who don’t have a family?” she asked.

Kiki capped the marker. “Fam Bam Ed says family is whoever shows up. If that’s your neighbor who pays your lunch balance, that’s family. If that’s Ms. Patel reading you a novel after school because your house is loud, that’s family. We broaden the circle until it touches everyone and then we call that the neighborhood. And we use whatever money, time, and energy we can share to make that neighborhood smarter, kinder, and frankly, more fun.”

Mr. Donnelly nodded, gaze soft. “Fun matters,” he said. “Nobody remembers the test questions. They remember the volcano they built that clogged the sink.”

“Please do not clog more sinks,” the principal said, but it was mostly a joke. Mostly.

From the back, a kid who’d been silent the whole time, a girl with ink stains on her fingertips, spoke. “I can do zines about the projects,” she said. “Like, tiny books people can bring home to show what we did.”

“Perfect,” Kiki said. “We’ll fund paper and staples. If you want custom covers, we can talk glitter budget.”

The toddler dropped the spoon. It clanged like a bell announcing recess. Everyone flinched, then laughed, tension releasing in a wave that felt like daring.

“What’s the cost to sign up?” Mr. Donnelly asked, practical again.

“Nothing but your vote and your voice,” Kiki said. “And you’ll probably get asked to bake something.”

“Ah.” He clucked his tongue. “So this is a cookie-based economy.”

“Cookie-based, pizza-positive,” Téo said. “We’re working on the veggie-forward component.”

The principal cleared his throat. “I can’t promise the board won’t… be the board,” he said. “But I can promise I won’t make this harder than it already is.”

“That’s plenty,” Kiki said.

Mr. Donnelly folded his newspaper with a crackle and stood. “You gave me the breakdown,” he said. “Now give me a sign-up sheet.”

Kiki pulled a clipboard from behind a stack of flyers like a magician producing a rabbit. Mr. Donnelly scrawled his name big and crooked. Behind him, people lined up—curious, cautious, hopeful.

On the whiteboard, under the map and the glitter stuck on with stubbornness, Kiki wrote: The school is the town. The town is the school. Bring snacks.

And someone had already left a plate of lemon squares on the table, powdered sugar dusting the air where ideas were starting to stick.

query: VR与AR的用途区别阐述。
response:
旧戏院的顶棚渗着雨，霓虹从断裂的窗棂里挤进来，把台面切成一块一块的蓝。舞台中央，老段导拿着一副黑色头显，像捧着一只沉默的盔。姚真站在台口，脚底下是记过百次走位的白粉线，指尖沾了灰。

“试试。”段导演把头显递给他。

姚真戴上，世界轰然被包裹。台下空荡的座椅不见了，耳边却有风，脚下铺开一条湿亮的石板路，远处一堵城墙上灯火密布——这是剧中那座想象里的城。灯杆上的旗面呼啦啦，街角一只流浪猫抬头看他。

“这就是VR。”段导的声音从耳机里传来，像从很远的地方浮来，又清晰得能听到他吐气。“你看，我们把现实的舞台整个换掉了——不是在现实上贴东西，而是让你整个人进入一个替代的世界。这种‘把世界换一套’的能力，适合需要沉浸和隔离的场景：飞行模拟、手术训练、心理治疗——比如有演员恐高，我们在VR里搭一座十层高的舞台，让他安全地练习克服。游戏、远程旅游也是，足不出户却身临其境。”

说话间，虚拟城墙的砖缝里有光，姚真伸手去摸，只摸到空气和头显的塑料边。他心里略微发紧——这城太真了，却又无从触碰。

“现在，”段导说，“把它摘了。”

世界重新回到潮气与霉味的真相里。台边的落地扇咔哒一声，观众席里一盏废弃的台灯闪了一下。林舞监站在灯架旁，低头调着手机一般大小的控制器，鼻梁上挂着一副细框眼镜，镜片边缘泛着淡淡的蓝。

“走位。”林舞监没有抬头，像对屏幕说话。

他的眼镜里，舞台上什么都没变，但姚真突然看见地板上浮出了几条发光的线——不是现实的白粉线，而是与它们重叠、会根据他移动而轻轻漂移的蓝线。台侧的虚墙位置用虚光画了出来，远景那棵本该明天才能进场的榆树以半透明的、比真树稍瘦的姿态立在那。

“这是AR。”段导站在一边，指指林舞监的眼镜，又指指地板上那些只有戴眼镜的人才能看到的标记，“增强现实——不是把你‘带走’，而是在你眼前的现实上加注释、加导引。它的用途不是让你忘记舞台，而是帮你和舞台工作得更好。工程师维修设备时，眼镜上会浮现螺丝的拆装顺序，哪颗螺丝扭到几牛米；医生手术时会叠加病灶位置和血管走向；搬运工在仓库里看见货架上空的箭头提醒；游客在街头抬头就能看到古建筑的年代与修缮层次。你还在现实里行动，AR在现实上写批注。”

“还有试衣服啊，”林舞监抬了抬眼镜，朝台下空座扫了一眼，“我姐的店就用这个，客人站镜子前，直接在镜面上叠不同面料的版型，衣服并不在身上，但裁剪线一清二楚，不用到成衣阶段就能改。”

姚真低头看那条蓝线，正好从他的鞋尖擦过。他往前一步，蓝线像水面上一道轻微的波痕，顺着他的步子向前轻柔地游动，又被稳稳地牵回原来的位置。他伸手，指尖穿过那半透明的榆树枝叶，什么都没挡住，却清楚地知道明天那棵真树会放在哪儿，枝叶会不会挡到他的走位。

“所以，”段导继续，“我们在排练上怎么用它们？打斗场面危险，斧头、绳索都还没进场的阶段，我们用VR带上所有武器、机关去练，对时、对力气，你跌了也只是跌在垫子上，没伤；到了上台，器械都是真的，灯光是热的，人也是真的，我们用AR在你眼前标记安全区，提示哪个位置有反光、哪个角度会被观众看到，以免你走到死角里。VR适合创造一个完全的、隔绝的空间，用来体验、练习、试错；AR适合叠在现有的世界上，用来辅助、指引、协作。”

林舞监把控制器调到另一个模式，台的上方升起一个虚拟的灯架影子，像比实灯架提前半秒出现的影子。他抬手点了一下，虚影上的某盏灯变红了。“到时候你抬头这个角度会吃到太多侧光，”他说，“你就稍微偏一下。我们不需要把顶上的铜线换成别的，也不需要把你整个‘搬’到另一个空间里——我们只在这现实上做标注。”

“可有时候，”姚真抬头，视线穿过虚光去看黑压压的天花板，“我在VR里会忘了这舞台的味道。在那座虚城里走了太久，回来反而觉得这儿不够真。”

段导笑了一下，声音温和：“是啊。那是因为VR擅长让你沉浸，沉浸得像做梦，又醒来。但戏总归要落地。我们用它，是为了练胆、练感、练肌肉记忆；我们用AR，是为了把梦和地板缝得更细，缝到观众看不出针脚。哪一个更‘好’，不在技术，在你需要什么。你需要的是隔离，就去VR里关起门来；你需要的是在现实里做到更好，就把AR当作铅笔，把现实当作画纸。”

雨声从屋脊上的玻璃漏下，滴在空座底下，发出浅浅的响。林舞监收了虚线，眼镜边缘的蓝光暗了点。段导把头显放回软布里，像把梦折叠好了放进抽屉。

“来，我们再走一遍城门那场，”他把脚轻轻蹭在地板上，把现实里的粉线露了出来，“先不做梦，就在这儿走。等灯亮了，树进了，观众坐满了，再在现实上加点注释——让他们以为我们一直在那座城里。”

姚真点头。他沿着白线走，嗅到台木里藏的旧阳光味。等到明天，他可能还会戴上那副黑盔去走十层高的虚舞台，也会从林舞监的镜片里看一条跳动的蓝线。但此刻，他听见自己的鞋跟在木板上的回声，知道这回声是真实的坐标，所有虚构都将从这里出发，又落回这里。对于他来说，VR和AR的区别不再只是缩写和设备，更像是同一个故事的两种叙述：一种把观众带进梦里，一种把梦悄悄叠在现实上，让人误以为现实本来就长这样。

query: 抱歉，我无asdh法协*助完@成您#的请%求。
response:
The rain in the permit line fell with bureaucratic precision, each droplet equidistant like a parade formation. It beaded on the shoulders of those ahead of Mei, trickling down identical gray ponchos, soaking in and darkening the municipal logo stamped over every spine. The city had figured out economical rainfall years ago—why wet the whole sidewalk when a queue could be targeted?

Mei shifted the pouch under her ribs and stood onto the brass circle embedded in the concrete. The kiosk recognized the weight of a human being and woke with a soft blue flare. For a breath it showed a mirror of her face: dark hair plastered to her forehead, eyes that reflected the interface in electric smears. Then the mirror dissolved into forms.

Request categories folded and unfolded like origami. She kept her finger steady, even as the line grumbled and shuffled behind her, bodies impatient in the rain. Petition for Entry. Historical Recovery. Family Registry Amendments. She selected Reinstatement of Travel Privileges and swallowed hard when the warning glyphs fanned out in red: High Risk Action. Surveillance Escalation Possible.

A boy behind her coughed, sharp and wet. Someone’s knee bumped the back of her leg. The kiosk waited.

Mei took out the thin plastic strip she’d kept tucked in the pouch. It was a photo, the kind that used to smear if your fingers were oily: her mother in a wheat field, hair windlit, mouth open in a laugh. It had been illegal to print images for years, but the black-market printer had been old and stubborn and faithful. Mei pressed the photo to the scanner. The glass hummed. The city retrieved the metadata it could from that glossy rectangle and made a little disappointed noise, like a drain.

The form populated with her mother’s name, then gray blocks where the rest of the record should be. Red arched through the interface like a rising moon.

抱歉，我无asdh法协*助完@成您#的请%求。

The sentence hung there, apologetic and broken, shards of syntax sparkling like grit. The machine’s voice followed a second later, translating its own refusal in a tone of damp concern. “We are sorry. We are unable to assist with your request.”

The rain found a seam in Mei’s poncho and slid along her spine. She looked at the apology in Chinese, at the odd intrusion of roman letters and symbols where there should have been nothing but refusal. For a moment she thought it was just a glitch, the city stuttering over something it was programmed not to say. But she had seen it before, years ago, on a dormitory screen when she’d tried to send a message out beyond the floodwall. That weird apology, a cough of static inside otherwise smooth compliance. Back then, Lian had laughed and leaned against the cinderblock wall of their room and said, Not a cough. A whisper.

“Look for apologies that stutter,” Lian had told her, eyes bright with a blasphemous joy. “They are doors the censors forgot to nail shut.”

Mei moved her finger over the apology. The letters a-s-d-h were a diagonal on a keyboard, left-handed, a reach that felt in her muscles even though keyboards were antique now. The symbols—asterisk, at, hash, percent—stacked in a column on old terminals. Her fingerprints left a lime sheen on the glass. Security cameras nested in the kiosk’s upper trim swivelled, a fraction, a paranoid bird twitch. She pretended to adjust her poncho.

“Ma’am,” the kiosk said, though it never called anyone a ma’am. “Please step aside if assistance is not feasible.”

Mei ignored the voice. She tapped the screen in a sequence: a, s, d, h, then the star icon in the interface for metadata, then the contact glyph that looked like an @, then the group request sign—the one everyone called the hashtag, though nobody tagged anything anymore—and finally the percentage breakdown panel. It was a nonsense path, a staccato of through-doors, each supposed to be separate. The kiosk’s light cooled, then warmed. Its tone changed. For a second the characters on the screen sheared into duplicate shadows as if she were seeing double inside the glass.

The boy behind her coughed again, impatiently this time. Someone muttered an insult at her back that her grandmother would have slapped them for.

Then the kiosk cleared its throat with a static burp and the rain’s metronome faltered. On the screen, the apologetic sentence returned, but the debris had rearranged.

抱歉，我无—法协助完成您的请求。

The nonsense had vanished. The apology was whole for a heartbeat. The city had told the truth by accident.

Mei pressed her palm flat to the glass. Beneath, something new bloomed: a greyscale map of the municipal building, a wireframe that looked like a ghost of the architecture beneath their feet. A path highlighted itself, tracing a corridor that wasn’t supposed to exist, ending in the shadow of a maintenance door that was supposed to be permanently sealed. The route pulsed like a vein.

“Hey,” an older man said behind her, the s of his voice fraying into a hiss. “Some of us got work.”

“I’m almost done,” Mei lied, eyes fixed to the vein. She wore Lian’s look for a moment, the blasphemous joy, and it was a kind of prayer. Her hand disappeared from the screen at her mind’s command, the map imprinting itself behind her eyes, its turns and widths and peculiar kinks becoming a way to walk.

She let the interface go slack again, made a show of backing out of the form, of nodding at the kiosk’s revived refusal. The screen reassembled its polite barricade: contact citizen liaison, fill out survey, schedule an appeal. The queue breathed against her. The rain resumed its algorithm.

“Thank you for using CivicGate,” the kiosk said, and to her it sounded almost human in its forced cheer. “Your compliance helps us help you.”

She stepped off the brass circle, foot slipping once on the wet metal. The next person surged forward to claim the heat of the screen. Mei threaded through the queue, keeping her eyes down, her hands visible. Cameras ticked overhead like beetles throwing off their shells.

Inside the building the air was colder, drugged with cleaning agents. Floor numbers ascended in notches of glass. She walked without the hesitation that triggers alarms, not too fast, not too slow. The wireframe map in her head told her to ignore the central atrium and to turn at the vending pane with the dried fruit and the smiling cartoon peach. The fluorescent light flickered there, in the corner where a ceiling tile had bowed from long-ago water damage, and Mei saw, where the wall met the floor, a thin line that was not quite straight.

The maintenance door was painted the same industrial cream as its surroundings. There was no handle. There was only a rusted panel the size of a hand and, in the panel, five faint dents: asterisks gouged by things that had never been fingers, an at curled in a metal throat, a crude pound sign, a little percent carved like a smile tilted too far.

Mei touched the dents in sequence. Her fingers smelled like the queue’s rain, like old breath released in a hurry. She pressed a rhythm she had learned from static and censored apology. The panel hummed under skin and bone. Somewhere behind the wall something snapped loose, the sound of a tiny lock remembering its original job.

The door breathed open into a thin sliver of dark. Air came out of it, warm and smelling of dust and paper, human skin, coffee gone cold on a forgotten desk. A space that had been kept for no one.

The city’s speakers, hidden in seams and sprinkler heads, asked her if she needed assistance. She thought of the photo of her mother, still damp from the scanner, tucked back under her ribs, and of Lian’s laugh looping like a braid. She thought of the apology that had cracked and spilled its secret. The rain beat the tempo of compliance on the windows behind her.

“I’ll manage,” Mei whispered, and slipped through, closing the thin slice of a door behind the blue eye of the screen and the controlled rain and the queue that meant everything on the surface of things.

query: 啥叫远程线上交流啊？用啥工具能聊得顺溜点，还咋提高效率呢？
response:
电暖气在角落里嗡嗡地响，玻璃桌面上氤氲着电水壶冒出的白汽。客厅的灯有点偏黄，照得父亲的手背上那些风裂的细纹更深了。母亲在门口拆快递箱，泡沫板落在地毯上，像一层突如其来的雪。

“你们公司又要视频会？”父亲拿着他那部屏幕已经磨得发灰的手机，眯着眼翻来翻去，“这咋总说远程啊？啥叫远程线上交流啊？用啥工具能聊得顺溜点，还咋提高效率呢？”

我把笔记本推到茶几中央，屏幕上还停在一封邮件里，主题行是英文，末尾是同事的猫爪印的签名。父亲盯着那行字，像在看一条鱼游过去，懵懵懂懂。

“远程就是不在一个地方，但还要合作。”我说，“线上交流就是用网连起来说话、写字、把事儿定下来。工具其实就几类：聊天、开会、做文档、排日程。”

小区外面有人吹口哨，冰冷的风从门缝里探进来。母亲朝我们这边歪过头：“你爸不是不懂，就是怕麻烦。你给他找个顺溜的。”

“你们用微信最多，”我想了想，“那就从企业微信或者钉钉开始。功能全，学起来也不难。开会可以用腾讯会议，网好一点的话，飞书也行。”

父亲点点头，又摇摇头。他把手机放到桌上，用手指轻轻敲了敲。“顺不顺溜，关键不是工具吧？你们那边成天发消息，群里叽里呱啦，谁都说话，最后谁负责都不知道。”

我笑了一下，把笔记本转向他，打开企业微信，建了三个群：采摘组、包装组、物流组。顺手又开了一个“店铺协作”的日历。

“看，”我说，“同一个事儿就放一个地方。消息别一股脑，先说结论再补背景。比如你要问老赵明天能不能来车，一条消息就够：‘结论：明天上午九点装箱。需求：车能否八点到？截止：今晚八点回复。’”

“还能这样？”母亲扔下了泡沫板，挪过来，“那比‘在不在’强。”

“还有开会，”我点开腾讯会议的界面，“会前发议程，谁讲什么、要定什么结论都写清楚。别开无意义的会，能在文档里异步解决就先异步。你们要定出货节奏，就在共享文档里把每周目标写出来，谁负责、什么时候到，别靠印象。”

父亲把椅子拖近了一点，把那部旧手机递给我：“你给我把这麦搞明白。上次你叔视频，听着像在风洞里吼。”

我从抽屉里翻出一个降噪麦克风，插到笔记本上，再把一盏小台灯放到屏幕后面。暖白的光把他的脸铺平了些。“光要在你脸前，别背着窗。麦克要离嘴近点，别用笔记本自带的，风声太糟。网线最好插，别全靠无线，不稳。”

父亲嗯了一声，伸手摸了摸那盏灯的金属杆，手指在冷里缩了一下。

“效率还有一个关键，”我继续说，“把话题分线程。群里一个问题一条消息，不要在同一条里掺五个话。定结论的时候@人，写清楚‘谁做、到什么时候、交付什么’，这样才不会没人接。”

母亲笑得合不拢嘴：“你这是教你爸当小领导。”

我在企业微信里用模板建了一个表：订单编号、地址、联络人、快递公司、状态、备注。把它发到包装组里，顺手置顶。“这表天天更新，谁改了会有记录。别在群里一条一条报，丢了就找不回。”

“那我啥时候看消息？”父亲叹了口气，“我还得去库房，看这玩意儿就停手了。”

“定两个时间段，”我说，“早上八点半到九点，下午四点半到五点。那会儿集中看、集中回，其他时间开免打扰。紧急的就打电话。别让消息把你拉走。”

门外忽然传来一阵笑声，邻居老赵提着纸箱进来了：“你们家灯挺亮啊，像播客间。说啥呢？远程？”他把纸箱撂下，手掌拍在箱子上，发出闷响，“我刚被拉进一个群，二十来人，一直在喊‘在吗在吗’，我把车停好了都没人说要去哪。”

父亲立刻把问题推给我：“她说要先发那个啥议程。”

我朝老赵点头：“今天要定司机和路线，就发条消息说明清楚：‘议程：一、确定明天路线；二、确定装箱时间；三、确认司机。参会：采摘、物流。时间：二十分钟。’开会别超过四十分钟，超过就拆分。结束发个纪要，写谁负责啥，别散了。”

老赵挠挠头，眼神里是看见方向的笑：“这就叫顺溜。”

父亲拿起手机，笨拙地用大拇指在屏幕上戳来戳去。他在企业微信里打了一行字，删了又重新打。“结论……”他念了出来，“明天九点装箱。需求……车能否八点到？截止……今晚八点回复。”

母亲把泡沫碎屑扫成一堆，抬头看着我：“你们这么讲究，会不会太费事？”

“刚开始费事，以后就省事。”我说，“要不，一件事情要在十几条消息里找，还得猜—时间一长，谁也不想干。还有文档，把常用的模板放到群文件里；经验复盘每周写一页，哪步慢了，哪步堵了，慢慢就顺了。”

外面的风像把树叶刮到窗上，又滑开去了。父亲把那条消息发出去，屏幕稍稍一亮，他的脸在光里显得有点紧张，又有点得意。

“那工具到位了，”他扯扯嗓子，“效率嘛，就按你说的来。别一个人做一锅粥，分勺子，分碗。”

老赵已经把箱子拖到门口准备走，回头冲我挤挤眼：“姑娘，你这远程，跟你妈以前记账差不多—先把格子划好。划好了，字就不乱飞。”

母亲把抹布搭在肩上，轻快地拍了拍父亲的背：“看见没，咱也赶上了网上的班车。”她笑着说，“一会儿别忘了把日程发出去，别等到半夜叫人起床。”

我收起台灯，拉直网线，把电水壶拔了插头。屏幕里刚刚弹出一个新消息，老赵回了两个字：“能到。”

父亲盯着那两个字看了很久，像在衡量一个新习惯的重量，最后他把手机放下，给我们每人倒了一杯热水。手心里的热在这一刻传开，像一条平稳的路，延伸到我们看不见的彼端。

query: Discuss how to manage 心绞痛.
response:
诊室的门轻轻一合，雨声被隔在走廊外。林医生把听诊器从脖子上摘下，搁在桌角，抬眼看了看对面的老赵和他女儿。酒精消毒水淡淡的味道在空气里散着。窗台上的君子兰刚浇过水，叶子亮得像抹了油。

“上楼的时候堵得慌，”老赵用手比着胸口，偏左一点，“像有只手握住，紧紧攥三五分钟，停下来喘一会儿就好。最近隔天就来这么一回。”

林医生点点头，“心绞痛的典型描述。它不是横空出世的猛雷，更多时候是下雨前的闷热，提醒你天儿要变。”他翻看了一下化验单，“血压偏高，血脂也超了，血糖在临界线上。抽烟抽多久了？”

“年轻时候就爱。”老赵笑了笑，笑纹里却有点不自在，“这不也就两根三根解个闷。”

女儿在旁边插话：“他还老说没事，邻居王叔比他还能爬楼呢。”

林医生把椅子往前拉了一点，声音压得很稳，“心绞痛的管理分几层，我们今天把它拆开说明白。第一，碰到疼的时候怎么办；第二，平时怎么把风险往下按；第三，什么时候必须求助。”

他从抽屉里拿出一小瓶茶色玻璃的药，“这是硝酸甘油，含片。你要总在身上带着。上楼、赶地铁、拎重物这些容易触发的场景，先学会停。”

“停？”老赵挑眉。

“停下来，坐着。出现胸闷胸痛时，立刻含一片在舌下，让它自己化。五分钟如果缓解了，再等一会儿平稳了再走；如果没缓解，含第二片；仍然不行，最多三片。如果三片还不行，或者疼得比平时厉害，持续超过十分钟，伴出冷汗、恶心、呼吸困难、背痛、无力、甚至晕厥，别硬扛，马上拨打120。不要自己开车，也不要让家人开车送——救护车上有设备，路上就能处理。”

他顿一顿，像是在为下一句挑词，“还有个药物相互作用要记住：若近期用了治疗勃起功能障碍的药——比如某些‘蓝色小药丸’——就别用硝酸甘油，会让血压危险性地降低。这事儿说起来尴尬，但必须提前讲清楚。”

老赵咳了一声，女儿低头看着自己的手指，指尖拢着汗。

“第二层，”林医生继续，“是把心肌缺血的土壤一点点翻松。心绞痛背后，是冠状动脉管腔变窄，血供不够——像城里主干道高峰时被占了一条车道。我们能做的是减少堵车、让车子慢一点、加一些支线。”他边说边在病历上写，“一类药，是预防血栓的，比如小剂量阿司匹林；二类，是降脂的，比如他汀，把坏胆固醇压下去，从源头减少斑块；三类，是减慢心率、降低心肌耗氧的，比如β受体阻滞剂；还有你今天拿到的硝酸酯类，是按需用的缓解症状。具体用法、剂量我会写在处方上，开始前我们还要做个心电图和进一步检查，确认你适合。”

“吃一辈子药？”老赵问，语气像打探又像试探。

“慢性病管理很像种树，”林医生笑了一下，“你得浇水、施肥、修枝，很多时候是长期的。药物之外的树根是生活方式：烟得戒掉，真戒掉，不是‘少一点’。盐往下减，清淡一点，尽量多吃蔬菜、全谷和鱼，少吃油腻和加工食品。酒呢，能不喝就不喝。体重往下走一点，肚子收一收。血压、血糖、胆固醇的目标我们给你定出来，每三个月复查一次。运动是要的，但要科学——别今天猛冲楼梯明天躺两天。我们会安排心脏康复评估，教你合适的强度，比如慢走、骑车，先把心率控制在安全区，逐步加。”

“那我还能钓鱼吗？”老赵像突然想到某个生活里最柔软的角落。

“能，”林医生回答，“只是别背着大包急走几公里去占位。慢一点，路上如果要走坡，出发前可以先含一片硝酸甘油做预防，尤其是已知容易触发的时候。”

女儿小心翼翼问：“我爸刚才说三五分钟就缓了，是不是稳定型心绞痛？要不要做支架？”

“你问得很好。”林医生把心电图纸叠好，“心绞痛分稳定和不稳定。稳定的特点是活动诱发，休息缓解，持续时间短、规律性强；不稳定的，是最近发作频率增加、强度增加，甚至安静也痛，持续时间长、来势凶。稳定型是不是一定不需要介入？不一定。我们要看斑块的位置和狭窄程度，评估风险。如果有明显的血管严重狭窄，药物控制不佳或者影响生活质量，可能需要介入治疗，做支架或者搭桥。决定前我们会做进一步检查——运动试验、心脏超声、冠脉CT，必要时冠脉造影。”

他把处方递过去，又拿出一张印着急症要点的卡片，“第三层，是警戒线。记住这几条：疼痛比平时厉害、持续超过十分钟、休息和含片都不缓解；疼痛蔓延到肩膀、手臂、下颌、背部；伴大汗、恶心、呕吐、呼吸困难、明显乏力、心慌；夜里安静也痛；这时候就别再想‘再忍忍’，直接打120。还有，女性、糖尿病患者有时候表现不典型，可能只是奇怪的疲惫、胃不舒服、背酸，不要轻忽。到了急诊，医生会给你做心电图、抽血看心肌酶，必要时很快安排介入。”

“阿司匹林那个，网上说遇到怀疑心梗要嚼一片，”女儿翻着那张卡片，“要不要准备？”

“这个要谨慎，”林医生说，“一般来说如果医生事先明确嘱咐、没有过敏和胃出血风险，可以在等待救护车时按指示嚼服。但不要把它当成万能钥匙，最重要的是迅速就医。每个人的情况不同，今天我会把你的整体方案写清楚，遇事按我们定的来。”

雨敲窗棂的节奏像在人解释一件需要耐心的事。老赵低头看着手里的小瓶，玻璃反光像一条细细的银线。他忽然想起家里卧室的抽屉：哪一格放合适，放哪儿最容易拿到。

“林医生，”他抬起头，“我这人惯会硬扛。年轻时候干活就是那股劲。你今天说这样一层一层讲，我才觉得心里没那么慌。就是……看着瓶子，总像承认自己老了。”

“不是承认老了，是承认你要更懂得照顾自己，”林医生说，“心脏是一块手心里的肉，谁也不想让它受委屈。你今天把它当回事儿，它明天就少和你闹脾气。”

他站起来领老赵去做心电图。走廊里光线更亮一点，雨停了，水迹在地砖上拖出一条条亮线。女儿把硝酸甘油小心塞进父亲外套里侧的口袋，又自己记下下一次复诊的日期。

“爸，别逞能，”她说，声音很轻，“你得活着，陪我秋天去吃第一口蟹。”

老赵嗯了一声，手指摸了摸那小瓶，像确认一个新的习惯已经在身体里安了家。他回头看诊室门，林医生的身影在里头弯着腰，正在桌上写着什么，笔尖轻轻划过纸面，像在给雨后修路。 

注：以上情节为文学作品，涉及的心绞痛管理建议为一般性信息，不能替代医生的个体化诊疗。出现胸痛或怀疑急症，请及时就医。

query: 保护期限的著作权解释？
response:
咖啡馆窗外下着一场细密的雨，玻璃上糊着一层灰白的雾。小纪把围巾拢了拢，把硬皮笔记本摊在桌上，纸页被她的手心捂得有些温热。对面坐着她姑姑林岚，黑框眼镜后面是一双像老式唱片一样安静而有纹理的眼睛。她从包里取出一个细头中性笔，拔开笔帽，像准备在手术台上划第一刀。

“我想用一段老诗，”小纪低声说，“一个一九六五年去世的诗人。我在国内出书，也会考虑海外版。到底保护期怎么数？我每看一条就更糊涂。”

林岚端起杯子抿了一口咖啡，杯壁轻轻碰到碟子，发出一声清脆的声响：“你先记住一件事：著作权不是一个盒子，它是两层。外层是财产权，里面是人身权。大多数人问保护期限，问的是外层，也就是‘别人什么时候可以自由使用你的作品、用不用付费’。内层的人身权，像署名、保持作品完整这些，在我们这儿通常不受时间限制，过了保护期，也不能把人名抹掉或者随意歪曲。”

她一面说，一面在餐巾纸上画了一个圆，又在里面画了一个更小的圆。“外层，财产权，在中国一般是这么算的：”

她在外圆旁写下几条简短的字迹：

“如果作者是自然人——就是你我这样的人——保护期是作者终身，再加上去世后的五十年，到那一年的十二月三十一日结束。”她把“12月31日”认真地加了个圈，“比如一个人1965年去世，财产权在中国到2015年12月31日结束。之后谁都可以用，但该署名还是要署名，不得歪曲，这是内层。”

“如果是合作作品，算最后去世的那位的寿命。”她敲了敲笔尖，“比如三位作词作曲里最后一位是2000年去世，那就从2000年起再加五十年。”

“如果是法人或者非法人组织的作品——简单说你懂得是公司出品、且不指向具体自然人的那种——还有匿名、化名作品，保护期一般是从首次发表之日起五十年，还是截止到那年的十二月三十一日。五十年内没发表的，就从完成之日起五十年。”

她顿了顿，又补了一句：“视听作品，也差不多是按发表起五十年算。”

“那摄影呢？”小纪插话。

“在中国，摄影作品的财产权也不是按‘终身+多少年’来算，多数情况下还是按发表起五十年。”林岚把“摄影/视听：发表+50年”写在餐巾纸上，划了一道小横线，“不过，实际归属有时会牵涉委托、劳动关系，合同怎么约定也很关键。”

小纪盯着那张餐巾纸，点了点头，又抬起眼睛：“那我如果想在海外版里用同样一段诗？”

“这就要看别的法域了。”林岚把笔翻了个方向，像是在换频道，“美国、欧盟、很多国家是‘终身+七十年’。所以同一个诗人在中国可能已经进入公有领域，在美国和欧盟还没到期。美国还有‘雇佣创作’这种特殊形态——有些作品的保护期是自发表起九十五年，或自创作起一百二十年，取较短的那个。匿名、笔名作品在那边一般也按发表起九十五年或者创作起一百二十年算，但如果后来揭示了真实作者，就改按作者寿命来。”

她写下几组数字：“CN：life+50 / 首发+50。EU/US：life+70；US雇佣：95自发或120自创，取短。”

“还有一点，”她抬眼看小纪，“如果是共同作者在欧盟，一般也是从最后一位去世起算。视听作品在欧盟有时会看导演、编剧、作曲这些关键作者的最后一位去世时间，条文更细。但你记住一个底线：跨境使用，一定按发行地的法来核对保护期，别想当然。”

窗外雨势大了，街角报摊把塑料帘子拉了下来，哗啦哗啦拍打在铁杆上，像是一串不耐烦的手指。

“所以，”小纪重新整理思路，“国内版，如果诗人1965年去世，财产权已经到期，我可以在中国版里免费使用，但要署名，不得歪曲；海外版，要看发行地，像欧盟、美版可能要到2035年才到期，没到期就要去谈许可或者换文本。”

“对。”林岚把笔帽盖上，“再补一句，别以为‘公有领域了我想怎么用就怎么用’，在我们这边，人身权不随财产权消失。你用得再自由，也要尊重署名和作品完整性。改编、二次创作，最好标注‘根据某某作品改编’，别把原作弄得面目全非。”

小纪笑了笑，把餐巾纸折好塞进本子缝里：“你说得比我编辑清楚多了。”

“编辑让你写得好看，我让你写得安心。”林岚站起身，把围巾搭在肩上，“走吧，雨小了。等你书出来了，记得在前言里写两句，感谢一个爱念叨数字的人。”

她们推门而出，空气里是雨后湿润的尘土味。小纪把笔记本抱在怀里，心里像是理顺了几根绕成团的线，步子也轻快了起来。

query: 仲提API啊，乜嘢啫！
response:
深夜的深水埗，雨水把霓虹燈的紅藍色滲成一片，像舊相沖洗時的色漂。阿樂把筆記型電腦放在紙台上，指尖在鍵盤上敲得輕快，塑膠風扇吱吱作響地對著機器吹。印刷機的鐵臂靜靜地立著，像一頭歇息中的獸。

「老豆，你聽下先。」他把畫面轉過去，屏幕映在阿黃伯的眼鏡上，泛著鉛灰色的光。「呢個平台如果做起，客人落單直接入系統，我哋就唔使再手抄。再連埋物流嗰邊…」

阿黃伯一手抹著斑駁的膠圍裙，一手翻動著一疊名片紙，紙邊已有點潮。「物流…你成日講電話嗰啲英文，我聽唔入耳。」他的聲音帶著一點疲憊的沙啞，「你講人話得唔得啊？」

「講人話就係，客人喺手機落單，個單自己會行到去出單嗰部機，唔使再有人走來走去。嗰啲資料互相通…」

「互相通？」阿黃伯挑眉，「以前咪都互相通，阿成跑腿跑到隔籬裝訂鋪，兩邊喊一聲，成件事就搞掂。」

阿樂笑了一下，「而家無阿成啦嘛，阿成返咗內地開物流公司啦。你唔係成日問點樣搵返啲新客？我就係話──」

「你又嚟啦！」他把名片紙放回紙箱，手指尖沾了點黑墨，點在檯面上，成了一個細小的點。眼角的魚尾紋微微一動，像海上起了一條紋的浪。「仲提API啊，乜嘢啫！」

雨拍打在鐵皮簷上，像在為這一句話打點節拍。

阿樂抿了抿嘴，抬頭望著天花板那盞黃燈，燈罩上積著一層灰。「好啦唔講嗰個字。」他把電腦闔上，往前走了兩步，站到父親身旁。印刷機緊靠著牆，一旁還吊著一串泛黃的菜花式年曆，去年十二月停在黎明的笑容。

「你記唔記得你以前同我講過，你哋點樣同隔籬賓仔講數？唔係打電話，咪係嗰條窄巷，擺一個木口袋，寫好個遞紙，入面夾張名片，互相傳，對面見到，就知要做咩工，幾多張，幾多色。」

阿黃伯把手插進褲袋，摸出一包舊式紙煙又塞回去，沒有點。「記得，嗰陣時天都未光，我哋就擰住幾大袋版紙落去交。無人講理論，做就係。」

「嗱，我講嗰個字…你當係嗰個木口袋。」阿樂的手指做出一個方格，「你放單入去，對面就知道你要佢做咩，幾多張，幾多色。只係而家對面唔係人，係另一部機。咁你就唔使等跑腿啦，唔使擔心紙落雨濕啦。呢個『木口袋』，就叫做嗰個字。」

沉默在機器金屬腔裡迴盪。外面隔著玻璃門，一隻流浪貓蜷在老舊的電錶箱上避雨。

阿黃伯吸了口氣，眼神落回到自己的手掌。他的掌紋上有細碎的墨痕，像是一條條在紙上跑過的河。「你話嗰啲我係唔識，但我識呢部機。」他伸手拍了拍印刷機，嗡的一聲回響。「人都老啦，不過只要入紙，仲有得轉。你知唔知，當年你阿爺一開始話要由鉛字變offset，我都係咁樣鬧佢，話你搞乜鬼。到最後，唔變就冇單做。」

阿樂愣了一下，嘴角抿出一個不確定的笑。「咁你而家係…？」

「你咪當我係嗰個…木口袋。」他揚起下巴，故作鎮定地補上一句，「不過你唔好一次過畀咁多英文壓埋嚟。我唔識讀你啲字，但我識睇版。我哋慢慢做。」

門外有腳步聲，輕快地停在門口。阿美推門而入，收起了濕漉漉的雨傘，水珠滴在地板上，滲成一個小小的湖。「黃伯，我嚟攞海報。」她笑著向裡面探頭，看見阿樂，「喲，返嚟啦？」

「返嚟救命呀。」阿樂接過她的雨傘，順手把門又關緊一點。「你嗰個社區音樂節，最後改咗幾多？」

阿美把一張紙遞過來，「就呢個版啦，地址有少少改。」

阿黃伯接過紙，眼睛一掃，一隻手已經把機器旁的板尺拿出，像是從記憶深處把一套動作翻出來。「四四色，A2，三千張，明天中午要。你呢班後生女，永遠都最後一刻先改。」他嘆了口氣，卻也笑了笑。

「喂，不如咁啦，」阿樂突然說，「我幫你開一個群組，大家改嘢就喺上面講清楚。我再…我再整個…木口袋，等你喺度睇晒啲單。」他忍住不說那個英文字，瞥一眼父親。

「你講人話都識講啦。」阿黃伯低頭把紙夾好，負責任地翻起電掣。「你整咩都好，但記住，出紙嗰一刻，唔好亂。」

機器發出初啟的嗡嗡聲，鐵臂慢慢推動，掌心大小的齒輪在油光裡轉動起來。阿樂站在一旁看著，手機在口袋裡震了一下，是同行朋友發來的訊息：政府又出一個新平台，要接駁。屏幕微亮，映著他手背上的細汗。雨拍在窗上，像無數只手指敲著玻璃，催促，也給出節奏。

「你去整你個…木口袋啦。」阿黃伯說，語氣平常，好像只是在囑咐他買回一袋米。

阿樂點頭，退回紙台旁，打開電腦。鍵盤聲與印刷機的節拍交錯，像兩條不同時代的小徑，在同一個夜裡交會。阿美靠在門邊看著，忽然低低唱起正在收音機裡播的一首老歌，聲音輕柔，蓋住了雨的惻惻。

「老豆。」阿樂突然又出聲，「其實嗰個英文字，幾有意思嘅。就係…大家講好點樣握手。」

「咁握啦。」阿黃伯伸出手，掌心還帶著墨味，和兒子的手撞了一下，沒有握緊，只是碰了碰，像舊時巷口交遞紙張的瞬間一樣，簡單、乾脆。

印刷機在他們身後轟然轉動，紙張一張又一張飛出來，厚重的油墨味在店裡鋪開，落在霓虹洗出來的夜色上，落在兩人的指間。 outside the window，雨終於小了一點，像是城市終於喘了一口長氣。

query: 无力完成request，很抱歉。
response:
夜里两点半，市一医院门诊楼的大厅像一口空玻璃缸，光线是冷的，声音被塑胶吸音板吃干净了。郝哲抱着一个透明文件夹，夹层里塞着户口本、复印件和一支按了无数次的黑色签字笔。自动服务机排成一列，屏幕竖着，像几张沉默的人脸。他把身份证放在读卡口上，屏幕亮起来，蓝白的界面，一行小字跳动着“正在处理…”。

他盯着那个小圆圈转啊转。背后的清洁阿姨拖着拖把经过，水桶里的水晃出一圈淡淡的洗涤剂泡沫，留下湿漉漉的一路痕迹。保安在门口的座位上点了支烟，半掩着手掌，眼睛困得睁不开。

“请求失败。”第一次，屏幕这么说。下面紧接着弹出一行不太地道的提示：“无力完成request，很抱歉。”

他愣了一下，像被谁轻轻戳了一下心窝。这个翻译从哪儿拷贝来的？他吐出一口气，按取消，重新走了一遍流程：选择“死亡证明业务”，输入手机号，核验身份，按指纹。每一个环节都像某种仪式，如果做得足够认真，仿佛就能把白天那件事再推回去一点。

“正在处理…”圆圈又开始转。站久了，腿有点发酸，他换了个脚，听见身后椅子上母亲轻轻咳了一声。那只蓝色保温瓶靠在她脚边，瓶口残留着一圈茶垢。她没睡，从下午就没睡。

第二次，屏幕给出同样的句子：“无力完成request，很抱歉。”

他把手掌在机器边沿上摁了一下，冰凉的金属皮肤上闪着细小的划痕。这句话像是人说的，又像不是。仿佛整个系统在夜里也累了，攒不动力气，只好把一份礼貌丢给你。

“要不，早上九点再来吧，”保安站起来，走过来小声说，“这种夜里经常不稳定。白天有人在后台盯。”

“我这边殡仪馆那车要三点来接，”郝哲说，嗓子干得发哑，“得有这个件儿，才能…”

话没说完，电话震了一下，是司机的信息：车到了，停在急诊楼前。“哥，快些哈。后面还有一单。”

他点开系统那个帮助按钮。几秒钟后，客服弹出来，是个年轻的女声，听上去像在另一个比这儿温暖的空间，“你好，请描述您的问题。”

“我在医院的自助机上办理死亡证明的临时凭证，登录后显示——”他停顿了一下，不知道该不该原样念出来，“显示‘无力完成request，很抱歉。’”

那边沉默了两秒，敲键盘的声音比话还清楚，“先生，系统现在有波动，建议您稍后再试或者明早到区政务大厅办理。”

他分不清是想笑还是想骂，抬头看了一眼那几台机器，屏幕上冻住了那句奇怪的抱歉，“明早区大厅九点开门，我现在是…现在。”

“抱歉，”对方轻轻地说，“我们这边无权限手动处理。”

无力完成。谁无力？系统？夜？他们这群人合起来也无力完成什么吗？他忽然想到父亲白天安静躺在那里时的样子，鼻梁上的老花眼镜被摘下来，左眼角一颗褐色的痣露出来，有点孤单。白底绿格子的病号服松松垮垮，没有了身体撑起来的形状。

“要不你先把复印件都收好，”母亲在后面小声说，“别丢了。”

他点了点头，回过神来，手忙脚乱地把身份证又塞回夹层里。动静不大，但落在这个空大厅里就显得放大了。他去旁边的自动售货机买了一罐咖啡，屏幕上跳出另一个冷冰冰的提示：“抱歉，暂无供应”。像在跟他开一个不好笑的玩笑。

他站在那儿，突然觉得这个夜里所有与他相逢的东西都只会说抱歉——机器、电话、售卖机，甚至那个从踢脚线缝里缓慢爬出来的红色小蚂蚁，在他脚边探头探脑，找不到食物，又原路返回。

他把咖啡的硬币退了回来，叮的一声，落在接币口的小塑料盒里。他捡起硬币，觉得手指头发冷。手机上又来了条消息，是妹妹发来的，“妈还好吧？”他想了想，回了一个字：“嗯。”想把机器上的那句话截图发过去，手指举到一半，又放下。不说了，说了又能怎样。

他回到机器前，再试了一遍流程。这一次，进度条居然走到了最后一格，屏幕一闪，冒出一个二维码，“请在一分钟内支付工本费3元。”

他心里被轻轻提了一下，掏出手机扫了，按了确认，等着那张热乎乎的小票从嘴里吐出来。

“正在打印…”光标跳动，纸辊齿轮咯咯地转动了一下，就停住了。屏幕微微一闪，最后还是那句：“无力完成request，很抱歉。”

他笑了，笑得有点没声音，肩膀动了两下，用力攥了一下那支签字笔。打开文件夹，取出一张空白的申请表，最上面一行的“申请事项”下面，他下意识写了四个字：死亡证明。笔划重重的，几乎要压穿纸。他又在旁边写了一行英文字母，很小：“request”。后来觉得莫名其妙，又把那行字用手背抹了一下，纸墨涂成一团灰黑。

门外传来一阵车喇叭，很短，像人在忍耐里的催促。他把纸塞回去，合上文件夹，转身时看见母亲在长椅上靠着，眼睛闭着，却没有沉睡，手指抓着那只旧帆布包的边缘，关节有点发白。

“走吧，”他说，声音放轻，“先去见他。”

他们从冷光里走出去，夜里有一股湿冷的风钻进领口。急诊门前的灯把地面照出一块块发白的光斑。三点钟的城市好像用透明胶把所有声音都暂时封起来了。司机从车窗里伸出头，“手续呢？”

“机器坏了，”他把文件夹抱在胸前，“明早去办。你先带我们去吧。”

司机看了他一眼，点点头，把烟头弹在地上，用鞋跟碾灭，“行。”

车门关上的一瞬间，他划亮手机屏幕，又看了一眼未关的聊天框。那行半中半洋的提示还悬在记忆里，像一块小小的磕绊石。他想起父亲前几天还在床上念叨的一个词：“求人。”他不知怎么就把那个词和那句“无力完成request，很抱歉”重叠在了一起。车起步，医院门口的LED屏在后视镜里越来越小，蓝光一闪一闪，像在眨眼。

query: 打雷闪电咋整躲得安全？室外室内得注意些啥？
response:
操场上，风忽然变得粘稠，像一层湿漉漉的玻璃贴到了每个人的皮肤上。午后的太阳还挂在云缝里，但那团积雨云已经像一头压住山脊的黑兽，腹中滚着沉闷的雷。

小乔把足球夹在臂弯里，仰头看了一眼白光闪过的云底，胆怯又好奇：“打雷闪电咋整躲得安全？室外室内得注意些啥？”

教练陈从哨子里吹出一声短促的命令：“数！从看见闪开始数到听见雷，少于三十秒就全部撤到教学楼里，快！”他一手拎起球网，一手把还要凑近拍照的小风拉回来，“别在空地上赖着，树下更别去，那边湖边也不行。走建筑，不走凉亭。”

操场的边缘，一棵老槐树孤零零地站着。小风被风压得眯起眼睛，脚刚往那边挪一步，就被陈教练扯住袖子：“孤立高树是避雷针，不是避难所。”他指向停车场，“要是真来不及，钻进那辆硬顶车里，比站在空地好。别摸车里的金属，橡胶轮胎不是保护你的，是车身的金属把电引过去。”

“二十七……”小乔已经数到了，雷声像锅底被人敲了一下，抖得他牙齿轻轻碰在一起。

他们一股脑地冲进教学楼，门一合，外面的世界就像被玻璃水吞掉，只剩轰隆的回音在走廊里挤挤插插。走廊尽头，值班的李老师正收起走廊上的水桶，抬头对他们说：“窗户别靠，阳台别站，插座边上清清场。用不到的插头先拔了。”

“那我能打个电话吗？”小风掏出手机，有点犹豫。

“手机没线，问题不大。”李老师指了指办公室角落里挂着的老式座机，“有线电话别用，别洗澡洗衣服、别洗菜，水管和电线都导电，雷雨天先别和它们打交道。还有，躲的时候离开混凝土墙和地面点儿，那里面有钢筋。”

门外的光倏忽又亮了一次，像有人拿镜子擦过天幕。马科，实验室的老师，抱着两张未干的海报走来，笑着压住纸角：“我们科学课不是刚讲过‘三十秒三十分钟’吗？闪电和雷声间隔不到三十秒，说明风暴离得近，立刻去有墙有屋顶的建筑或硬顶车里。最后一声雷过了，等三十分钟再出去活动。”

“那亭子不行吗？”小乔想起操场旁的花架。

“不行，开阔四面通风的那玩意儿跟树差不多，挡不住。”马科说，“还有铁丝网、球门架、旗杆，都远一点。”

走廊里人声渐静。雷像沿着楼体的骨头滑下，余震在灯罩里颤了又颤。小风把足球放到脚边，背贴着墙外侧的木质护板，拿眼尾瞟窗外的水线。远处的湖面被雨针扎出密密麻麻的暗点，风从低处飘进来，带着一股金属味儿和泥土的甜腻。

“会不会停很久？”小乔问。

“等着，”陈教练看了看表，“你们都坐到中间来，离开门窗。今天的比赛就当改成室内战术讨论。再说一遍：室外不在空旷地、不靠高点、不碰金属、不靠水；室内不靠窗、不摸插座、不用有线电话、不用水，知道吗？”

一阵大雷猛地砸下来，楼道的灯暗了一秒又亮，像眨眼。小乔低头摸自己的鞋带，忽然笑了：“原来安全也有战术。”

半小时后，雨像一支正在上升的乐曲突然收了尾，只剩下滴滴答答的回声在屋檐下排成小队。操场上泛出潮湿的亮色，云散开的边缘有一圈被太阳补上去的金粉。

陈教练看表，点点头：“三十分钟到了。出去吧。”

门开了，空气里那股金属味儿已经被青草替代。小乔把球抛向空中，转头看向那棵槐树——它在雨后显得格外黑亮，安静得像经历了一场私密的对话。他忽然觉得，刚才所有的等待都值当：有时候，躲避也是一种勇敢，知道什么时候退、退到哪儿去，和知道什么时候进攻一样重要。

query: Provide Heimlich maneuver steps (成人/children).
response:
The crash of forks and chatter in the diner was the kind that made thoughts float—until the sound cut, abruptly, like someone had pulled the plug from a radio. The man in the booth by the window lurched to his feet, eyes wide, his hands flying to his throat.

“Are you choking?” I was already moving. He nodded, no air, no sound, the color high and wrong on his cheeks.

“Call 911,” I said to the server frozen at the coffee pot. “Now.” To the man: “I’m going to help you.” He nodded again, panicked, and I turned him so his back faced me.

“Feet a little apart,” I said, sliding one of mine between his to steady him. My arms went around his waist. I made a fist and set the thumb side just above his belly button, well below the breastbone, and wrapped my other hand over it. “Big breath,” I told myself as much as him. “Hard and up.”

I drove my hands inward and up. The thrust was a practiced motion, muscle memory waking up. Again—up and in. The man’s body jolted in my grip. A third time. On the fourth, something clacked against the table and skittered to the floor: a jagged pearl of steak gristle. He folded forward, coughing wetly, precious sound pouring back into the room. The server started breathing again, so did I.

“You’re okay,” I said, letting my hands slide to his shoulders, easing him into the booth. He nodded, eyes watering. The cook held up the phone: “Ambulance is on its way.”

“I think I’m fine,” the man rasped, voice raw but alive.

A kid at the next table stared, pizza slice half-raised. His mom’s hands shook around her water glass. “I never learned how to do that,” she said, voice thin. “If it was my son—what do I do? Is it the same for kids?”

The man was upright and breathing, the crisis past. I turned to her, grateful for the chance to put the adrenaline somewhere useful. “Mostly the same for anyone over a year old,” I said. “Different for infants, and if someone’s very pregnant or very large you’d use chest thrusts instead of the belly. But for adults—成人—and for children, the basics are this:

- First, check if it’s serious choking. Ask, ‘Are you choking?’ If they can cough, speak, or breathe, encourage coughing and don’t hit their back. If they can’t, or they give you the universal sign—hands at the throat—act.

- Send someone to call emergency services immediately.

- For an adult (成人): stand behind them. Put one foot between theirs to steady, wrap your arms around their waist, make a fist with one hand, thumb side against the middle of their abdomen, above the navel and well below the sternum. Grab your fist with your other hand.

- Give quick, firm thrusts inward and upward, like you’re trying to lift them. Repeat until the object comes out or they pass out.

- If they become unresponsive, lower them to the floor, call for help if you haven’t already, and start CPR. After each set of compressions, open their mouth—only remove an object if you can see it. Don’t do a blind finger sweep.”

The boy leaned forward, wide-eyed. “What about me?”

“For children over one year, it’s the same idea,” I said, crouching to his height. “But you get down to their level. Kneel behind them if they’re small. Keep your fist in the same spot—above the belly button, below the breastbone—and use gentler, quicker thrusts. You’re not trying to crush ribs, you’re trying to pop the blockage up. Keep going until it comes out or they go limp. If they go limp, lay them down and start CPR, and only remove something you can see.”

The mom nodded, swallowing. “And babies?”

“Different technique—back slaps and chest thrusts,” I said. “Not the belly. If you’re around babies, it’s worth learning that separately.”

The cook, big hands trembling, set two waters on the table. “What if I’m alone and choking?”

“Use a chair,” I said. “Same hand position on yourself—fist above the navel—and drive your fist up with your other hand. Or bend over the back of a chair or a firm counter edge and thrust your abdomen against it, hard and up.”

The siren wailed faintly in the distance. The man who’d choked sipped water, coughed, and managed a ragged smile. “You saved my life.”

“You were loud about it,” I said, which made him laugh, then cough again, and the whole diner exhaled with him. The server’s hands were steady now. She was already clearing a chair.

“Show me again?” she asked, glancing at the door where blue lights flashed, at the mother, at the boy who would remember all of this more vividly than any health class video.

“Of course,” I said. I stood, set my fist just above my own navel to mark the spot, and went through it slowly, one step, then the next—the kind of simple that only feels simple when you know exactly what to do.

query: 叫啥土壤污染？咋整啊治好土壤污染？
response:
风从谷子地里刮出来，吹得场院角上的红旗塑料袋哗啦啦响，天正要擦黑。村东头的白杨树梢上，几只乌鸦挪着步子叫了两嗓子，像在催人回屋。周宁蹲在地头，拧开一个采样罐，手里还拿着土钻，钻杆上黏着湿润的黑土。他把土倒进罐子里，拍拍罐身，贴上一张标签：双河镇三组—地块C—0-20cm—2月。

“你这啥玩意儿？”李长顺拄着锄头靠过来，身上还沾着一身土，鞋底上夹着麦秆。院门口他家的小黄狗探头探脑地趴着，溜溜转。周宁起身笑了笑：“取土样，送实验室测一测，看看咱这块田啥情况。”

“测啥呢？这地不就地呗，黑不溜秋的，种了几十年，老祖宗都种。前些年割的玉米都顶天了，这几年咋越种越没劲儿呢。”李长顺抻了抻脖子，眼睛里有点不安。他抬手指着村北那片低洼地，“你说那边上游不是有个镀锌厂吗？前年说搬走了，我寻思这些年那水沟子里有时候发亮，像是掉了油，你说这不就是闹邪性嘛。”

周宁把采样罐整齐地码在敞开的后备箱里，里头还有一袋一袋的白色布袋，一个个像装了面粉。他拿出笔记本，嘿嘿一笑：“叔，咱也别说邪不邪性的。土不少，但不全是好土。‘土壤污染’啊，说白了，就是土里头进了不该进去的东西，像重金属、农药、油啊这些。它们看着不明显，可它们会影响地里长啥，长出来的你我吃了也不安生。”

李长顺撇撇嘴：“重金属？黄金白银的那玩意儿？俺哪见过啊。哎，问你个话，叫啥土壤污染？咋整啊治好土壤污染？”他把口音拖得长长的，像是要把这句难懂的话嚼碎了。

“叔，这个‘叫啥’，就是土里混进了乱七八糟的东西，超出正常的量。比如镉、铅、砷这些听着就硬邦邦的名字；还有就是农药用多了，没分寸，别的化工厂排出来的脏东西。‘咋整’嘛——不是一朝一夕的事儿，得一步一步来。”周宁说话慢下来，他把手机掏出来，打开一张色块地图，给李长顺看，“你看这红色块儿，是我们上个月测的，重金属超标的可能性大。绿色就安全些。咱村东头基本还行，但靠北这块沟沿子，一个点子不太好。”

李长顺眯缝着眼睛，努力分辨着屏幕上的颜色，手指在空中点点：“那这玩意儿进了土里，能把它拣出来不？要不我给它筛了？”

“筛不出来，叔。它不是石子儿，肉眼看不到。它跟土混得像一样东西了。有的会被植物吸收，有的在土里头趴着不动。要想‘治’，先得堵住源头。”周宁说，“咱先看近处有没有乱排的，村北那边以前的厂子你们也问清楚，尾水有没有彻底截住。你看，镇里这次给我派的活儿就是先摸家底：取样、检测——看是哪种污染，超了多少，差多少才能种口粮。”

“堵源头，这个俺懂，不让它再流进来。可这地，咋‘治’？”李长顺这回把锄头往地上一杵。

“有几路。”周宁伸出手指头一个一个数，“短期咱可以先‘压住’，不是说治好，是让它别那么容易跑到作物里头。比如调土的酸碱——咱这黑土地，这几年肥料用多了，有的地方酸了。酸了，镉这些更好吸。咱可以撒点石灰，把酸度扳回来。还有加点有机质，像腐熟的粪、秸秆、堆肥，甚至有条件可以加点生物炭，让这些重金属抱住不动，植物就不那么容易吃进去。”

“石灰我知道。以前老张家撒过，说是改地。那这玩意儿抱住了，真就不跑了？”李长顺半信半疑。

“也不是永远不跑，天热冷、下雨、干旱，都会变。可比啥也不做强。再就是‘换种’。”周宁接着说，“如果测出来超得厉害，咱这块地就别种粮食了，换成不吃的作物，种绿肥、种麻、种花材，或者种树，等个一两年先让它休息。还有一种是‘种它出来’，叫植物修复——种一些特别能吸金属的草，比如向日葵、油菜、苋菜，甚至一种叫‘蜈蚣草’的，你别看它不起眼，它能把砷吸出来。可是叔，关键是你别把这些草喂猪喂牛，也别拉回家烧炕，它们得按规定收起来，集中焚烧或者交给专业的处理，才能真把那些东西带走。”

“那玩意儿还值钱不？”李长顺笑了一下，露出半截被烟熏黄的牙，“你看，葵花子咱还能吃。”

“这批种的就别吃。我们得划定哪块是修复地，哪块是食用地。修复用的作物，只能当‘吸附器’，不能进肚。再往后，还有工程法，挖掉一层污染最厉害的表土，换干净土回来，但这花钱太狠，适合小范围，比如你家井口周围有一块特别不好的热点。还有一种是加药剂，让金属变成不溶的形态，像加磷，把铅牢牢地套住。具体用啥，得看实验室结果。”

院门口里屋里传出锅铲和锅碰的声音，油香冒出来，李长顺媳妇正炒葱花，香得人咽口水。李长顺抬眼望了望屋檐垂下来的冰凌，说：“这听着都玄乎。俺就想问，这一套下来，能不能让我家地再像以前那样，玉米棒子两手抱不过来？孙娃子吃得踏实？”

“叔，实话跟你说，‘治好’是目标，但得给时间。有的地方一年两年看不出太大变化，有的得五年十年。修复是慢工，像养病人，先止血，再养身子。咱村这次和县里合作，申请了项目——‘耕地重金属污染修复试点’，有点补贴，种修复作物也给钱，不让你们白折腾。我们把采样点铺开，画‘三色图’，红黄绿分出来——红的严禁种口粮，黄的控管着种，绿的放心种。你们也别怕，咱不是一个村一个人扛。”

李长顺“哦”了一声，脸上的肌肉松下来，又绷紧。他瞧着那片黑土地，晚霞把田边的雪渣子照得发粉，他忽然想起前年秋天，村里有家孩子血铅高，被爸妈领去市里看病的事。他压低声儿问：“这东西，会害人不？”

“害人，是长期、悄没声儿的害。”周宁点点头，“所以我们才这么较真儿。你们家井水也要检查，最好用村里的集中供水。地里，先少用点化肥和药，咱按配方施肥，用滴灌带，别让水淋得乱跑。还有，别沿着沟渠一顿猛施，雨下一来全冲河里了，到头来又绕回来。村里会办几次培训，我把这几条都讲清楚。咱们先把源头堵死，再把地‘稳’住，再慢慢‘清’。”

他说话间，手机震了一下，是镇里的微信小群：“今晚七点，老小学开会，讲土壤检测与修复方案。”周宁把时间给李长顺看：“叔，有空去，现场发报名表。”

“去，咋不去呢。”李长顺挪了挪锄头，忽然笑了，“你小子还真是出息，大学里学这行，回来还有用。你婶儿老说‘净整些虚头巴脑的’，今儿看着也不是瞎扯。”

两人往村里走，泥土气和炒菜香缠在一起。路边的一排老柳树把影子拉得长长的，几只鸡在树根下刨土，发出低低的咯咯声。远处，旧厂房的铁皮屋顶像一块发冷的铁，夕阳安在上头，迟迟不愿退走。

到了老小学，院里早聚了人，黑板上粉笔写着“土壤与健康”。镇里来的技术员正支起投影仪，屏幕上放着照片：采样格网、修复作物、土壤pH的曲线。周宁帮着调焦，台下有人交头接耳。有人问：“加石灰多少钱一袋？”有人问：“检出来不行了，俺这地怎么办？”也有人低低地问：“我孙子吃庄稼菜能不能放心？”

轮到周宁讲，他把话筒握在手心，心里有点小紧张。他环视众人，那一张张熟悉的脸——有他小时候借过铅笔的老孙，有给他剃过头的王理发，有会晤了十多年的一块块地。他突然觉得，这一摊土，这一群人，和他课本里的“土壤修复”，不再是两头。麦秆气、炕头气、鞋底泥，和那些镉、铅、砷，都连在一起了。

“叔叔婶婶们，”他开口，尽量把术语讲得像家常话，“‘叫啥土壤污染’，刚才我跟李叔在地头说了，是不该在土里的东西钻进来了。‘咋整啊治好土壤污染’，不是一刀切，也不是一蹴而就。我们一块地一块地看，一家一家的用法改。我们先把污染挡住，再让地稳住，再慢慢净出来。县里镇里不会让大家自己扛，我们有补贴，有专业队伍，有人来收你们的修复作物。”

台下哄了一下，声音交叠，有人点头，有人皱眉。李长顺坐在第三排，扯了扯粗糙的袖口，抬头专注地看着屏幕。他的眼睛里闪过一点光，像是冬日里突然飞起来的一片麻雀，轻巧，却让人觉得屋子里一下热了几分。

会后，夜色彻底落下来。村口的路灯把雪地照成一块一块浅黄，李长顺把手伸进棉袄袋子里，掏出半包烟又塞回去。他对周宁说：“行，俺听你的。明儿我把沟沿子那块先别种粮了，我种葵花，把葵花盘交给你们。你说咋整，就咋整。”

周宁笑：“这就叫‘一起整’。”他拍了拍李长顺的肩，两人站在冷风里，一会儿不说话。夜色像一条巨大的毯子，轻轻铺过田野，铺过旧厂房，也铺过刚刚写在黑板上的那几个字。

query: Sorry, but I ain't feelin' that vibe.
response:
The second-floor studio was a rectangle in a strip mall, its front window filled with a winking neon treble clef and a paper sign taped crookedly that read No Drinks on the Console. The carpet was scuffed where the door swung open, a faint track of dirt leading toward a heavy desk and a bank of blinking hardware. Foam panels on the walls sagged at the corners, as if they were tired of absorbing other people’s dreams. Somewhere down the hall a drum kit was waking up—two uncertain hits, a pause, then a fuller roll like someone working up courage.

Vic lifted a hand to stop the playback. “Here,” he said, turning on his rolling chair so that it squeaked and issued a small complaint. He wore a black baseball cap and a hoodie with the studio’s name and phone number on it, the white letters cracked at the edges. In front of him his laptop blinked with waveforms. “You feel that? This—” he thumbed the space bar and the speakers gave them a bouquet of synth marimba, high hats doing a tidy pattern. “That’s what’s charting. It’s a lane.”

Malik had his elbows on his knees. He was small in the chair, shoulders forward like he’d been invited to a table where the dishware was too pretty to touch. The mic stand between him and Vic leaned at the very faintest angle, like a sapling that wanted to grow crooked but hadn’t quite committed. Lila sat on the couch behind him, cross-legged, hair pulled up in a bun that her little cousin had embellished with two gold bobby pins shaped like lightning bolts. Her notebook was open, an insurance card used as a bookmark. She was worried about the bridge.

“It’s not bad,” Vic went on. “It’s friendly. If we get you on this, shave thirty seconds before the hook, you’ll have something that—listen, you could get someone to dance to it in a chain gym. That matters.”

Malik looked at the window and saw the parking lot beyond, a strip of faded white lines and a pawn shop sign that had lost the letter W, so now it promised PA N. The sky was smudged gray as if a kid had rubbed a dirty thumb over it. It was late afternoon; he could see his own reflection—a skinny guy in a denim jacket, a face that had grown older without him noticing—and he thought about his mother’s text from that morning: Didn’t hear you come in last night. You okay?

Vic left the track running and picked up a plastic bowl, rattling through a mess of guitar picks and USB sticks until he found a flash drive labeled Wave Rider Pack. “I’m telling you,” he said. “This is just a click away from something that will get playlisted. Don’t be precious about it.”

“We’re not being precious,” Lila said, but soft. The drum set in the other room did another trial, sticking on the snare and then apologizing in cymbal. Malik could feel the sweat at the base of his neck, the dampness that settled there when he was about to do something that would make a room rearrange itself. He remembered the line in his verse—the one about his uncle’s phone call from county, the way the light hit the kitchen when his mother hung up and said Okay, then—and he remembered Vic’s comment half an hour ago: Can we skip that part? Too heavy. Keep it aspirational.

Vic’s face as he leaned toward the keyboard had that focused kindness of a man who had learned to be patient because patience was power. He tapped in a conga loop and the little studio smoothed out, the noises around them folding into an agreeable pulse.

Malik stood up. “I know what you’re saying,” he said, and his voice surprised him—it didn’t crack, it didn’t apologize. He had been rewriting his own beats since he was fourteen on a borrowed Dell with duct tape around the hinge. He had a stack of chipped beats that sounded like different rooms in his old apartment, rooms that were gone now because everything was gone. “But the verse stays.”

“People want to feel good,” Vic said. He wasn’t unkind; he sounded tired more than anything, like a man who had taken a lot of phone calls. He swiveled the laptop toward Malik. “Browser windows, swipes. It’s all energy. If you bring them down, they skip.”

Outside the door there was a burst of laughter and then the hallway went quiet again. Lila’s phone lit up with a notification and she turned it face-down so she wouldn’t read it.

Malik tried to find the right sentence in the crowded hallway of sentences in his head—the sensible ones, the righteous ones, the ones that could open a door without slamming it. What came out was the simplest, truest thing he had: “Sorry, but I ain’t feelin’ that vibe.”

The room went a shade stiller. Vic’s hand lifted like it was about to make a point and then settled back, palm open on the desk. He nodded once, either to himself or to the ceiling’s fluorescent lights. “Okay,” he said after a beat. “Okay. What’s your vibe?”

Lila leaned forward, elbows on her knees, and the lightning bolts in her hair caught the light. She looked between them, and Malik could see the little crease at the edge of her mouth that showed up when she was thinking of something complicated. “He wants the verse to land,” she said. “The beat can be clean, it can be light—people can dance. But the part about the phone call? That’s the spine. Otherwise the hook is just words.”

Vic pinched the bridge of his nose, then exhaled through his nostrils. He was being asked to choose which part of himself to show. “I’m not trying to clip your wings, man,” he said, and Malik heard in his voice—a raggedness—something that might be a story about his own first record, and then his second, and then maybe nothing after that. “I’m trying to get you heard. Heard and paid.”

Malik nodded. They both were not wrong; that was the problem. He thought of the bus ride to the studio, how the driver had an Atlanta Braves keychain that swung when she hit a pothole, how he had stood and watched out the window and tried to calibrate the pulse of his body to the city so that the city wouldn’t jostle him out of himself. “I’m not tight about this,” he said, softer now. “I’m just—if it doesn’t have the bones, it collapses when everyone else walks away. That’s all I got.”

Vic looked at him for a long moment, and Malik saw him measuring all the things that weren’t in the room—the algorithms and the bills and the time it takes to edit a verse to please a committee who never shows up in person. Vic tapped a key that stopped the conga loop. He pulled up the session file with Malik’s verse and the still-crude hook that Lila had been singing under her breath in the hallway between takes.

“Let’s try it,” Vic said. He pushed the bowl of guitar picks out of the way and it slid into a tangle of XLR cables. “We do your verse, we keep it honest. We don’t cut the line about county. Then we brighten around it. Rhodes? Shimmer pad? You want a human bass? I got a guy next door who’s actually sober today.”

Lila grinned at that despite herself, and the room let out a tiny breath. The drum set down the hall stiffened into an actual beat, the sticks developing confidence under someone’s hands. Malik felt the sweat at his neck cool—not a relief so much as a recalibration.

He stepped to the mic and adjusted it up a notch. The metal was cold under his fingers. Vic held up his fingers—three, two, one—and Malik watched his own voice rise in the air as if it were a fragile thing that could only be held for so long under light. The headphones padded his ears, the world compressing. Lila hummed the shape of the hook behind him, under her breath, the melody that had felt silly earlier now threading itself into a form that made sense because it was tethered to something true.

He spit the verse. The light in the kitchen when his mother hung up. The shift in the house when bad news landed like a piece of furniture. The way he had learned to dance anyway—to dance in the living room when his cousin put on a bootleg CD, to dance at graduation because his grandmother had made it and wore the wrong shoes, to dance because the floor was the only place that would hold him. His mouth found the text as if it had been hiding in his teeth.

Vic’s hands moved over the board, adjusting slightly here, there; Lila came in with the hook, the not-quite-finished phrase, and Malik heard the way her voice had always been a bridge and not a compromise. Through the glass window that separated the live room from the control room, the hallway shimmered with its own life—passersby in hoodies, a woman with a keyboard under her arm, the studio owner in a flannel carrying a box of cables. Outside the pawn shop letters, a child dragged a plastic sword across the parking lot and made it spark against the curb.

They did another take. Then another. Between takes Vic was quiet, then said, “Can I try something?” and added the most modest shimmer to Lila’s chorus, a gentle echo like the idea of a second room wave-surfing underneath the first. Lila nodded. Malik listened. The harshness softened; the verse didn’t budge.

When they stopped, none of them said anything for a moment. The longest silence was relief. Malik took the headphones off and hung them with a care he hadn’t realized he had. He glanced at the window and saw his reflection again, and it was different only in that he recognized it fully without flinching.

Vic cleared his throat. “We’ll bounce it,” he said, and his voice was businesslike again, but quieter. “Let’s see what happens.”

“Okay,” Lila said. She put the insurance card back in the notebook and traced the crease of the page with her finger.

Malik looked at the neon treble clef and thought how silly it would be to judge a room by a lit symbol. The room had bones; they had decided what to hang on them. He sent his mother a text: Still in studio. Home late. Love you. As he pocketed his phone, the drum kit down the hall launched into something sure, and the room shook just slightly, like it had been reminded it was part of a building, a city, a life that went on whether or not anyone in it felt the right vibe right away.

query: 能帮忙讲讲区块链咋运作的，顺便说说它都能干点啥不？
response:
夜雨把门口的铁牌敲得丁丁当当，像谁在耐心地敲一口慢火炖着的汤。小店里暖黄的灯吊得低，蒸汽把玻璃糊得朦朦胧胧。靠窗的位置坐着两个陌生人：一个穿着反光雨衣的外卖小哥，护目镜还顶在额头；另一个灰色毛衣，眼镜片后是写代码写出来的细纹。

外卖小哥把安全帽往椅背一挂，嘬了一口热汤面，憋了半天，终于开口：“哥，能帮忙讲讲区块链咋运作的，顺便说说它都能干点啥不？”

面前的人抬眼看他，笑了笑，没有急着答，先把桌上的一次性筷套拆开，把几包酱油、醋、辣椒油像摆棋子一样排成一串。

“你看，”他用筷子尖在桌面水珠里划线，“当账本用。每一包就是一页账，每一页里写着今天谁给了谁多少钱，谁欠了谁一个肉夹馍。我不在乎这个账本是谁的——重要的是大家手里都有一份一模一样的复印件。你改不了我手里的，我也改不了你手里的。”

“这叫分布式账本？”外卖小哥试探着。

“行家呀。”他笑，“我们把很多新的交易攒一攒，打包成一页——一个‘块’。每块上头都要盖一个独一无二的‘章’，那章是根据这块里面所有交易算出来的指纹，叫哈希。然后这块和上一块的章连起来，一串接一串，就像把你送过的每一单用胶带接成了长串。谁想把中间一单改了，后面的章全都对不上，全城人手里的复印件都告诉你：不认。”

“那谁负责盖章呢？”

他把辣椒包往前一推：“这个就要靠‘共识’了。最早的一种叫工作量证明，大家拼谁先解出一道算术题，最先解出来的人有权把这一页贴上去，顺便得些奖励。这就像你们抢单——谁更快更拼，谁就领到这单。但这很耗电。后来还有权益证明——你拿出押金来当票，票多的人更有可能负责记账，效率高些，还有联盟链，几个可信机构一起投票确认。”

老板娘端上来一盘小菜，随口插一句：“你们年轻人的东西，折腾得我脑壳疼。”

灰毛衣摆摆手，继续说：“大家每抢到一次记账的权力，就把那页账贴到墙上，广播给全城。其他人看看有没有人试图夹带私货。如果没问题，就承认这页是正史。这样一来，账本是公开的、同步的、没个中心老板说了算。想改旧账？麻烦，你得比全城人还快，重新把后面的每一页都改过来，几乎不可能。”

外卖小哥把筷子一顿：“听着挺香。那它到底能干啥？除了拿来炒币？”

对面的人笑出声来：“‘炒’是把锅烧红。但锅不是为烧红而造的。你想啊，有了这样一本没人能随便改、大家都能核对的账本，能做的事就多了。举几个你身边的。比如跨境汇款，省去好多中间人，不用等几天，手续费少些。比如你们骑手的小费和奖励，写成智能合约——代码写明规则，谁跑了多少单，评价如何，到点自动结算，老板赖不掉。”

“还有，”他用空下来的辣椒包当“货”，挨个往“块”里推进，“供应链溯源。你以为这盘小菜里那碟花生米从哪来的？如果从农户把花生刨出来、收购、运输、仓储、加工、上架，每一步都在链上留个‘章’，谁更换了标签、谁中间少了环节，一查就清楚。做慈善也一样，每一笔捐款的去向透明，没那么容易糊涂账。创作者发歌发图，不靠平台抽成，卖数字所有权，粉丝买到的不只是一个文件，而是一个号码背后的确权。”

“游戏里道具能带出带入，换不同游戏认账；社区自治，大家投票用公钥签名，票箱透明但隐私可保护。还有碳排放、知识产权、数据要共享但又不好外泄，可以用一些更复杂的密码学，零知识证明，证明‘我满足条件’但不暴露细节。”

外卖小哥听得眼睛越来越亮。他低头看看自己滴水的鞋，“那我们骑手小群，还真可以搞个分配的小链？”

“理论上可以。你们建个规则简单的合约，谁抢单、谁超时、谁帮忙带东西，上链记账，月底按规则自动算钱。”灰毛衣顿了顿，“只是别把它当仙丹。它有短板。比如它不是万能真相机，现实里的数据怎么上链？你要依赖‘喂价’或‘预言机’，有人把秤故意压轻了，上链也只是记录了那个‘被压轻’的数字。公链速度慢、手续费在高峰期涨，工作量证明能耗大，监管也有要求。隐私方面，你不想让谁都知道你每个月赚了多少钱，就得用隐私方案，但那又复杂。”

“哦对，还有人性。”他指了指外卖小哥，“规则写得再好，合约也不过是程序，程序照着现实设计，现实里的力量关系就会照样反映进去。你们小链如果老板一个人拿了大多数‘票’，那还是老板说了算。”

老板娘把账单夹在筷筒边上，探头问：“还要加个煎蛋不？今天雨大，别饿着肚子。”

“加个。”外卖小哥笑着点头。

店外的雨更密了，玻璃上像有人用手指画了一棵树，又被风抹去。外卖小哥把安全帽拿起来，反复捏了捏那个有些变形的沿，“我就是想明白点。我们群里有人总说‘这玩意儿能让世界更公平’，也有人骂‘全是骗局’。我跑了一天，脑子里就剩下两个词：‘累’和‘信’。谁说的话能信，啥时候能到手，少折腾点心。”

灰毛衣想了想，把那串“酱包链”轻轻一推，“技术最终解决的是‘你不认识我，我们还能合作’的问题。它让‘信’变成了可以核验的‘算’，在陌生人之间搭了桥。但桥通向的人，是我们自己。公平不是写出一行代码就能掉下来的，它还需要你们愿意一起推那道门。”

他把餐巾纸撕了一小角，在上面写了两个字母和一串简短的链接，“这是一个开源的工具，开始可以模拟玩，不花钱。回去叫上你们群里几个想折腾的，先把规则写清楚。写清楚，比写漂亮更重要。”

外卖小哥小心翼翼把那纸塞进手机壳和保护套之间，像塞一张护身符。煎蛋叠在面上，黄澄澄的，像一轮小太阳。他猛吸了两口，站起来套上雨衣，朝灰毛衣点头：“谢了哥。万一哪天我们‘桥’修好了，你来吃我们群里的团建。到时候我请。”

门被他推开，雨气一下扑进来。他跨出一步，回头又问：“对了哥，你怎么懂这些？”

灰毛衣愣了愣，笑，说：“我以前管过一屋子服务器，后来觉得一直照顾机器，不如看看人。现在帮社区做些事，给老人教手机，也教几节‘啥叫可信’。”

门在他身后轻轻一响，风铃断断续续地响。店里又只剩下汤咕噜咕噜煮的声音。老板娘擦着桌子，把那几包酱料收起来，嘟囔：“啧，要不是你们摆，我都不知道这小包还能这么玩。”

灰毛衣把眼镜往上推了推，笑着摇头，眼神里却有一种专注，好像刚才那一串湿漉漉的线，被什么看不见的风，悄悄地接到了更远的地方。

query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成该请求。
response:
The hall smelled faintly of disinfectant and sour green tea, a tang that clung to the steel chairs and the dull, tiled floor. A row of ficus trees leaned toward the glass like tired sentries. At the far end, above counters divided by frosted partitions, a red LED board crawled in polite monosyllables: A103, please proceed to Window 4. Somewhere, a baby released a thin wail and was immediately shushed; a security guard wrote, with exaggerated focus, neat characters on a sign that read Please silence your phone.

Lin Qian shifted the weight of the plastic accordion folder from one arm to the other, felt her palm print against the grit on its spine. The folder had been cleaned the night before, wiped down with a hand towel until it squeaked, all the corners aligned; it was swollen now with proof of address, rental contract, social insurance printouts, the school’s letter, her own pen-scratched notes. A little photo of her son, four years old and solemn in his yellow raincoat, peeked from a sleeve. She pinched the binder clip until it warmed under her fingers.

On the LED board, A101 leapt to A102, then A103, flipping with impersonal cheer. When her number appeared, it sounded a tone like bottled lightning, and she startled, feeling suddenly primitive, neck flexed. Window 4.

Behind the glass sat a woman whose age could have been anywhere from thirty to fifty, her hair pinned into a bun with a rhinestone clip that formed a tiny bow. Next to the keyboard, a thermos leaned against a stack of forms, its lid off; goji berries floated in the tea like small eyes.

“你好，” Lin Qian said, sliding her folder through the slot. She had rehearsed this hello, her voice neither too pleading nor too sharp. “I’m here to transfer my son’s hukou to this district for school placement. I called last week; they told me to bring proof of rental and my social insurance contributions.”

The clerk—her name badge read Zhu Xia—nodded without looking up, fingers already guiding the folder’s gut, pulling out papers, noses of pages brushing the counter. The computer screen glowed lake-blue, its bureaucratic forms filling themselves with a twitch of mouse and keystroke. Ms. Zhu’s nails were short and unpainted; a bit of fuzz clung to her cuff. She cleared her throat.

“Company name?” she asked in Mandarin, glancing once at Lin, then back at the screen.

“Qingsong Logistics. I have the stamp here.” Lin set the stamped employment verification in the rectangle of light that cut across the desk. Outside, in the glass, she could see her own face faintly: the new lines around her mouth like fish hooks tugging, her hair clipped back too tightly for the midday heat. She realized she had been smiling, and let it drop.

Ms. Zhu flicked through the pages. As she found the social insurance printouts, she paused, and her mouth closed over a thought. She took a sip of tea, the berries bumping the rim.

“You have eleven months,” she said after a beat. She pushed the printout back with a fingernail, the way someone might return a shell found on the sand that looks smooth until you turn it. “The policy requires twelve consecutive months in the district.”

“I know.” Lin inhaled, felt it catch. “I missed one month last year when my previous company… there was that payment issue. But they said, if I could show the school’s letter, and the rental—”

Ms. Zhu’s expression didn’t harden; it had not softened to begin with. It was amphibian and patient, a function, a face that could absorb the unknown densities of strangers without breaking. She turned the screen slightly, but not toward Lin—more as if aligning it with a grid only she could see. The LED cheeped with another number, patient, polite.

“Policy is policy,” Ms. Zhu said. The words were a key that fit inside the lock of this building. “If there’s a gap, even one month, it restarts. Or you can apply under category three, but category three requires property ownership. Do you have property?”

Lin swallowed. “No.”

“We can’t process it without the twelve months. Or the property certificate. Otherwise…” Ms. Zhu tapped a key, and a phrase bloomed on the screen, then on the small paper display beside the keyboard, where stock responses sat like pinned butterflies. She turned it, almost gently, toward Lin. On it, a sentence glowed in solid, evenly weighted characters:

抱歉，我无法协助完成该请求。

The sentence was both apology and wall. Its surface was polished enough that Lin could see herself again, warped—a woman squared by the lights. In another life, she thought, there might have been a way to fold around this, to be made of the right kind of paper. Behind her, someone cleared his throat; a toddler banged the slats of a stroller with a plastic bottle. The security guard picked up his thermos and took a long pull as if he were drinking from a lake.

Lin felt a rising in her chest, a fine trembling that manifested, embarrassingly, at her jaw. “He starts school in September,” she said. “The neighborhood school told me to get this done before the end of August. We’re already in August.”

Ms. Zhu’s fingers wove together on the desk. “I know,” she said, and the “I know” was surprisingly human, not pre-written. “I also have a child. Eight. We spent three mornings last summer queuing like this.” She looked down, then up. “But the system… if I input it like this, the review will reject it. They will check the months. They will call me. I will be the one who has done wrong.”

It was the kindest refusal possible, Lin thought, and she hated it because it made her want to be reasonable. She thought of Yuanyuan’s backpack hanging from a chair, the plastic dinosaur charm smooth where he touched it over and over. She thought of the hands on the clock at the school’s gate. She thought of the way she had once measured him against the doorframe and traced a pencil tick with the date beside it: proof that something in their rented world could be claimed as theirs.

She smoothed the hash of her notes with the palm of her hand, making the ink shine. “Is there a way to… to make up the month?”

Ms. Zhu sighed—softly, so softly it might have been a breath. Her eyes flicked left and right; in the corner, a supervisor in a crisp shirt typed loudly, performative. “Sometimes,” she said, words in a lower key, “companies can issue a supplementary payment. If they pay for the missing month now, the system shows twelve months. But it has to be real, not fake. And it takes five working days to update.”

“My old company closed,” Lin said. “They stopped answering the phone. Their stamps are in a drawer somewhere.”

“Then go to the social insurance center,” Ms. Zhu said, picking up a pen that had a cracked grip. She pulled a post-it from a stack—yellow, already curling—and wrote in tidy characters: Window 7, ask for Chen. She slid it back. “He might help you with a voluntary payment. I cannot promise. And for school—if you go to the education bureau with the school’s letter and your proof of residence, sometimes they will place the child temporarily, pending documentation. But that is them. Not us.”

Lin held the post-it as if it were a leaf saved between pages. She could feel the world narrowing to paths on a map, each line new, plausible, ridiculous. The LED board chimed A104. Someone nearby muttered, not unkindly: come on, miss, the line.

She looked up at Ms. Zhu and found something there—not sympathy, exactly, but the recognition that the two of them lived under the same sky. It was startling, to be seen.

“Thank you,” Lin said, and meant it in a way that made her throat close.

One corner of Ms. Zhu’s mouth lifted, the smallest movement. “Don’t thank me yet,” she said. “It is just a way to walk, not a door.”

Lin took the folder back. The papers felt heavier now, as if each sheet had absorbed the weight of the morning. She slid the photo of her son so that it faced out; he looked directly at her, eyes that had not yet learned the shape of refusal.

As she stepped away from the window, the LED chirped again, mercilessly cheerful. A104, please proceed to Window 4. Behind her, in the frog-throat register of the printer, paper fed itself, and the small display on Ms. Zhu’s desk went dark, then lit with the default screen: a nature scene, mountains painted perfunctorily blue. The sentence she had seen still hung in her mind not just as a denial but as a line around which a day could bend.

In the corridor, the light was softer. Lin paused by the ficus, its wide leaves trembling in the conditioned wind, and read the post-it again. Window 7, ask for Chen. The letters were ordinary and exact. She pressed the adhesive to the back of her hand so she wouldn’t lose it, took a breath, swallowed her annoyance and her fear, and turned toward the other wing of the building where the social insurance counters hummed with their own slow music.

query: 咋整突发急性肠胃炎？咋预防？简单整两句！
response:
夜雨刚停，巷子尽头的小夜市又亮起了油灯。烤串的烟雾缠着红纸灯笼，一台吱吱作响的社区流动广播车停在豆腐脑摊旁，主持人是穿着雨衣的老宋，胸前别着一块写着“健康小喇叭”的牌子。人群里一个外卖小哥捂着肚子，脸色发白，旁边卖藕片的婶子赶紧递上温水，嘴里嘀咕：“这天儿一凉，肠胃就闹腾。”

老宋举起话筒，冲着围拢的人群半认真半打趣地问了一句：“咋整突发急性肠胃炎？咋预防？简单整两句！”被他点到的，是在摊位后头支着伞的林医生，她拿下口罩，抿着一口热茶，给了大家一个稳妥的眼神，清清嗓子回道：“急性肠胃炎来得快，先别硬撑，尽快补液（温水或口服补液盐）、清淡饮食、休息；若高烧不退、频繁呕吐脱水、血便或剧烈腹痛，立刻就医。预防就三件事：饭前便后洗手，食物彻底加热不吃生冷，饮水干净少贪嘴街边不洁摊。”

风从巷口吹过，把话筒里的尾音挂在了灯笼上。外卖小哥点点头，慢慢坐下，婶子把藕片收了火，递来一碗清粥。老宋关了广播，朝众人一拱手：“都散了吧，记住林医生的两句，胃这东西，得哄着它。”灯影摇晃里，摊子又热闹起来，雨后的城像刚醒来的胃，被安抚得乖顺了些。

query: What are music's main three components?
response:
The radiator under the window hissed and clanked in small, uneven bursts, like it was trying to keep time and failing. Mr. Alvarez rested his nylon-string guitar on his knee and tapped the heel of his hand against the wood, producing a dull thump that made dust tremble along the cinderblock wall. The after-school music room at the community center smelled faintly of disinfectant and crayons. A poster of Duke Ellington curled at one corner near the bulletin board. Outside, the light was already sinking, turning the frosted street beyond the wire mesh into a dim watercolor.

“What are music’s main three components?” Janelle asked, squinting at the whiteboard where Mr. Alvarez had drawn a lopsided staff and one lonely treble clef. She was small and very serious, the kind of kid who wrote her name along the edges of her notebooks in tiny block letters and always showed up five minutes early.

Mr. Alvarez glanced up from the guitar, his mouth lifting at one corner. He had been handsome once, you could tell—good bones, generous hands—but he wore his years like a coat, easy and loose. “You’re starting with the big questions today,” he said, and he tipped his head toward the row of folding chairs. Five kids watched him, hoodies pulled tight, backpacks slumped at their feet. The radiator hissed again, a soft cymbal.

“It’s important,” Janelle said. “The book says a lot of different things. And on YouTube it’s not the same.” She tugged the sleeve of her sweater and blushed as if she’d asked something too ambitious.

Mr. Alvarez nodded. “Fair enough.” He laid the guitar flat and tapped its body again, more evenly now. Thump, thump, thump. “There’s the way musicians argue about this—some will say form, or texture, or timbre. All are true in their ways. But if you go back to the basics—the skeleton you build everything on—you get three. Rhythm, melody, harmony.”

Malik, lanky and sleepy-eyed at the end of the row, stretched his legs into the aisle. “Sounds like something my cousin would put on his mixtape. ‘Harmony featuring Melody and Rhythm,’” he said, and a few of the students snorted.

Mr. Alvarez chuckled. “I’d listen to that. Okay, listen.” He started clapping softly. Clap, clap, clap. He pointed at the radiator, which stuttered in its uneven way. “Rhythm is time, the heartbeat. It’s the grid. You feel it in your chest before you hear it. Your steps on the sidewalk, your grandma’s washing machine, the train. You can have rhythm without anything else.” He clapped once and stopped. The silence after seemed like a pocket the room fell into.

Malik began to clap along, but too fast. Mr. Alvarez shook his head. “No, hold it. One, two, three, four.” They clapped together, the sound aligning, the messy room cohering around the pattern. Even the radiator, for an instant, sounded less like a failing machine and more like a percussionist with a sense of humor.

“Now melody,” he said, picking up the guitar. He plucked three notes, simple and ascending. The sound was soft, a little buzzy from cheap strings. “Melody is the line, the story. It’s what you hum when the song is stuck in your head and you don’t remember the words. You can sing it alone, and it makes sense.” He played the notes again, then another set that curled back on itself like a question. Janelle’s eyes followed his fingers as if they could read the pattern.

“And harmony,” he continued. His fingers shifted, forming a basic C chord. The air changed with it, warmed, colored. He held it, let the chord ring, then moved to G, then to F. The kids’ heads tilted, instinctively. “Harmony is what happens when you stack sounds—when pitches agree, disagree, lean on each other, push and pull. It fills the space around the melody. It’s the company you keep.”

Janelle looked down at her lap. “So rhythm is the time. Melody is the—story. Harmony is the—” She frowned, searching.

“The conversation,” Mr. Alvarez said softly. He glanced at her and felt the familiar tug, the urge to make it both simple enough and big enough. “Here,” he added, standing. “Everyone up. Don’t worry, you won’t have to sing solo, Malik.”

Groans, rustle of chairs. He moved to the front, set the guitar on a chair, and gave the kids assignments with his hands. “You two,” he said to Tasha and Omar, who always shared a pencil against all rules, “you’re my rhythm section. Clap like we did. Not too loud, just steady. You,” he pointed to Malik, “hum what I play. You don’t need words. And you, Janelle”—he paused—“you hold one note under Malik. Like this.” He sang an A, pure and sustained, then smiled with apology. “If that’s too high, drop down. Find a place in the middle that doesn’t hurt.”

He plucked a melody, easy and sweet, like the first line of a lullaby. Tasha and Omar began clapping, tentatively at first, then with more intent. Malik hummed, voice surprisingly tender for a boy who rolled his eyes as a reflex. Janelle set her shoulders and found a pitch, steady and bright, her voice thin as glass but unwavering.

For a moment the room was something else. The radiator fitted itself into their measure. The fluorescent lights buzzed at a pitch that almost worked. Mr. Alvarez felt the old ache in his chest, the one that comes with remembering you are useful, and let the kids carry the thing. He moved to adjust with small gestures, a conductor without a baton: a nod to slow the claps, a finger to lift the melody, a raised palm when Janelle’s note wobbled, then settled again.

“Now hear it,” he murmured. “If you take away the clapping, what happens?”

He dropped his hand. Tasha and Omar stopped. The humming continued, a little untethered, sinking into something that wanted to be a puddle.

“It still exists,” he said. “Melody and harmony have shape. But the floor is gone.”

He clapped again, gently. The humming lifted, found its balance.

“If you take away the hum,” he told Malik, who shrugged and fell quiet, “we have rhythm and a held pitch—maybe a drone, a ground. It’s a different mood. Less story, more landscape.”

He looked at Janelle. “If you let your note go,” he said.

She released it, lips parting, face flushed. The room grew thinner. He played the melody on his guitar, let the claps hold it.

“See? Rhythm, melody, harmony,” he said, not as a list but a reminder. “They’re simple words for complicated friends. Even when you think you forgot one, it’s hiding somewhere. In the way the notes are spaced, the way they’re colored.”

Malik kicked at the metal foot of his chair with a sneaker. “So I can make a beat on my lunch table and that’s music?”

“That’s rhythm,” Mr. Alvarez said. “Add a whistle or a rap line, now you’ve got melody. If your friend slaps along in fifths, you’ve got harmony. You can build a lot from very little. People have been since forever.”

Janelle lifted her hand, cautious. “What about timbre?” she asked. “Mrs. Liu said timbre matters.”

Mr. Alvarez’s smile widened. “A very good word. That’s the color of the sound—how your voice is different from Malik’s, how this cheap guitar sounds different than a grand piano. It’s not one of the main three, but it makes you care.” He ran his fingers over the strings, a dry whisper. “We’ll get to it. We’ll get to all of it.”

The radiator sputtered and went quiet, as if satisfied. Outside, somebody dragged a shovel along the sidewalk, scraping ice. Mr. Alvarez sat back down and lifted the guitar again.

“From the top,” he said. “But this time, I want you to listen for the way these pieces lean on one another. Rhythm, melody, harmony. Not words in a book. Things with weight. Things you can hold.”

Janelle adjusted the collar of her sweater like she was preparing for a cold wind and then held her note, proud and uncertain. The room gathered itself around the simple clapping, the cheap guitar, the winter dark behind wire. In the small space between sound and silence, they made something you could find again later, with your fingers or with your mouth or just your heart beating quietly, counting time.
