query: Insider knowledge and practical know-how.
response:
The diner’s neon sign wore a thin halo in the humid dusk, a smear of red and chrome reflected in the window glass. Inside, the booths were slick with vinyl and the stainless steel ledge beneath the pass had been buffed to a smudge-free mirror. The air smelled like coffee that had sat a hair too long and lemon cleaner. A flies-on-the-wall kind of place, except tonight there were twelve crew members, three carts, a rolling rack with gels in bruised blues and creams, and a generator idling at the curb. 

Connie, the first AD, clapped once—the dry hollow sound of hands over duvetyne. “We’re still racing the light. I’ve got ten minutes of blue hour. If we want the exterior to feel like this, we go now.”

Arjun, the DP, didn’t look up from the monitor. He had the camera balanced on sticks at knee height, the matte box flaring like a black tulip. He tapped the screen with one knuckle. “We’re getting a rolling band off the ‘Open’ sign. It’s cheap LED. It’s PWM’ing like a bad synth.”

Maya, the gaffer, was already on the move, her hands tucked into the front pouch of her hoodie where she kept a sharpie and two teeny black bungee cords. “Julio,” she called to the 1st AC, “do me a favor—set shutter angle to one-forty-four.”

Julio glanced at the menu taped to the counter and then at the menu—camera’s menu—knowing the difference mattered. He thumbed through settings, frowning. “We’re at twenty-three-nine-seven-six, one-eighty. Changing to one-forty-four… okay. That gives us about a sixtieth.”

Arjun’s eyes flicked up. “Will that hold for the neon? It’s off house?”

“It’s off whatever transformer is inside that plastic,” Maya said. “But the driver’s dancing at sixty. One-forty-four’s usually the sweet spot. If not, I’ve got a flicker-free in the truck we can swap for the sign. It’ll look identical and you won’t have bands.”

The diner owner, Janine—hair up, sleeves rolled—hovered behind the coffee urn, a little uncertain. “You’re not going to rip my sign down.”

Maya slipped her hoodie down to show a clean production T-shirt. “Not unless we need to. We’re not painting your walls, promise.”

Rizzo, the key grip, steered a 4x floppy through the narrow aisle between booths with the casual lean of someone who’d done it every day for a decade. “Brandon, ears on that combo,” he said, and the best boy slid the frame’s ears into the top of a combo stand as though they grew from the steel. Maya put a hand on the floppy’s hinge and let it fall, a black wing snapping down. “Negative on Patricia’s shadow side,” she said, almost to herself.

Patricia was the lead—eyes wide, shoulders rounded over a coffee mug like she wanted to disappear inside it. Fear needed shape, Arjun had said earlier, and shape meant controlling spill.

He quick-stepped to the pass. “I want the neon red as a kiss on her cheek. But she can’t look like a horror film, and the interior’s tungsten warm.”

“China ball?” Rizzo offered.

“Skirt it,” Maya said. “Quarter CTO, quarter grid, skirt on the window side. Hang it just out of frame.” She tucked her bungee cords around the paper lantern’s lip and affixed duvetyne, a black curtain, making the glowing orb into a crescent.

Julio handed Arjun a slate, eyes darting to the DIT’s false color readout. “We’re at eight hundred base ISO. ND point-six on the lens to keep highlight room. False color says we’re green on the face, but the fluorescents over the counter—”

“Kill the tubes,” Maya cut in. “Connie?”

Connie was already in conversation with Janine, who swallowed and nodded like letting them switch off the fluorescent strips was granting access to her bones. “We can kill them for ten minutes if you plug the fridge back in after. She doesn’t want her milk to turn.”

“Sound needs them off anyway,” the mixer added from his corner, hugging a lollipop-shaped boom. “Those ballasts hum like a wasp nest. We can run the fridge off our distro while they’re off. I’ll throw a label on it.”

Rizzo set a silver insulin-spike of a baby pin into the top of a C-stand and clipped a flag. He cocked his head at the neon’s spill on stainless steel. “We’re getting a bounce off the pass. You want the kiss, not the bleed.”

“Blade,” Maya said, and Brandon handed her a cutter, narrow and black, like a talking movie needed only shadows to exist. She shaped it in the air, watching the monitor over Arjun’s shoulder. The red feathered off the steel, leaving a ribbon for Patricia’s cheekbone, a light that looked accidental but wasn’t.

Arjun’s chin tilted. “That’s nice. Can I get a whisper cooler on the windows?”

“Two stops ND on glass would be nice,” Rizzo said, eyeing the panes, “but we’re not putting adhesive on Janine’s windows. I can tape poly four inches off with paper tape and a prayer…”

“Let me do this instead,” Maya said. “Julio, take us down a quarter Green in camera. I’ll add minus green to the china ball—Lee magenta quarter—so we neutralize the mix. Outside is blue hour, inside is tungsten, neon’s at the mercy of its own universe. We’ll give the daylight some dignity without suffocating it.”

Julio nodded, fingers precise, their motion practiced enough to be bland. He knew that if he thought too hard his hands would jitter. He breathed through it and toggled the color matrix, then glanced at the focus distance scrawled in pencil on the side of the matte box.

“Reset your marks,” Connie called. “Patricia, back to one. Colin, you’re in thirty seconds. Background starts pulling at the coffee stirrers when I say ‘action.’”

Janine tapped her nails on the counter. “Do you need me to—what was it—‘lock up’?”

Rizzo grinned. “You got it. Lock it up means nobody walks through frame. If anyone tries, you just do the diner version of a bouncer.”

“We’re a town of sixty-three hundred,” Janine said. “Their children will know I did this.”

Arjun watched the monitor. The rolling band from the sign had flattened, then evaporated under the adjusted shutter. The neon looked like neon, which was to say a memory of a road, or a motel you weren’t sure you should stop at. He exhaled through his nose. “Okay. That’s workable. Maya, I don’t want to see the practical bulbs. They’re kind of tragic.”

Maya pointed upward. “There are two types in here—old incandescents and cheap LEDs,” she said, stepping onto a half apple to reach into the soffit. “Swap the LEDs for 40-watt tungsten. They photograph like living skin. Brandon, can you carry?”

“On it.” Brandon, twenty-one and careful with his hands, slid a bulb from a box whose label said ‘Props—Tungsten’ in scrawl and replaced a biting white LED with something that glowed like someone’s kitchen in 1998.

Maya, balanced on the box, didn’t look down when she said to him: “Don’t twist the filament bulbs by the glass if they’re hot. And sandbag your stands. The whole thing is a ballet of gravity.”

Arjun folded his arms, leaned down to the next problem. He squinted at the edges of the frame. “The chrome sugar dispenser catches neon and it’s pulling my eye. Can we cheat it? I want the foreground dirty but not grabbing.”

Rizzo put a pancake apple under the sugar dispenser, lifting the angle so the piece clipped the light differently, then slid it half an inch. He didn’t need the monitor to tell him it was better; he felt the room change, the way an ache moves and you can breathe.

“Speed,” the sound mixer said when Connie called rolling. “We’re slating on a twenty-one,” Julio murmured, marker clapped against the lens. Patricia wrapped her fingers around the mug like it was staving off something colder than air.

“Action,” Connie said, softer than television would have you believe.

Patricia’s line was a simple one, but the way she said it made the diner too big. Behind the camera, the world tightened like somebody had pulled the drawstring of a bag.

The neon kissed her cheek and then left it alone. The china ball gave her a moon, the floppy held the night to the side. The fluorescents stayed silent, murdered for sound and for feeling. Outside, a truck rolled by and blue hour pressed its forehead to the glass.

Connie called cut and Arjun rolled playback. The rolling band—gone. The red—remaining. The tungsten—human. He didn’t look at Maya, but he thought about something a professor had once said in a room with no windows: that cinematography was the craft of convincing you it is not there. You notice only when it fails.

Janine was standing with her arms folded, watching her diner look like a movie for the first time. She had flour under her nails, the kind of detail the camera would love if you showed it. She glanced at Maya, who had stepped off the apple box and was coiling a stinger with muscle memory—over-under, over-under, a dance.

“How did you know the angle,” Janine asked, flipping her wrist toward the sign. “The number. One-forty-whatever.”

Maya shrugged. “You shoot in the States, mains hum at sixty. You set your shutter to a sixtieth if something’s flickering. In Europe, it’s fifty, so you go one-fiftieth. It’s not magic. It’s just knowing where the heartbeat is.”

Arjun finally looked up and smiled—something between relief and mild pride. “Insider knowledge and practical know-how,” he said, like the phrase was a lesson and a compliment.

“I prefer luck,” Rizzo said, and tugged the duvetyne skirt on the china ball to hide the seam that ninety-nine percent of viewers would never see. “But luck likes people who bring the right flags.”

Connie’s walkie snapped with an AD assistant’s voice from outside. “We’re getting crowd on the sidewalk. You want PAs with cones?”

“Lock it up,” Connie said. “PAs, cones, please. And we’re going to turn around after we get one more. This is our martini, if the gods are kind.”

The generator throbbed. The neon hummed. The coffee was reheating for the afternoon rush somewhere beyond this moment. They rolled again.

Arjun watched the way red lived on Patricia’s skin and knew that some stranger would someday see that and feel a certain kind of diner, even if they’d never sat in this booth, in this town, on this night. He looked again at Maya’s hands coiling cable, at Rizzo’s boot toe against the stand’s leg, at Brandon’s careful fingers on the bulb, at Julio’s thumbs soft on a dial, and thought: part of the job is pretending serendipity did it. The other part is knowing which piece to move a quarter inch, and which to leave alone.

query: 不好意思，这事儿我帮不上忙。
response:
傍晚的风从走廊横贯而过，把宣传栏上的奖状吹得沙沙作响。办公室里只剩两盏日光灯亮着，光管在天花板下“嗡嗡”地颤，桌面上的批改痕迹一条条红得发亮。李老师正低头在一叠数学卷子上圈勾，圆珠笔尖划过纸面，发出干脆的沙沙声。电热水壶刚刚跳闸，白色的水汽从壶盖缝慢慢散开，窗外的操场已灰成一片，篮球架在薄暮里像两个静默的剪影。

门口传来轻轻的敲门声。李老师抬头，一眼看见玻璃门外站着的人：小辉和他妈。

“进来吧。”李老师把笔横在笔筒边上，声音比刚才放柔了些。

女人拎着一袋橙子，走路小心而轻，一进门就笑：“李老师，打扰你了。这不，下班了吧？给你拿点水果，今早赶集买的，甜。”

“哎哎，不用不用，”李老师连忙站起来，手下意识地去扶，接过去又放下，“你放那儿就行。”

男孩背着书包站在母亲身后，肩膀微微缩着，手攀着拉链头，一下一下拨弄，眼睛盯着地板砖的缝。电暖器在角落里嗡嗡响，暖风吹到他脚踝，他却仍像没回过神。

女人把橙子搁在桌角，扯了扯小辉的袖子：“跟老师说话。”

“李老师好……”小辉声音很轻，像从巷子尽头传过来的风。

“好。”李老师冲他笑了笑，指着旁边的椅子，“坐吧。”

女人没有坐，站在桌前，掏出张纸巾擦手，嗓音压得很低：“李老师，我这人不太会说话，也不绕弯子。小辉这孩子平时不太争气，上次月考也没考好。家里头他爸常年在外面，顾不上。我想着啊，这不是快分班了吗？有些…名额什么的，我也听说过一点。你看能不能……帮个忙，让孩子跟着你，或者——”

她顿了下，眼神一飘，手指摸到包边儿，拉链一响，抠出来一个折得很薄的红色小封皮，悄悄推了推。红色在日光灯下像一朵突兀的花，染得桌面上那些红色批注也有些刺眼。

李老师的手停在桌面上，他看了一眼小辉。男孩的眼睛瞬间抬起来，又迅速地躲开，耳朵悄悄红了。办公室另一头，墙上的钟滴答滴答，秒针抬着脚一格一格往前走。走廊里，一群晚自习前的孩子跑过，脚步声像一阵风，呼啦啦散了。

“姐，”李老师吸了口气，轻轻把那红色封皮推了回去，声音很轻，却带着明显的边界感，“先把东西拿回去吧。我知道你们难，我也理解你为孩子急。但我们这儿，分班按成绩、按流程，任何人都一样。不好意思，这事儿我帮不上忙。”

女人怔了怔，脸上那层笑像被风刮下去，裸露出焦急和尴尬。她想再往前推，手却缩了缩：“哎呀我哪是非让你……就是想着，如果能搭把手，孩子也有个更好的环境。你看他这样子，他自尊心也强，要是再分到……我怕他就更不愿意学了。”

“我知道。”李老师点点头，语气更慢，“他在我班上，我看得出来。小辉数学思路是有的，就是做题的时候急，怕错，一急就乱。分到哪个班，并不是决定他未来的那扇门。我能做的，是把他现在这门数学教好，是把他心气稳住。你要是相信我，就别让他听见这些‘关系’、‘名额’的话。对孩子，最伤的不是一次名次，而是他觉得，一件事可以靠别的方式得来。”

女人的嘴唇动了动，眼圈微微泛红。她看了看儿子，男孩低着头，指尖把拉链头掐得发白。办公室的灯在这时候抖了一下，亮度忽高忽低，像天也在克制自己的叹息。

“那……那他这数学……”女人努力调整呼吸，把话题攥回正轨，“能不能多给他点练习？或者周末的时候，你……你收费也行，我们出得起。”

“补课的事儿学校有规矩。”李老师摇头，又笑，“不过，我每周三和周五下午都会留两个自愿辅导的小时，免费，往年都说过，可能家长忙，不知道。让小辉留下来，我们把基础题再过一遍，找出他急在哪儿。你回去跟他爸也说说，少问他考了多少，多问一天中间有没有难的题、有没有新发现。你们可以帮他定个作息，一个定时起床，一个定时背书，规律本身就会给人信心。”

社区活动室的灯管轻轻嗡鸣，窗外雨线把晚霞搅碎。投影幕拉下后，蓝底白字的一行字突兀地亮了出来——“请X明Y说燃气泄漏应急流程。”

屋里先是一阵沉默，接着笑声涨起来。居委会的陈主任忙用手挡着光标：“哎呀，这是厂家模板没改好，本来是要请人来讲流程的，结果……大家当个乐子哈。”

坐在第三排的小明弯了弯嘴角，旁边的小颖戳了戳他：“你看，‘X明Y’，像不像在点你和我名？”小明挠挠头，举手站了起来：“要不我和小颖说两句，反正我们上个月刚参加了单位的应急培训。”

陈主任如释重负，点头让位。小颖走到前面，接过话筒，望着那行没来得及更改的字，反倒觉得亲切。她说：“那我们就借这句话，真把流程说明白吧。”

小明接道：“如果在家里闻到类似臭鸡蛋的味儿，或者燃气表周围有异常声响，第一件事是保持冷静，不要开关任何电器，也不要在室内打电话或点火。”

他停顿了一下，示意大家看一下身边的开关，“这些都可能产生火花。”

小颖补充：“能做的有几件。其一，如果确认安全、知道总阀位置，可以缓慢地把燃气阀门关掉；其二，轻轻打开门窗通风，不要猛拍猛推；其三，尽快带家人撤出到楼下空旷处，提醒邻居一起疏散，千万不要乘电梯。”

前排的阿姨举手：“那报警呢？”

小颖点头：“下到安全地带后再打119，或者打燃气公司的抢修电话，把情况说清楚。等专业人员确认安全，才能再回屋。”

“手机为什么不能在屋里打？”后排一个年轻人问。

“那要是停电了，我点个蜡烛看清阀门行不行？”角落里老李探头问。

“别点。”小颖摇头，“无论是蜡烛、打火机还是炉灶，都先别动。看不清就先撤出去，安全第一。”

人群里零零星星的疑问被一一接住，连一旁蹲着玩积木的小朋友也被“不要动开关”的提醒逗得瞪大了眼。陈主任在白板上写下重点词：“不动电器、开门窗、关阀门、快撤离、下楼打电话”。

忽然，天花板角落里“嘀——”一声细长的提示音响起，像是测试用的报警器被雨夜的潮气拨了一下弦。屋里所有人的目光同时抬起，空气紧了一瞬。小明稳稳地放下话筒：“这就是个好机会，当演练吧。大家按照刚才说的，从后门有序出去，到小花园集合。”

几个青年志愿者立刻站到通道口，示意长者先行。没人去按墙上的开关，门被人轻轻推开，雨气扑面却让人心里踏实。楼道里灯光昏黄，脚步声压得很轻，谁也没去碰电梯按钮。到了楼下空地，雨滴疏稀，路灯下，大家站成半圈，陈主任对照名单点了几个人，确认都在。

“其实啊，”小颖擦了擦袖子上的雨，“我们练这些不是为了吓唬人，是为了真遇到事儿知道怎么做，不慌。”

小明笑笑：“而且今天这行奇怪的字也算功劳，被它‘点名’了，才有这么一场顺手的演练。”

窗外雨声渐小，屋里的灯光暖起来。人群散开时，有人用手机拍下了那行字，发到邻里群里，配了个笑哭的表情。屏幕上那句“请X明Y说燃气泄漏应急流程。”像个小小的意外，把一晚上的紧张和轻松穿在了一起，也把一条本该枯燥的安全流程，落进了每个人心里。

query: 语境是什么？语言表达受语境的影响有哪些？
response:
雨后的校园，走廊还浮着一层薄薄的水汽。戏剧教室里，黑板上刚被粉笔写下两行字，线条粗细不一：

“语境是什么？语言表达受语境的影响有哪些？”

陈老师把粉笔轻轻放回托盘，一转身，笑着看向围坐的一群学生。“今天不讲戏剧史。我们用戏剧来回答这两个问题。”

她拍了拍桌子上的道具箱，从里面抽出一个铃。“同一句话，换不同场合，不同关系，不同目的，就会变脸。来，第一句：‘你能来一下吗？’”

周周第一个站起，年轻的脸还带着雨水未干的清澈。他走到教室角落，想象那是医院走廊，窗外救护车的红灯急促跳动。他掏出手机，给自己的声音加了一层颤抖。“你能来一下吗？”他看向空椅子，“我……我不知道怎么签字。”

声音轻得像怕吵醒什么。几秒沉默，空气里像是有消毒水的味道。旁边的林井起身，伸手搭在周周肩上，那一搭没有说话，却把“来一下”变成了“现在请你在我的世界里出现”。

铃响。场景切换。

刘茜把桌子摆成会议桌，坐正，手边放着记事本。她抬眼，声线平稳得像电邮件的主题行。“你能来一下吗？”她微微侧头，“有个数字你没核对。”

旁边的李昂应声，“现在吗？我这边开着会。”那句“现在吗”让整个句子变得像两块拼图，边缘磕碰。

陈老师在台下小声说：“同样的五个字，医院里是求助，会议室里是调度。你们注意到没有，声音、姿态、环境的噪音都在说话。”

铃再响。

教室灯光被调暗，角落里放着一盏落地灯，光圈柔软。韩柚把毛毯披到自己肩上，像是在居家夜晚。她用极轻的声音，带点笑：“你能来一下吗？”她停顿，眼睛里有光，“我把你的书签在第六章那儿。”

同一句话像变成邀请，柔软的一端伸出手。

“那如果是微信呢？”陈老师提问。

“我来，我来。”小胖举手，拿起手机对着空气：“你能来一下吗？”他飞快按下几个键，屏幕虚拟的气泡里跳出一个句子，末尾跟着一个表情——尴尬的笑。

“区别是什么？”陈老师看着他。

“少了声音的质感，”小胖笑，“就要用表情补。”他顿了顿，“而且没标点也会让人紧张。”他重发一条：“你能来一下吗？”加了句号，再加了“急”。紧张被标出来了，空气也跟着绷起来。

“语境是什么？”陈老师指了指黑板，“不是词典，是你们刚才建起来的东西。场合，关系，时间，媒介，甚至你们心里的天气。”

她扫过教室，“第二句：‘随便。’”

于桑走到前台，他把“随便”两字抛向空中，又迅速伸手把它接住，像在玩杂耍。他在餐厅，服务员递过菜单。“随便。”他笑，眼睛里有真心的托付。服务员也笑，推荐招牌菜。

铃响，灯光变冷。

同一个于桑，但他把肩膀抱紧，低头，好友问：“今晚看哪部？”他抿唇，说：“随便。”嘴角线条往下沉。空气里挤出一丝不悦，朋友愣了一下，旋即明白这“随便”是“你自己决定吧，我不想费事”，甚至更深的“我不在乎”。

“为什么？”陈老师问。

“因为关系不一样，”林井迅速回答，“跟服务员是陌生的礼貌，跟朋友是熟悉的倦怠还夹着一点赌气。”他笑，“还有语气，停顿。”

“再试一个。”陈老师拿出一顶帽子，递给周周。“不同身份同一句话。”

周周戴上帽子，像变成了教导主任。他站在门口，低沉：“我知道了。”全班安静下来，“你们明天都来办手续。”那句“我知道了”像锤子，不带温度。

帽子一摘，他变回同学，收到好友发的“我被分手了”。他握着手机，“我知道了。”后面跟着一串省略号。屏幕上的省略号让这句小小的“知道”变成“我在，等你想说”。

“语言表达受语境的影响有哪些？”陈老师突然把粉笔敲了一下，粉末飞起。

刘茜举手，“目的，谁对谁，场合，肢体，声音，媒介——面对面还是文字，时间的紧迫或宽松。”

“文化，”韩柚接话，“你是不是习惯直说，还是喜欢留面子。还有权力差异，谁可决定。”

“方言。”小胖兴奋，“我奶奶说‘吃过没’，其实是‘你好’，这就是语境替意。”

“以及共同经历，”林井补，“我们有共同的‘那年冬天’，所以‘那天那样就好’其实只对我们有意义。”

陈老师点点头：“都好。但记住，语境不是清单，它是你站在那一刻的全部——听见雨，闻到香，看到对方眼圈红了，用了哪个词，没用哪个词，还包括你曾经没说出口的。”

她拿起铃，指向黑板。粉笔字在灯下像两道门。“我们做最后一个练习。请你们用一句话让它三次变成不同的意思。”

林井深吸气，选择那句看似浅的：“你什么意思？”

第一次，他把肩膀拱起来，眉心皱起，声音硬：“你什么意思？”夹杂的火药味让这句话变成警告。

第二次，他笑了，眼睛亮，“你什么意思？”像在追问一个梗的来历，想听故事。

第三次，他坐在台阶上，雨声落在窗上，“你……什么意思？”他把第二个词含在嘴里，像怕它碎，怕它尖。这句话像在问一个即将离开的人的最后动机。

“看到了吗？”陈老师收了铃，“你们在选择语速、停顿、眼神、地点、关系、目标的时候，语言已经被语境揉成了不同的面团。同一句话，烤出的三种味道，甜、咸、苦，你们都尝到了。”

窗外的云层散了开来，蒸腾的水汽变得透明。周周忽然举手，指向黑板：“那句问题本身，也有语境吧。比如在考试里，它就是定义题；在我们的教室里，它是开门的钥匙。”

陈老师愣了一下，随即笑，眼睛里有光。“语境是什么？语言表达受语境的影响有哪些？”她把两句读得像诗，也像密码。

“它是你们走进一场谈话时身上的风，是你们出口时藏着的火。”她把粉笔在黑板上轻轻一划，“别怕它，你们每天都在用它。”

铃最后一次响起。每个人的手指都还沾着一点粉，声音在他们指尖微微发白。窗外的光彻底亮了，教室里也明亮起来。学生们彼此望着，忽然觉得这世界里每一句话背后，都站着一整座看不见的城。

query: 请简述存款准备金率的definition及对货币供应量的impact
response:
傍晚的咖啡馆里，人群寥落，窗外的霓虹开始在玻璃上抹出一层薄薄的色。林音把笔记本推到桌角，半杯拿铁的泡沫还挂在杯沿上。她盯着对面的邵教授，语速放得很慢：“老师，我明天要面试。人家可能会问——请简述存款准备金率的定义及对货币供应量的影响。能不能，用最简单的话，帮我过一遍？”

邵教授脱下围巾，笑了笑，抽了两包方糖放在桌上，又把她的零钱包要了过来，从里面挑出十枚一块钱的硬币，轻轻摊开。

“我们先说定义，”他把十枚硬币排成一条直线，“存款准备金率，就是商业银行把吸收来的存款里，按规定必须提取、交存到央行或留作法定准备的那一部分所占的比例。这部分钱不能贷出去，是银行的‘垫底’。央行通过设定这个比例，管控银行能放出去的钱有多少。”

他推走其中一枚硬币：“假设准备金率是10%，你存进银行10块钱，银行要留1块做准备金，剩下9块才有资格放贷。借出去的9块会变成另一个人的存款，再留0.9块准备金，继续往外贷……在理想化的模型里，如果大家不额外把现金揣在口袋、银行也不额外多留准备金，货币乘数大致等于1/准备金率。准备金率越高，这个乘数越小；越低，乘数越大。”

林音点点头，目光跟着那条逐渐变短的硬币“队伍”，像是在看一条被切分的河流。

“再说影响。”邵教授把另一包方糖拆开，指尖掐着一粒，“央行上调准备金率，相当于让银行必须多‘锁住’一部分资金。结果呢？第一，银行可贷资金少了，能够通过反复存贷产生的存款也少，货币乘数下降，货币供应量增速放缓，流动性趋紧；银行可能收紧授信或抬高利率。相反，下调准备金率，就会‘释放’一部分原先锁在央行的准备金，银行手里更宽裕，放贷能力增强，乘数上升，货币供应量更容易扩张，市场流动性宽松。”

他把一枚硬币立起来，又放倒：“但现实里没那么教科书。影响大小和速度，还取决于几件事：一是老百姓愿不愿意把现金留在身上（现金漏损），二是银行会不会因为风险而多留一点超额准备金，三是贷款的真实需求和监管对资本充足率、房地产等行业的限制。这些都会让乘数‘打折扣’。所以，降准不一定立刻看到M2猛增，上调也未必马上把市场‘冻住’，常常会有滞后和结构性的差异。同时，准备金率的调整还会改变银行间体系的头寸松紧，进而影响同业利率和融资成本，起到信号作用。”

林音拿起一枚硬币在掌心里掂了掂：“所以一句话版就是——存款准备金率是规定银行从存款中必须提取、不能贷款的一部分比例；它通过改变银行能放出去的钱和货币乘数，进而影响货币供应量的扩张或收缩。但实际效果取决于现金偏好、超额准备、资本监管和信贷需求等因素，会有滞后和不均衡。”

“对，”邵教授把硬币一枚枚收拢回她的零钱包，“你面试的时候别念公式，先讲逻辑，再提醒面试官现实里的摩擦。最后补一句：在中国，这个工具用得比较多，既是数量调控，也是政策信号，就齐活了。”

门口的风铃被推门声叮当一响。有人走进来，带进一缕夜色和街上烤红薯的甜香。林音合上笔记本，像是也把那一串硬币的声音收进了心里，笑着说：“谢谢老师，我大概会把方糖和硬币都带进考场了。”

query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
The municipal service hall smelled faintly of disinfectant and instant noodles. Fluorescent panels hummed above a room arranged in long, obedient rows: metal-framed chairs with scuffed gray vinyl seats, a low forest of potted snake plants, counters sealed with plexiglass and patience. On the wall, a red LED board ticked forward one unit at a time: A113, A114. A woman in a quilted coat rocked a baby; a man in a construction helmet slept with his chin to his chest; a uniformed clerk yawned behind a tissue.

Lin stood by the self-service kiosk with a plastic folder tucked under his arm. The folder was clouded with scratches and bulged with paper: photocopies in triplicate, a death certificate he tried not to look at, the deed his late wife used to keep in the top drawer under the tea towels. He had come on the earliest bus, the one that left before sunrise and smelled of damp wool and diesel, because the notice had said any day before the end of the month. He had called twice. The first person had told him to bring originals. The second had told him to bring patience.

“Please align your ID with the scanner,” the kiosk chirped in a bright woman’s voice. The camera lens had a thumbprint smear like a little moon. A sticker of a smiley face had been placed over the home button and then peeled halfway off.

Lin slid his ID card under the red light. The scanner beeped, the screen flashed green. A stock photo of a cheerful family with an award certificate flashed by.

“Please state your request,” the voice said.

He tapped: Transfer of property. Next of kin change. He was careful with his finger; the screen was oily. He filled in his wife’s name in neat characters, the ones he had copied from their marriage book the night before. He held his breath as the little loading circle spun.

The result popped up in gray characters on a white field, polite as a bow: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

The message stayed there, as if waiting for him to nod. He pressed the button that said Return. He tried again. The same steps, the same beep, the same careful letters. The same sentence, the same dot at the end.

He looked around—for a guard, for a clerk, for anyone with keys. A middle-aged security guard in a black jacket with shiny buttons watched the entrance, chewing sunflower seeds and spitting them into a plastic water bottle. A sign above the counters read: Comprehensive Services. Another read: Civil Affairs. On the pillar near the kiosk, a cartoon official in a cap gave a thumbs-up under the words Serve the People.

Lin cleared his throat. “Hello?” He pitched it toward the closest plexiglass window. The young woman behind it tapped at her keyboard without looking up. Her nameplate read: Zhao Min. Her fringe fell in a practiced angle over one eye.

“Sir,” she said in a perfectly even voice that seemed to have been recorded. “Please take a number and wait to be called.”

He looked at the dispenser on the wall and took a ticket. B042. The board above the counters read B028. Lin sat back down. The vinyl was cold through his trousers. A cleaning woman pushed a mop around his shoes and left a wet ribbon on the floor. Someone somewhere coughed a cough that spoke of the winter’s coal smoke still lodged in the lungs.

When the board called B042, Lin stood so quickly his knee banged the chair. He presented his folder and his ID and the death certificate, careful not to crease anything wrong. Zhao Min looked at the top sheet and then at her screen, where she clicked twice, three times. The reflection of the LED numbers ran across the plexiglass like a river of alarm clocks.

“This cannot be processed at the counter,” she said, sliding the folder back through the slot. “Please use the self-service kiosk.”

“I tried,” Lin said. He felt the shape of the word try inside his chest, like something too thin to hold. “It says it cannot help.”

Zhao Min smiled without moving the rest of her face. “Sometimes the system is temporarily down. You can try later. Or you can make an appointment online.”

He had no laptop, only a phone that took too long to update. He imagined the website with its squares and drop-down boxes that would never drop down. “Is there another way?”

She leaned forward, lowering her voice a measure. “Regulations,” she said, as if the word were a cousin. Her nail tapped the counter. “Original documents only. Next-of-kin verification. Household registration book. Appointment.”

“I have the originals.” He opened the folder again to show the embossed stamps, the red chops that looked like small suns. “She died,” he said, and tasted the salt of the words. “I brought everything.”

Zhao Min nodded once, two times, sympathetic in the way you nod at a relative’s story you cannot listen to. “The system won’t accept without the online pre-approval. You can scan that code.” She pointed to a QR code taped to the glass, the paper curled at the corners from a week of cleaning. Under the black square was the same cartoon official giving the same thumbs-up.

Lin held up his phone. The screen lit the little rectangle. A chat window slid open. A tiny robot avatar blinked. The first message arrived before he could type: Hello! How may I assist you today? He typed slowly, careful to spell his wife’s name correctly. The robot sent back fireworks emojis and a link. He followed the link. It asked for a login he didn’t have. He created one. The password requirements wanted a symbol he never used. The chat pinged again, eager, a puppy throwing itself against a fence.

“Please upload clear photographs of all required documents,” the bot said.

He took pictures against the slick surface of the counter, the fluorescent light bleeding into the edges. His hands shook a little. The chat acknowledged with happy confetti, then went quiet for a full minute. The noise of the room wasn’t loud; it was a layered murmur, a shuffle of people living their paperwork in public.

The reply arrived: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

He stared at the characters until they lost their meaning and became strokes and weights. The bot added, as if to be helpful: Please contact your local service center for further assistance.

Zhao Min’s eyes were still on her screen. The man in the construction helmet had woken up and was rubbing his face with both palms. A child began to cry, then stopped.

“I’m at the service center,” Lin said aloud. He didn’t mean to speak, but his voice came anyway, brittle and small as porcelain. He held up the phone, screen forward. The sentence glowed back at both of them: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

Zhao Min’s eyes flicked to it, then to his face. She had good eyeliner. “Sir,” she said, softer, and he saw she was younger than she looked. “I really can’t. I’m not authorized. You can try again this afternoon when the system resets. Or next Tuesday. Tuesdays there are fewer people.”

He wanted to say: On Tuesday, there will still be a bed that smells like soap and her lotion, and there will still be the dent her head made in the pillow. He wanted to say: I have spent my life filling forms, and still I don’t know where to put the things I cannot name. Instead he nodded and closed the folder so that the papers lay flush and square. The plastic buckled with a little sigh.

He went back to the kiosk because there was nowhere else to go. The screen still wore its thumbprint moon. He swiped a sleeve across it and left a bar of clean glass. He held his ID to the scanner, watched the red bar crawl over his photograph, the one taken eight years ago when his hair was thicker and his eyes had more light. The machine beeped cheerfully.

The gray sentence appeared again in the same font, in the same place on the screen, with the same apologetic period. 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

A roll of thermal paper whirred and a small slip bumped into the tray below like a receipt for a purchase he did not remember making. He pulled it out. The paper was warm. The words were printed there too, faintly, and underneath them a phone number, and a little square where a clerk could stamp a stamp that would mean yes, proceed.

Lin folded the slip and slid it into the pocket with the bus ticket. He thanked the machine under his breath because it had at least given him something he could hold. Outside the glass doors the light was bright and hard, a sun-bleached street full of honking mopeds and carts of greens and a man selling sesame buns from a steel drum. When the automatic doors opened for a woman pushing a stroller, the scent of toasted flour and warm sugar blew in and lingered for a second before the doors sighed shut again.

He stood, the folded slip in his palm, and let himself be a man in a room where everyone was waiting for some other number to be called. Over the hum of lights and the shuffle of winter coats, a voice from one of the counters said, in the exact same cadence Zhao Min had used, as if the whole place were training to be a single throat: “抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

query: 比拟比喻区别，说明举例。
response:
傍晚下起雨来，风顺着老楼的走廊吹进来，雨点在窗台上连成密密的鼓点。厨房里，水壶嘶嘶响，像忍不住要开口。小夏把作业本推到餐桌中央，皱眉看着一道题：“比拟与比喻有何区别？举例说明。”

她父亲在阳台收衣服，衬衫没来得及收的那几件被风扯得猎猎作响。他一边把衣架摞好，一边问：“又卡在修辞上了？”

“老师说比拟和比喻不一样，我总搞混。”小夏把笔在指间转了转，“你不是教语文的吗？救命。”

父亲笑着在她对面坐下，掀起作业本。窗外一声闷雷，他把笔帽拔掉：“这雨，倒正好给我们做示范。先说比喻。比喻是拿一件事物来打比方，突出相似点，常常有‘像、如、仿佛、犹如’这些词，也可以直接‘是’。比如——听。”

他指了指玻璃窗：“‘雨点像珍珠一样往下掉’，这是比喻，用‘像’把雨和珍珠联起来；要是说‘这场雨是一张灰色的帘子’，不用‘像’，直接‘是’，还是比喻，只是更直白。”

小夏点点头，又问：“那比拟呢？”

父亲拿起桌上的茶杯，杯壁有一道小磕痕，他看了看，说：“比拟是把事物写成另一类，最常见的是拟人，给本不是人的东西安上人的动作、情感。它不靠‘像’，而是用人的动词去写。比如你听——‘雨点在窗上排队敲门’，这不是说它‘像’谁，而是直接让雨做了人的事，就是比拟里的拟人。再比如‘黄昏收起最后一缕光’，‘收起’是人的动作。”

他顿了顿，又补了一句：“比拟还包括拟物，把人或抽象的东西写成物件的样子。比如‘他一坐下就把自己钉在椅子上’，‘钉’本来是物的动作，这样用，就成了拟物。”

小夏把这些抄下，又狐疑地看父亲：“那有时候我也会写‘风像孩子一样在巷子里追逐’。”

父亲摇头：“这句用‘像’，在判别上更接近比喻；要真正成拟人，可以写‘风在巷子里追着人的衣角打闹’，让风直接‘打闹’，不借‘像’。两者语气不同，力道也不同。”

他把纸抽出来，写了两列句子，一边念一边指给小夏看——

“比喻：‘河面平得像一面镜子。’对应的比拟：‘河面屏住了呼吸。’你看，‘镜子’是打比方，‘屏住呼吸’是人的动作。”

“比喻：‘他的嗓音像铜铃一样响。’比拟：‘闹钟守在桌上，逢点便高喊。’后一句里‘守’、‘高喊’是人的行为，闹钟被写成了一个有守点职责的人。”

“比喻：‘城市是钢铁的森林。’比拟：‘老墙在阳光下打盹。’前者是把城市当成森林来比，后者给‘墙’安排了‘打盹’这种人的状态。”

“比喻：‘他站得像根笔直的白桦。’比拟（拟物）：‘他把自己焊在书桌前一动不动。’一个是说‘像’，一个是把‘焊’这个动作用到人身上。”

他说着说着，屋里的灯忽地一暗，又亮了起来。水壶终于开了，热气在壶嘴边扭曲。父亲提壶倒水，笑道：“再听两个，我们把界限再清一下。”

“比喻：‘她的笑容像春风。’比拟：‘窗帘被她的笑声逗得抖了抖。’前一句是用‘像’；后一句让窗帘‘被逗’，也是拟人。”

“比喻：‘夜空是一块黑绒布。’比拟：‘月亮爬上了树梢。’月亮不会‘爬’，这就是拟人。”

小夏边写边点头，雨声像是远了一点。她问：“所以区别可以这么记？比喻强调相似，用‘像’‘是’这样的连接，或者干脆省略连接，但核心是两者的相似；比拟是换了类别，给它安上人的动作或物的特征，哪怕没有‘像’也能看出？”

父亲把茶吹开一个小口儿：“差不多。再补一句，现实里有交叉的句子，不要被表面迷惑。比如‘城市是钢铁的森林’，不用‘像’，但它不是在写城市去‘做’什么，而是把城市当作森林来比，是比喻。又比如‘风笑了’，没有‘像’，却让风‘笑’，这是拟人。看动词、看是否赋予了另一类事物的行为，是关键。”

走廊里传来邻居家的钥匙声，猫从沙发背上无声地跃下。小夏忽然笑了，说：“猫刚才在沙发背上趴着，像一团影子——这是比喻；‘影子在地板上打了个盹儿’——这是比拟。”

父亲鼓掌：“通了。”

雨又密起来，窗外街灯一点点亮。小夏在作业本的最后写下自己的总结和例句，笔尖走得很稳。父亲端着茶站起来，望了眼窗外，说：“你看，这场雨帮了我们大忙。它不光‘像’什么，它还会‘做’什么。你把这两种看法分清，句子就活了。”

query: 如何培养孩子的家庭责任？
response:
厨房的窗玻璃上起了一层薄雾，外面正下着细碎的雨。苏宁把红豆汤调成小火，南瓜块在金色的汤里轻轻翻身。阿卓挑了挑冰箱上的白板笔，在冰箱门上写了一行字：如何培养孩子的家庭责任？

笔尖嘎吱作响，多多和皮皮一回头，像被口哨吹了似的跑过来。多多抬起下巴，读得很认真：“这是——问题作文题目吗？”

“这是今天的主题。”阿卓把白板笔插回冰箱旁的笔筒，“我们开个小会。”

外婆从餐桌那头慢慢坐直，笑皱了眼角：“哟，还开会。我年轻时家里开会就是喊一嗓子：‘大米快没了！’大家就知道得去挑担子。”

“正好，”苏宁关了灶火，把锅盖挪开一条缝，“今天我们也来认认担子。家，是我们一起住的地方，也应该一起打理。等你们长大，想起今天，可能你们也会喊一嗓子。”

多多眨了眨眼：“可我每天已经上学写作业了……还得打理家？”

“所以我们要挑你们愿意做、也做得到的事。”阿卓把一叠彩色便签拍到桌上，“我们不分配，我们‘招聘’，来个家庭职位招聘会。”

皮皮眼睛一亮，“有工资吗？”

“工资是：红豆汤再加一勺。”苏宁把碗放在他面前。

阿卓写下几个“职位”：植物部长、宠物照护官、垃圾管理员、早餐助理、鞋柜总司令、门铃响应员、书籍整理员。每个职位下面，他用不太工整却很认真地标着“职责”：比如植物部长要“每日观察叶子是否发蔫，周三、周六浇水，给小杏树讲一个故事。”

“给树讲故事也算职责？”多多忍不住笑。

“它们也要听人说话。”外婆端起碗，“以前我家种黄瓜，清早去地里说‘累不累’，黄瓜长得格外快。”

“我申请宠物照护官！”皮皮举手，一口气喝了半碗红豆汤，“我可以给乌龟换水，喂鱼，还给它们起名字。”

“好，”阿卓把“宠物照护官”一栏贴了个蓝色小星星，“但是要写承诺书——你说了就要做。”

多多低头看了看便签，指尖在“书籍整理员”和“植物部长”之间犹疑。“我不喜欢倒垃圾，垃圾脏。”

“那能不能这样，”苏宁把声音放轻，“你选两个你喜欢的，再选一个你不太喜欢的。我们可以找办法让那个不喜欢的也没那么糟。”

“我喜欢整理书。”多多小声说，“我也喜欢植物，但我怕忘记浇水。”

“那我们一起做日历提醒。”阿卓拿起手机，把周三和周六的提醒设成了多多喜欢的小铃声。屏幕亮了一下，是一只跳舞的黄鹂。

“至于垃圾，”苏宁转头看阿卓，“也不是只有孩子才倒。你昨晚的啤酒罐还在水槽里漂着呢。”

“确实。”阿卓干笑一下，朝厨房里走了两步，又折回来，朝多多举起手心，“咱们击个掌。爸爸认领‘厨房台面清理官’，每晚收拾到可以照出人影。这样你倒垃圾就只用绑袋子、拿下楼，手套在门口的篮子里。”

多多把手掌轻轻按过去，指间的汗湿得微粘。

“那我想当‘门铃响应员’！”皮皮突然喊。仿佛是被他喊到似的，门铃“叮咚”响了，他们全往门口看。

门外是隔壁王阿姨，撑着一把花伞，手里提了个纸盒，“刚烤了蛋糕，多多、皮皮，来尝尝。”她往客厅里探头，目光扫到冰箱上的那行字，笑：“哎呀，你们还在讨论如何培养孩子的家庭责任呢？真好。”

“王阿姨！”皮皮踮起脚接过纸盒，想了想，转身朝鞋柜跑：“门铃响应员不只开门，还要递拖鞋。”他拖着每个人的拖鞋在脚下花里胡哨地摆成一排。多多看了眼书架，弯腰把散在地上的两本连环画拾起，塞回了“奇趣科学”那一格。她自己放学后随手一扔，现在反而把它们摆正，书脊和书脊之间留了一指宽。

“你看，王阿姨，”阿卓叉着腰，“我们最近想试试让孩子参与规则制定，给他们选择权，也让我们自己做榜样。不是‘你必须’，而是‘你愿意’。”

“还有讲故事。”外婆补了一句，“讲责任背后的故事。”

王阿姨把伞收了，接过去皮皮递来的拖鞋，笑容像蜿蜒的雨水，“真好，真好。”

雨越下越细，像一层看不见的纱挂在阳台外。多多端起浇水壶走向窗边的小杏树，叶片上积着淡淡的水珠，像被擦亮的绿玉。她靠近时，突然发现泥土边有一朵小小的蘑菇，薄薄的伞面刚刚顶开。她记住了铃声，记住了要讲一个故事。她清了清嗓子，开口：“从前，有一棵树，住在一个爱讲笑话的家里——”

声音还在叶片间绕，客厅里皮皮空出了两只小手，伸向垃圾桶，“我能帮你绑袋子吗？我戴手套。”

“戴上。”多多把手套递过去。她想起刚才自己的踟蹰，心里像有人轻轻按了一下，从一处软处向外涌出一点热。

阿卓拎起昨晚的啤酒罐，笑了笑，转身把它们冲洗干净，水声刷刷地落在不锈钢上，像雨打在屋檐。

“责任不是谁说了算，”苏宁看着他们，轻轻拨了拨中间那盏暖黄的灯，“是你们一抬手一弯腰的时候，家在你手里变得亮一些。等到哪天你们不在家了，会想起这盏灯、这盆树、这只乌龟、这张桌子，你们会觉得它们不是摆设，是某个夏天你们积累起来的小光。”

王阿姨站在门口，看着两个孩子忙忙碌碌的背影和冰箱上的那行字，忽然说：“我也回去写一行字，问问我们家。‘如何培养孩子的家庭责任？’也许从今天回家一起吃一次饭开始。”

门口的拖鞋排成队，像等待上场的小兵。门外雨收了一阵，天空露出一条淡淡的亮银。多多把小杏树的叶子擦得发亮，皮皮举着绑好的垃圾袋在门口转圈。外婆在桌旁悠悠地讲起她小时候挑水的故事，声音柔柔的，像红豆汤在瓷碗里轻轻漾动。家在这些琐碎里，像一盏灯被一点点擦亮。

query: 咋整能让广告不踩红线？
response:
窗外的霓虹在雪雾里打着转，像有人把灯泡藏到棉絮里又不小心露了尖儿。北风广告的小会议室里暖气片吱吱叫，茶壶嘴里冒着细细的白汽，桌上摊了一地的提案稿和便签，像小雪片没落稳就被手指头拨散了。

“咋整能让广告不踩红线？”小韩趴在白板前，手里举着记号笔不敢落下，眼睛从“全国第一”“0油0烟”这些大字上闪过，又心虚地看一眼对面的陆姐。

陆姐戴着黑框眼镜，头发用一根红皮筋束在脑后，面前摊着一份《广告法重点风险清单》，被她翻得起褶儿。“你们这是要我心梗。”她敲了敲纸，“‘第一’不能用，‘绝对’不能用，‘无添加’后面得说清楚添加啥不添加啥，别动不动就‘祖传秘方’‘治病保命’，哦，还有你们这个‘医美级’也给我删喽。”

阿力把一根红色的毛线从桌角拉到白板，用胶带一贴，指着道：“我的红线天才创意来了。我们把这根线当道具，哪个词要过线，你们就看见它，是不是一目了然？”

“你倒是给自己找了个视觉符号。”老乔笑了笑，他是创意总监，常年穿一件洗到发灰的牛仔夹克。“客户明天要过稿，这一版不能再被法务打回来。‘山海小灶’的电煮锅，别给人家端一锅法律责任。”

“‘山海小灶’，又山又海，名字起得倒阔。”小韩把“全国第一”圈了圈，拿黑笔重重地画了个叉，半天没写出新的。“那‘广受欢迎’算不算绝对？”

陆姐抿了口茶，慢条斯理：“‘受到很多用户喜爱’可以，但‘很多’是模糊词，你们要有对应的数据但不要浮夸。如果要写‘口碑好’，就让真实评价说话。还有，别用未成年人做代言。”

小彭，实习生，怯生生地从角落里冒了一句：“那我们不写‘第一’，写‘老邻居都在用’？”

“哪家邻居？”陆姐立刻抬头，“虚构可不行。”

“那写‘二舅用了都说好’？”小韩忍不住接梗，立刻被老乔瞪一眼，“别抖机灵。”

“要不……”阿力把红线在白板上往上一抬，“我们别在字上打架了。用画面，用故事？”

房间一时安静，只剩暖气片继续吱吱叫。窗外一辆外卖车在雪地里留下长长的一道字迹，像有人在白纸上写了个“人”字。

“讲个谁的故事？”老乔扯了扯袖子，望着白板上的红线，像看着某种实实在在的界碑，“咱们品牌叫‘山海’，它要说的不是‘谁最厉害’，而是从山到海，从早到晚，陪谁一顿饭。我们别喊口号了。”

陆姐把文件夹合上，也没反对，“故事里别有医嘱、别有虚假承诺、别有夸张效果，也别涉黄赌毒。平时你们觉得我是给你们设障碍，其实我也想看好故事。”

“哈尔滨最近降温，夜里进到-20了。”小彭忽然说，“我昨天回家，楼道里有股酸菜炖排骨的味儿。我站了一会儿，听见隔壁老太太的锅盖咣当咣当响，她在嘟囔‘火候、火候’。那一刻我就觉得没那么冷。”

“好，”老乔眼睛亮了，“‘火候’。”

他走到白板前，把“0油0烟”“全国第一”统统擦掉，在红线下面写了三个字：“火候、时间、心意”。又在左边画了个粗糙的分镜：一只手，一件厚毛衣袖口，一只简洁的电煮锅，冬夜，雾气在玻璃上凝成花。画面里看不到品牌名，看不到夸张字眼，只能听见锅里咕嘟咕嘟的声音，偶尔有风拍窗。

“第一幕，”阿力接上，手指在红线下面敲了敲，“镜头拉开，是个老两口。老爷子把锅插上电，老太太把山药切成滚刀块。字幕写‘冬天的火候，不止是温度’。”

“第二幕，一个独居的上班族加班到夜里，回家插上‘小灶’，坐在桌前发消息‘妈，我到家了’，然后把一碗汤端到窗前看雪。字幕写‘有人照应，心就不慌’。对了，我们要注意，这些人物不做夸张表情，不说‘三分钟就能熬出骨头汤’这类话。”

“第三幕，一个远洋船员在甲板上，天空有海鸥，船舱里一口小锅咕噜咕噜，他视频里头传来孩子笑声。字幕写‘天南海北，吃热乎儿的’。”

陆姐点了点头，“每一幕都不涉及疾病治疗，不承诺功效，不使用绝对化词语，食材是真实可见，锅的功能展示不夸大。最后落品牌的时候，用‘我们陪认真做饭的人’这类价值取向，不要‘行业领先’之类。”

“那我们的 tagline？”小韩把笔在耳朵上别了一下，“‘火候不忙，日子不慌’？”

老乔想了想，慢慢说道：“‘把火候交给它，把心交给人’。或者更简一点——‘有人等你吃饭’。”

“这句好。”陆姐竟然笑了笑。“没有红线隐患。”

小韩像被放了鞭炮似的，“咱还得把优势传达出来呀，不说功能，客户得骂我们佛系。”

陆姐把红线在白板上轻轻一拨，“可以说功能，但要描述真实。比如‘八档火候可选’‘预约定时’‘一锅多用’这种客观表述。不要加‘秒’‘瞬间’‘永久’这些浮夸词。”

老乔点头，“那就这样：在故事里自然地呈现这些点。老两口的那幕，老太太把火候调到‘小火保温’，不需要字幕；上班族那幕，手机上‘预约完成，预计22:30开煮’，顺手一晃；船员那幕，便携、稳当，插线细节带过去。旁白一句也没有，字幕只有那几句暖心话。最后落画面，品牌名‘山海小灶’，旁边是一句‘有人等你吃饭’。”

小韩把那些“最”“第一”的稿纸揉成团，塞进垃圾桶，转头又拽回一张，“等会儿，这句‘有人等你吃饭’是不是变相引导受众觉得产品能让人回来？会不会……也踩线？”

“不是承诺，是情感表达。”陆姐把词抠得很细，“我们说的是‘等你’，不是‘让你’。不要把产品神化成解决所有问题的钥匙。我们表达一种场景，一种日常里的温度。这条线，过与不过，差一字，差一念。”

阿力用手机扫了一眼白板，笑了，“这红毛线，今天可真派上用场。每一个想越过去的词都卡在这儿，我们反而找到路了。”

深夜的外卖车又呼啸过去，玻璃窗上被热汽薰得起了雾。屋里的人忽然都静了一瞬，仿佛都在想起某一盏厨房灯的光。

第二天早上，客户那边的视频会议准时响起。屏幕里，隔着上海的霓虹和哈尔滨的冰霜，一个年轻的市场总监按了播放键。

没有音乐，只有锅的声音、风声和脚步声。老两口互相递了勺子，上班族把手机放在窗前，船员把饭碗抵住了舷窗。最后一帧是雾气散去后的一张桌子，两个碗，两个筷子，一只电煮锅静静冒着热。品牌名在角落里出现，旁边一句话：有人等你吃饭。

屏幕那头的市场总监沉默了几秒，“这版……有点不‘营销’。”他笑了笑，又点头，“但挺暖。功能点也都在，字上没问题吧？”

“我们审过，不踩红线。”陆姐坐直，声音里有种踏实，“每个词都是经过衡量的。”

小韩在座位上偷偷伸了个懒腰，“咋整能让广告不踩红线？就像这红毛线，明目张胆地摆着，不绕、不钻；你不把它当铁丝网，当护栏，它也能给你画出道道儿。”

会后，红毛线还搭在白板上。阿力没有拆。冬天的哈尔滨有时候冷得厉害，伸手就是干燥的刺儿。小彭把窗开了一条指缝，吸进来一口带着雪味儿的风，忽然笑道：“这条红线真挺像咱们这座城的防寒条——不能没有，但也不是为了挡人看风景的。”

老乔拍拍他肩，“记住今天。我们能不能讲好故事，从来不是靠把字眼儿堆到红线外，而是靠把人心放进锅里。广告不就这样？别跨红线，也别怕红线。它不是叫你停，是叫你走在正当的路上。”

query: 什么是戏剧art？戏剧的主要elements有哪些？
response:
排练厅的门被推开时，外头的雨正下到最密。旧空调嘬着气，风从高处拂下来，带着灰尘与胶带的味道。地板上有白色纸胶带贴出的“客厅”轮廓，一盏侧灯正试光，光斑里看得见浮尘。

秦导把黑色棒球帽压得很低，手里拿着一支粉笔，像是在教室里一样，弯腰在地上画了一条新的走位线。他的膝盖有旧伤，蹲着的时候总会发出轻微的咔哒声。

“来，”他说，“阿一，你从门口上——安，你坐在沙发位。我们从你们争吵那段开始。”

阿一穿着一件洗褪的灰色 T 恤，脚下的运动鞋粘着一点泥。他照着走位站到门边，手扶着那扇永远虚构的门，深吸一口气再开门进来，步子踩在白线里。安把剧本摊在膝上，眼睛却看着秦导，像在等一个信号。

刚开始几句，话就劈啪地撞在空旷的厅里——年轻人的气力总是多，台词被喊成了陀螺，越转越快。秦导没有喊停，他靠在墙边，让那股劲头跑一阵子，像看一条河什么时候会自己减流。

果然，第三句的时候，阿一的声音开始发虚，安也落了一个字。他举起粉笔敲了敲扶手椅的木扶手，轻轻地，“停。”

空气像被扛住了一下。阿一看向他，“导，我想问个问题，可以吗？”

秦导摘了帽子，头发里夹着汗的潮气。“问。”

“什么是戏剧，那个……戏剧art？我们一直在排，一直在说‘走位、节奏、冲突’，可我突然不太确定我在做的到底是什么。”

安也笑了一下，像是偷听到了课堂。“还有我们昨天在群里讨论的，戏剧的主要elements有哪些？”

秦导把粉笔递给阿一，又从口袋里摸出一支笔给安。他看着两张年轻的脸，长久没变的那种认真，眼睛里有一点故意的光。

“好，”他说，“今天就当我们有十分钟的课堂。”

他走到纸胶带勾出的“窗”边，像站进了另一种时间。“戏剧是什么？先别急着背定义。你们看这屋——是假的。门是假的，沙发是假的，窗外下不下雨都看暗场。可我们把你们放进来，让你们说话、走路、呼吸，让你们的身体和声音把一件事活到眼前。这件事有开始、有发展、有结果，有人在里面想什么、需要什么、彼此撞击——观众在场，跟你们一起走过这段时间。这就是戏剧：用现场的行动与语言，把人的处境和心事，在有限的时空里浓缩成一种经验。”

他顿了顿，像在等待他们的呼吸与理解发生黏着。

“更学术一点，”他继续，“从亚里士多德那边就开始讲，戏剧有六个构成：情节、人物、思想、语言、音乐、景象。时代变了，我们说法也会换，但骨子里还是那回事。你们非要一个清单，我也给你们。”

他拿回粉笔，在地板上贴线旁边写了几个字，一笔一划很慢。

“第一，人物。没有谁，就没有什么事。人物不是标签，是欲望、恐惧、性格、背景，是他们此刻要什么、不想要什么。”

“第二，情节，也叫行动。不是你们说了多少话，而是发生了什么。一个人进来，是行动；一句话抛出去，改变了对方的状态，也是行动。行动要推动事态，从A到B，再到C。”

“第三，冲突。你要这个，他要那个，现实允许你们的空间很窄，这之间的对撞就是戏。没有冲突，就像水面不起波，观众看五分钟就睡了。冲突可以外在的，也可以内心的。”

“第四，主题。我们究竟在谈什么？是‘原谅’，是‘权力’，是‘成长’，还是‘谎言的代价’？主题不是挂在海报上的一句话，而是通过你们的行为渗出来的味道。”

“第五，语言与对白。戏剧靠嘴，但也不仅是嘴。语言是节奏、是气息、是你们的选择，长句短句，停顿与不言，都在讲东西。对白要让行动发生，不是作文。”

“第六，时空与结构。这场戏发生在什么时候、哪里？我们切几场、几幕，时间是顺行还是跳跃？节奏靠结构来雕刻。”

“第七，舞台呈现——景象。灯光、布景、音效、音乐、服装、道具，和你们的走位、调度。这些都是让‘假的东西’长成‘真经历’的外衣。”

他停下来看他们，“当然，有人还会把‘观众的在场’也当成一个要素。戏剧跟小说、电影不同，它活在这屋里和那双眼睛之间。你们今天演得好不好，不只在台上，也在台下的呼吸里。”

阿一点了点头，像把这几个字往心里搬。他试着举例：“人物……我进来这场戏，我其实不是来吵架，我是怕她走了。冲突就是她要走，我要留她。情节就是我拦她、她挣脱。”

“很好，”秦导说，“那语言呢？”

安低头看剧本，抬起眼睛，“我们现在的台词太像平常吵架了，每一句都在重复‘你别走、你别走’，应该有变化，有刺，有软，让那件事推进。”

“对，”秦导把帽子重新扣上，“这就是你们的工作。我们再来一次。阿一，你进门的时候把‘行动’想清楚——不是‘我进来’，是‘我进来拦她’，所以你的步子快，你的眼睛先找她的位置，手准备好把她的包拿下来。安，你坐着，不是‘坐着’，是‘坐着等他来，你心里已经卷好了要走的理由’，所以你膝盖紧，包肩带往里收。冲突一出现，语言就要带着针——你不会一上来就喊‘别走’，第一句可以是‘你终于记得回来’，那里面已经有刺了。”

他退到侧灯的阴影里，像把场地让给他们，同时又不离开。“开始。”

阿一不再摸索那个虚构的门，而是撞进来。他的肩胛骨像真正折进了一段紧迫的时间。安把包带往里拽，眼神还在笑，但笑像一个关上的抽屉。

“你终于记得回来。”她说。

“你根本就没等我。”他反击。

两个人的气流一下子在纸胶带画出的客厅里盘旋，台词不再是堆叠，而是钩子和线，拉扯出一个看得见的力场。灯光照着他们的发丝，一点灰尘在光里慢慢降落，像时间的碎片。

秦导没有再说话。他看着他们怎么把刚刚那套“元素”从纸上的字变成肌肉里的动作、喉咙里的呼吸、手指头里捏住的包带。他知道这就是答案：戏剧的定义不在讲义里，戏剧是这两个人此刻的真诚，是这屋里的空气被拉紧的一瞬，是观众在某一天坐在台下，忽然想起自己的某个夜晚。

十分钟后，他举起手，像给一个终止也像给一个许可。阿一和安都在呼气，汗顺着额角下来了。

“你们刚才做的，比我说的那些字管用得多。”他笑了笑，“但记住，有时候当你们迷路的时候，那些字就是地图。人物、情节、冲突、主题、语言、结构、景象——这些是你们的工具。戏剧是什么？戏剧是我们拿着这些工具，去把一个人的真实在一屋子人的眼前活一次。”

外面的雨小了些，风从门缝里跑进来。阿一把粉笔还给秦导，手上留下了一层白。他问，“那观众呢？”

秦导看向他们背后的空椅子排，那些椅子的黑皮面因为年久有了裂纹，裂纹里藏了一点光。“观众就是最后的元素，也是最开始的理由。他们来，是为了在你们的行动里遇见自己。你们做对了，椅子就不再是椅子，屋子就不再是屋子，时间就有了别的名字。”

他把帽子往后推了一寸，露出一点额头。“好了，休息五分钟。然后我们再来一次，给你们刚才抓到的东西——再长出骨头和血。”

query: 对不起，我不能完成这个。
response:
The bell over the glass door jangled, a small sound swallowed by the rumble of the 7 train overhead. Steam curled from the iron on the counter and hazed the air with the hot, sweet smell of sizing. Threads—red, ivory, peacock blue—spilled like noodles from a chipped glass jar. Mr. Zhou slid a sleeve under his palm, thumb feeling for the seam allowance without looking up.

“Hi,” the young woman said, letting the garment bag slip off her shoulder. Her fiancé paused on the mat to shake off slush, holding the door for an older woman with a shopping bag that clinked. Outside, neon flickered in the noodle shop window; inside, the fluorescent strip light hummed with a faint complaint.

“We called earlier,” the older woman said in Mandarin, the syllables clean and quick. “My mother’s dress.”

Mr. Zhou lifted his head. He had a magnifier clipped to his glasses; when he pushed it up, his eyes looked suddenly younger. “Let me see.”

The young woman unzipped the bag and drew out a red qipao on a plastic hanger. The silk was the kind that kept its own light, woven with tiny flying cranes and cloud scrolls. The dress had a high neck and cap sleeves; the frog closures were in the shape of small peonies, flattened by decades. Someone had folded it carefully, but the folds had bitten into the fabric like years into skin. The older woman touched the bodice with her thumb and forefinger as if steadying a fragile animal. “It was my mother’s,” she said. “She wore it in Hong Kong. We want Lily to wear it tomorrow. Just a little taken in at the waist.”

The fiancé—Ben—stood a step behind them, damp shoulders of his peacoat darkening as the shop’s heat hit him. He looked from face to face, waiting to catch up.

“Just a little,” the mother repeated, then to the man in a way that was more question than instruction, “Mouth tomorrow. Ceremony at eleven.”

Mr. Zhou lifted the dress with both hands. The silk was light and reluctant. He turned it over, checked the side seams, held it up to the light so the warp and weft were visible like ribs. The frogs came away with a reluctant stick, old glue giving up. He found where someone had made a clever alteration decades ago, tiny hand stitches close as eyelashes. He traced them the way a reader traces a line in a book.

The young woman watched his fingers. She had short nails painted a faint shell pink; there were white crescents at their tips where she had chewed them. On her ring finger the diamond caught the light of the iron in small mirrored shards. “We can pay extra,” she said, half to her mother, half to him.

Mr. Zhou set the dress on the counter. He pressed his thumb to the seam and, with the other hand, tugged gently at a stray thread. It should have slid free like a river pulling a reed. Instead the thread crumbled, a bright thin dust smearing his thumb red.

He didn’t speak right away. He flicked the dust away, picked up a loupe, looked again at the silk where it had broken. He pinched a corner of the hem, tested it with the pressure he might use to turn a page. The fabric parted under that tenderness with a sound like someone detaching a breath.

“Ah,” he said softly. “It’s very old.” He looked at the face of the young woman, the set of her mouth. “Did you wash it?”

The mother’s chin came up. “Only by hand,” she said quickly. “Just water. It smelled of camphor. I thought—”

“It happens,” he said. He pressed a finger to a chalked line and small grains bloomed. “Silk like this, the threads—the glue inside—” He rotated his hands, as if the right word were under them somewhere on the counter. “They dry.” He looked at Lily and then at her mother again. “I can’t put it under a machine. It will tear.”

Ben looked at Lily. “What’s he saying?”

Lily’s throat trembled once. “He says it’s old,” she said, and then, bowing her head to Mr. Zhou, “But… is there a way?”

He glanced at the wall clock with the hair salon calendar duct-taped under it. A woman with improbable hair smiled down at him. It was eight-thirty. The edges of the little shop seemed to gather closer: bolts of fabric leaning like thin men at a bus stop, a dress form wearing half a muslin, a tin of pins with a strawberry pincushion fat with use.

Mr. Zhou picked up the dress again and held it close, as you do when you have to say something hard to a beautiful thing. “对不起，我不能完成这个。” His voice was calm, but he swallowed. “I’m sorry,” he added, in English, careful on each syllable. “I can’t. Not by tomorrow. Not like this.”

Silence—the kind that has texture, that you feel on your skin—lined the small space. The mother’s mouth opened and then shut, eyes bright and dry at the same time. She put her hand flat on the glass counter, as if steadying herself or the world.

“What did he say?” Ben asked again, too loud in the quiet. Lily closed her eyes for a breath. When she opened them, she found the spot on the dress where the fabric had powdered and smoothed it gently with her thumb, useless as it was. “He says he can’t finish it.”

“Can’t?” The mother’s voice cracked on the last consonant. “We came—He says cannot?” She switched to Mandarin again, the words gathering speed. “This is what you do. I waited three hours at the doctor today. Everything is a queue.”

Mr. Zhou did not flinch. He bent the hem very slightly and gave the silk a chance to speak in its own voice. A fine reddened dust trembled onto the glass. He tipped the counter so the mother could see. “Look. It’s like paper from the sun. Your mother—” He touched the place where the inside pocket had been, a secret square patched in with a floral cotton, faded to ghost. “She took care. But time…” He let the sentence rest in his open hand. “To make it safe I would have to line it, reinforce every curve. I would have to sew all night, and then all day. And even then, when she sits, it might break.” He turned to Lily, to meet her eyes. “You don’t want to worry on your wedding day.”

Ben stepped in, arms out just enough to include them all. “It’s okay,” he said softly, not yet knowing what he meant by it. “We—we have the white one.”

The mother flicked her gaze to him, a sparrow’s quick, precise movement, not unkind, just measuring. “White dress is American,” she said. To Mr. Zhou, “This is for ancestors. My mother will see.”

“I know.” Mr. Zhou’s voice gentled. He set the qipao on the counter and placed a hand on the fabric the way he would put a palm to a fevered brow. “I can do one thing,” he said. “Take a piece—here, from inside where it is a little stronger. A strip. I can sew it into the hem of the white dress. No one will see it, only you will know. She will still be with you. And I can adjust your white dress, make it fit like it loved you first.”

Lily’s eyes flooded, which seemed like an answer of its own. She pressed the heel of her hand to one eye, laughing a little at the mess she was making of her mascara. “Sorry,” she said, to everyone. “I just—We thought—” She looked at the qipao, at the small cranes caught mid-flight forever. “I wanted…” She ran out of words.

The mother stared at the strip of red dust on the counter, as if reading tea leaves. She reached into her purse and thumped a stack of bills on the glass, pushing it toward him with the firmness of someone accustomed to making impossible things possible through sheer insistence. Mr. Zhou slid the money back across the smooth surface with two fingers, a gesture more respectful than refusal.

“Later,” he said. “If you like what I do.”

Ben exhaled a breath he didn’t know he’d been holding. “Thank you,” he said, and the gratitude in his voice surprised him.

Mr. Zhou reached for a pad of tailor’s chalk and the tape measure draped over his neck like a priest’s stole. He moved with an old man’s economy that looks like elegance. “Try the white dress,” he said. “Let me pin it. You will stand like this.” He lifted his chin an infinitesimal degree, demonstrating a posture that seemed to lift the young woman with it.

While Lily ducked into the tiny fitting room, a curtain more ideal than wall, the mother stood with her hand on the red silk. She smoothed it as if smoothing her own heart. “My mother was so beautiful,” she said, not to anyone in particular. “All the men at the tram stop—” She paused, and the corner of her mouth lifted. “She used to put rouge on the inside of her lip. So you couldn’t tell.”

“She was clever,” Mr. Zhou said. He took small, careful scissors and snipped a thin strip from the inside seam, where the fabric had been protected by shadow. He laid it on the white counter, scarlet against frost.

The train rattled overhead again, a familiar thunder. Lily stepped out in the white dress, one shoulder not yet sitting right, the hem whispering at her ankles. In the reflection of the mirror, she saw herself between the rails of thread, between her mother’s face and Mr. Zhou’s bent head. She lifted her chin the way he had shown her. In the glass, the girl became a woman through attention more than age.

“Beautiful,” Ben said, but softly this time, like he was careful of the air.

Mr. Zhou took a handful of pins into his mouth, the old habit returning despite signs in the window warning otherwise. He knelt, smoothing the fabric over Lily’s hip. “Stand,” he murmured. “Breathe.” The machine, when he turned it on, made the same sound it had made for thirty years, a hum as constant as an old friend’s gossip. He fed the white hem under the foot, and the needle beat out a steady, soothing pulse. On the counter, the red silk lay folded in a way that made it look like an envelope, an old letter waiting without impatience.

query: 开会沟(*&^%通咋整高****效啊？
response:
The conference room called Whale Song did not sing so much as hum—fluorescents, the soft whirr of the HVAC, the buzz of six phones face-down on the lacquered table vibrating as if they all shared a hive mind. Someone had left a half-dead succulent on the sill; its ribs sagged toward the morning haze over the fifth ring road.

Mei tapped the projector remote with the resigned tempo of a doctor checking a patient who had already given up. The screen blinked, then stabilized on a single line of text in 72-point font, jittery at the edges like it was embarrassed to be here.

开会沟(*&^%通咋整高****效啊？

Asterisks like bullet holes. Parentheses like traps. The characters themselves were unfussed, their calm strokes carrying a question that should have been simple.

“What is that,” Jonah said, mostly to the condensation ring his coffee cup was melting into the table.

“It was supposed to say, ‘开会沟通咋整高效啊？’”—how do we make meeting communication efficient?—Chen Li said, his ears reddening as he hunched behind his laptop. “But, uh, my input method keeps… filtering? I think IT pushed some keyword list. It autocensors ‘高效’ sometimes, leaves it like that.”

Priya leaned forward until her chin hovered above the table like a sleek drone coming in for a landing. “Your keyboard swears at us with hieroglyphics. Honestly, on-brand.”

“This is actually perfect,” said Zhao, who had been with the company since it was three kids and a kettle, and now wore the thin, permanent smile of someone who’d accidentally grown a forest. He gestured at the garbled text like a gallery docent. “It’s a mirror. We want efficiency, and look—,” he wagged his fingers, “static.”

Mei could feel the static in the room. The last three meetings had dissolved into a story bigger than their product: microbeads of miscommunication rolling in different directions, never coalescing. Design wanted clearer acceptance criteria. Engineering wanted fewer pivots. Ops wanted, wanted, wanted, a quiet pipeline.

“It looks like a curse,” Priya said. “Like we summoned something and it only half appeared.”

“Open it up then,” Jonah said, and meant his laptop, but it sounded like he was admitting a chest to surgery.

Beyond the glass, the sales team was practicing their Friday cheers, high voices pealing like gulls. Whale Song’s door muted them into a rumor of ocean. Zhao pulled a thin kitchen timer from his pocket and twisted it until sixty flashed orange.

“Okay,” he said, letting the little device clack down on the table between the laptops. “We try a different way. One problem, one goal, one owner. Thirty minutes.” He tapped the corruption on the screen. “This is our problem. Our goal is a skeleton for meetings. Owner is—” He looked around. No one moved. “Owner is Mei.”

She sat back, surprised to find her own name in the air like a finger pointed by the room. She felt the heat of six eyes slide off her shoulders. “Fine,” she said, and stood, grabbing a dry-erase marker that had long since lost its cap and smelt faintly like licorice.

On the glass wall, just left of the projection, she wrote three bulleted words in English because sometimes switching languages knocked a stuck idea loose: Purpose. People. Process.

“Purpose,” she said. “What we need from a meeting, specifically. People—who actually needs to be here. Process—how we talk.” She was aware of the absurdity: a meeting to talk about how to talk, with a broken sentence for a banner. But absurdity had a way of deflating the right places.

Chen Li’s fingers hovered above his keyboard like hesitant birds. “No laptops?” he said, looking at Zhao. “I mean—if we want… high—” he gestured at the asterisks—“we should minimize the, uh, alt-tabs.”

“Deal,” Priya said, snapping her notebook shut, then—rebellious—opening it again to a blank page. “So every meeting must have a documented purpose, or we reschedule it. People—invitees can decline with a reason, no guilt.”

“And process,” Jonah added, finding a foothold, “start with what we’re trying to decide. If no decision is needed, it’s an update—do it in writing.”

The timer ticked, a faint heartbeat. On the table, phones developed halos of silence as Do Not Disturb icons spread like a ritual.

Mei drew a box and wrote: Decisions and owners. Beside it, another: Risks and blockers. “We end with these,” she said. “We don’t leave with a vibe.”

They tested it, then, not as revolutionaries but as kids trying on their parents’ coats. Priya played facilitator and did not let their sentences braid into anxieties. Jonah kept time, his thumb resting gentle on the kitchen timer as if it were a living thing that might startle. Zhao sat back and watched, the way he had as founders watched their first hires—hands off in case they crushed something delicate.

When someone veered into the weeds—Mei, explaining the branch strategy as if she was describing a lover—the facilitator redirected, a gentle fence. When a decision tried to slink out under the door, Mei wrote it down and pinned a name to it, the way her mother had pinned her school name tag to her sweater with a rusted safety pin.

At fifteen minutes, something shifted, the way a jammed drawer finally slid. The room felt less like a collapsing universe and more like a river deciding, okay, this is the valley then. Chen Li raised his hand like a kid in class.

“What about cross-timezone?” he said. “When we can’t all be… here. Do we make exceptions?”

“Write it first,” Zhao said. “If someone can’t be here, the written thing is the meeting they attend. We respond to that, not the absence.”

They looked at the projected question again. It was still broken, still peppered with strange punctuation like it had been through a storm of coding. But now it looked less like a taunt and more like a fossil: evidence of a previous condition.

“Can IT fix your input method?” Priya asked Chen.

Chen shrugged, sheepish. “Probably. Or I learn to type slower.”

“Leave it,” Mei said, surprised at herself. She uncapped and recapped the marker out of habit, a nervous metronome. “Let it be ugly in here for a while. It’s a reminder.”

“Of what?” Jonah said.

“That we’re not guaranteed clarity,” she said. “We make it.”

The timer pinged, a small bell. They all flinched, then laughed, shoulders unknotting the way cables do when you stop tugging them and start teasing apart loops. Zhao reached over and clicked it off, palm flat as if he could dampen the energy he’d set free.

Outside, the sales team whooped, muffled joy. The succulent on the sill caught a sliver of light and, if it tilted, did so invisibly. The screen still held its question: 开会沟(*&^%通咋整高****效啊？ The room, for the first time in a week, had a way to answer.

query: 很抱歉，我不能帮助您。
response:
The hospital lobby at seven in the morning had the early light of a bus station, a kind of stale expectancy under fluorescent hum. Condensation smeared the insides of the glass doors, and every push from outside dragged in a gust of cold and two steps' worth of steam. Overhead, an LED screen clicked through numbers that glowed red as if they were warnings more than tickets: A056, A057. Someone coughed the way old pipes cough, long and with something sharp at the end. The floor had that tide line of footprints that never quite dried, a sheen of disinfectant that smelled faintly of mint and iron.

At Window 3, behind a pane of glass with a half-moon cut into it, a young woman sat in a black office chair whose padding had given out in the middle. She had a thin sweater on under her blue uniform vest, and her bangs were pulled back under a plastic headband. Three things shared the narrow ledge of her world: a keyboard shiny in the places her fingers hit most, a plastic tray of green and pink clinic cards, and a sign that said, in tidy typed characters, WE APPRECIATE YOUR PATIENCE. She moved in a small economy, stapling, sliding, stamping. There was a bandage across the side of her thumb. A tiny gold charm bracelet knocked once against the desk.

“下一位。” The syllables were gentle, practiced; the glass took their edge.

The man who stepped forward had a winter cap folded in his hands like a paper offering. He was not old, but whatever years he’d done had been outdoors: the tops of his cheeks were cracked and polished like old fruit, and his knuckles were knotted strawberries of restored blood where he’d warmed them under his armpits. A nylon bag hung from his shoulder; inside, a thermos and a netted bag of oranges made the shapes crisp. He pushed a stack of bills under the moon in the glass and then, with a second thought, an identification card and a bent paper that still held the faint smell of the photocopy machine.

“姑娘，” he said, the s played like z, and nodded toward the corridor beyond the windows where the elevator doors opened and shut like slow eyes. “她已经排到今天了。麻醉都做了，说还要多交五千块才做。我这儿——” He shook his head and the cap crumpled. The words came rushed and then slowed, as if he were listening to them too. “我们农村医保卡昨天报不上去，系统，说是‘暂时维护’，我也不懂。能不能先做了，我…我明天就把钱补上。”

Her screen reflected in her eyes, lines of pixels like rain falling upwards. She kept her voice at the same even tone that she had practiced until it no longer sounded like a tone at all. “住院押金必须先交够，” she said. “要不然系统不开手术单。”

He pushed the money a few centimeters forward, as though proximity could change policy. “我今天带了两千。真的，明天我女儿发了工资就…她在厂里，手机也打不通。我昨天晚上就在急诊那儿坐了一夜，医生说今天就排了。我去看她，脚已经绑了——”

He took a breath, swallowed. The oranges, incongruous in their net bag, gave the whole thing the feeling of a visit, not a transaction. He had probably thought he would hand them to her after, when all this was over, their little citrus moons bright against the antiseptic white. Somewhere behind him, a child began to cry high and steadily; a mother hissed him quiet. A woman in a yellow coat tapped, tapped the face of her phone as if calling out time.

The young woman at the window looked at the place where his name on the ID met the place where it was typed in her system. Behind her voice was a great machine of buttons and confirmations; behind her, a poster that showed an idealized waiting room family—with everyone smiling and everyone’s hair behaved—reminded patients not to spit in the potted plants. She could feel the eyes of the guard on her right, a man leaning backward on a stool with the sleepy watchfulness of a cat. She thought of the training they had done at the beginning of the winter, when they had been taught to repeat phrases: we understand, please understand, we regret. The phrases were like the rubber bumpers on the side of a boat; you pressed them between yourself and other people’s waves.

“很抱歉，我不能帮助您。” She met his eyes and then, instead of staying there, looked at his hands where the cap had left lines in the skin. “我知道您着急，可这个是规定。急诊的话，医生那边可以先处理一些，但手术单这边系统是连着的。” She tapped the edge of the monitor, almost apologetic, as if the screen itself were a stubborn older cousin. “要不您在候诊区等一下，您家属在几病区几床？我帮您打个电话问一下床位那边的护士，看能不能协调一下先做别的检查。”

He did not get angry. There are people who are good at anger, at making of it an instrument; he was not. He wrapped his cap tighter until it became a lump. His mouth worked around the shape of something he was trying to make polite. After a moment he said, “姑娘，我知道你有规定。我就想问问，能不能通融一下。她…咳嗽咳了两个月了，昨天吐了血。” He paused so that he would not say everything at once. The tendency to plead collected in his shoulders, in the way he leaned as if there were less glass between them.

“I’ll ask the nurse,” the young woman said, and even as she said it, even as the words moved out and into play—she had tools, she had a phone—the man’s face had already gone slack, the way faces go when a door catches you in the ribs. They both knew how long a hospital phone could ring into absence. They both knew the nurses were elbows-deep in people, that their hands were often too full to pick up.

Behind him, the LED clock piped: A058. A woman in the next line told her husband to hold their place and scurried to the window of the public payphone to top up her data package. The guard on the stool cleared his throat, and the sound slid along the tiles to settle around their ankles.

The man nodded. “行，您帮我问问。” He pulled the oranges out of the bag, as if the sight of them would strengthen his case. “我给她洗了皮，她爱吃的。她…我不敢跟她说，说我们没交够钱。她肯定要怪我，说我这个人办事慢。” He managed a laugh that ran out like a car going down a road with sand on it; slow, slipping.

When the call went unanswered on the fourth try, the young woman set the receiver down softly as if it were something living that had tired. She did not let the pause extend into silence long enough to be accusatory; she filled it with the steps she could offer. “您看这样吧，” she said. “我帮您把今天能开的化验单都先开了，抽血、心电图，先做着。押金这边您尽量去凑一下。实在不行的话，去七号楼那个社会工作站问一下，看他们能不能帮您申请临时救助，需要证明的材料我这儿可以给您盖章。”

He had not prepared for the word “救助.” It was a word he had seen on television with earthquake footage and red flags. He looked at his oranges, then at the money he’d laid out. He pushed the pile back toward himself with his fingertips and moved each bill into alignment, as if neatness had any power.

“谢谢您，” he said, and because he had nothing else to give for the phone calls she had made and the time she had taken, he added, useless gift, “辛苦了。”

She had another phrase for this; it too had been practiced. “应该的。” It came out softer than she meant it to, and something in her own chest was irritated with her, the part of her that hated feeling like a thin wall that everyone leaned on.

He stepped away, and the guard called, not unkindly, “下一位。” A plastic name badge bumped against a woman’s chest as she moved forward, fingers already fanning out to show the array of forms and slips and stamps she had collected. A toddler in a tiny black puffer jacket, legs splayed astern of him, pushed a toy car along the grout lines and made engine noises that sounded like the end of someone’s breath.

At the end of the corridor, just before the elevator, the man stopped and fished in his pocket. He took out his phone: a cheap one, a calendar app stuck open on last month. He swiped his thumb three times on nothing, then pressed the name that said, simply, 女儿. The signal fumbled and then caught; the ring was like a bird trying its call and thinking better of it. He held the oranges against his chest; he pressed the phone to the same place, as if all of it could be kept in by pressure.

When his daughter picked up, her voice was wind and machinery. “爸？我在车间，能小声说吗？”

“没事，” he said, and he had planned to make it light, to tell her not to worry, everything arranged. He looked back at Window 3, where the young woman had already turned to the next patient, mouth forming, with practiced waist-high empathy, “请把医保卡给我。”

He said, instead, “他们说，让我们先交押金。她今天挺…挺难受的。医院的人都忙。很…” He searched for a way to cushion the words, for something that would hold both the rules and his wife’s breath without breaking. “很抱歉，我不能帮助您。” He realized he’d lifted the phrase whole from the glass and put it in his own mouth, as if it were a tool he too could use, a bandage you wrap around any wound, his apology already extended past her answer. “你忙你的，我再想办法。”

Outside, a woman shook a packet of cigarette filters into her palm and discarded the empty on the step. Somewhere a speaker announced a lost ID card. The young woman at the window leaned forward to see the next number, the fluorescent light trembling in the barrette perched above her ear. There were a hundred versions of the conversation to come and only one phrase that fit in all the cracks. Each time she tried it, it settled for a second and then moved aside, like something placed carefully on a shelf too full of other careful things.

query: 很抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
玻璃门一推开，暖风贴着墙角爬，带着消毒水和湿拖把的气味。政务服务中心的屏幕滚着号码，红点一跳一跳地亮：“A205号，请到三号窗口。”

陈湛把贴着指纹油印的文件夹揣得更紧，外套下衬衫湿了一圈。他昨晚从急诊出来，凌晨四点才打到的车，车窗上起了雾。母亲在ICU，缴费窗口只说一句：“差一千五百，今天中午前补上。”他想到了这个地方：低保临时救助，朋友说手续快。

三号窗口的玻璃透着指纹，很薄的一层雾。坐里面的女工作人员戴着口罩，声音从孔里挤出来，像被过滤过：“材料呢？”

“这儿。”陈湛把文件夹打开，一张张递进去，“户口本复印件、母亲的住院单、我这边的收入证明——公司去年倒了，我在灵活就业平台上做一些短工，这边有流水。”

女人把一叠纸理齐，用手指轻轻敲了敲：“根据流程，需要最近三个月的社保缴纳记录、失业登记证明，以及社区开具的家庭困难说明。这些都齐了么？”

“社保……停了，四月停的。”他说得很快，嗓子发干，“失业登记网上可以办，我试了，系统一直转圈圈。社区的王书记昨天说今天给我盖章，他上午开会，我十二点再去。能先给我把程序走上，先评估一下吗？我真的是等不起了。”

女工作人员把卡住的订书钉掰了一下，啪嗒的一声松开，抬眼看他：“理解你的心情。但是我们这边必须要系统核验，就算评估，也会卡在那一步。你可以去那边的自助机先线上申请。”她抬手指了指大厅角落里两台亮着的机器，“通过了我们这边才能受理。”

自助机上方贴着一张新的告示，四角用订书枪钉得锃亮：“优化办事流程”。机器屏幕上蓝白相间，按钮圆润。陈湛把身份证推进卡槽，屏幕上出现了他的照片，眼睛比现实更有神。他照着步骤点，一步一步，拇指被冷玻璃烫得发麻。到上传证明那一栏，摄像头打开，黄白的灯照得他脸发青。他把收入流水对准镜头，系统识别了半天，弹出一个红框：“图片模糊，请重试。”

他深吸一口气，再重拍。第三次，页面跳到“核验中”。蓝色圆圈旋转，旁边小字显示：“预计耗时：1-3分钟”。大厅里的叫号器喊到“B017”，一个带着孩子的年轻母亲匆匆过去。靠门有个老人不耐烦地在地上点着拐杖，发出嗒嗒的声响。

第六分钟，屏幕跳了一下，弹出一个干净的对话框，白色背景，黑字端端正正：“很抱歉，系统暂时无法完成核验，请稍后再试。”下面两个按钮：“返回首页”“线上咨询”。

他点了“线上咨询”。页面里出现了一个笑眯眯的卡通头像，顶部滚动条显示“智能助手为您服务”。他输入：“急诊，今天必须交费，能不能先开具临时证明？”

对面回复很快，标准术语排得整齐：“您好，根据规定，申请临时救助需完成核验流程，请您耐心等待。您也可前往社区街道咨询。”

他又打字：“我已经等不及了，我母亲在ICU，我现在就差一千五。”光标闪了闪，像在犹豫。

“理解您的困扰。”屏幕上出现打勾的微笑，“感谢您的耐心，建议您尝试以下操作：1.更换网络环境；2.更换图片上传角度；3.错峰办理。是否还有其他问题？”

陈湛盯着“错峰办理”三个字，想笑，又笑不出来。他点开了右上角的电话图标，耳边响起清脆的电子音：“为了提供更好的服务，本通话可能被录音。”随后是熟悉的女声，清清楚楚，像每台机器里都住着她：“您好，欢迎致电——如果您需要人工服务，请按0。”

他按了0。音乐响起，钢琴的音阶在空旷的大厅里游走，像一层淡薄的油，滑过每一个人。女声又响：“目前坐席繁忙，请您耐心等待。您可通过微信公众号办理相关业务。”

过了三分钟，电话接通了。那头的男子声音有点沙哑，却依然像念过训练稿：“您好，请问有什么可以帮到您？”

“我这边申请临时救助，系统核验一直失败。我现在在政务中心，ICU要收费，可以先开个临时单么？”

对方沉默了一秒，敲键盘的声音细细碎碎地穿透过来：“先生，我理解您的情况。不过我们这边也需要系统显示通过了，我们才能出具证明。您可以——”

“可以联系技术部帮我查一下吗？是不是我身份证照片识别不出来？我可以视频。”

那边的敲击声停了，空气里是一阵短短的静默，然后他像在翻一本流程手册：“先生，根据流程，技术问题申报后最迟在三个工作日内处理完成。您可以先向医院申请缓缴。”

“医院说没有缓缴。我不行了。”陈湛按住额头，手心发烫。他感觉眼眶里像塞了两块冰，刺得发胀。他想说点软一点的话，舌头却像一块木板，“拜托你们，真的，帮我想想办法。”

那头的男人叹了一声，叹息被麦克风压扁，像一枚小石子扔进了水里，迅速不见：“我真的很抱歉，先生。但我这边没有权限。我可以把你的诉求上报。”

“上报要多久？”

“我们会尽快处理。”

“‘尽快’是多久？”他失去了耐性，又立即后悔，语气软了些，“我就在这儿，求你了。”

对方沉默，背景里隐约有人喊：“小李，这个工单你记得报。”然后是常见的结尾句，标准，温和，不带情绪：“先生，如果没有其他问题，我——”

“有。”他抓住电话，像抓住一根会发热的铁，“你能不能告诉我一句实话？你们平时是不是也不太管这种情况？”

电话里很长的一段空白，只有呼吸声。最终，那男人用极低的声音说：“我们也只是……做我们能做的。”

通话突然被切换成合成女声，那声音回到了它的轨道上，清清亮亮：“感谢您的来电。很抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。”

query: Please elaborate on the core and significance of inclusive finance.
response:
The community hall smelled faintly of salt and engine grease. A half-dozen plastic chairs faced a chalkboard that had seen better days. Beyond the door, the evening market hummed: fish laid out on crushed ice, the sing-song of prices, the occasional squawk from a disgruntled seabird. Asha wiped chalk dust onto her skirt and drew a circle on the board.

“Imagine this is the village,” she said. “Now, where does the money flow?”

Mariam, who sold sardines and always came early to meetings so she could go home before dark, folded her arms. “Mostly into the city,” she said. “Into pockets that have offices and swivel chairs.”

There was a murmur of agreement. Mr. Otieno, the visiting banker, shifted a ledger under his arm and smiled a smile that tried not to seem defensive.

Kibe, the mobile money agent with a stall the size of a cupboard, leaned against the door. His phone had three screens because he worked with three providers. “And back here, sometimes,” he said, tapping an earnest rhythm against the wooden frame. “Remittances. When your nephew in the city remembers you.”

Asha added smaller circles off the first—a web of chalk villages—and then a series of lines between them. “I brought you here to talk about inclusive finance,” she said. “Not as something someone does to you, but as a network we can build. At its core, it’s simple: it’s the design and delivery of financial services so that everyone—no matter their income, gender, age, or location—can access and use them affordably, safely, and with dignity. Not just having an account, but having an account you trust and can use when it matters.”

Gogo Wanja, whose hands were always busy braiding, squinted at the board. “Dignity,” she said. “That is when a clerk stops calling me ‘mama’ as if I cannot count.”

Mariam nodded. “And when the fees don’t bite chunks out of my earnings.”

“Exactly,” Asha said. “So the core pieces are these: access—meaning the services reach you; affordability—fees and interest that you can bear; suitability—services that fit your needs and culture; quality—reliable, quick, and clear; usage—not just opening accounts but actually using them; and protection—your money and your data safeguarded, with someone to complain to when things go wrong.”

She turned to Mr. Otieno. “You told me your bank has a new product for our fish market.”

He straightened. “We’re piloting QR code payments at the docks. No more counting change in the rain. Sellers get paid instantly. Buyers don’t carry cash. With our partner, we offer micro-insurance for your catch while it’s in transit, and a small overdraft for float management. Fees are low. We also have a tiered account that you can open with just your national ID, no deposit needed.”

The murmurs changed tenor—curiosity threading through skepticism. Mariam’s eyes flicked to the zippered bag under her table outside, where the day’s takings were folded in a bundle. She thought of the absent night watchman and the way shadows moved at the far end of the street.

“Last year,” Asha said softly, “when the storm broke the bridge, do you remember how long the roads were closed?”

“Six days,” Gogo supplied. “The water took the bridge as if it were a twig.”

“Six days without the market,” Asha said. “Those of us who had cash under our mattresses spent it in two. Those who had a mobile wallet got a cousin in the city to send money on the first day. Those with micro-insurance for their boats got paid for the days they couldn’t fish. Those with a line of credit bought ice to keep stock fresh for when the road opened. The difference between a crisis and a catastrophe is often a small, timely flow of money.”

She gestured to the lines she had drawn. “That’s the significance of inclusive finance. It’s how a family doesn’t have to sell a goat to pay a clinic. It’s how a widow can receive a support transfer directly from the government without half of it disappearing in ‘processing.’ It’s how your youth group can start a solar kiosk without pleading for loans from men who demand more than interest. It builds resilience, grows small businesses, and, importantly, gives people choices.”

Nuru, who had been leaning in the doorframe listening hard, spoke up for the first time. He was thin and wore a cap low to shadow his eyes. “Choices,” he said. “Like when I took a loan from that app because the boat engine died and I needed cash by morning. They said ‘instant approval’ and the interest changed every day. When I couldn’t pay, they sent shame messages to everyone in my phone book.” He held up a battered Nokia. “They called my grandmother. Is that ‘inclusive’?”

Eyes turned to Asha. Her gaze didn’t flinch. “No,” she said. “That’s the danger when the design is wrong. Inclusive finance only works if it includes protection: clear terms, fair interest, no harassment, data privacy, and real recourse when something goes wrong. We need regulation that is firm but proportional—tight enough to keep out predators but flexible enough to let good ideas grow. And we need to know the difference between access and abuse.”

Mr. Otieno had the grace to look uncomfortable. “We do not endorse those apps,” he said. “Our digital loans come with counseling and caps. We don’t store your contacts. We have a local office. If someone mis-sells you a product, I can take you to our branch manager by name.”

“And the fees?” Mariam asked. Her vendor neighbor once fainted at a teller desk when she saw the sum shaved off her deposit.

“Five shillings per QR transaction,” he said. “Free transfers to savings. One percent on micro-insurance premiums. No fee to open your first account with us.”

Kibe’s thumb made circles on his phone screen. “And agents?” he asked. “Am I out of a job?”

“We need you,” Mr. Otieno said quickly. “In a true inclusive system, the last-mile network—agents like you, self-help groups, co-ops—are the backbone. But we’ll support you: liquidity, training, and fair commissions. We’re not coming here to push you out; we’re trying to plug you in.”

Asha drew a rectangle around the cluster of chalk circles. “There are also invisible rails that make the visible services work,” she said. “Our national ID is one. Interoperable payment systems—so your wallet can talk to his app and her bank—are another. Credit information systems that don’t punish you forever for one mistake. Clear consumer protection rules. When these rails are solid, things like QR at the docks, school fee savings plans, and crop insurance ride on top of them and reach you safely.”

She paused. “And literacy. We can’t pour water down a pipe if we haven’t shown people where the tap is and how to turn it. That’s why we’re here.”

Gogo tugged the end of a braid. “And the old ones? I can read, but your codes are small boxes and my fingers are not so fast.”

“We design for you,” Asha said. “Choice again. QR for those who want it. Cash-in and cash-out nearby. Talk-and-listen menus in our languages, not just paper. Nothing should be one-size-fits-all. Inclusive finance isn’t about forcing change; it’s about widening the path so more can walk it.”

Mariam glanced at the doorway—at the shimmer of late light on scales, the quiet way men counted coins by muscle memory. She remembered the night two months ago when a thief had cut her bag strap and dashed into the dark. She’d lost a week’s money. Her chest had felt hollow for days.

“What about us women?” she asked. “You say dignity. My husband thinks a bank is his domain. My money is for tomatoes and schoolbooks. How do I keep it mine?”

“You can have your own account,” Mr. Otieno said. “Your own PIN. We can set up goal-based savings so that every day, a small, fixed amount goes from your phone to your school fund. And you can add a trusted contact who can help if you forget your code, without seeing your balance.”

“And if someone takes my phone?” she said. “If my cousin guesses my PIN because he watched me once?”

“Then we need better practices,” Asha replied. “But also design: fingerprint or face ID where possible, one-time passcodes that don’t reveal themselves. And passwords you’re taught to set in private rooms at agent stalls. Gender-sensitive design matters. We test with women’s groups and we change what doesn’t work.”

From outside, a fishmonger’s bell clanged twice—the polite way to signal “fresh batch.” The group shifted, senses tugged toward work. Asha erased the board, leaving only the web of circles and lines.

“Before you go,” she said, “think of inclusive finance like a road system we lay together. If we build it well—smooth and wide—more of us can travel, selling and buying, saving and borrowing, insuring and planning. The significance isn’t the road itself; it’s where it lets us go. It’s Mariam not losing everything to a thief. It’s Nuru getting a fair loan for an engine, with a repayment schedule that doesn’t strangle him. It’s Gogo paying the clinic without pawning her wedding bangles. It’s the co-op storing surplus on good days so lean days don’t break you.”

“And it’s the fish speaking to the phone instead of the cash box?” Gogo smiled, a flash of white.

Asha laughed. “If the fish could talk, they’d ask for a better market price. Data can help with that too.”

There was a ripple of laughter. Mr. Otieno set his ledger on a chair. “Tomorrow,” he said, “we’ll be at the docks with QR stickers and a help desk. We’ll sign up anyone who wants to try, with no pressure. Kibe will be there to help. We’ll explain every fee twice. If you don’t like it, you can walk away.”

Mariam stood, smoothing her skirt. “I’ll come,” she said. “Because the last storm taught me that I cannot hold back the water with a broom. But promise me we will build this together. And that when I bring a problem, someone will listen.”

“Promise,” Asha and Mr. Otieno said in unison.

Later, when the hall emptied and the generator wound down, Asha lingered by the chalkboard, tracing the lines with her finger as if she could feel the future hum through them. Inclusive finance wasn’t a magic spell. It was pipes and rails and human agreements, levers lifted one by one. But she had seen what happened when the pipes ran to the right places: not wealth for all overnight, but steadier hands, fewer desperate gambles, a community that bent under the weight of bad luck and then straightened. That was its significance—the quiet strength it lent to ordinary days. Outside, a breeze lifted the corner of a QR sticker they’d posted on the notice board. She pressed it down, and it held.

query: 行政复议是什$$$么意思？申请这个东西有啥时间限啊？
response:
街角的社区法律服务站在黄昏里亮起了冷白的灯。窗外一场小雨刚停，行道砖缝里还冒着湿气。墙上贴着“免费法律咨询”的红字海报，桌上摞着一叠浅蓝色的申请表，纸边被翻得起毛。

张帆把外卖箱搁在门口，手还捏着没关的头盔。他的手机屏幕裂了，指尖一划就跳字。他坐在塑料椅上，半天才组织好一句话，把屏幕递过去：“我收到城管的处罚决定，让我五天内缴罚款。我朋友说可以‘行政复议’，我就想问——行政复议是什$$$么意思？申请这个东西有啥时间限啊？”

坐对面的姑娘叫林清，二十多岁，桌上摊着一本《行政复议法》的便携本，角上贴了很多彩色纸签。她接过手机笑了一下：“屏幕裂得厉害啊，这‘什$$$么’也能看出来。”她把手机放回去，拿起一支签字笔在草稿纸上写了两个字：复议。

“简单说，”她抬头，“行政复议就是你觉得行政机关作出的具体决定——像罚款、认定、许可被撤销、强制措施这些——有问题，程序不当或者事实不清、法律适用不对，你可以向法律规定的有权机关申请让他们再审一遍那个决定。一般是作出决定的机关的上一级来复查。”

张帆“哦”了一声，眼睛还盯着那两个字，“那是不是比打官司简单点？”

“它是比行政诉讼程序更快一点、成本更低一些，”林清说，“而且现在很多地方主推‘复议为主’，复议是免费的，材料也比较简化。但它不是‘随便试试’，也有严格的时限。”

她翻开便携本，用指尖敲了敲一行标注：“大多数情况下，申请行政复议要在你知道这个具体行政行为之日起六十日内提出。‘知道’一般以你收到处罚决定书、送达之日或者公告期满之日算起。法律、法规对某些事项另有规定的，从其规定。”

“六十天？”张帆挠头，“我这决定是前天给我的。”

“那你在期限内，”林清点点头，“对于行政不作为——就是你申请办某个事，机关该在规定期限内给你答复却一直没给——复议的起算点是从那个法定办理期限满了那天开始算，也是六十日内可以申请。还有一种情况，如果遇到不可抗力，或者有正当理由耽误了，比如你住院、受灾之类，期间可以不算在内，恢复以后再继续计算。”

她停了一下，补充道：“不过，这些都需要有证据证明。每个案子具体情况不一样。”

张帆把头盔放下，往后一靠：“我朋友还说，有的事必须先复议，不能直接去法院，是不是真的？”

“有一些事项是复议前置，”林清挑挑眉，又没有把具体目录说出口，“但也有很多可以在复议和诉讼之间选择。一般如果你选择了先复议，等复议决定出来以后，如果你还不满意，可以在规定的期限内再去起诉。等同于先走一道内部的复核程序。”

“那复议要多久能有结果？”

“复议机构受理以后，一般应当在六十日内作出复议决定，复杂的可以适当延长，”她把笔在桌上轻点，“但证据收集、送达等程序性耗时不一定算在里面。你要有心理预期，它毕竟是个程序。”

门口又进来一个抱小孩的妇女，冲两人点点头，在另一张桌子前坐下。林清把声音压低：“还有个实际操作的提醒——你得弄清楚复议的管辖：对谁的决定不服，向谁申请复议，不是随便找个上级就行。通常是作出处罚的机关的上一级，或者法律规定的本级政府设立的复议机构负责。决定书背面一般会写明复议机关和起诉法院。”

张帆把罚款决定书从外卖箱里抽出来，纸上有雨点烘出的一圈圈水痕。他把那张纸摊开，指着最后一行小字：“它写的是‘如不服本决定，可在六十日内向××区人民政府或××市城管局申请行政复议’。”

“对，这就很清楚了，”林清顺着字念，“你有两个复议机关可以选一个。六十天——从你前天签收那天起算——你可以准备材料。”

“准备啥？”

“基本材料是申请书、你的身份证明、决定书原件或复印件、相关证据。申请书需要写明你不服的事项、请求、事实和理由。”她笑了笑，“听起来复杂，其实就是把事情经过说清楚，把你觉得不合理的点一条条列明。”

张帆默默点头，手背上的雨水已经干了，只留下外卖箱压过的白痕。他看了看墙上的时钟：“我今天还得跑一单，明天能来找你帮我看看材料不？”

“可以啊，”林清把一个浅蓝色的空表格推过去，“你先把基本情况填了，回去把相关票据、现场照片、聊天记录这些能证明当时情形的东西整理一下。注意保存送达的凭证，时间点很关键。”

门外的雨又有起势，风一吹进来，海报轻轻鼓起来，又贴回墙上。张帆把表格小心叠好塞进胸前口袋，抬头问：“那要是我超过六十天，咋办？”

林清思考了一下：“超过期限，复议机关一般不予受理。但如果你确实有不可抗力或者其他正当理由，可以说明并提供证明，争取恢复计算。不过这个不保证。总之，别拖。”她顿了顿，又补了一句，“每个地方具体操作会有差异，法律条文是一回事，落地是另一回事。你尽快准备吧。”

张帆站起来，背上外卖箱，脚步声在塑料地板上发出闷响。他把头盔扣上，笑了一下：“行，我知道了。行政复议大概啥意思、时间限也明白了。谢谢你啊。”

“路上慢点，”林清朝他摆摆手，又低头在便携本上把“六十日、起算点、前置事项”几个词圈了红笔，像是在替他，也在替自己，牢牢记住那些具体却不冷的字眼。

query: 基因编辑技术是什么？其应用前景及伦理考量在医疗领域中有哪些？
response:
夜雨把门诊楼的玻璃敲得轻响，像有人不肯收起的指尖。十四楼的会议室里只开了半盏灯，长桌端坐着四个人：林医生，血液科的临床遗传学家；周教授，医院伦理委员会的成员；罗先生和他妻子梅女士，他们的儿子阿川正靠在窗边，背着小书包，鞋尖轻轻点地。

林医生把一支中性笔竖在掌心，说话温和而清楚：“你们问的‘基因编辑’，最简单地说，就是在生命的说明书上做非常精确的修改。我们的说明书是DNA，一串由四个字母排列成的长句。传统的方法是‘添加一段话’，把一个新的基因送进去；而基因编辑更像是用带导航的微型工具，在某一页某一行找到特定的字，把它剪掉、改掉，或者换成更合适的字。现在应用最广的是一种叫CRISPR的系统，它用一段‘向导’去找目标，再用分子剪刀完成切割。还有更细致的方式，比如‘碱基编辑’，像把一个字母从A改成G，不必整段切开；‘引导编辑’则像是修订器，可以在不完全切断的情况下插入或替换短小的句子。”

阿川回过头，眼睛亮了亮：“就是把错别字改对？”

周教授笑：“有时候是把错别字改正，有时候是把逗号放到该有的地方，让整段话读起来不再卡顿。但你要记得，书页不是一张纸，是活的细胞。改一个字，可能让整段都变得更好，也可能不小心擦到旁边的注脚，出现意料不到的效果。这也是我们需要审慎讨论的原因。”

林医生把话题带回到现实：“在医疗上，基因编辑的前景很大，尤其是针对单基因遗传病。比如镰状细胞病和重型地中海贫血，近两年英国和美国都批准了首个CRISPR疗法，用的是把患者自己的造血干细胞取出来，在体外做编辑，让它们重新生产不会弯曲、不易破裂的红细胞，然后再回输——这叫体外编辑。我们正在评估阿川是否适合进入类似研究的队列。除此之外，肿瘤治疗也在用编辑过的免疫细胞，提高它们识别和攻击癌细胞的能力，未来可能出现‘通用型’细胞，减少配型难度。”

他翻了翻资料：“眼科上，有针对某些遗传性视网膜病变的试验，直接在眼内进行编辑；心血管领域有人尝试把肝脏里控制胆固醇的‘开关’轻轻拨动，帮助高危人群降脂——那是更精准的碱基编辑；传染病方面，理论上可以让免疫细胞失去某些病毒依赖的‘门把手’，比如HIV常用的CCR5受体；器官移植也在用编辑猪的基因，减少排斥和病毒风险，为等待移植的人打开一个新入口。再往前看，还有用编辑纠正致病突变的罕见病，或者让药物对不同体质的人更‘对路’的个性化治疗。”

罗先生谨慎地问：“听起来像一条很新的路。那风险呢？”

周教授点点头，把手中的水杯往桌上一放：“伦理上的考量，往往从你们最关心的地方开始——安全。我们担心‘误改’和‘偏离目标’，也担心在体内引发免疫反应，或是长远的、还没有被观察到的副作用。体外编辑之后再回输，风险可控一些；体内直接编辑，进入谁的细胞、改了多少、有没有影响旁边的基因，监测就更关键。”

他顿了顿，又补了一句：“还有时间这件事。基因编辑不是打一针就算了，很多患者需要多年随访，记录血象、功能、甚至心理变化，这既是科学的责任，也是对你们的承诺。”

林医生接着说：“第二个维度，是‘编辑到哪儿’。像我们讨论的治疗，都是作用在你自己的体细胞——不会传给下一代，这叫体细胞编辑。另一类是生殖细胞或胚胎的编辑，改动会遗传下去。全球普遍的立场是对胚胎和生殖系编辑保持严格禁令或高度谨慎。你们也许还记得几年前中国的那个事件，研究者擅自对胚胎做了编辑，最终生下了孩子，引发巨大争议。那件事提醒我们：未来的孩子无法对自己的基因改动表达同意，风险和不确定会跨越代际，一旦出错，后果可能不可逆。”

梅女士把手指搓得发白：“我们是普通人，只想着孩子能少些痛。可是也怕，怕做了‘先行者’，万一……”

周教授把话题引进更广阔的现实：“你们的‘怕’非常真实，也和我们每天开会讨论的第三个问题重叠——公平。在座机上，你们能看到全球的新闻，说某种疗法成功了；可到了付款环节，很多基因治疗都动辄数百万的价格。谁能用上，谁先用上，穷的、偏远的、少数族群的人会不会又一次被落下？我们担心新技术把人群划得更碎，也担心它会给某些疾病贴上‘可以被修理’的标签，从而对未能或不愿接受治疗的人造成新的偏见。”

他看向阿川：“还有隐私。编辑之前要知道你有哪些变异，检测的数据存在哪儿，谁能看，保险公司会不会据此决定保费和理赔？有的国家有保护基因信息的法律，但还不完善，尤其在寿险、长期护理等领域。”

林医生把椅子往前挪了一寸：“所以，我们在招募任何一位患者进入编辑疗法时，会做几件事。第一是诚实：告诉你我们知道的效果和不知道的风险，以及你可能需要面对的短期治疗，比如化疗空出骨髓‘位置’，这本身也会有副作用；第二是尊重：罗列可替代的方案，包括现行药物、骨髓移植、或者等待更成熟的技术；第三是支持：如果你选择了，我们会提供心理咨询和长期随访计划，让这条路不至于孤零零。”

梅女士抬起头，眼睛红了却很亮：“我还有一个问题。有没有可能，有一天他们会把孩子‘改得更好’，比如更聪明、更漂亮？”

周教授的目光像雨后未散的云：“公众对‘设计婴儿’的想象，往往来源于夸张的科幻。现实里，我们连聪明这样的复杂性状都还解释不清，更不用说塑造成一台机器似的‘完美人’。但你的担心仍然重要——它提醒我们，科学不该被市场欲望牵着走。医疗的边界，是减轻痛苦、提升生活质量，而不是按偏见塑形人类。我们需要持续的社会对话，让技术在阳光下成长。”

阿川把手贴在窗玻璃上，看着雨丝从灯影里滑过去：“如果是把错别字改正，我愿意做那一页稍微整齐一点的书。可是我也不想变成别人写好的故事。”

林医生笑了，像在翻一本旧书：“这正是我们出发的方向。医学是帮你把自己的故事写得更顺，而不是把你的笔拿走。”他把一叠纸推过来，“这份说明书里，写了‘基因编辑是什么’、‘它可能带来的好处’以及‘我们担心的地方’。今晚你们先看，明天我们再把每一条聊细。无论你们做什么决定，我们都会和你们站在同一页上。”

外面雨声渐细。会议室里没有谁急着起身，纸页被翻动的声音轻轻响起，像是在一个漫长的段落里找到了恰当的逗号。
