query: Explain core 伦理 in scientific research.
response:
The rain had started midafternoon, tapping the high windows of Building C like someone drumming fingers on a desk. When Dr. Lin sent the message—All-hands meeting, 5 p.m., mandatory—nobody argued. The centrifuge coasted to a stop; a pipette clicked and was holstered. By the time everyone shuffled into the seminar room, damp shoulders and laptop lids beaded with water, she was already at the whiteboard.

She uncapped a marker and wrote just one word in the center, clean and deliberate: 伦理.

“Ethics,” she said, turning. “We need to talk.”

Qian slid into a chair nearest the radiator. Amir leaned against the back wall, arms folded, eyes weary from a week of staining and restaining. Xiaoyu opened her notebook and, almost unconsciously, drew the same character in the margin.

“I got a call from the 伦理委员会,” Dr. Lin continued, voice even. “The IRB. Our consent forms for the wearable sensor study? The translation misses a clause about data sharing. They caught it; we didn’t. It’s fixable. But it’s a crack in the foundation.”

She drew a line under the character, as if to anchor it to the board. “This is not a scolding,” she added. “It’s a reminder. We work with cells, with code, with data. But under all of it is 伦理. If we ignore it, nothing we do can be called science.”

Mr. Zhang, the lab manager, cleared his throat softly. He was old enough to have lived through labs where order and cleanliness masked a dozen unspoken shortcuts, and he kept two watches—one for time and one for compliance. “Lin, do you want me to—”

“Let me start,” she said. “Then I’ll ask all of you to argue with me.”

She tapped the marker against the board. “First: honesty and integrity. No fabrication, no falsification, no plagiarism. These are big words; the sins are small and quiet. Qian, last week you sent me a figure with an unusually smooth curve. When I asked for the raw data, it took three days to find.”

Qian sat straighter, the breath catching in his throat. “I—yes. The files were on my desktop. I renamed—”

“I know,” she said, softening. “I’m not accusing you of anything. I’m using us as an example. Honesty begins with the lab notebook that someone else can read, with filenames that outlive you, with raw data that is never, ever destroyed. If you clean data, the code that does the cleaning is versioned and explained. If you remove outliers, the criteria are prespecified. If a result is negative, it still exists.”

Amir smiled, rueful. “If science were marriage,” he said, “transparency would be fidelity.”

“Exactly,” Dr. Lin said. “Which brings me to objectivity and transparency. We preregister our hypotheses when we can. We make our analysis plans public before we are tempted by noise. We share code and data whenever it’s ethical and legal to do so. That’s not performative; it’s accountability. If someone can’t reproduce our work, I want them to come into this room and tell us how to do it better.”

Xiaoyu raised a hand, tentative. “Dr. Lin, I read about p-hacking. It sounded like… curiosity gone bad.”

Dr. Lin nodded. “Curiosity with sharp elbows. It’s looking at the data first and then deciding what you were looking for. Sometimes exploration is fine—discoveries are born from wandering. But you must label what is exploratory and what is confirmatory. The ethics here—伦理—is about not fooling ourselves or our readers. If you don’t know, say you don’t know.”

Mr. Zhang, who’d rescinded more keys than anyone liked to admit, added, “And not fooling your future self. I’ve seen postdocs leave and two years later we can’t explain a figure because the only record is a JPEG in a ‘Final_Final2’ folder.”

Laughter eased the air. Outside, a motorbike buzzed through the rain.

“Second,” Dr. Lin said, and drew a new circle on the board. “Respect for persons. You hear that as a slogan, but imagine your mother signing a consent form for a study. Would you want her to be rushed? Would you want the language to be vague? We don’t treat consent as a box to tick. We ensure understanding, avoid undue inducement, and honor the right to withdraw without penalty.”

Amir shifted against the wall. “We used the term ‘anonymized’ in the draft protocol. Mr. Li from data protection wrote ‘pseudonymized’ instead. I thought it was semantics.”

“It isn’t,” Dr. Lin said. “Anonymization means no one—including us—can reidentify the person. Pseudonymization means we can, with a key. The ethics are different. If there’s a key, we guard it. We minimize who has access. We store clinical data on encrypted servers, not on your laptops. If a journalist calls, we don’t confirm participation. If a patient asks for their data to be deleted and we can honor that without compromising the integrity of the analysis, we do it.”

Qian glanced at Xiaoyu. “What about images?” he asked. “We took photos of the electrode placements for documentation. They’re in the shared drive.”

“Faces blurred, tattoos and scars obscured, consent specifically for images,” Dr. Lin said. “And we never post those on social media. Ever.”

She drew a third circle. “Beneficence and non-maleficence: do good, do no harm. We weigh risks against benefits—not abstractly, but with numbers and with imagination. A sensor that might cause a rash is a small harm; a disclosure that might cause someone to lose their job is a great harm. In animal work, the 3Rs—replacement, reduction, refinement—are not paperwork. If you can use organoids instead of mice, you do. If you must use mice, you use the fewest and you alleviate suffering. Ethics is how you hold a mouse, not just how you euthanize it.”

Mr. Zhang nodded, eyes going somewhere far off. “My first PI told me, ‘Be kind to animals because one day you will wish someone is kind to you.’ It stuck.”

“And justice,” Dr. Lin said, sketching another circle and connecting them with lines. “Who bears the burden of research, and who benefits? If our recruitment is only from people who can afford to take time off work, our results will lie to us and to the world. We seek diversity, not to tick a box, but because truth lives there. We compensate participants fairly, not so much that it coerces, not so little that it insults. When we publish, we don’t pretend that this device will save everyone when we’ve only tested it in the young and healthy.”

Xiaoyu hesitated. “Is it unjust if we work mostly with students because they’re easy to recruit?”

“It’s convenient,” Dr. Lin said. “It’s also biased. We can do better. Ethics isn’t only ‘don’t be evil.’ It’s also ‘be curious about what you’re missing.’”

Amir pushed off the wall and took a step closer to the board. “What about the sponsor? Shandong Lifeline paid for half the sensors. They asked me to pre-approve the abstract and offered to ‘help with language.’ Conflict of interest?”

“Always assume conflicts exist,” Dr. Lin said. “We disclose funding sources. We disclose when a company has a stake. We keep the right to publish regardless of outcome, and we won’t let a sponsor edit our conclusions. If we’re offered gifts, we say no; if we’re offered consulting, we seek approval and we draw a bright line. When you speak at a conference, you say who paid your ticket.”

Qian chewed his lower lip. “Authorship,” he said. “I helped with the data collection on Amir’s last paper. I didn’t write any of it. Do I qualify?”

Dr. Lin smiled, and the corners of her eyes softened. “Authorship is credit and responsibility. The usual criteria are: substantial contribution to conception or design or data acquisition; drafting or revising the manuscript; final approval; and accountability for integrity. If you only carried boxes, no. If you designed the sampling protocol, yes. If you ran the analyses and can explain them, yes. We err on the side of fairness. Ghost authorship and gift authorship hurt everyone. If you’re on a paper, you must be able to defend any part of it to a stranger on a train.”

“Which has happened,” Amir said, and the room chuckled.

“Mentorship is part of 伦理,” Dr. Lin went on, quieter now. “I am responsible for your training. If you make a mistake, it’s my mistake too. If you feel pressured to produce results, tell me. We do not create a culture where sleep deprivation is a badge. Rest is ethical. Saying ‘I don’t know’ is ethical. I want to hear your doubts before they become headlines.”

Outside, the rain eased. The radiator hissed like a cat exhaling.

“Peer review?” Xiaoyu asked.

“We do it generously,” Dr. Lin said. “We don’t scoop ideas we see in review. We declare conflicts. We critique the work, not the person. And we accept critique the same way.”

She set down the marker. The board was a web of circles and lines, the character in the center now almost like a heart with arteries.

“I could make this a checklist,” she said. “But checklists can’t see. What I want is for you to develop good eyes. When you’re tempted to toss a data point because it ruins your narrative, ask what story you’re serving. When someone dangles a shortcut, taste the metal. When a participant looks at you and doesn’t understand, stop. When we write, tell the truth without sparkle that distorts.”

Mr. Zhang stood and walked to the light switch, then thought better of it. “Should we… draft a lab charter?” he ventured. “Not for the shelf, but for the wall.”

“Yes,” Dr. Lin said. “But first, we practice. Qian, you’ll upload all raw data by Friday with readme files. Amir, you’ll send the sponsor our publication independence clause again and decline language help. Xiaoyu, you and I will rewrite the consent in plain Mandarin and English, and we’ll pilot it with Ms. Chen from the community advisory board. Mr. Zhang, you'll review animal use and see if the organoid proposal can move forward.”

“And the IRB?” Amir asked.

“I’ll call them back tonight,” she said. “I’ll tell them we’re grateful.”

They gathered their notebooks and laptops. Chairs scraped the floor; the room rearranged itself to ordinary. In the doorway, Qian halted, then turned back.

“Lin,” he said, haltingly. “When I was a kid, my grandfather used to say, 做人要正—be upright. I thought it meant standing straight when you’re scolded. I think now it’s more like what you wrote.”

Dr. Lin looked at the board. The rain had stopped completely; the city beyond the glass was rinsed and reflective.

“It’s the same,” she said. “Upright in data, upright in code, upright with people. If we get that wrong, our science is clever fiction. If we get it right… then maybe what we do will deserve to exist.”

They filed out into the corridor. The smell of agar and ethanol followed them; the hum of incubators felt steadier than before. In the emptied room, the word remained on the board a moment longer, and then the walls, as they had for decades, listened and stored what they could.

query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成该请求。
response:
The phone’s glow turned his palms chalky blue. Lin tried to keep his breathing even, though the bedroom behind him was filled with the soft scrape of his mother’s cough and the ticking of the wall clock, a cheap plastic face that thought it was keeping time.

He tapped the “Help” icon in the hospital app for the third time. A cartoon stethoscope bobbed in a cheerful loop as the chat window spun up. He typed fast, thumbs scraping the glass.

“Payment stuck after identity verification,” he wrote in Chinese. “Urgent deposit. Dialysis tomorrow morning. Can you push through?”

The hourglass flickered into three dots, then a polite reply that felt like a door sliding shut.

抱歉，我无法协助完成该请求。

“Really?” he said aloud, as if the phone could hear his incredulity. He glanced toward the hallway where his mother slept, the little nightlight making thin shadows of the wicker chair and her walking stick. The bitter, herbal smell of the medicine she’d been steeping all day was lodged at the back of his throat.

He dug his nail into the split seam of the sofa cushion and typed again. “Who can assist? I have the funds. Identity check failed because front camera broken.”

Three dots. The same sentence came back with a different timestamp, like a stamp from a different office but the same ink. 抱歉，我无法协助完成该请求。

Outside, the corridor echoed with footsteps. Someone laughed too loudly, then shushed themselves, a whisper bouncing off concrete floors. The building was old; the elevators coughed before they took you anywhere.

Lin lifted his head. “Ma?” he called softly. The coughs had stopped, replaced by a thin wheeze. “I’ll be right back. I’m going to the convenience store. I’ll come back with something for your throat.”

He slid into his sneakers and grabbed a jacket, the kind you buy from a stall without trying it on. The night air was wet, that southern damp that slicked your skin no matter how clean the air conditioner tried to keep the apartment. He locked the door and jogged down the stairs because the elevator would take too long to decide.

On the ground floor, the security guard looked up from his tiny TV. “Little Lin, you still awake?”

“Bank trouble,” Lin said, already pushing through the glass doors. “Gotta go three blocks to the 24-hour.”

He could smell the convenience store before he saw it: detergent and microwaved buns and new plastic. The clerk, a girl with a rabbit clip in her hair, nodded hello without peeling her eyes from a show on her phone. Lin grabbed two lemon lozenges, a bottle of warm water, and stood under the light, dialing his bank’s customer service.

A recorded voice greeted him with the script now everyone knew by heart. “For service in English, press two.” He jabbed one and waited. The music was a sound no one had composed, just an algorithm’s idea of reassurance.

When the line clicked and a woman’s voice came through, he spoke too fast at first. He had to slow down to make sense.

“The verification won’t work. I have to deposit for a morning procedure. I have money in my card. The hospital app connects to your bank. It’s stuck. Can you—”

“Sir,” the woman said in that careful tone that suggested both empathy and its limits, “if the camera is not working on your device, our system cannot verify your biometrics. Are you able to use another phone?”

“My old phone is with a cousin in Huizhou. It’s midnight. My mother’s sleeping. I can’t leave her to go across the city. Can you waive it?”

“We cannot waive biometric security,” she said. “We can unlock your account at a branch with your ID.”

“All branches are closed,” Lin said, trying to keep the plea out of his voice. “The hospital needs the deposit before morning.”

“I’m very sorry,” she said. He could hear the hum of other calls behind her, the low machinery of the city. “I understand the urgency.”

He bit down on the lozenge and felt the sharp sugar crack. “You don’t,” he whispered, surprising himself. He thanked her anyway, hung up, and rubbed his eyes until stars came. He bought the lozenges and water, nodded at the rabbit clip girl, and walked out into the street where the damp had sealed the city in a clear film.

The hospital’s exterior lights were white enough to make indigo of the sky. He watched a delivery truck back up to the loading dock, the driver staring straight ahead, his face lit a pale rectangle by the cab’s tablet. Lin crossed the car park and went inside. Fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, the benches lined with sleeping people whose bodies had adapted to new ways of folding.

The self-service kiosk stood like an altar, glowing blue. He touched the screen, the smoothness making his fingertips suddenly too dry. “Deposit,” he selected, “Dialysis,” “Tomorrow,” “Patient: Lin Mei.” The screen spun. A small camera icon glared at him like an eye that didn’t blink.

“Facial recognition failed,” the screen told him in a stale white box. “Please try again.”

He tilted his face, the angle the app usually preferred. It whirred once, thought, then spit out the same box. He could feel his heartbeat in his jaw. He pressed the assistance button.

A nurse in soft shoes hurried over. Her hair was tied with a blue elastic that matched the walls. “Yes?”

He explained, the phrases coming out in a blur: broken camera, urgent deposit, mother’s wheeze in the hallway, everything that made the night smaller. The nurse listened with her body angled toward him, hands held together like she was catching the story before it fell.

“Our kiosk uses the phone’s camera,” she said. “If the camera is broken, the system won’t let you authenticate.”

“Can I show you my ID here? Can you push the deposit manually?”

Her eyes flicked toward the desk. A man sat with his elbows on the counter, impression of a supervisor, the tie undone but the authority intact.

“I can ask,” she said quickly. “Wait.”

She crossed the lobby and leaned to speak to the man. Lin could see their silhouettes reflected in the glass door: her curve forward, his hands opening, then the slight inward shrug that meant this wasn’t a thing he could change. The nurse came back with the apology ready.

“抱歉，我无法协助完成该请求,” she said, and the way she said it wasn’t the flat script; it came with the weight of the night. “I’m sorry. We have to follow the protocol.”

The phrase cracked something in him because he had seen it already twice, once from the thing in the phone pretending to be a person, and now out of an actual person who had to pretend to be a line of code.

“Tell me what I can do,” he said. He wasn’t pleading; he was asking this as if the answer were a shape he could build with his hands.

“Do you have a neighbor with a working phone? If you log into your account on their device, we can process the deposit. If you don’t want to log in, the bank branch opens at eight.”

Eight meant too late. Eight would arrive and the dialysis slot would be gone, the bed assigned to someone whose biometrics had passed. He thought of Uncle Wang in 304, whose daughter worked nights. He thought of the kid in 206 with the electric bike that hummed so loud on Sundays. He saw the path unfolding under his feet like a boardwalk he hadn’t planned to walk tonight.

“I’ll try,” he said.

The nurse touched his sleeve lightly, a gesture that meant nothing and everything, then went to the next person, whose need was a different shape.

The corridor back at his building smelled faintly of fried scallions. He knocked on Uncle Wang’s door, then remembered that the old man’s hearing aid was probably on the end table under a newspaper. His knuckles stung. After a long minute, the door opened a crack, chain still latched.

“Oh, Lin,” Uncle Wang said, his voice already softening at the edges of sleep. “What is it?”

“I need to borrow your phone for ten minutes,” Lin said, under his breath, trying not to broadcast urgency like it was contagious. “For the hospital. Just the app.”

Uncle Wang looked over his shoulder into the apartment, where a plant had been coaxed into a respectable green under a grow lamp. He undid the chain and waved Lin inside. “Come. What’s the password again? My daughter set it; I never use it.”

On the coffee table, the phone lay under a lace doily, like a prized plum. Lin sat, logged out the elder’s account, logged in his own. The authentication prompt appeared. He held the phone up. The camera caught his face, mapped it with lines he couldn’t see. For a moment, the phone thought, its algorithms shuffling through their little stack of truths. Then the green tick. He exhaled and realized he had been holding his breath.

He entered the deposit, a sum that made his stomach cinch. The app sent the request to the bank. He waited. The spinning circle spun, and for a second he imagined it spinning all the way down a drain. Then it stopped. “Payment processed.”

On the way back to the hospital, the city’s damp lay on the street like a sheet. He moved faster than he needed, not because time was suddenly thick, but because his body needed the motion. At the kiosk, he pulled up the record. The bed number was assigned; the morning slot held his mother’s name. He took a photo because evidence mattered even when the screen said so.

In the lamplight of the ward, he stood outside his mother’s room. She blinked awake as he opened the door. “Ah Lin?” she said, voice small and rough.

“We’re okay,” he told her in a tone he hoped sounded like a hand rubbing a back. “It’s done.”

He set the lemon lozenges on her bedside table, half a joke, half an offering. Her mouth twitched, then smoothed. “Always trouble,” she whispered, closing her eyes again.

He sank into the chair and watched the machines that did what they were designed to do. Outside, the nurse walked past, her shoes whispering on the floor. Somewhere in the building, a printer coughed a page into the tray, a clerk slid a rubber band around a stack, someone else’s request—possible or not—moved through the pipeline.

On his lap, the phone buzzed with a notification from the hospital app. “Appointment confirmed,” it said. The words were so simple you could fold them up and carry them in your pocket. He felt the night settle around him, not lighter exactly, but less like a wall.

He thumbed back to the chat window where the refusal sat like a stamp. The sentence was still there, but it didn’t hold anything anymore. It had been a barrier until he found the gap alongside it. He didn’t reply. He closed the app, and the screen went dark, only his own reflection floating for a moment before the black took it.

query: De@@scr#ibe b^ack**up me!!thods an&&d relev%an#ce.
response:
The office still smelled faintly of sawdust from the model room, though no one had cut foamboard in weeks. Morning light came in pale and clean through the high windows of the converted warehouse, warming the edges of drafting tables and the plants Laila kept rescuing from construction sites. Somewhere in the back, the server closet ticked like a nervous metronome.

On her monitor, the folder names were all wrong. The proposal package for the 14th Street library was now a smattering of symbols and clipped syllables. One entry—gray, unopenable—read: De@@scr#ibe b^ack**up me!!thods an&&d relev%an#ce.

“God,” she said, thumb pressing into the bridge of her nose. “Is this a joke?”

Priya, her intern, drifted over with a mug of coffee so full it trembled. “I didn’t touch anything. I just tried to drag the latest CAD to the shared drive and it made that… chime of doom.”

“You mean the bonk,” Laila said. They both stared at the folder, as if looking hard enough might turn the symbols back into words. Next to it, a progress bar had frozen at twelve percent. Somewhere, a machine beeped three short, one long. Laila’s stomach tightened. In her head, the city’s procurement officer said: Bids due at noon.

She called Jonah.

He arrived thirty minutes later with a backpack that clinked softly—tools, or snacks. He had the kind of quiet that settled a room. Priya showed him the screen, the gibberish, the spinning beach ball.

“Fun,” he said under his breath, crouching by the server closet. The door was ajar. Inside, the NAS—the toaster-sized box that had seemed so simple when they’d installed it—was blinking an amber light like a warning on a small, resented spaceship. He put his ear to it.

“Drive failure?” Laila offered, hands on her hips. She wanted to sound competent. The afternoon she’d read the manual felt like a hundred years ago.

“Looks like one went. RAID’s doing its job, but it’s limping. When’s the last backup?”

“Last what?” Priya asked.

Laila looked at the whiteboard by the kitchenette. Someone had written in Expo marker: Don’t microwave fish. Under it, in her own handwriting: BACKUPS? and a little star. The star had seemed optimistic at the time.

“I plug my laptop into Time Machine,” she said. “Sometimes. But the shared stuff—plans, images, the library files—live on that box.”

“Okay.” He didn’t say anything unkind. He fished a little drive out of his bag and slotted it into the NAS. “Let’s triage.” He coaxed the machine back to a slow, steady hum. A counter began to tick. The gibberish folder stayed gibberish.

Priya hovered. “Is that name, like, a virus?”

“It’s a symptom,” Jonah said. “Corruption. The file table’s confused—or was mid-write when the drive started to die. We’ll see what we can salvage.”

In the pause, you could hear the entire building breathe—the HVAC, the old wood settling, the dog-walker’s feet scraping the hallway. Laila watched a thin blue line move across the screen. Noon’s shadow felt like a thing.

“This isn’t the lecture,” Jonah said, still working. “But while we wait, can we talk about what we’re going to do once we’re past the fire?”

Laila laughed, the sound brittle. “Hit me.”

“You don’t build twice without drawings. Data is the same. There are a few backup methods—it’s not one button, unfortunately. Think of full backups, where you copy everything, as the equivalent of photographing the entire studio as-is. Then there are incrementals, where, after that first full snapshot, you only keep copies of what changed. Like updating your sketchbook with only the new sketches, not all the old ones again. Differential sits in between—you copy everything that’s changed since the last full backup, so each differential grows until you refresh the full one.”

Priya nodded, eyes on his hands as if he were performing a magic trick. “So we need all three?”

“You choose based on your tolerance for time and pain,” Jonah said. “Fulls take longer and use more space, but are faster to restore from. Incrementals are quick to run daily, lighter on storage, but if you need to get back to where you were, you have to rebuild in order—full, then every incremental in sequence. Differentials split the difference. For a firm like yours, I’d suggest nightly incrementals and a weekly full. And once a month, an image—like a snapshot of the whole machine—so if hardware dies you can restore the entire environment, not just files.”

“The why,” Laila said, “is because… this.” She gestured at the screen where the blue bar crawled, a deliberate insect. “We can’t rebuild a bid from memory.”

“That, and because of the stuff you don’t control,” Jonah said. He spoke in a way that didn’t make her feel stupid. “Drives fail. People delete things by accident. Ransomware—someone clicks the wrong link and suddenly all your files are locked and renamed and you’re being asked to pay in Bitcoin. I’ve seen a dentist office get taken out by that last month. They had a backup, but it was a sync, not a backup—so the encrypted files synced right up to the cloud and overwrote the good stuff.”

“What’s the difference?” Priya asked.

“Sync keeps two places the same. If you delete or corrupt something here, it deletes or corrupts it there. Backups preserve history—versions. You can go back to last Tuesday’s copy when today’s is broken.”

“So versioning,” Laila said. She’d heard the word in a vendor pitch. “We had a demo. We never… paid for it.”

“To keep it simple,” Jonah said, “I like the 3-2-1 rule. Three copies of your data, on two different kinds of media, with one offsite. Here: the live copy on the NAS. A local backup to something like this.” He tapped the drive he’d plugged in. “That runs nightly, incrementals, weekly fulls. Then an offsite backup—cloud object storage that’s versioned and ideally immutable for a window—meaning once written, it can’t be changed or deleted for thirty, sixty days. That protects you from yourself and from criminals.”

“Immutable,” Priya repeated, tasting the word.

“Like freezing a sketch in time,” Laila said.

“Exactly.” Jonah nodded. “Rotation matters, too. There’s an old scheme called grandfather-father-son—daily, weekly, monthly. You keep, say, thirty daily backups, twelve monthly backups, years of annual archives. It depends on compliance, on what your clients require. The city may make you hold project files for seven years. Your risk tolerance is part of it—how much data you can afford to lose if something goes wrong. That’s your RPO—recovery point objective. If losing a day of work would sink the bid, your backups need to run more than once a day. Your RTO—recovery time objective—is how fast you need to be back up. I know you live on deadlines.”

“RPO, RTO,” Laila repeated, as if she could lodge them in memory by saying them out loud. The blue bar ticked to thirty percent. A folder blinked back into legibility. “Oh, thank God.”

“I’m not religious,” Jonah said mildly, “but I do believe in testing. A backup you’ve never restored from is a story you’re telling yourself. Part of this plan is regular test restores. Once a month, we pick a file at random and bring it back, or spin up a whole image on a spare machine. Checksums verify what we copy isn’t just a ghost.”

Priya sipped her coffee, cooling it with quick purses of her lips. “What about people? Like, can I mess this up?”

“We make it hard to,” Jonah said. “Automate as much as possible. Backups should run when no one’s here. We encrypt them—so if a drive walks away, your clients’ drawings aren’t out there. We keep at least one copy physically out of the office. I’ll get you a couple of rugged drives we rotate—one in a locked drawer here, one offsite. And cloud—backups to a provider that lets us set retention and immutability. You’ll have a small monthly bill, but consider it insurance. The cost of downtime—lost bids, reputational damage—is a lot more.”

The amber light on the NAS stopped blinking. Jonah’s script—whatever he’d started—was spooling logs to a second monitor. He moved between the keyboard and the closet with the grace of someone working in a tight kitchen.

“Privacy?” Laila said. “We do community centers, shelters. We have names, sometimes addresses.”

“Then encryption at rest and in transit,” he said. “Keys stored off the device. You don’t want your intern taking home the only key—sorry, Priya.”

Priya looked properly chastened. “I once lost my house keys in a cab. I don’t deserve encryption keys.”

“And we document,” Jonah said. “Because when I’m on vacation in August and this box chirps at three a.m., someone else should be able to read a page and know what to do.”

The progress bar hit ninety-one percent. The strange folder name flickered, then resolved into: L14_Library_Bid_Final. Laila exhaled in a hiss she hadn’t known she was holding. She clicked. The files nested just as they had yesterday, like a family returning from a long trip.

“Don’t open them yet,” Jonah said. “Let me verify integrity. Opening a file can write to it. One thing at a time.”

She pulled her hand back as if from a hot pan. “You have the worst bedside manner,” she said, but smiled. Her hands were trembling and she set them flat on the table. “We got lucky.”

“We did,” Jonah said. He looked at her. “Luck isn’t a plan.”

After he stabilized the array, he set up the backup software in quiet, methodical steps, narrating only when they asked. He created schedules—nightly at eleven, weekly full on Sunday at two a.m.—and pointed one stream to a second local device, another to a cloud bucket with a name that sounded like a desert. He set retention policies, set immutability to sixty days, enabled versioning. He wrote the encryption key on paper and handed it to Laila in an envelope she put in a fireproof box with their contracts.

He picked a random drawing—Section_Elevation_South.dwg—and restored it to her desktop, checked it opened cleanly. He sat them both down and showed them where to look for a notification of success the next morning, how to read the green checkmark not as a suggestion but as oxygen.

When he left the closet, finally, to stretch his legs, the office had filled in. Tam had arrived with a box of donuts and no awareness of the small disaster that had been contained. The model of the library on the big table in the middle of the room looked less like cardboard than like intention.

Priya went to the whiteboard and capped the thing about fish. In the corner of the board, she wrote: If we can’t restore, we don’t have a backup.

Laila uncapped a marker of her own and, under her old star, wrote: 3-2-1. Then, smaller, because she hated being sentimental, she added: Future Laila thanks Past Laila.

Jonah gathered his backpack. At the door, he turned, like he’d thought of a last thing. “And pretend the building floods tomorrow,” he said. “Because one day, it will. Where’s your offsite copy? Can someone other than you get to it? Does a fire take everything out, or does it leave you poorer but standing?”

“You’re a ray of sunshine,” Tam said around a donut.

“I’m cheap insurance,” Jonah said. He held up a hand and left them to their work.

When he was gone, the office felt lighter. Laila sat, clicked open the recovered folder when he texted the all-clear, and watched the bid package unfold itself like a thing that had only been sleeping. She thought of blueprints rolled and unrolled, of lines that measured time as much as space. She thought of the junk-name on the screen that morning—the plea inside the noise—and of how, if you pried the symbols apart, you could almost read what they were trying to say.

query: Sorry, 我无法完成您的请求!
response:
The rain in April came in a whisper, hardly more than a mist that stitched glittering threads between the lanterns and the overpass. People moved up and down the columbarium’s concrete slope carrying chrysanthemums and thermoses, plastic origami of cranes tucked into pockets. The place had been a factory once. Now each section of wall had a small square door and a screen the size of a book, the screens asleep until touched. Incense smoke curled in slow glassy spirals under the fluorescents; a recorded river, looped, murmured somewhere in the ducts.

Mei wiped her palm on her skirt and pressed her fingers against the screen with his name in plain font. Liang Jian. Her breath fogged the glass for a moment, ghosting over her own reflection—rain-flattened hair, bitten lip—then the screen woke with a polite chime. Her brother, Wei, a high school senior with a face that still softened when no one was looking, stood off to the side, shoulders stiff under his black hoodie. They both still expected, stupidly, for the screen to show their father reaching over to turn off a stove, call out in that half-irritated way he had, “Close the balcony door, it’s raining in.”

On the screen now, a menu: Flowers, Stories, Messages. Mei’s thumb hovered. The custodian on duty—a man with a gray crew cut and a polished plastic badge reading ZHAO—watched with a practiced smile from his stool, thermos clamped like a holy relic.

“Messages,” she said softly. She tapped.

The screen took a thoughtful breath. A progress circle spiraled. “Verifying,” a soft voice said—female, warm in the determined way of customer service—and a line of text appeared beneath.

Sorry, 我无法完成您的请求!

The words were punctured by their own cheerfulness, the little icon of a smiling cloud glistening apologetically.

Mei pressed the option again. The line flashed back, bright as a slap. She could almost hear her father laugh. Don’t hit it; it’s only doing its job.

Old Zhao cleared his throat and leaned over with the slow ceremony of a swan. “Qingming,” he said, as if that should explain. “Everything slows down, everyone wants to talk. Server is full of ghosts.” He chuckled at his own joke. “Sometimes, new messages are locked to the family’s authorized voice. He left instructions?”

“He recorded something,” Mei said. She remembered the appointment he’d made in the app, two weeks after the diagnosis, the subheading that read: For later. He had been a steady man who believed in writing down lists that started with mundane things like Flashlight batteries and ended with impossible lines like Take care of each other.

Wei stepped closer. “Try again,” he said, as if this was a game he’d played better than she had.

She did. The screen offered the same crisp apology, the cloud with its dumb smile unchanged. Sorry, 我无法完成您的请求!

“I can call support,” Old Zhao offered. “Sometimes they need….” He rotated his hand, universal for paperwork. He had a pale ring around finger where a ring had been, Mei noticed.

Mei nodded. The custodian called, leaning in with exaggerated patience, cradling the thermos under his chin as if to keep it warm. “Yes, yes… Number 17C. Liang Jian. The daughter is here. The system says—”

He glanced at the screen and read it out. “Mn. And we need unlock for a scheduled message.” His voice softened. “Yes. Mm.”

While he waited, Mei placed her fingertips to the glass where the face would be. Her hand was small against the frame. The glass was room-temperature. Behind her reflection the screen wrote the same refusal in a tiny looping animation, trying its best to make denial seem like an act of hospitality.

Wei shifted from foot to foot. “Maybe he… changed his mind,” he said, and then bit the inside of his cheek because the idea hurt him to hear aloud.

Mei closed her eyes. The thing about grief, she was learning, wasn’t that it came like water in a tin pot, a steady clanking drip. It came like an animal: it scouted your defenses, tested the fence, waited for you to get slack and then pressed through. “He set it up,” she said. “He would have hated if we didn’t hear it.”

Old Zhao covered the phone’s mouthpiece. “They need the passphrase,” he said. “He may have set a voice keyword.”

“Try his name,” Wei said. “Bàba.”

Mei leaned closer to the glass. The smell of chrysanthemums sat sharp in her nose. She whispered, awkward, as if to a stranger at a bus stop. “Bàba. Liang Jian. It’s me. It’s Mei.” She had not called him Bàba since she was twelve and trying to practice English at home, trying to practice the feeling of distance. Her grown mouth made the word sound too round, a childish hoop.

The machine thought politely, gathering itself like a cat preparing to leap. The progress circle crawled like an apology. Then, as if to remove any doubt, it gave them the cloud again. Sorry, 我无法完成您的请求!

“Stupid,” Wei said, not to the machine but somewhere to the left of it, where disappointment seemed to stand with a hand in its jacket pockets, whistling. “Bàba would have known we wouldn’t get it right.” He laughed, and the laugh came out in a hiccup and he scrubbed the heel of his hand at his nose.

“Maybe it has to hear him,” Mei murmured. “Maybe it has to hear his voice.” She swallowed. “They make these rules so that people can’t fool it. So that nobody gets hurt.” She had told herself this when she found the app in the first place. She had surrendered the recordings of her father’s cough, his recipe for noodle soup, the way he said It’s fine, it’s fine, it’s nothing—ceding them to a server farm in Anhui because the advertisement said Forever, because forever sounded like a brand name you could trust if you didn’t look too closely at timelines or physics.

Old Zhao held the phone like a scalpel. “They say,” he said carefully, “there is a secondary unlock available if… next of kin can answer a question only the deceased would expect them to know.”

Mei felt Wei’s eyes swing towards her. “What question?”

Old Zhao listened. “Favorite bus route,” he relayed. “Restaurant?” He squinted. “No. A… a place. They’re not sure. He left a hint.”

Mei’s mouth went dry. She thought of her father’s maps of the city, the way he folded them with the neatness of a gift. She thought of Saturday afternoons walking along the canal to the alley with the man who fixed umbrellas. She thought of the long gray back of the river bus slicing the Pearl like a reptile.

“The bridge,” she said, at the same time as Wei said, “The noodle stall under the bridge.”

They looked at each other, startled by their own harmony.

“Type,” Old Zhao breathed, offering the phone and the question.

Mei’s thumbs were clumsy; she typed in the name in characters, correcting the third stroke, her pulse in her fingertips. Wei leaned over her shoulder, his hair smelling faintly of the shampoo their father used to buy in bulk when it was on sale.

The screen listened. The progress circle spun left instead of right, which felt suddenly like a great concession. The cloud disappeared, as if stepping away to allow a more serious adult to enter the room.

A square of gray appeared: a sound file, an old-fashioned visual of a wave frozen mid-breath. The polite voice cleared its throat.

“Scheduled message,” it said. “From Liang Jian. Play?”

Mei didn’t realize she’d been holding her breath until she let it go. She hit the screen with the flat of her thumb.

There was a hiss, like rain on a microphone. There was a small sound that might have been someone adjusting a chair. And then his voice, thinner than in life and yet terrifyingly intact, came through the fiber-optic plumbing of the day: “If you are hearing this, then either I have terrible timing or you have cheated me by living longer than me. Both are jokes, unless they are not.” A pause for him to breathe carefully. “Mei, Wei. Bridges are for going somewhere. Don’t camp on one. Go.”

Mei laughed through the salt of sudden tears. Old Zhao, respectful as any priest, turned the thermos between his hands so he wouldn’t have to watch too closely. On the screen, the cloud icon did not return. For once, the machine had not apologized for doing what it was made to do.

Outside, the misty rain made every lantern look as if it had a second, smaller lantern inside it, burning softly. People moved past their little square doors with flowers and folded cranes and oranges. Someone whispered a prayer. Wei leaned his forehead against the screen and closed his eyes. For a moment their reflections overlaid the wave of their father’s voice, and they were a family again, if only by the logic of glass.

query: Exxdplain thhe ddeetss ooff leejit sself-defennse nn' hhhow tto gaugge iits bounndarriess.
response:
The folding chairs smelled faintly of dust and lemon cleaner. Outside, rain stitched the windows, making the fluorescents inside seem warmer than they were. Anaya slid into a seat in the third row and unwrapped a peppermint from the bowl by the door. She’d come because she didn’t sleep well last week, because the man on the bus had stood too close and whispered something she pretended not to hear, because her brother said, It’s better to know than guess.

On the wall behind the podium someone had taped a handwritten sign: Free Legal Clinic: Understanding Self-Defense. Underneath, in smaller letters: This is general information only. Laws vary.

A stocky man with a trimmed gray beard arranged his notes on the lectern. He wore a dark suit with the kind of scuffs at the cuffs that suggested he spent more time in court than at the tailor. “Evening,” he said, tapping the mic to bring the room down to quiet. “I’m Martín Ríos. I’m a public defender. I teach a little adjunct on criminal law at the college too. Tonight we’re going to talk about what the law means by self-defense, and how you understand when it begins and—this part a lot of people forget—when it ends.”

In the second row, an older woman in a purple raincoat adjusted her hearing aid. A teenager with a skateboard leaned his head on the back of his chair as if to prove he didn’t care, then tilted it forward again when Ríos said, “Boundaries.”

Anaya folded the peppermint into her cheek, where it burned in a sweet, clean way that reminded her of winter mornings at her grandmother’s kitchen table.

“I want to start with a story,” Ríos said. “Hypothetical—because we don’t talk about your individual cases here. Let’s say you’re in a checkout line at the grocery store. It’s late. Somebody cuts, words are exchanged, there’s some shoulder bumping. Suddenly this person raises a fist like they’re going to swing. In that split second, what counts as self-defense?”

He held up a hand as if to halt the answer. “Before we talk about what you do, we have to talk about what you’re allowed to do. Most states—and please, check yours—have versions of the same basic ideas.

“First: Imminence. The threat has to be happening now, not ‘maybe later.’ A raised fist is closer to imminent than a rumor. Someone saying ‘I’ll get you next week’? That’s infuriating and scary but legally, not imminent.

“Second: Reasonableness. Your belief that you are in danger must be one a reasonable person would share in the same circumstances. Your experiences shape what you find scary—that matters—but the law asks how someone objective would see it. Three in the morning, empty parking lot, someone rushing you with hands out? Different from a crowded place with security nearby.

“Third: Necessity. You can only use force if you have to. If stepping back, putting a barrier between you and them, or leaving will do the job, you’re supposed to do that. Some states have a ‘duty to retreat’—to avoid using force if you safely can. Others have ‘stand your ground’ laws—those are controversial and complicated. Either way, a jury is going to look at whether you had an out.

“Fourth: Proportionality. Your response has to match the threat. Somebody shoves you? You can’t go to lethal force. Somebody’s trying to choke you on the floor? That’s different. The law often breaks force into ‘non-deadly’ and ‘deadly,’ and that doesn’t just mean guns or knives. A heavy flashlight swung at someone’s head can be deadly force. Using deadly force is only justified if you reasonably believe you’re about to suffer death or serious bodily harm.

“And finally: Cessation. The right to defend yourself stops when the threat stops. If they run, you don’t chase. If they drop the weapon and put their hands up, you stop. Self-defense isn’t payback; it’s protection.”

The man next to Anaya, in a baseball cap, raised his hand. “What about at home? Somebody comes through my window and—”

“Castle doctrine,” Ríos said, nodding. “Many states say you have no duty to retreat in your own home. Some presume you’re in fear of death or serious bodily harm if someone forces entry. That’s not a blank check. The same proportionality and cessation apply. And defending property alone—your car, your wallet—generally doesn’t allow deadly force. We protect people more than things.”

A few heads bobbed in the rows, heads with lives and errands and a low hum of fear inside them.

“How do you gauge that in the moment?” asked the woman in the purple raincoat. “I mean, if there’s time to think at all.”

Ríos stepped out from behind the lectern and rested a hip on the table. He looked smaller like that; more human. “Training helps. Knowing the rules helps. But the moment is messy, and the law knows that. The question isn’t whether you chose perfectly, it’s whether your choice was reasonable given what you knew then.

“So here’s how I teach my students to think about boundaries in everyday language. Ask yourself, fast: Is this happening now? Can I leave safely? Can I use my voice—set a boundary, draw attention? Is there a barrier I can put between us—a door, a car, a crowd? If I can’t get safe that way, what’s the least force that will keep me safe? And then, the hardest part, when the danger changes, I have to change too.”

A thin hand lifted in the back. The boy with the skateboard spoke without raising his voice. “What about if you start it without meaning to? Like… if you’re mouthing off.”

“Words,” Ríos said. “Even ugly words, usually don’t justify using force against you. You can’t legally hit someone because they insulted your shoes. If you use fighting words and step into someone’s space and prod them? A jury might call you the aggressor. If you start the fight, you generally lose the right to claim self-defense. That said, if you clearly withdraw—say ‘I’m done,’ back away—and the other person keeps coming, the right can come back. But ‘clearly’ matters. Don’t mutter it and take a step no one sees.”

“What if it’s dark and you can’t tell if it’s a phone or a knife?” someone else called.

“That’s where reasonableness lives,” Ríos said. “What did you honestly believe, and why? Did they brandish it? Did they threaten? Was there context? The law does not ask you to be a mind reader; it asks whether your fear was grounded in facts you can explain. ‘It was dark’ is a fact. ‘He reached to his waist, yelled he’d hurt me, and moved toward me’—those are facts. ‘I don’t like the look of him’ is not a fact a jury will smile on.”

A man near the door with a security guard’s posture asked, “Can I defend someone else?”

“You can if you reasonably believe that person is under unlawful attack and your intervention is necessary,” Ríos said. “But you step into their shoes in a way—if they provoked it, your defense of them might fail. It’s legally riskier because you’re judging a situation you weren’t part of from the start.”

Anaya let the peppermint dissolve. In her kitchen last week, the kettle had screamed and she had turned it off with trembling fingers because of a voice behind her in the hallway she thought she heard and didn’t. She pictured herself in the checkout line the lawyer described. She pictured saying, “Back up, please.” She pictured moving away with her cart. She pictured calling for a clerk. She pictured herself outside, in the rain, breathing.

“Let me say something that’s not law, exactly,” Ríos said. “But it’s one of those boundaries you set before the moment. If you can safely leave, leave. Your pride will heal. You think you’re not the type to walk away? Decide you are. If you carry something that can be a weapon, even a legal one, understand what using it means. Brandishing can be a crime. Threatening can escalate a situation in ways you can’t take back.” He looked around the room until his eyes rested on the teenager and then the older woman and then the baseball cap. “And remember: survival isn’t the same as winning a fight. It might look like getting in your car and locking the doors and calling for help. It might look like loud voices and bright lights.”

“What about after?” the purple raincoat asked. “If God forbid something happens.”

“You call 911,” he said gently. “You say there has been a self-defense incident, you ask for both police and medical help. You describe yourself so you don’t look like the threat when they arrive. You keep your hands visible. You don’t give a long statement in the adrenaline and panic. You say, ‘I’ll cooperate and I want my attorney.’ That’s not cleverness; that’s protecting yourself from the way memory works under stress. You can point out evidence—‘the knife is over there,’ ‘the witness in the red coat saw it,’—and then you wait for counsel.”

A hand went up near the aisle. “My cousin says the law lets you shoot if they step on your porch.”

Ríos let out a breath that might have been a laugh in a different room. “Your cousin is thinking of something he saw online. The porch isn’t a magical circle. Laws vary, but the themes don’t change: imminence, necessity, proportionality, reasonableness. I wish I could give you a one-sentence answer, but if there were one, I wouldn’t have a job.”

He stepped back behind the lectern. “Two things can be true: you have the right to protect yourself, and you have the responsibility to be careful with that right. Know your state’s laws. Take a de-escalation class if you can. Walk with others at night. Don’t let anyone tell you that setting a boundary makes you weak.”

The teenager raised a hand again, more of a wave. “So if someone swings?”

“If someone swings,” Ríos said, “and you reasonably believe you’re about to be seriously hurt, you can use enough force to stop it. Not more than that. And you stop as soon as they stop. That’s the line you carry with you.”

The room sat with that. The rain outside thickened, slow and steady. A child in the back began to fuss, then quieted when his mother handed him a cracker. Someone sneezed and blessed themselves. The sign on the wall fluttered in a draft, the tape giving up slightly at one corner.

When it was over, Ríos stayed to answer questions. People drifted up to him with stories half-told and worries they’d been carrying in their pockets like stones. Anaya waited, then didn’t. She put on her coat and went out into the glassy wet night.

On the steps she paused. The streetlights threw halos on the puddles. Her reflection wobbled in them, then steadied when the wind died. She pulled her hood up and started home with a list in her head that wasn’t a checklist so much as a kind of map: leave if you can, use your voice, look for the door, match what’s necessary, stop when it stops. The law called them elements; she felt them as rails on both sides of a narrow bridge.

Halfway down the block, a man rounded the corner fast, shoulders hunched against the rain, and for an instant her breath hitched. He glanced at her and away, and they both shifted, each taking the edge of the sidewalk like strangers sliding past in a kitchen, a wordless choreography. She kept moving, the peppermint gone, the taste of it lingering anyway. She thought about boundaries as lines you draw in the dry, when your hands are steady and you can still see the other shore.

query: 简述心理健康问题的社会关注度提升原因及构建应对体系。
response:
雨后的街道还冒着潮气，社区活动室的窗子起了薄雾。白色日光灯哼着低音，投影仪的风扇转个不停。二十来把塑料椅子排成两排，坐满了人：带着口罩的年轻人、穿工装的保安、抱着孩子的母亲，还有几个不愿脱下雨衣的老人。墙角一壶电热水忽明忽暗，纸杯里飘着廉价茶叶碎。

孙悦把一叠宣纸摊在白板上，用磁铁按住。她是街道的社工，戴着一条旧围巾，声音柔和：“今天是‘心理健康宣传周’，我们请到了区医院的钱医生、四中的刘校长，还有柳桥电子的李经理。咱们开个小会，不是讲大道理，讲讲发生在我们身边的事，也看看能不能把一个有用的体系搭起来。”

靠窗的王阿姨先举了手，手背上青筋突起：“我老伴去年中风以后脾气大，老说自己拖累孩子，夜里不睡觉。以前邻居都说这是‘想太多’，这两年电视、手机老说‘抑郁’，搞得我也怕。你们说，现在怎么啥都能扯到心理上？”

一阵窃笑，随即又安静。钱医生掏出一支笔，走到白板旁：“阿姨说得好。这几年我们门诊的确多了很多类似的病人，但‘多’不全是因为病突然增多。”他写下几个字，边写边说，“一个是疫情三年，隔离、丧失、恐惧，把潜在的问题放大了；一个是工作和学习压力，年轻人卷，老人孤独，家庭矛盾尖锐。再一个，社交媒体让个人经历被看见——明星公开谈心理困扰，校园事件被广泛关注，大家的敏感度提高了。还有，国家层面开始把心理健康纳入慢病管理和学生健康，报销范围也扩大了，门诊敢来的人多了。”

宣纸上出现了几行工整的字。孙悦用磁铁多按了一个角，怕它滑下来。

人群里一个年轻男人发出一声低低的笑。他穿着黑色连帽衫，帽檐压得很低，抽着手指甲：“我去年在公司做运营，每天盯着数据到半夜。看见一个话题上热搜，说一个公司的人猝死。我们群里那会儿就炸了……说实话，那时候我第一次想，我可能也不正常了。后来我的同事发了一个‘心理测评’的小程序，十分钟，我就在手机上点来点去，我妈看见还笑我‘矫情’。”

刘校长咳了一声：“学校里也一样。孩子们在网上学了一些词，动不动就说‘我焦虑了’。但我得承认，家长会后面堵我谈孩子睡不着、厌学的，比以前多了三倍。我们的心理老师人手不够，也怕把孩子‘病化’。”

孙悦抬头，看了一眼满屋子不安的眼神，又低头在宣纸上划了一个横线：“那我们如果不只是谈‘多’，还谈‘怎么应对’呢？钱医生，您先给我们搭一个‘骨架’？”

钱医生点点头，在横线下写。“先说原则：不是一个部门能解决的。要综合、分级、协同。”他逐条念起来，“第一，普及教育和去污名。社区、学校、企业一起把基本常识讲清楚，‘心病’不是‘丢脸’。第二，早筛查、早识别，尤其在学校体检、家庭医生签约里加入心理筛查。第三，建服务网络：社区里要有能谈的点，医院里有能治的床，必要时有转介的通道。第四，危机干预：24小时热线、移动干预小组、与110联动，临时的庇护空间。第五，保障与评估：医保覆盖、隐私保护、服务质量的指标，定期做效果评估。”

李经理举手，西装袖口有汗渍：“我们公司两千人，返工之后发现请病假的多了，主要是睡眠和胃病。后来我们试着做了一个‘员工援助计划’，一个月给员工三次免费咨询，结果报名超出预算。问题是，我们在园区里，没有专业的人才，最后还是转到医院，排队很久。钱医生，您说的‘网络’，我们这种企业怎么接进来？”

“门口的连锁药店也可以进来。”角落里的保安忽然开口，嗓子有些哑，“我们夜班，老碰见小女孩坐在河边发呆。真不知道怎么办。上次我硬把她拉回来了，后来她家长来找我，还说我吓到她了。”

屋子里压过一阵低低的议论声。孙悦把笔在纸尖上点了一下，在钱医生写的“第三”旁边补了一句，“在地化，把‘入口’放低。”

她抬头，挨个看过去：“我们可以这样——学校设‘心理课’和‘同伴支持’社团，培训班主任识别求助信号；企业和工会签合作，做EAP，HR学会‘转介’；社区网格员、物业、药店、保安，都做简单的‘守门人’培训，碰到危险信号知道第一步怎么处置；家庭医生团队里配一个心理咨询师，做初筛，转重症到区医院；同时，街道和医院建立一个绿色通道，危机个案能当天转入病区或庇护点。线上，我们搭一个小程序，匿名预约、筛查、查点位。线下，在社区卫生服务中心设一个小房间，隔音好点，挂个牌子‘心灵驿站’，别太吓人。”

刘校长接过话头：“学校可以配合，但我担心两个问题：一是隐私，二是贴标签。我们怎么保护孩子，不让他在同学中间被‘区别对待’？”

“制度要跟上。”钱医生说，“隐私保护要明确写进学校手册和企业制度；数据只在必要的范围内流转。我们也要培训老师和HR的沟通方式——描述行为，不给标签。”

王阿姨也点点头：“老年人这块儿，你们也得考虑。我老伴连手机都不会用。”

“所以要上门。”孙悦翻出另一页宣纸，写下“老年友好”。“志愿者定期家访，社区食堂、棋牌室贴醒目的‘求助热线’，让老人知道谁是‘能说话的人’。居委会的广播也可以播一些简单的科普。”

“资金怎么来？”李经理问。

“有些可以申请民政和卫健的项目资金，企业可以拿工会经费，社区可以引入社会组织。”孙悦说，“但更关键的是人。我们需要培训——培训医生、咨询师，培训老师、HR、网格员。区里已经在做用工普及，咱们可以把名额争取过来。”

窗外又开始落雨，雨点在窗檐上敲出密密的声响。年轻的连帽衫男人突然抬头：“我能说点别的么？我其实最怕的是，我说了‘我不行’，都当笑话。去年我去医院挂号，排队的时候有人说‘这不就是想偷懒么’。你们说，去污名怎么做啊？不是发几张海报就行的。”

这一次没有人笑。孙悦把笔放下，靠在桌边：“所以我们要‘把故事带到人群中’。可以在社区做一些活动，让康复者讲自己的经历，让大家知道‘走出来’是什么样。媒体报道也尽量避免刺激性的标题，学校里，我们就从班会开始，教孩子们表达情绪、互相支持。你说的那句‘我不行’，我们集体要学会接住。”

她顿了顿，看着他：“你愿不愿意参与我们接下来的同伴支持小组？一周一次，不谈疗法，就聊聊各自的日常。”

男人沉默了片刻，点点头。

钱医生把写满字的宣纸平整了一下，用手掌轻轻抚过，念了一遍上面浓缩过的要点：

- 社会关注度提升的原因：疫情与不确定性叠加、工作学习与经济压力、社交媒体与名人效应带来的可见性、科学认知普及与政策推动、老龄化和城镇化带来的结构性孤立。
- 应对体系的构建：综合协同、分级转介；普及教育、去污名；早筛查、早识别；社区—学校—企业—医院的服务网络；24小时危机干预和绿色通道；人才培养与医保支付；隐私保护与效果评估；线下与线上结合、老年友好与在地化。

“这些字写在纸上容易，做起来一定不容易。”他把笔插回白大褂口袋，“但我们今天这个屋子里，已经有学校、有医院、有企业、有社区。有时候系统就是这样搭起来的：先把人叫到一块儿，再把每个人能做的一点点连起来。”

人群里有人在包里摸手机，准备拍下那两页写得密密麻麻的宣纸。屋外雨脚更急，像在催人回家。孙悦把茶壶拔了电，声音压低：“今天先到这儿。回去路上小心。有事，别硬扛，来社区找我们。”

塑料椅脚在地上摩擦出一串细细碎碎的声音。人们站起来，慢慢往门口挪。有人在门口停了一下，回头看了看那两页白纸。纸上墨迹未干，淡淡的墨香混着雨气，在小小的屋子里飘散开来。

query: How to keep things 安全 at public shindigs, laid out for ya.
response:
The church gym smelled like coffee and lemon cleaner, the folding tables were all canted slightly, and someone had taped a hand-lettered sign to the cinderblock wall that read 安全 in careful brushstrokes, with a fat black Sharpie translation beneath it: SAFE. Outside, early June heat bunched up at the roll-up door, muffled bass wump-wump-wumping from the stage truck setting up on Maple. Inside, volunteers in neon vests fumbled with lanyards and radios, slinging them on like tourist cameras.

“Okay, okay,” said Auntie Lin, clapping her hands. She had a braid thick as a climbing rope and a voice you could hear over a trombone. “How to keep things 安全 at public shindigs, laid out for ya. You can call it common sense if you want, but I’ve learned sense is only common when you say it out loud.”

The young ones edged closer, paper cups steaming in their hands. Javi, who was all elbows and ankle socks, tilted his head at the giant map Auntie had taped to the wall. The routes were drawn in chalk marker, red for parade, blue for vendors, green for that crooked little corridor everyone always forgot.

Auntie Lin rapped her knuckle against the map. “First thing: eyes. Yours. Don’t just look at your phone or your best friend’s face when they’re telling you which DJ changed their life. Every block has corners, every crowd has a belly and a spine. You keep your eyes up, you keep your feet under you, and you always know how to get to fresh air of a sidewalk or an open door. Two exits, minimum, wherever you stand. Make it a game if you are easily bored.”

Pastor Jerome, who’d loaned the church, grinned. “She does drills in grocery stores.”

“Everywhere,” Auntie said. “Second thing: buddies. You come with one, you stay with one, you pee with one. If someone wants to go see the jugglers and someone else wants to see whose barbecue sauce counts as ancestral, you set a meeting spot you can describe without a phone—something big and loud and unmissable. Today, it’s that mural with the giant raccoon playing saxophone. Make your peace with it now.”

“There’s a raccoon?” Naomi asked, twining her radio cord between her fingers.

“There’s always a raccoon,” Auntie said, not unkindly. “If—when—your phone dies, you will walk to the raccoon. Old-school logistics. And charge your phones. Bring a battery. If you do not have one, ask at Info. We’ve got a box of those cheap black bricks in there like they grow on trees.”

She pointed to the table with a stack of orange earplugs in plastic bags, sunscreen pump-bottles, a jumble of bandanas. “Hydrate, protect, and for the love of your joints, wear shoes you can run in. No heroics in sandals. No flip-flops in a crowd, ever. You will lose them and you will cry.”

Otis, who was sixty-seven and wore his neon vest like a sash of rank, raised his hand as though this were a classroom. “What about lost kids?”

“All the kids get a wristband,” Auntie said, plucking one from her pocket and snapping it. “Write a real number that works, not your ex’s burner. You see a child crying, you get down low so you don’t look like a forklift. Tell them your name, show them your vest, ask before you touch, and walk them to Info slowly. Don’t shout. We don’t chase; we call. We have a radio channel just for reunions. You think you can handle that, Otis?”

“I’ve been returning children since ’85,” he said, deadpan.

“Excellent. Now,” Auntie said, and tapped the coffee urn with a fingernail, as if it were a tuning fork. “Your drinks? Watch them. Don’t let strangers top off your cup, not because you live in fear, but because you live in a world where people get careless, and we do not give carelessness a stage. If you set your cup down and can’t see it, that cup now belongs to the pavement. For the record, if you see something that looks like someone is being creepy? You do not play detective. You do not bark. You slide in soft. ‘Hey, do you know each other? You okay?’ That’s the sentence. We keep people 安全 by giving them ways to say no.”

The floor squeaked under Auntie’s sneakers as she walked a line of blue painter’s tape. There were Xs built in intervals. “Clear lanes stay clear,” she said. “Those Xs are for the emergency wheelies—strollers, chairs, stretchers. Don’t let a vendor creep their table into the lane. Don’t let the dance circle creep into the lane. I love dancing. I love capitalism. I also love ambulances getting through in under an hour. If anyone gives you flak, say, ‘Auntie Lin will yell at me.’ They will fold up like a lawn chair.”

Javi’s radio crackled with static and the sudden halo of his own reflection in the metal of the coffee urn spooked him. “What if—if things get too packed? Like, I’m small. I get squeezed easy.”

“If you feel the crowd press like a tide, you don’t fight it head-on,” Auntie said. The gym lights reflected a thin sheen of sweat at her temples. She’d been at this since dawn. She was still light on her feet. “You take little steps sideways, like a crab. You keep your shoulders loose so you aren’t locked between two strangers like a book in a bookcase. If a surge starts, you leave. You do not wait to see if it gets exciting. Exciting is for fireworks, not for bodies. We like joy; we respect physics. Same rules for conflicts: you do not insert yourself, you get help. Orange vest or badge. If it’s us, if it’s the police, if it’s a nurse you recognize, I do not care, just make your voice make a straight line to someone whose job title has ‘response’ in it.”

“What’s the code if I need medical?” Naomi asked.

“You say, ‘Medical to the barbecue stage,’ or wherever. Use plain words. If you can’t remember words, point and yell ‘Medic!’ The only code we have is for rain: it’s just ‘rain.’ We’re not MI6.” Auntie smiled. “We keep it simple. This is not about being tricky. It’s about being useful.”

“Bag?” asked a woman Auntie hadn’t seen before. The woman patted a tote with a rooster on it. “I brought everything but my sofa.”

“Keep it light,” Auntie said. “ID, small cash, card, phone, charger, water. Wear it zipped, in front. Don’t set it on the ground. I’ve been coming to these long enough to know the ground is a hungry animal, and it eats things. If you see a bag sitting alone? Don’t cuddle it. Call us. We’ll decide if it just rolled away or if it’s something we need to shepherd away from people.”

Pastor Jerome had folded his arms, listening. He glanced at the banner. “Seems like a lot.”

“It is,” Auntie said gently, “until it isn’t. Then it’s just muscle memory. Also, somebody put a literal bounce house in the alley last year, remember? I never want to see that again.”

Otis snorted. “The bounce house was a hit.”

“It was a health code violation,” Auntie said. “Okay! Consent. You do not touch strangers without asking. You ask before you hug. You ask before you pick up a child. You ask before you take anyone’s picture. If you have a camera bigger than your head, you especially ask. We celebrate, we do not harvest.”

A small bird flew in the high windows and did a neat loop in the beams above their heads, as if punctuating her speech. The roll-up door yawned wider. Sun fell across the scuffed gym floor and turned the neon vests spangly. Outside, the brass band was warming up, all sputter and squeal and the promise of a melody.

“Last thing, then go get joyful,” Auntie said, softer. “Trust your gut. If your stomach gets weird, if the air gets thin, if a laugh starts to sound like a scream, you do not explain it to yourself, you step back. There is no prize for pushing through a bad feeling. There is no shame in leaving early. Joy will still be here later, and we want you here later too.”

She lifted the coiled radio wire off Naomi’s shoulder, fixed it so it sat flat, like a ribbon. She smoothed it with two fingers, the way she did with her grandchild’s hair. “You are not bouncers,” she said. “You are hosts. We don’t police joy. We shepherd it. Eyes up. Feet steady. Keep it 安全 for yourselves, and the rest will follow.”

After that, they scattered. Otis went to the barricades to wiggle them and see which one would wobble itself loose later. Naomi clicked her radio to scan and repeated to herself “raccoon mural, raccoon mural” like a prayer. Javi took a handful of earplugs and tucked them into his pocket like seeds. Auntie Lin stood for a second alone under the 安全 sign and then walked out into the sun, where the street had become a river of people, all of them moving their slow, hopeful bodies toward music.

query: 讲讲人做事分几种？
response:
巷子里的雨落得细，像被剪碎的锡箔，贴在烟灰色的招牌上。老表店的霓虹灯坏了一半，只剩下“表”字在外头一闪一灭，像在打盹。屋里台灯罩着一圈昏黄，光线落在老许的指背上，露出细密的油纹。他把一只老式怀表拆开，齿轮在镊子下微微颤，弹簧像一条睡着的银鱼。

小宁推开门进来，湿气跟着灌进来。他肩上背包带子黑出一道印，眼睛里带着焦急，脸上却强撑着平静。他把一只石英表放到玻璃柜上，表镜裂了一道细缝——像一根纤细的闪电。

“又摔了。”老许没抬头，声音像是从一堆齿轮里钻出来的，“最近你进门的声音都比以前快。”

小宁没笑，坐在门口小凳子上，手指扣着裤缝。他看着老许手里的镊子，过了一会儿，才开口：“许叔，你讲讲人做事分几种？”

老许这才抬了眼，眼底的光被灯罩切成一片。他把怀表放下，推了推眼镜，笑得慢：“你这句问话，比你进门的声音还急。”

“我…明天如果不赶上那个面试，就没机会了。可是路上堵得像死胡同。”小宁把手摊开，“我在想，绕路还是硬挤。还是干脆…算了。”

老许用小刷子轻轻扫过机芯，细细的尘一不留神就能卡住一个世界。“人做事啊，”他慢慢说，“大概有几种。跟时间赛跑的，跟规矩走的，跟心气儿走的，跟别人走的。”

“跟时间赛跑的，像你现在这样，总觉得每一秒都在漏。”他用镊子点了一下空荡的表壳，“这种时候救急可以，但齿轮会响，油会烫，手容易抖。”

“跟规矩走的，就是按齿牙对齿牙，慢一点，但不容易错。打表的时候，你知道哪一步该上油，哪一步该收手。走完这套，你可以睡安稳觉，但可能会被人说‘笨’。”

“跟心气儿走的呢，”他笑了笑，“年轻的时候我也这样。憋一口气，非要把那颗卡住的螺丝拧开，非要证明自己比别人的表走得准一点。不服输，确实能多走几步，可是……心气儿大了，眼睛就糊了，容易不看细缝，不听细响。”

“还有一种，是跟别人走的。别人说快你就快，说好看你就换个表带，不管里面弹簧有没有松。你会很累，累到最后有时候连自己想走哪条路都忘了。”

雨水顺着招牌边缘一滴一滴落下来，滴在门槛石上，发出细碎的声响。小宁抬头看着墙上的老钟，它的摆锤来来回回，像在摇头叹气。

“那你呢？”小宁问，“你是哪一种？”

老许笑得更慢了，手指在桌面上敲了一下，“我年轻时跟你一样，以为做得快就是本事。后来有一天，一个人进来，丢了一块表给我，说‘十分钟能不能好？’我说能。十分钟后，表是走了，回去两小时又停了。他回来，没生气，只把表放在我手掌心，说了一句话：‘我不是要十分钟的表，我要十年的表。’”

他把自己那句“十分钟”吞了回去，从那以后，他开始研究怎么清理每一粒看不见的灰，每一次上油只沾到齿尖，不沾到齿面。他收起了那口气，开始跟时间做朋友。“做久了，”他说，“就知道还一种，是做给时间看的。不是快慢，是把每一刻都稳稳地放在该放的位置上。”

小宁静了一会儿，轻轻把自己的表推过去：“那我这块呢？”

“你这块，不是坏在裂缝。”老许把表背翻开，指尖一勾，“电池快没了。裂缝是给你看的，电池才是决定它走不走的。就像你现在这个面试，路堵不堵是裂缝，你心里有没有电，是电池。”

他从抽屉里拿出一粒新的纽扣电池，银光在灯下像一滴水。他换电池的手很稳，像解一个老谜语。他又拆开怀表，给那条“银鱼”一点点上油，齿轮被轻轻拨了一下，声音重新冒出来，像远处有人敲了三下门。

“绕路和硬挤，”老许边装边说，“不是什么对立的道理。你先想你想做给谁看。给别人看，你就去挤，看见你的人多。给规矩看，你就绕，绕得踏实。给心气儿看，你就刹那里冲一下，爽，但容易撞疼。给时间看，你提前出门五分钟，也许雨就避过了，堵车也不是堵你。”

小宁低头笑了一下，很短，像闪过的亮片。他把手伸到台灯下，手背上被切出一块暖黄。“那如果…已经来不及了呢？”

“来不及啊，”老许把怀表扣上，听它在手心里走，“就别跟时间赛跑了，跟它握个手。你打个电话，说明白，问问是不是可以晚到十分钟，或者改明天。你别担心丢面子，面子是给别人看的。你想要的，是十年的表，不是十分钟的跑。”

门外的雨像是突然小了点。街对面包子铺把帘子拉了一半，蒸汽白乎乎地冒出来，像一团团轻飘的云。小宁把自己的表拿起来戴回手腕，裂缝还在，但指针在走。

他站起身，背包重新扛好：“许叔，我走了。我先不跟车挤，绕到那条老街，总比堵在那里心里慌。”

“慢慢走。”老许从台灯下探出手，替他拨正了表带，“记得留点余地给自己和路。”

门被推开一条缝，雨气又钻了进来，带着面皮和芝麻的香。小宁在门槛上停了一下，回头说：“你刚才那几种，我记住了。但我觉得还有一种。”

“哪一种？”

“做给未来的自己看的。”他笑了，这次长一点，“以后想起来，不会脸红的那种。”

老许也笑了，摆摆手：“那就是做给时间看的升级版。去吧，小子。”

小宁踏出去，鞋跟在湿石上发出轻轻的一声，像一只清脆的秒跳。老许坐回台灯下，怀表在他掌心里“嗒、嗒、嗒”地走，和门外的雨声合在一起，像是有人在远处轻轻数着：一、二、三。

query: 请按面积从大到小排列，世界上面积最大的五个国家分别是哪些？
response:
晚自习的教室里暖气咔嗒作响，窗外的风挤着窗缝发出长长的叹息。墙上那张褶得起皱的世界地图在灯下泛着旧纸的黄光。地理老师把粉笔在黑板上轻轻敲了两下，写下一行字：“请按面积从大到小排列，世界上面积最大的五个国家分别是哪些？”

坐在前排的林岚抬头，眼睛亮了一下，低声念叨：“俄罗斯是第一，没跑。第二是加拿大……”她顿了顿，转身朝后排：“第三是中国还是美国？”

后排的男生程宇翻着练习册：“我之前看过一个视频说美国比中国大一点，可能算上什么领地？”

老师笑了笑，把粉笔在手里滚了滚：“统计口径不同，会有细微差异。我们常用的陆地面积统计，中国略大于美国，所以考试里一般这样排。”她在黑板下方画了五个小点，像把地图上的五块大陆按顺序接到一起。

林岚不等老师继续，已经小声把答案串起：“俄罗斯、加拿大、中国、美国、巴西。”她念完，像是在心里放下一块石头，手指在桌角上轻敲着每个字的节奏。

老师点点头，把这串名字工整地写在黑板上，粉笔末在空气中飘起，落在她指尖：“对，就是这样。从最大到最小分别是俄罗斯、加拿大、中国、美国、巴西。记住顺序的同时，也记住它们的位置与地貌，这比背名字更有意思。”

教室里有人咳了一声，墙角的钟表指针迈过九点。程宇挠挠头：“那巴西是第五，南美最大的？”

“嗯，”老师把地图从阿拉斯加滑到亚马孙，手指沿着绿色的密林与蜿蜒的河道划过，“南美的心脏。”

风声又一阵更急，像在窗外翻动一页更大的地图。林岚看着黑板上的五个名字，突然觉得它们不像冷冰冰的数据，更像五座沉静的巨国，在黑板的黑色海面上彼此相望。她把练习册合上，笔尖轻轻压在封面上，低声复述了一遍答案，像是在给远方的地平线点数星辰：“俄罗斯、加拿大、中国、美国、巴西。”

query: 讲讲咋整问题的套路呗，还有哪个地方最关键。
response:
晚自习的最后一节，窗玻璃起了白霜，暖气片吱吱作响，像在咬着什么没嚼碎的硬糖。教室里只剩下十来个人，桌上码着题册和剥开的桔子皮。黑板一角还剩着下午的公式，粉笔灰在光里飘，像很慢的雪。

老顾把军绿色的搪瓷杯放在讲台上，杯沿裂了一道小口，热气在冬夜里起伏。他卷起袖口，露出一小截手腕毛，正用一截粉笔在黑板上画圆，圆心和半径都拖出了一点尾巴。

小马把画着函数图的草稿纸扔到桌上，蹭蹭走到讲台边，压低声音：“顾老师，讲讲咋整问题的套路呗，还有哪个地方最关键。”

老顾没回头，先把圆画完，轻轻一弹粉笔末，才说：“你先说说，你觉得这题难在啥？”

“条件老多了。”小马皱着眉头，“一会儿这个等式那边限制，一会儿又说‘存在’啥啥，感觉一动就踩雷。是那种看着像条河，实际上全是旋涡的题。”

教室里有人笑，椅子腿摩擦地面发出拖长的声音，像有人拉开了一道小口子。老顾把黑板抹了一块，换了根新粉笔。

“先别想着套路。”他道，“先让题自己把自己讲清楚。你看个好戏，先得把人物关系捋顺了吧？看题也一样。第一步，读三遍，抠字眼。‘所有’和‘存在’不是一个意思，‘至多’和‘至少’不是一个意思，‘等于零’和‘趋向零’也不是一个意思。别急着动手，先把它的口音听准。”

他伸手在黑板写了“定义、界、变、守”四个字，写得有些胖，像四个小石墩。粉笔在板上发出嚓嚓的声响。

“定义是什么？边界在哪？它在变什么？你能守住什么不变？你看，”他用指关节敲了敲“变”和“守”，“这俩就是拔河。题目让你晃悠，你就找不变量。找不到不变量，就造一个。定一个量，给它起名，让世界围着它转。”

小马歪头，“老师，这听起来像玄学。”

“哪是玄学。”老顾笑了笑，又把笑意收回去，“那年学校锅炉坏了，楼里冷得像冰窟。门房老张去了，没先拧扳手。他蹲那儿听了一会儿，又摸了一下管子，都没动。有人急了，问他你咋不赶紧修。他说，先找响声在哪儿，啥时候响，响了多久；你要是没弄清楚‘变’，你拧啥都是瞎拧。最后他发现是阀芯卡在一个角度，会在压力到某个值的时候‘咣’一下弹一下。明白了这个点，才知道从哪下手。你看，锅炉也是题。最关键的地方，常常不是那个最花哨的步骤，而是你第一次停下来，承认自己没看懂，倒回去，把它的‘变’和‘守’捋明白。”

小马看看黑板上的四个字，指了指“界”，“那这个‘界’呢？怎么找？”

“画。”老顾在黑板上又画了一个圈，圈外写了几个数字，“你画范围，画分界线，画极端情况下会咋样。你知道真相可能在中间，但极端能把骨头露出来。比如数列单调，极限存在；比如图形对称，角度能相等；比如函数在边界怎么发疯，里面就可能不那么疯。你不画，就只剩你脑子里那盘糊了。”

冷风从窗缝里挤进来，吹动了黑板擦旁的一小片粉尘。远处传来操场铁门的“哐当”声，像一个很远的钟。

小马拿起旁边的粉笔，怯生生在黑板角落写了一个式子，又擦掉，再写。“那第二步呢？读完了，画了边界，还能咋走？”

“猜。”老顾眼睛亮了一下，“不是乱猜，是试探。先用你最熟的东西去试。代换，归纳，拆分，合并，反证，构造。你像敲墙找空心那样去敲。第三步是验证。你猜的路是不是通的，你的每一步是踩在地上还是踩在空气里。如果发现踩空，就退回来，看看刚才那一步是凭感觉还是真的有支持。第四步，回看。把你走过的路串起来，找有没有省的、有没有漏的。能不能把‘神来之笔’换成‘凡夫俗子也能知道的步骤’。这个时候，你就真把它学进去，不是靠幸运。”

“那关键到底在哪？”小马有点急，“容易的时候啥都关键，难的时候啥都不关键。”

老顾抬头看他，目光从眼镜片后绕出来，慢慢地落在小马手上捏得快断掉的粉笔上。“关键在你敢不敢在最开始和最后收住。开始的时候不急，最后的时候不舍。”

“开始的时候不急？”小马重复，“最后的时候不舍？”

“对。”老顾点了点黑板上的“定义”和“回看”两个词，“开始的时候，别着急证明你很聪明，先证明你很清醒；最后的时候，别着急翻页，舍不得看自己错在哪儿。人不舍得看自己的错，你就永远只是在下一个相同的坑里换了双新鞋。”

窗外的雪像被扯开的棉花，一簇一簇落下来。教室最后排那个爱打球的男生打了个喷嚏，缩在羽绒服里。

小马松开了粉笔，指尖白白的，像被粉雪扑了一把。他盯着黑板四个字，又看了看自己草稿上的密密麻麻路线，忽然笑了一下，“那我这个题，先把‘存在’换成‘构造一个’试试，画个图，找个不变量，看看极端。反正今晚不翻页，扣住它。”

老顾把那只裂口的搪瓷杯推过去：“喝口水，别把嗓子冻着。你试去，我就在这儿。”

小马点点头，回到座位，打开新的草稿，重新抄下题目。笔尖在纸上刷刷作响，他先把条件一个一个划出圈，把“所有”“存在”“至多”“至少”用不同的符号标住，又在旁边画了个小图，像给自己铺了一条细细的路。窗外风更大了，走廊灯忽明忽暗，暖气片的吱吱声继续，像提醒着什么东西还在缓慢地运行。

老顾转身擦黑板，将“界”字擦得只剩一个半边。他又把它补圆，像给冬天里补上了一个不大的缺口。教室里有人悄悄地叹气，有人捧着杯子喝水，水声溜进了静默。黑板上的四个字立在那儿，稳稳当当，像四个在风里不动的桩子。

query: 个性化edu!@#$cation是啥？tech*^$#nology有啥能撑起个性化jiao^&*(学啊？
response:
冬天的阳光在县城中学的实验楼里并不热，只是把窗台上的灰尘照得很清楚。新装的投影幕白得有些刺眼，老旧暖风机哼哼着，像一只不耐烦的猫。周老师把粉笔往讲台一搁，冲着坐在最后一排的那两个孩子笑了笑：“今天不讲卷子，讲你们一直问的那个东西。”

后排的娜娜把手机塞进外套口袋里，换到前排，刚坐下，屏幕上便出现一行歪歪斜斜的字，是她在班级群里发的——个性化edu!@#$cation是啥？tech*^$#nology有啥能撑起个性化jiao^&*(学啊？羞得她把围巾往上拉。

“这就是今天的问题。”周老师用手指轻轻敲了一下那行字，粉笔灰从指尖飘起。他的视线从学生们脸上一一扫过，停在李安脸上——这个总低着头画直线的小孩，总在做题时把步骤写得工工整整，却在英语朗读时永远小声得像蚂蚁。

后门推开了，穿着羽绒服的姚工走了进来，鼻子上架着一副看起来很贵的眼镜。他是县里的校企合作项目派来的工程师，带来了一台新设备和一套“个性化学习支持系统”，名字起得很顺耳，却也让人有点警惕。姚工把一个扁平的盒子插到投影仪上，屏幕上的蓝色小圆圈开始跳动。

“先说个性化education是啥。”周老师没让姚工开口，自己把话接过去，声音平和，“不是一个人关在小黑屋里做自己的题，也不是让机器取代我。它是被看见——被看见你的长处、你的节奏、你学得特别容易的部分、特别难的地方，你对世界的好奇心是什么。它是让你不必被一根尺子量到底。”

姚工在旁边点头，打开了系统。屏幕上出现了一张复杂的图谱，像是冬天的藤蔓：一个个小节点连成线，节点上写着“分式的约分”“因式分解”“一次函数的斜率”“过去完成时”“光的折射”。每个节点旁边有不同颜色的圆圈，有的亮得发光，有的暗淡像被雨淋过。

“这是知识图谱。”姚工用手势缩放，“我们让系统记你们在每个知识点上的掌握程度，它不是只看一次卷子就打分，而是通过你平时的练习、口头回答、项目作业，甚至你写的步骤和你读英文时的语音。看，”他点开“过去完成时”，一排小条出现，娜娜的条是嫩绿的，李安的条是半绿半灰。

李安的眼睛动了动。周老师知道他最在意的是灰色。他走到李安旁边，低声说：“灰不是失败，是提醒。系统会在这里给你找更适合的材料，给你多两句例子，再把你读出来的语音抓一点，告诉你哪里错。”

姚工又点开一个窗口，是语音识别模块。屏幕上是昨天下午的英语朗读作业，李安的声音被显示成波形，某个词“worked”的尾音被红色标记。“这不是打分，”周老师说，“是技术帮我听得更细。你看，我有时候在教室里一次听四十个人，耳朵是活的，但也会漏。machine帮我补，但是我决定怎么用。”

教室里有轻微的窃窃私语。窗外的操场还堆着霜，白得像白纸。娜娜举手：“那 tech*^$#nology能撑起啥？除了图谱和语音？”

姚工露出一个职业笑容：“不少东西。自适应练习，你做一道题错了，它不是直接给你答案，它会查你错的是概念还是步骤，给你下一题更小一阶梯。还有间隔重复，你背的单词它按你忘记的规律在恰当的时间推给你，省你把不该花的时间全花在熟的词上。再比如推荐算法，按你兴趣——你喜欢植物，我们就把‘光合作用’的项目作业设计成观察你家门口的槐树，而不是让你空背。做实验？我们有个AR模块，戴上最普通的纸盒眼镜都行，能让你在桌子上看见分子长什么样。没有网络？我们准备离线包，不让谁因为家里没Wi-Fi就错过。”

“还有学习分析，”周老师补充，“不是用来排名，是让我看见谁本周总卡在一个地方，谁的情绪曲线下滑了。我们装了一个简易的注意力记录，不是拍你，是看你在做题时的停顿时间告诉我你在犹豫，我就知道该过去坐你旁边。你们的数据不出校，先跟你和家长说清楚。”

李安很慢地抬了手：“老师，个性化会不会让我总是做简单的题？我怕变成被系统保护的那个人。”周老师哼了一声，笑：“这就是为什么机器不可以当驾驶员，只能做后视镜。我给你布置的挑战不会少，它只是帮我把台阶铺得更均匀，不把你推下楼。个性化不是降低标准，是把标准分解。更重要的是，它让标准不止一种——有时候我们要看你解决问题的路径，有时候看你讲清楚一个东西的能力。”

姚工点点屏幕：“比如项目学习。咱们县有梯田，你们测过没有？我们会给你们设计个小项目：用一次函数去计算水流速度，写报告，拍视频，告诉你们为什么你们家那块田灌起来总比隔壁快。这个项目里，每个人路径不一样——有人做数学，有人写文案，有人拍摄——但是都达到了学习目标。”

门口站着一个人，穿着棉袄，手里拎着保温桶。吴阿姨，李安的妈妈。她犹豫了一秒才走进来，坐到后排，拧开保温桶，淡淡的米香飘出来：“我就想问问，老师，这些东西会不会把孩子变成只盯着屏幕的那种？我们家里没电脑，手机也老卡。个性化是不是就是一个人戴着耳机学习？”

周老师把粉笔在黑板上轻轻划了一道，把白线断在中间，像是示意边界：“不会。个性化不是孤立，是连接。你看今天这个系统，它只是让我们更了解每个孩子，然后我安排一对一的解释，小组合作的时候不再把你和不合适的搭档一直绑在一起。我会让李安跟你家的那条沟做水流测量，让他跟小鹏一起，或者跟娜娜一起。课堂还是课堂，书还是书。耳机是工具，不是墙。”

姚工也把话说软了些：“系统也可以用在低带宽、低配置的设备上，我们可以给你们每周发纸质路径图，告诉你们这周哪些内容是‘必须掌握’，哪些是‘可以拓展’。孩子不需要时刻在线。”

周老师在黑板上写了两行字，一行是“被看见的差异”，一行是“被尊重的共性”。他转身，像是要把这些字也写进每个孩子的脑子里。教室突然很安静，只有暖风机的声响和吴阿姨拧盖子的细碎金属音。

“那隐私呢？”后排有人问，是自习室常驻的陈校长，声音沙哑，“孩子们的语音、行为数据，谁看，谁存多久？”姚工早备了答案：“本地存储，脱敏处理，经过家长同意再用。算法透明，我们每一条推荐都有理由，不会出现‘为什么我总被推到简单题’这种不明不白。老师和学校决定权在前，企业在后。”

周老师推开讲台抽屉，拿出两本薄薄的册子，一本封面上印着一条龙特有的蜿蜒，一本是普通的田野照片。他把龙的那本递给娜娜，把田野那本递给李安：“你们今天回去试一下。娜娜，你读这本，把里面的古文挑一段，我们用自然语言的解释给你配现代文对照；李安，你测一下那条沟，把数据带给我，我们把它放进一次函数图里，看看斜率是不是你想象的那样。”

娜娜抱着册子，眼睛亮得像春天刚刚冒头的芽。李安的手指在封面上敲了一下，像试琴。他还想问什么，嘴唇动了动，最后把话吞下。一旁的吴阿姨悄悄看他一眼，那一眼里有担心，也有一种不常见的安静的信任。

散会时，操场上太阳偏了，影子被拉长成墨。周老师收起投影仪，把那张知识图谱关掉，只留下黑板上两个词。姚工把设备装回包里，绕到周老师身边：“周老师，这些功能还有很多，眼动追踪、情绪识别，其实——”

“不急。”周老师摆摆手，“先从能帮到孩子的开始，从不会吓到他们的开始。个性化的第一步不是炫技，是问一句‘你今天哪里卡了’，然后听得比以前更真。”

他提起那两本册子，像提起两盏灯。门口的风有点冷，吹动了走廊上悬挂的精神文明宣传栏里一角纸——上面写着“因材施教”四个字，被阳光照得透亮。

晚上，校门外的街灯亮了，摊位上的铁壶冒着白气。李安和吴阿姨走过去买了两碗馄饨。吴阿姨把册子往包里塞，问他：“个性化edu!@#$cation，到底是个啥？”

李安想了想，把筷子在碗里敲了两下，像在找节拍：“可能是老师看见我需要什么，再让我自己也看见。tech*^$#nology就是他背后那只手，帮他握稳了，不替他开车。”

吴阿姨“嗯”了一声，馄饨汤热得上脸。街角的那只流浪猫缩在摄影棚的门口，睁了一下眼又合上。夜色里，学校的窗子有些还亮着，有人还在教，有人还在学。个性化的故事就是在这样的光里慢慢展开——不是一个响亮的新名词，而是一次次被看见的眼神、一次次被调整的作业、一条条被走过的路径。技术只把灯调得亮一点，路还是人走出来的。

query: 未成年人保护有哪些具体措施？
response:
雨刚停，社区小礼堂的窗玻璃还挂着一层薄薄的雾。塑料折椅一排排摆好，老旧的投影仪在白墙上打出一块有些斑驳的光。刘雁把话筒试了试，指尖在按钮上停了一秒，听着“滋——滋——”的电流声渐渐平稳。

“今晚聊的，是大家这几个月常提到的事。”她笑着扫了一圈，“关于孩子怎么保护、怎么管、怎么会更好。”

最后一排坐着个戴黑色帽衫的小男孩，帽檐压得低，他的手指在椅子的边缘上蹦跳出微微的节奏。他叫游游，十五岁，进门的时候跟妈妈的手挽得很松，像随时要脱离。

“我先说个故事吧，”刘雁晃了晃手里的蓝色册子，“前阵子我们做家访，一个十三岁的女孩在班级群里被同学编排，说她‘妖’。她开始不去学校，成绩掉下去，爸妈也不知道到底发生了什么。最后靠老师的报告，学校开了欺凌处置会议，我们社工介入，给她做了三次心理辅导，两个孩子的家长也受了训。现在，那孩子每周还会来小站画画。”

前排的陈叔在凳子上换了个姿势，他是这里的退休保安，嗓门向来大：“那是好事。可是啊，话说回来，未成年人保护有哪些具体措施？我们知道的都是零碎，手机乱七八糟的信息太多。”

刘雁点头：“好，咱们就把零碎拼成完整的图。”

她把册子放到投影仪旁边，一条一条说起来，声音不急不躁，像雨后的风。

“第一块，是学校层面。现在各个学校都有反欺凌的预防与处置机制，明确了谁负责接到报告、谁组织约谈、怎么记录。老师遇到怀疑虐待、性侵、严重欺凌——法里有强制报告制度，必须在规定时间内向公安或者民政报告。而且学校里有心理辅导室，学生可以匿名预约。我们也和三所学校签了合作，外面的心理师每周进校园坐诊。”

游游的铅笔从衣兜里滑出来，他手背贴着木椅，一点点把笔推回去。

“第二块，是家庭。”刘雁看了一眼坐在他身边的李佳，“区里做了‘家长学校’，大家可以学如何跟孩子沟通、如何识别抑郁或焦虑的表现。出现家庭暴力，孩子可以申请人身安全保护令，法院会出禁令，限制施暴者接近。监护责任如果严重缺位，民政能介入，做临时照料，必要时更换监护。”

李佳的眼睛像烫了一下，手心里的纸巾攥紧了。

“第三块，是社区。”她往堂门外看了一眼，那条路亮着两点车灯，“我们社区驿站建立了‘未成年人保护联络员’，有问题可以来找我，或者找门口那位穿蓝背心的小王。每周三晚上，我们开青少年兴趣小组，写词、打篮球、还有机器人。还有一个重要的：对有侵害未成年人前科的人，很多行业不让他再接触儿童，比如教育培训、托育机构入职前要查背景。这是为了防止风险再发生。”

陈叔摸着自己俩条粗糙的手指，点点头：“这条好。”

“第四块，是网络保护。”刘雁的声音轻了些，“平台要求有内容分级和未成年人模式，视频、直播、游戏都有防沉迷和实名认证。未成年人晚上规定时段不能长时间游戏，这大家也都体会到了。我们也教家长设置手机里的家长监护，帮孩子过滤色情、暴力、诱导消费的内容。发现网暴，平台要及时处置。你们也可以向网信举报。”

“第六块，是社会支持。”刘雁接回话筒，“区里有‘12355青少年服务台’的热线，孩子可以匿名打，聊学习、情绪、纠纷。妇联的‘12338’也能帮家长咨询法律问题。我们这一片还有一个临时避护点，如果孩子短期需要离开家，有床、有热饭。”

她停了一下，看向座位，像在寻找某个目光：“还有，很多人关心‘文身、酒吧、网吧’这类场所的管理。现在规定禁止给未成年人文身，娱乐场所要查未成年人的身份。不适宜的广告不得向未成年人投放。大家可以监督，发现违规拍照发给我们或市场监管。”

门口雨伞上的水珠滴进塑料盆里，发出一声轻响。游游缩了缩肩，这个细小的声音越过纷乱的对话，落在他耳边。

“那……”李佳终于开口，她的嗓子有些发紧，“如果一切都做了，可孩子还是不愿意跟我们说话呢？”

刘雁把话筒轻轻挪低，像是只对她说：“愿不愿意，常常不是一个‘措施’能解决，是时间、信任、还有他相信自己没有被放弃。你可以先不问问题，先陪他做点他喜欢的。比如……你今天肯来，已经很重要。”

这时，陈叔又举起手，嗓音变得俏皮：“那我们老头子能做点啥？别光站在门口吼。”

“您可别小看自己，”林涛笑了，“学校门口那一眼就很有用。还有，路灯下遇到疑似欺凌、推搡，介入的时候先保护孩子，再打电话，别自己硬扛。还能干的——把小卖部门口的香烟远远收起，别让孩子眼睛里都是这些东西。”

前排有人笑起来，后排有人不动声色地点头。

投影仪的光突然跳了一下，屏幕变黑又亮。刘雁按了按遥控，不好意思地摊摊手：“老伙计了，今天可能也累了。”

散场的时候，礼堂像被人轻轻吹了口气，声音稀薄下去。游游站起来，帽檐还是压着。他走到那张摆着册子的桌子前，拿起一本蓝色的小册。他翻到里面，看到第一页赫然印着几个大字：“未成年人保护有哪些具体措施？”下面的条条框框用黑体列着，但他没细看。他只盯着封底那行小字：“需要帮助时，请拨打12355”。

“这个你拿着。”刘雁的声音在旁边，很轻，“有时候，有些话先对陌生人说也行。”

游游把册子塞进帽衫的袋子里，指尖却在封皮上停了一下。他从门口走出去，夜色像一块柔软的布，把街道裹住。雨气里有泥土的味道，和远处麻辣烫的香。

李佳追上他，像往常一样伸手想挽住他的手臂，又在半空中收了回来：“要不要去吃辣烫？”

他摇了摇头，又点了点头，像在与自己斗争。走到路口，他突然停了停，把手机掏出来，屏幕把他的脸照得更白。指尖在数字上滑过，停在一个号码上。他没有拨出去，只是把号码加入了“星标联系人”。

在路灯下，两个人的影子并排拉长，又慢慢被风轻轻吹散。远处的社区礼堂里，投影仪彻底熄了，白墙恢复成最普通的一块白，仿佛什么也不曾发生，又仿佛一切才刚刚开始。
