query: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。
response:
At noon the bank was a cold, white aquarium. Overhead, a video looped silently, a laughing couple on a beach stilling mid-sprint every thirty seconds before dissolving into a chart of interest rates. A jade plant leaned toward the window and found only its reflection; outside, buses rasped and coughed at the curb, their doors gasping open and shut. The security guard dozed in his chair, chin hitting his chest and lifting again in a slow nod.

Ms. Lin stood at Counter 3, her bag open like a small suitcase on the polished ledge. The papers inside had all been ironed with her hand that morning: marriage certificate, household registration booklet, death certificate that smelled faintly of ink. The red chops bled through the thin A4 pages in tidy circles. She placed each document where the young clerk—twenty-something, neat hair pinned back, glossy nails—tapped the glass.

“I want to withdraw enough to pay the shouyi,” Ms. Lin said, using the village word for funeral meal. “He—my husband—he has the account. I’ve brought everything.”

The clerk nodded. Her badge read “Zhao Yanyan.” She tucked a strand of hair that had escaped. Her blouse had a starched waviness, the kind you get from drying overnight on a balcony rail. “Auntie, I’ll check for you. Have a sit.”

She scanned. The machine made its discreet, shuttered noises. In the waiting area, a toddler clapped his palms on the low coffee table, leaving a fan of wet prints. Numbers ticked up on the red LED board: A083 — A084 — A085. Somewhere a printer hummed and released a warm sheet into an empty tray.

Ms. Lin didn’t sit. The counter glass was scuffed at elbow height and her reflection floated over the clerk’s monitor: a soft, square face with new hollows under the cheekbones, hair clipped blunt at the jaw. She had slept with her coat on last night, on the sofa with the TV flickering, as if not undressing would make the morning stay away.

The clerk’s mouth tightened at the corners. Her eyes went back and forth across the screen with the concentration of someone threading a needle. After a moment, she pursed her lips and leaned to the side, as if to see whether a different angle would make the list of requirements rearrange itself.

“Do you have a notarized certificate for inheritance?” she asked gently. “继承权公证书.”

“I have the death paper. The police stamped it.” Ms. Lin tapped the red seal. “They said the bank could release for funeral costs.”

“Yes,” the clerk said in the tone of someone repeating a thing she had learned on her second week. “We can release up to a certain amount for funeral expenses. But we still need the notary document. If there are other heirs, we need confirmation.”

“It’s just me. And the boy, but he works in Suzhou. He can’t come back till Tomb-Sweeping.” The sentence sounded like a complaint and she hadn’t meant it to. She pressed her thumb into the leather seam of her bag, where a thread was loosening.

The clerk clicked something decisively. She leaned closer to the screen. Ms. Lin, who had raised a son in an apartment with a television so small that faces got lost at the edges, read the characters inverted on the monitor as the clerk scrolled past them. They flickered, then settled in bold in the center, a polite sentence framed in gray: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。

The clerk’s face took on a blue cast from the monitor light. She glanced at Ms. Lin, then back at the sentence. It wasn’t even a human voice; it was the system, speaking for everyone in the building.

“I’m sorry,” she said aloud, translating without moving her lips. “The system won’t allow me to proceed without the document. If you go to the notary office on Wuyi Road—here—” she pulled a printed map from a stack and circled with a purple gel pen, “they can do it in three days if you pay the expedited fee. You’ll need your son’s ID copy and signature, and yours. Then bring this back and we can—”

“Three days,” Ms. Lin repeated. Her mouth felt full of dust. “He is in the freezer.”

The clerk kept the pen poised, as if the sentence would require a new symbol. “We can give you a small amount today if you can get your son on a video call, to confirm. Hold on.” She looked at the screen again, typed, waited. “No—sorry—only with a notarized temporary permit. The policy changed last month.”

Behind Ms. Lin, a man in a jacket with a glossy eagle on the back cleared his throat. The boy at the coffee table had moved on to the water dispenser buttons and was being extricated by a grandmother with wrists like cords. The security guard woke briefly and put a hand around his paper cup of tea, steadying it as if it might jump.

“Can you try again?” Ms. Lin said, though she had seen the characters, bright and cool and final. “Maybe it will let you.”

The clerk smiled a small, sad smile that said, I have tried before for other aunties. She tapped again, out of ritual. The same sentence floated up. 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。 The clerk’s finger hovered over the Enter key as if the key itself were the refusal.

She reached into a drawer and took out a smaller sheet. “I’ll write you a checklist. If you bring these exactly, it will be fast when you return.” The gel pen made the list cheerful in purple.

Ms. Lin nodded. Her hand moved on the documents, lining their corners to align with the edge of the counter. The marriage certificate still had a crease from 1987, a fold from a bus ride back from the county bureau that day. She didn’t notice when a photograph slipped from the file and fell to the floor until the clerk stooped and picked it up.

It was a print you get from the shop downstairs: glossy, edges a little furred. In it, Mr. Lin stood beside a fishing pond, a white plastic bucket at his feet. He had been taller then, or maybe happier; his shoulders were squared, his front teeth showing, his cap pulled low. The clerk looked at it too long, and then she passed it over with both hands, the way you pass a hot bowl.

“He looks nice,” she said, and Ms. Lin surprised herself by laughing, a dry bark that made the child at the water dispenser look up. “He was,” she said, and the words turned her mouth to salt.

At the exit, a woman with a lipstick mouth—a wealth manager, the placard on her desk declared—stood, hand hovering over Ms. Lin’s elbow without quite touching. “Auntie, let me give you my card,” she said warmly. “If you need any help… when things are settled, we have products for retirement. Steady yield.”

“I have enough,” Ms. Lin said, not to be rude but because it felt necessary to announce it, like saying her own name.

Outside, the heat had risen above the wetness of the morning. A bus sighed at the curb. Men smoking under the eaves flicked their ash into a communal pot of tea leaves. Ms. Lin folded the list, tucked it into the file, and slid the file into her bag. She took her number slip from her pocket and frowned at it, as if it had some use now. A083. She held it until her knuckles paled, then tore it in half, then half again, each rip small and clean, releasing a paper smell like rice glue.

When she looked back through the bank’s glass, she could still see the blue glow of the clerk’s screen, and for an instant, as the window took her reflection and the clerk’s face and the aquarium brightness and stacked them, it seemed as if the words hung there for her alone: 抱歉，我无法协助完成您的请求。 Then the screen refreshed, a new client sat down, numbers moved, and the line advanced without her.

query: 哎呀，不好意思啊，这事儿我是真帮不上忙。
response:
急诊大厅的自动门一开一合，带着点潮冷的风。天花板上的灯白得发青，把人脸照得像刚洗过。叫号屏哔一声翻一行，A245变成A246，之后又卡住不动了。人挤在一块儿，棉袄上的棉絮和酒精味混在一块儿，偶尔有鞋底摩擦地砖的细响。

我拎着个塑料杯，杯盖歪着，橙色的糖包漂在水面上。爸在靠墙的长椅上坐着，腰后垫了我卷起来的羽绒服，气喘着，箱子一样的胸口一抬一落，眼睛看着前面的宣传屏，上面一会儿是三高防治，一会儿是冬季防滑。妈把他的手背搓来搓去，小声说“再忍一会儿，就到我们了。”

王姨穿着个米色呢子大衣，领口有几根毛被风吹得竖了起来，她提着个印着超市LOGO的布袋进来，脚后跟一下没踏稳，踉跄了一下。我赶紧往前走了两步，“王姨这儿呢。”我喊她，她抬头看见我，脸上挤出笑，“哎呀，小韩，你们咋在这儿。”她低头看了看我手里的化验单，“爸这是……”

“咳喘了两天了，昨晚挺厉害。想住院观察几天。”我压着声音，“我想着您不是认识呼吸科的谁么，您看……能不能……”我话到这儿往下咽了，心里发酸，手指头在杯壁上来回摸。

王姨眼角笑褶子还没来得及收回去，听到这句，笑就慢慢垮了。她把布袋换到另一只手里，重新抓紧，手背青筋一跳一跳的。“哎呀，不好意思啊，这事儿我是真帮不上忙。”她叹了一口气，往旁边挪了半步，给我们让出点空间，“不是我不帮，真是不敢也没法儿。”

妈赶紧说，“没事儿没事儿，给你添麻烦了。”

王姨凑近一点，小声说，“你叔前些年不是还好使嘛，那还是以前。现在上边盯得紧，床位都是系统里排队，医生护士也都老怵，谁都怕拍照留痕啥的。我闺女去年调去科教科了，管培训那块儿，压根儿沾不着床位这事儿。我刚给她发了微信，她回我一句‘妈，别！’就不说话了。”她把手机递给我看，屏幕上只有一行短短的灰字，像从冷水里捞出来的。

我“嗯”了一声，嘴里涌起一阵苦味，仿佛刚嚼了片橘子皮。爸咳了一下，身子前倾，我赶紧把纸巾递过去。他接过去揉在掌心里，冲王姨挤挤眼，“嗓子这玩意儿，干的。不用住，打一瓶水就行。”

妈瞪了他一眼，“你少说两句。”

王姨把布袋放到脚边，弯腰摸了摸袋子里，“我刚从菜市场过来，买了点条肠、萝卜，医生说我自己血脂也高，少吃肉。”她说着又想起什么，从口袋里摸出几瓣糖蒜包着的纸掇给我，“吃个蒜，杀菌。”她又看了看爸，“老韩你别逞能，医生怎么说就怎么来。”

叫号屏又“哔”地一声，呼叫A247。前面有人“哎呀我的号”的叫，慌慌张张拎着包往前挤。有人手里提着输液瓶从我们面前走过去，透明的液体在管子里一滴一滴，照得人心里发冷。走廊尽头的保洁拎着拖把来回挪，拖把把地上一滩鞋印抹成淡灰色，空气里浮着一点橡胶和消毒水混合的味儿。

“要不你们先把片拍了，医生看完再说。”王姨把围巾往上扯了扯，“这制度就是这样，怨不着谁。我真帮不上忙啊。”她的声音软下来，“要是换以前……”

她没说完，手指在围巾边缘捻了一下，扯下一小绺毛，盯着那绺毛看了两秒，又吹了口气，像是吹走什么。

“知道的。”我点点头，把杯盖掰紧了，塑料壳勒得手心发痕，“我们自己排吧。”

“有啥事儿别憋着，能帮的我肯定帮。”她又说了一句，后头有人喊她，“王姐，轮到您了。”她应了一声，把布袋提起来，冲我们摆摆手，“先走了，你们看着办，注意保暖。”

她转身往窗口那边挤过去了，背影在人群里时隐时现。妈把我的袖口拽了拽，压低声说，“别难为人家。”

我“嗯”。手里那张化验单被我捏得起了毛边，纸角翘出来扎手。叫号屏上面数字一格一格地跳，像冬天慢吞吞的太阳从阴云后挪出来一点儿。我看了一眼爸，他靠在椅背上，闭着眼，眼尾有细细的纹路。妈把他的围巾解了一半，又给系上，冲他笑，“再一会儿就轮到咱了。”

对面的小男孩在妈妈腿上打盹，嘴角有条细细的口水痕。他妈妈把他往上提了提，拍了两下背。自动门再一次开合，风把门口的宣传单吹得立起来，扑扇两下又倒下去。我咽了口口水，把杯子递给妈，深吸了一口气，往前站了一步。人群里，一个声音压低了又抬高，碎碎叨叨，最后都被装进那一声“哔”的提示音里，吞了。

query: What is an 操作系统? What are the common 操作系统?
response:
The ceiling fan in Mr. Chen’s shop stirred the warm evening air, drawing ribbons of solder smoke toward the back door where summer cicadas rasped at the alley walls. A row of battered monitors glowed along the workbench like sleepy fish tanks, their blues and greens reflecting off jars of screws and the clear tape dispenser that had inexplicably become the shop’s communal ruler.

Jia stood on a plastic stool, one knee planted on the stool’s cracked surface, peering into the open belly of a desktop tower. Mr. Chen had set a cone of light over the machine; inside, the motherboard gleamed with tiny cities, and the fan spun up, whining, then settling.

“问吧,” Mr. Chen said, wiping his hands on a cloth and nodding toward Jia’s notebook. Ask.

Jia puffed out a breath and read, careful, as if summoning a phrase that might misbehave if said wrong. “What is an 操作系统? What are the common 操作系统?”

From the front of the shop, the bell tinkled as someone came in. The cat—named Kernel as a joke that only the regulars laughed at anymore—looked up from its spot on the laser printer and flicked an ear.

Mr. Chen leaned his elbows on the bench and looked at Jia over the frames of his glasses. “You got your school oral test tomorrow, eh?” he said. “They still making you ask the English question with Chinese words?”

Jia nodded. “Miss Lin says it helps us remember what we already know. She says language mixes like hot pot.”

“Language, computers, families,” Mr. Chen said, smiling. “All hot pot.” He tapped the side of the open computer. “操作系统… operating system. Imagine the shop is a big kitchen. The stove is your CPU. The pots and pans are like memory and storage. People come in with tickets—orders—‘fix my phone,’ ‘print my photos.’ Without someone in charge, all the cooks bump into each other, burn the soup, forget to pay the gas. The operating system is the head chef and the floor manager together. It decides which pot sits on the burner and when, who gets more flame, who waits. It keeps track of where the ingredients are. It talks to the refrigerator, the oven, the printer. It gives the menu—the interface—to the customers so they can ask for what they want without walking into the pantry themselves.”

“So it’s like… 管家,” Jia said. “A house manager.”

Mr. Chen nodded. “Yes. The OS sits between the hardware—things you can touch—and the software—things you can ask the machine to do. It has a few big jobs. Resource management: decide who uses the CPU, how much memory each program gets. File system: keeps your stuff in drawers and knows which drawer has your homework and which one has your grandmother’s photos. Device drivers: speaks the language of the printer, the Wi‑Fi card, the camera. User interface: the windows, icons, the commands you type. Security: locks the doors, decides who gets to do what.”

From the front, a tired-looking courier in a faded green jacket laid a cracked phone on the counter. “It just froze,” he said. “It shows a little robot and says no command. I swear I didn’t do anything. And I gotta be back on the road in twenty minutes.”

Mr. Chen nodded toward the green robot on the courier’s screen. “Android,” he said. “An operating system for your phone. See? It’s literally saying it can’t take orders right now.” He slid the phone across to Jia. “You answer your own question first. What are the common 操作系统?”

Jia flipped to the page with Miss Lin’s neat diagrams. “Windows,” she said. “Many people use Microsoft Windows for desktops and laptops. macOS for Apple computers. Linux—like Ubuntu and Fedora—for servers, and some desktops too. For phones and tablets: Android and iOS. There’s also ChromeOS, like the school’s cheap Chromebooks, and BSD… FreeBSD, maybe… that routers sometimes use? And… uh… older ones like Windows XP and 7, but they’re not safe anymore.”

“很好,” Mr. Chen said, blowing at a bent pin until it lifted. “Good. You can say, Windows and macOS are the big desktop ones. Linux is everywhere—on servers that power websites, on supercomputers, and in embedded devices. Android is built on top of Linux. iOS is Apple’s for iPhones and iPads. ChromeOS is a skinny jacket Google made for low-cost laptops, mostly web-based. BSD family is quieter but tough—like those aunties who never come to temple but always know what’s going on.”

The courier shifted from foot to foot. “Is it… bad?” he asked.

Jia looked to Mr. Chen, then took a breath and held down the volume and power buttons as she had learned. The green robot winked out, and the black screen offered white text. The cat’s tail twitched once as if scanning the log.

“You can put the analogy in your own words,” Mr. Chen said softly to Jia. “Make it yours. They’ll remember the picture if you remember it.”

Jia nodded. “Operating system is like… the night market manager,” she said, eyes on the phone as the recovery menu blinked to life. “You have all these vendors—the apps—wanting electricity, table space, customers. The manager decides who plugs in where so the lights don’t blow. They collect the stall fees—manage permissions—so no one steals. They fix the path so people don’t trip.” She tapped the volume button carefully, chose reboot. The phone sighed back into color, the courier exhaled with it.

“Common ones…” she continued, cheeks warming with the attention. “Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, ChromeOS. Some use command lines, some are more windows and icons. All of them are… translators between us and the machine.”

Mr. Chen grinned and slid the courier’s phone back to him. The man nodded and pulled a coin from his pocket, two yuan polished smooth by years in a palm, and pushed it back across the counter under the cat’s whiskers. “For good luck,” he said, and left with the green jacket flaring once in the doorway.

The shop quieted again. Outside, a motorcycle coughed and faded. Inside, the ceiling fan made its slow lazy rounds.

Jia turned the desktop tower back toward her. “So… why so many operating systems?” she asked, pencil hovering.

“Different kitchens,” Mr. Chen said. “Different chefs. Different tastes and tools. Windows grew in offices. macOS grew in art rooms and in Apple’s own way. Linux grew among people who liked to take machines apart and put them back together—and now it runs the largest parts of the internet. Phones needed operating systems that understand small batteries, touch screens, antennas talking all the time; Android and iOS evolved there. Each one has its own rules, its own best dishes.”

“One more question,” Jia said, though she hadn’t written this one down. “What happens if there is no OS?”

Mr. Chen leaned back on his stool and raised his hands, palms up, to the humming shop. “Then your beautiful metal and plastic is so quiet it hurts. Software could talk straight to hardware, but every program would need to know every way to speak to every piece. Imagine every customer here has to know how to run the soldering iron, fix the printer, align the laser, all to print a flyer. Chaos. An OS gives us a shared way to ask. It also stops bad programs from breaking the house. At least most of the time.”

Kernel leapt from the printer to the bench and nosed at Jia’s pencil. Jia scratched the cat under its chin. “So if my cousin says his phone is Android and mine is iOS, we’re really saying we eat at different night markets,” she said.

“More like the same night market with two parts who don’t share plates,” Mr. Chen said, chuckling. “But both are still making sure nobody steals the electricity.”

Jia closed her notebook and practiced the English again, rolling the words around her mouth like a marble. “What is an 操作系统? What are the common 操作系统?” She pictured a vast kitchen humming, the steam slicking the lights, the order tickets in a clip. Somewhere in there, the head chef swept a hand, and the pots moved into place.

Mr. Chen switched off the desk lamp. The shop slipped from spotlight to aquarium glow. “You’ll do fine,” he said. “Now help me fit this case back together before your mother calls and asks if I’m teaching you useful things or just keeping you out all night.”

Jia laughed and reached for the side panel. Outside, someone started singing two shops down, a song without words, just a held note that felt like a wire pulled tight and plucked. Inside, the operating systems hummed on in their glass boxes, invisibly preventing small disasters.

The expo hall hummed the way hives hum: a soft, collective vibration from thousands of feet on concrete and a thousand tiny worries about weather, shoes, sleep. Lin pressed her palm to the cool aluminum of her bib, the paper crisp against her chest, and stared up at the LED banner that spanned the entrance like a horizon that had been mounted and plugged in.

The banner glitched.

Letters slid sideways, pixels misfired in violet halos, and then a sentence—no, a question—wrote itself in shards across the scrolling ad for isotonic gel. “什X么是马拉%松运@动？参#加马拉~松的赛@前准+备及赛后恢~复方^法有哪+些？”

Lin felt it in her teeth, the way unfamiliar symbols tremble there before you let them out. Her mother had once said that language was a tightrope strung over a river of meaning, and that sometimes you fall in and come up soaked in the wrong words. Lin put the thought away, but the banner kept asking.

“What is that?” someone beside her said, laughing in a way that wasn’t unkind. The man wore a volunteer lanyard and a jacket the color of sprinting shoes. His name tag read NAVEEN.

“It’s Chinese,” Lin said. “Kind of. Like a Chinese sentence that got caught in a washing machine with punctuation.”

He squinted. “Can you read it?”

She read it aloud, stumbling through the static characters, and then again, smoothing them: “什么是马拉松运动？参加马拉松的赛前准备及赛后恢复方法有哪些？” Her mouth remembered. The meaning came up clear as a sky after storm: What is marathon running? What are the pre-race preparations and post-race recovery methods?

Naveen whistled. “The banner’s supposed to cycle through multilingual FAQs. That’s… extra. I think the freaky characters might be from the content filter. We had a spam plugin that mangled anything with certain word patterns. Somebody must’ve turned it back on.”

He was already on his phone, thumbs moving. Lin watched the crowd flow around them, a river of neon threading through rows of vendor booths, massage guns buzzing, cups of sample electrolytes sweating on plastic tables. The questions on the banner weren’t wrong. They were just wearing armor.

“My dad would love this,” she said before she remembered he wasn’t here to love anything. “He taught calligraphy. He believed the shape of a character could teach you how to stand.”

“What did he say about running?” Naveen asked, still scrolling through a labyrinth of admin panels.

“That it was like writing on the world with your body,” she said, and then winced at herself. The honest-to-goodness corn of it. “He didn’t run. He just liked metaphors.”

Naveen grinned. “I like metaphors. They’re like… gels for the brain.”

She laughed in spite of herself. Beneath the banner, a young boy tugged his mother’s sleeve and pointed upward. She answered in Spanish that she didn’t know, maybe it was a riddle. Lin wanted to tell him the answer, that there wasn’t one, that the question stuck on a loop above their heads was what running did best: uncover questions you didn’t know you had, make them loud, make them unignorable.

Naveen looked up from his phone. “I can fix it. Or I can leave it. It might be the most honest thing in here. Everything else is certainty and discounts.”

“Leave it,” Lin said. “If anyone asks, tell them it’s an art installation.”

“Art installation,” he repeated solemnly, as if practicing. Then, gentler: “Are you ready? First marathon?”

“Third.” The number surprised her; she still felt like a person pretending. “Still feels like the first.”

A pair of older women walked past comparing socks. A man with shin splints limped by while assuring someone on speaker that he was fine, he was fine. A nurse in scrubs pinned on a bib over her top, hands steady from muscle memory. The hall expanded on Lin’s inhale and shrank on her exhale. That was all running had ever been.

Her phone buzzed. A message from her mother: Eat something. Don’t forget sunscreen. He would be proud.

Lin typed back, I know, and added a heart, then deleted the heart, then added a different one. She watched the old forensics of habit play out on her own screen: the way her thumb hovered, the way she always thought to fix things before she accepted them.

“Do you want me to translate the sign for the PA?” Naveen asked. “We could make an announcement.”

“It’s okay,” Lin said. “Half the people in here are already doing what it says. They’re drinking tiny cups and stretching and arguing with their shoes. The other half are thinking about the parts no one dramatizes.”

“Like what?”

“After,” she said, and tried not to picture the ache that would hum through her legs like a remembered song. “The quiet after you cross, when no one is calling your name and there’s no more line to cut.”

A woman shuffled toward them in a hoodie with the hood up despite the heat. She had the narrow, luminous look of someone who had once been in a place only she could see, and had just returned. She stopped under the glitching banner and took a photo. She noticed Lin noticing and shrugged.

“For my daughter,” the woman said. “She learns Chinese on an app. She’ll love this.”

“It asks,” Lin said, because suddenly she wanted to offer something that was not a correction, “what a marathon is, and what to do before and after.”

The woman nodded like that was exactly right, smiled, and drifted away. The banner flickered: 什X么是马拉%松运@动？参#加马拉~松的赛@前准+备及赛后恢~复方^法有哪+些？

Naveen pocketed his phone. “There’s a quiet corner by the east exit where runners go to breathe,” he said. “If you need it. You can’t miss it. It smells like oranges.”

“I’ll find it,” Lin promised, because having a direction helped.

He gave her a thumbs-up and was swallowed by the ebb and pull of the expo, by a man waving an iPad and a group in matching charity shirts buzzing about pace bracelets. Lin stepped back, letting the tide carry her to a table where a woman with henna on her hands handed her half a banana and told her good luck, good luck, in a voice like a lullaby.

Outside, the sky was the color of unpolished steel. The city’s buildings looked like they had been sharpened overnight. Lin stood on the steps and watched people pin their fears to their shirts like bibs. She took a marker from her pocket and wrote two characters on the back of her hand, the ones her father had always traced in the air for her, the ones that meant endure and return. The ink bled a little, pools of meaning.

On her way to the start, she passed under the banner again. The question hung there above the field, imperfect, persistently curious, and it felt like a blessing. She didn’t answer it. She tightened her laces, breathed, and stepped into the corral where the world narrowed into a lane and widened into time.

query: 不好意思，我真帮不了。
response:
雨从傍晚就没有停。霓虹牌子在湿漉漉的蓝夜里像一块被反复擦拭的玻璃，反射出条条红光，斜斜地倒进吧台后面的镜子里。我一直把切好的青柠堆在冰槽边，手上还沾着它们萤绿色的汁。从门口进来的风带着雨味和街角烤串的烟气，掺着晚班电车远远过桥的哼声。

她推门进来用力过头，风把门拍在门框上，发出某种心脏被敲一下的声音。她的行李箱是灰色布面的，轮子在木地板上拖出两条潮湿的痕。我见过很多人深夜走进这家店，背上有不同的重量，有的是故事，有的是债务，有的是单纯的疲惫。她的重量是那种寂静的——落座时只让椅子腿轻轻一声，眼睛里像藏着一枚尚未启封的信。

“喝点什么？”我问，拿起杯子让冰块敲了一下玻璃。

她抬起头，眼睛在吧台上巡了一圈停在墙上的钟上，指针走到十点半的位置。她说：“热的，有吗？”

我笑了一下，说：“我能做热的威士忌酸，不像菜单上的，但夜里喝着暖。”她点头，握住杯沿时手指有些发红。

调酒的动作调子很熟，我很少在夜里卡壳或者犹豫，但在她第一口酒下肚，鼻尖因热气微微湿润之后，她开口问的那句，我直到她走后都在反复听着。

“你认识阿川吗？”她说。

我的手指在冒着白雾的金属壶上停了一下，接着又继续画圈，蒸汽在吧台灯下像薄薄的纱。我把杯子给她，回答得像我平常回答任何一个名字：“看人多不多吧，他常来，坐靠门那张，喜欢加一片柠檬皮。”

她低头笑了一下，像是承认这个描述正中她心里一个点。笑里有一种苦沫味，很轻，落在木头上不会留下痕迹。

她从包里拿出一个牛皮纸信封，厚度不大，封口处贴着一枚小小的红色贴纸，某个文具店里常见那种。她把它在指尖转了一下，说：“能不能帮我把这个转交给他？我明天早上的车要走，之前一直没找到他。”

我看着信封，像看着一个不该把它打开的人出现在门口。阿川不喜欢被找，他说过，甚至在某个雨停的下午笑着用了一个词——“清净”。很多人以为在酒吧里清净是不可能的，其实恰恰相反。清净是有人陪你坐着，愿意听你说，也愿意跟你一起不说。阿川讨厌被他说话以外的东西追上，他曾经把一个号码在我面前揉成细条，丢进烟灰缸。

但这不是我的事情，或者说，我的小事情是在冰块和酒之间、在梦和醒之间的小道上，不在信件和离别之间的大路上。我摸了一下吧台下放着的抹布，找寻一种能让我说出拒绝的质地。

“他是你的？”我问，不是为了猎奇，是为了给她多一点路说话。

“不是，”她说，停了一下，又说，“也许是‘曾经的’，这种说法很滑。总之，我不能再等他。车从北站走，五点半。车票已经买了，行李不多，能背着走。我们说好了见面，他没来。我就想……至少，让他知道。”

她喝了一口热威士忌酸，杯壁被她手上的温度烫出一圈缓慢的雾。酒的味道和她的词句混在一起，像走到桥头忽然吹来的风，有甜有苦，终究带走点什么。

我把手放在吧台上，指尖按住那一角纸，感觉它的纤维在软。夜里做决定尤其难，你面前是某个陌生人的把柄，背后是某个熟人的嘱托。阿川的嘱托并不多，他也不算让我为他保守秘密的人。但有些话像是酒里的一滴橙皮油，只要你知道里面有它，口感就不再平。

我吸了一口气，让声带像刚刚被蒸汽蒸过那样反复想清楚。然后我把手收回，说：“不好意思，我真帮不了。”

这句话从我的口里出来，比我预想的更小声，更像是落在吧台上的一滴水。她看着我，眼睛里不闪，不挪，也没有求我解释。那种看像一个安静的湖面，在某处底下你知道有一条鱼游过，但你看不见它的影。

她点了一下头，把信封收回包里，拉链响了一下，声音很直。她没说什么像“我理解”，也没说“那算了”。她只说了“谢谢”，然后把剩下的酒一口喝掉，呛了一点，把咳嗽压在喉咙里。

从她把椅子推回原位、行李箱的轮子再一次在木地板上留下一条潮湿的痕，到她打门出去那一刻，我一直站在吧台后边，肩膀有点紧，像是回忆起很久以前一场冬天里的球赛，那球擦过我的指尖然后换了一个方向。

门关上，雨声立即填满她的空位。墙上的钟走到将近十一点，电台里远处有人在播报明天的天气，“早上转晴”，他说，不像真的。

阿川在十一点半来。雨停了一点，挂在他肩膀上的布帆布包滴答地把剩下的雨水送到地上。他推门的力道刚刚好，门几乎没发声。他看见我，露出那种不想说也不必说的笑。他坐在靠门的位置，手指自然地在桌面上敲了两下。

“老样子？”我问。

他点头，“老样子。”我削了一片柠檬皮滑到酒里，看着皮上薄薄的油光一层薄膜似地破裂，把香带到酒面。他端起杯子，呼出一口气，像是琥珀里有一个已经被保存好的秋天。

我本该把刚才的事情搁在夜里某个角落，让它像落地的一滴水一样蒸发掉。可那封信的角似乎还摩擦着我的指尖，提醒我夜里有一个未竟的动作。我开口，伸手擦了擦吧台的水，说：“今天有人找你。”

阿川的手停了两秒，抬眼看我。他不上来问是谁，只是等我说。那一瞬间我几乎想把整个故事讲出来，甚至想把那封信从我的叙述里掏出来，放在他面前，让他自己做决定。然后我的喉咙里的某个东西把这条路按住了。我记得我刚刚说过那句“我真帮不了”，它在我脑子里挪来挪去，最后停在了一个答案上。

“她走了，”我说，“明早的车。她叫你别担心。”我不知道为什么用了这个词，也许是为了让夜里少一点重。

阿川微微笑了一下，“别担心。”他重复了这三个字，像是把它们捧在手里看了看，然后放回桌上。他低头喝了一口，眼睛在杯沿上擦过，像是看见了某个光的变形。

我们都没再说话，外面雨似乎停了，路灯下的水窝开始照出更清澈的黄。人走的人走，留的人留。我把吧台擦干净，把柠檬皮篮子里的剩余拢了一下，灯在酒瓶的玻璃里闪了两下像几只飞行疲惫的昆虫。

夜里我大概会睡不着，想起那个信封，以及那句从我口里出来的轻。也许明天早上会晴，她会坐上车，在阳台上晾过衣服后离开这座城市。也许阿川会把他的帆布包背得更牢一些，也许他不会。都不是我能帮的。我在这条街的尽头看着人来人往，假装自己是一个用手里的柠檬和酒制成平衡的人，而平衡的另一端，那些没人能帮的事，像雨停后挂在树叶上的透明一滴，在光里停留了一会儿，然后滑落到地上。

query: 如何培养良好亲子关系？
response:
晚饭前的六点半，厨房里蒸汽在黄灯下团成一小朵一小朵的云。林萧把姜切成丝，锅沿冒着轻响，阳台上晾着的毛巾还在滴水。门口的电子锁轻轻“滴”一下，儿子小宇背着书包进来，鞋底有点泥，裤腿沾了一道细细的粉笔灰。

“今天怎么这么晚？”林萧没有抬头，先把火关小了。她在脑子里倒数了三下——这是她最近练习的——再转身，笑得不那么着急。

“社团拖了。”小宇避开她的视线，往餐桌上一丢，书包侧袋里滚出一支笔。那支笔外壳被咬出一道坑。

手机在他的手里亮了一下。林萧伸手拿来一个玻璃碗：“先把手机放碗里充电，饭前我们都不看。我的也一起。”她把自己的手机也放进去，屏幕阖上的那一刻，厨房像突然安静了一秒。

小宇“嗯”了一声，把杯子拿到水槽边去冲。他回来的时候，把一张作业纸抽出来，黑色的印刷体喊着作文题目：“如何培养良好亲子关系？”

他把纸往餐桌上一拍：“我们老师出的题目。你说这谁写得出来。”

林萧笑了一下：“要不，我们边吃边想？先把菜起了。”她拎起锅，青菜的香味被热油裹着漫开。她不去追问今天社团里发生了什么，先让热气和味道填满空间。

饭碗落桌，小宇拿筷子的手有点僵。他吃了两口，就把筷子放下，指尖在作文纸角来回扣。林萧看着他手背上的细毛，想起下午老师微信里传来的两行字：“今天在班上有点冲突，他有点激动。我已经聊过了。”她喉咙里有个冲动往上涌——“你怎么又……”——但她用刚才的练习把它压回去。

“我看到你回来脸有点紧，肩膀也抬得很高。”她说，“我有点担心，也好奇。你愿意先说说今天过得怎样吗？不用着急，先吃几口。”

小宇没有看她，拿起筷子又夹了一块豆腐，他嚼得很慢。过了会儿，他把筷子放下：“赵辰又拿我的东西。数学题我没做出来，他笑我。我有点生气，拍了桌子。老师让我们分开。”

“听起来你很委屈，也有点被他挑衅到了。”林萧把自己的碗往他那边移了半寸，“我刚开始是想说‘你不该拍桌子’，但我知道你当时一定很难受。我们可不可以先把那个感觉留在桌上，看看它是什么样？”

小宇的肩膀慢慢落下来：“就是像被人捏住脖子那样。然后…我知道拍桌子不好，可是我脑子就嗡嗡响。”

“我也会这样。”林萧笑笑，“我今天开会，老板在我还没说完的时候打断我，我心里也嗡嗡响。我是去倒了一杯水，站在窗边看了两分钟的天。”她停了一秒，“等你愿意，我们可以一起想想遇到这种嗡嗡的时候，除了拍桌子，还能做什么。”

小宇点头：“我可以出去走两圈。或者我用老师给的那个‘暂停卡’，那张蓝的。”

林萧把一块胡萝卜拨到他的碗里：“好，我们把它写在冰箱上的‘嗡嗡清单’。还有，我有件事想跟你说。”她吸了一口气，“上周我冲你喊了，我很后悔。我那天太累又着急，没有好好听你。我现在跟你道歉。”

小宇抬了眼，眼睛有点红，“我也不该把门关那么响。”他用手指头推了推面前的餐巾，“我们可以…像你说的那样，遇到嗡嗡先停两分钟？”

“可以。”林萧把筷子放下，手掌平平地放到桌面上，“我们试试用两个规则：一是先描述发生了什么，不评判。二是用‘我’说感受，不用‘你总是’。比如你今天可以说‘我觉得很被忽视’，而不是‘你们都站他那边’。”

门口的锁又响了一下，陈浩拎着一袋葡萄进来，鼻尖还挂着外面冷空气的红。他在客厅的光里停了一下，看到桌上的作文题目，笑道：“哎，这题不错。”

“你晚了十分钟。”小宇看了看墙上的钟。

陈浩把葡萄放下，站在门口把鞋换好：“对。对不起，我在楼下绕了路，因为我想多买点甜的。你今天不好过，我想家里有个甜的东西。”他走到桌边，拿起小宇的作文纸，“老师问的是‘如何培养良好亲子关系’，我们能不能先说说，我们家里已经在做的是什么？再看还缺什么。”

小宇把纸拉回自己这边，拿起笔：“我们有‘饭前不看手机’。”他写下第一行。停顿了一下，又写，“每周三晚散步半小时，聊聊彼此的事。”

“还有‘先敲门’。”陈浩补充，“你喜欢你的空间。我们都在练。”

“对，”林萧笑，“还有‘每个月一次小项目’，比如上次我们一起装那个书架。这比我们坐下来讲道理更管用。”

小宇的笔尖在纸上咰咰地响，他抬头：“那‘不拿我和别人比较’也要写上。”

林萧眼睛一软：“当然。‘看见你的独特，不拿你做排名’。我还想加一个‘互相说正面的反馈’——比如我今天看到你帮奶奶提了米，我很开心。”

陈浩去洗葡萄，水声从水槽里轻轻落下。他把葡萄端回来，葡萄的皮在灯下发光。小宇伸手拿了两颗，嘴里含着甜，肩膀完全放松了。

“那我们冲突的时候怎么办？”他用笔尾敲了敲纸，“老师说要写‘遇到问题如何解决’。”

“我们刚才其实就做了一遍。”林萧笑，“先停、再听、再一起想方案。比如你说想‘出去走两圈’，我们就支持；比如我需要你下次用词温和一点，我也要说出具体的请求，而不是说‘你不要这么坏’。”

陈浩点点头：“我们可以写‘定期圆桌会’——周日晚十分钟，每个人说一件想调整的事，一件感激的事。我们把‘嗡嗡清单’贴冰箱，你喜欢用蓝笔写，我用黑笔。”

小宇在纸上写下这些，字一点点变得匀称。他突然把笔停住，望向两人：“那我今天数学只有六十八分，你们不骂我？”

林萧笑着摇头：“成绩是一个信息，不是你的价值。我们可以一起拆一下哪里掉了分，下次怎么学得更好。但这不会改变我们对你的喜欢。”她说着，伸手碰了碰他的手背，“你是你，不是一个数字。”

陈浩从葡萄盘里捏了一颗最大最圆的递给他：“如果你愿意，我可以明天晚饭后陪你看那些错题。我们做三道就好，别贪多。你也可以告诉我，哪一种讲法让你最不烦。”

小宇嘴角有了个小小的笑：“你别讲太多比喻就行。”他把最圆的那颗葡萄放进嘴里，故意发出一点夸张的“啪”声。

外面楼道里的脚步声渐渐远去，厨房的热气也平缓下来。林萧起身收碗，突然又想起来什么：“我们还有一个新习惯试试——每天晚饭后十分钟，只聊感受和这一天好玩的事，不谈作业、不谈安排。你教我们一个你今天学的新词，我们也告诉你我们工作里的笑话。”

“那我今天学的是‘共情’。”小宇举着笔，“就是…你刚才那样。”

“对，就是那个。”陈浩伸出手，和儿子用他们私下的“秘密握手”碰了一下——两下一上一下，最后指尖相触。林萧在旁边笑，看着两个她爱的人以这种小而稳的方式靠近。

作文纸上已经写了半页，留着一大片空白可以慢慢填。冰箱门上贴着他们之前的便签：周三散步、周日圆桌、每月小项目、嗡嗡清单、先敲门。门外冬夜的风凉，不会进来。屋里有热汤，有葡萄，有三个愿意练习的人。

“如何培养良好亲子关系？”小宇低声念了一遍题目。他在纸的最后一行写：我们不追求完美，我们追求在不完美里彼此靠近。写完，他抬头看了看父母，然后把笔盖盖上，把纸叠起，像收好了一个小小的约定。

query: 解释文艺复兴思想与影响
response:
傍晚的乌菲齐走廊像一条被黄昏慢慢拉长的琴弦，游客的脚步声稀稀落落，一阵一阵，像余音。玻璃窗外，阿尔诺河在雨后泛着微绿的光。馆员露琪亚把胸卡别回毛衣里，侧身让我站在一幅画前。

“波提切利的《春》。”她说，“你看，这里没有圣徒的殉道，没有末日审判。是风、花、肉身、神话——古希腊罗马的故事被重新请回了屋里。”

我点头。三位轻盈的女性像风中树叶。她说得很轻，像怕惊动她们。

“这就是我们说的‘人文主义’的一个入口，”露琪亚指着那一圈光滑的手腕，“把人的感受、理性、尊严放在画面中心。人不再只是通往来世的影子，而是此世的主体。那时候学者们提倡studia humanitatis——修辞、诗歌、历史、道德哲学、语法，不只是神学。皮科写《论人的尊严》，说人是上帝将自己放在世界中心的‘变形体’，能选择成为兽也能成为天使。这不是抛弃宗教，而是把人的自由和创造力抬起来。”

她把手往后抬了一下，带我到达·芬奇的《天使报喜》前。玛利亚的手指按着书页，书页仿佛被她呼吸微微掀动。

“看这书桌和花园的远景，”露琪亚贴近玻璃，“透视。线条收束到一点，空间像被数学支撑住。文艺复兴的另一个核心，就是用观察和理性去解剖世界，哪怕是为了画得更像。布鲁内莱斯基在大教堂前用镜子和板子实验透视；达·芬奇去解剖室看肌肉；艺术家在画室和工坊里像科学家一样做实验。他们不满足于套用传统图式——他们问：眼睛看到的是什么？光如何折射？物体如何占据空间？这种‘看’的态度，慢慢就推着科学往前走。”

我们在一幅圆形的《圣家族》前停住，米开朗基罗的颜色像从石头里爆出来。露琪亚指示我看约瑟的手臂——肌肉绷得像绳子。

“个体的力量。”她说，“佛罗伦萨立在小广场上的《大卫》其实不在这里，但你可以在这个圆里看到同一个气质——一个青年像城邦的良知一样站着。城邦之间互相竞争，政治上强调公民的德性，艺术上强调人的形体、意志、荣誉。赞助人——美第奇这样的银行家——用钱养画家和诗人，一方面出于喜好，一方面也是权力的装饰。文艺复兴把格调和财富紧紧系在一起，推动了艺术的繁盛，也让艺术变成可以动员的符号。”

我们往里走。有一个玻璃柜，里面躺着一本小开本，纸页边缘泛黄，封面是一只小锚绕着海豚。

“阿尔杜斯·马努蒂乌斯，”她笑，“威尼斯的出版社在这家伙手里变成了一种机器。他用斜体字，把古典作品编成便携的小书，像这样。再往北一点，古腾堡发明了活字印刷。它改变了知识的速度和地理：书变便宜了，思想可以越过修道院的墙。人文主义的文本——西塞罗、维吉尔、塔西佗——被校勘、印行；宗教改革的火种也是纸张点燃的：路德把《圣经》译成德语，普通人开始读。伊拉斯谟写《愚人颂》，用温柔的讽刺批评教会内部的腐败。思想奔跑起来，教会也学会了追，它设禁书目录、设改革的委员会。没有哪一种‘光’是不投影子的。”

她指给我看墙上的一抹灰影，是丢勒的版画，狮子般的自画像眼神锐利，像倒扣在画纸里的针。

“北方的文艺复兴有它的表情。”露琪亚说，“他们把人文主义揉进了基督教，更多关注道德、日常、细节。你看丢勒的细节和梵高的细节不一样——一个是用针刻出来的理性和秩序，一个是百年后的情绪震颤。但对当时的欧洲来说，印刷和通俗语言让这些差异在地图上彼此看见了。”

我们经过窗，黄昏像一层薄薄的琥珀贴在城市上。露琪亚靠着窗台，说：“影响是广阔又纠缠的。教育上，学者们把书院从神学的迷宫里引出来，训练学生的语言和判断，让他们去读古人的文本和历史。城市里，银行、工匠、商人跟学者、画家交往，知识和钱相互催化。哥白尼和伽利略用数学推翻了旧宇宙，把太阳推到中心；培根把实验立为方法。地理上，地图往西延伸，佛罗伦萨人维斯普奇的名字落到了新大陆，航海给欧洲带来了金属、香料、疾病与奴隶贸易——让欧洲对自身的信心无限膨胀，也让它在别处制造了漫长的伤口。”

她停了一下，像在选择词：“当然，‘复兴’不是一朝一夕的灶火。中世纪远不是黑暗，很多灯火来自它；‘文艺复兴’这个词，还是十九世纪的历史学家重新打磨出来的镜片。它也不属于所有人：女性艺术家艰难地在门槛上探头——你听过索福尼斯巴·安古索拉吗？她在宫廷里画皇后，却常被称为‘才女’而非‘大师’。工匠和穷人日常的生活并没有因此变得辉煌；意大利被外敌践踏，罗马在1527年被洗劫。艺术常常是权力的织物：教会也学会了用巴洛克的戏剧性召唤信徒。”

我们在一幅无名小匠画的圣母像前停下，圣母的手指粗糙了些，金箔贴得不平。我忽然觉得亲切。露琪亚把声音放得更近：“但它毕竟让一个问题变成习惯，直到今天也还在问：人是什么？我们如何自处？文艺复兴把人从图像的边角移到中心，把眼睛和心智当作可信的工具。它的代价、它的盲点——我们在后来几百年的战争、殖民、资本的轨迹里都能看见。可若没有那一代人把画布拉直，把语言磨利，把古书捧回桌上，我们可能也学不会怀疑与发问。”

走廊里最后一盏灯熄了，保安走来提醒闭馆。我们沿着楼梯下去，脚步在石头上敲出轻的回声。门一开，外面细雨像一层稍微冰凉的纱，我和露琪亚一起站在雨檐下，看街角卖报纸的小贩把今天的头条掀给路人。

“你写小说，对吧？”她忽然问。

“嗯。”我说。

“那你也在做同样的事。把人的话重新写回纸上，让他在纸上站起来。”

我笑了笑。雨水沿着檐沟奔跑，像手稿边被水渍渗出的一圈圆晕。我想到那些在书页间折下的小角——是读者把时间折成标记。文艺复兴也许不过是这样一个折角，让人翻回去时，忽然看见自己在页中。我们把伽利略、达·芬奇、皮科、伊拉斯谟的名字像书签一样插在历史里，不是为了膜拜，而是提醒我们：人的目光曾这么抬起过。至于光照到了哪里，哪里又留下阴影——走出檐下，才知道。

query: 啥是民宿，有啥要当心的？
response:
傍晚的雨把大理古城的石板路淋得发黑，檐角滴水，一串一串，像敲在手背上的凉意。阿卓拎着登山包在巷口犹豫，手机地图的蓝点在雨幕里乱跳。他被一盏黄色小灯吸引过去，木门上挂着一块手写牌子：青苔院·民宿。

门一推，湿润的桂花味扑了出来。院子不大，青石台阶上铺着麻绳，墙上钉了几把旧木拍子做装饰。主人是个四十来岁的女人，头发在脑后扎得利索，脸上带着雨后的潮红。她把抹布在掌心绞干，笑着接了话：“你们是阿卓吧？雨大，快进来。”

小叶把伞一抖，水珠叮叮当当掉在木地板上。她是阿卓的表姐，一路把他从火车站带来，跟主人用方言寒暄几句，转头对他：“你不是问我啥是民宿嘛，今天正好给你上一课。”

阿卓冲主人点点头：“阿姨，我就是想问，这民宿……到底跟酒店有什么不一样？”

主人“哎”了一声，手指冲着屋子转了一圈：“简单说，酒店是标准化的、像流水线，民宿嘛，你就当住进别人家的房子。可能是我家老房子改的，也可能是别人家的小院子、一个阳台、一个阁楼，风格、规矩都各自不同。我们自己打理，和客人靠得更近点，熟了还能一起喝茶聊两句。喜欢的人，说有生活味儿；不喜欢的人，说不够统一。”

她一边说，一边把钥匙递给他：“现在都不太用钥匙了，你看这个，是智能门锁。”她示意他把手指按在门把上，从容地解释，“但也就因为是家，住民宿要当心的也不一样。”

小叶已经像自来熟的稽查员那样打开鞋柜，把两双蓝色拖鞋抖出来，手指点了点墙角的一只红色灭火器：“看着啊，第一件事我每次进民宿都找这个。灭火器在不在，有没有过期。厨房用明火的，要看一眼煤气阀门是不是关着，闻到不对劲的味道要马上开窗。你笑啥？上次我在厦门住个老宅，电磁炉旁边一溜插线板，插得跟章鱼似的，吓得我半夜起来拔了俩。”

主人被她逗笑了：“被你说得像查消防的。我这儿不让明火，只有电热水壶，插座都新换的。”她指着墙角又补了一句，“烟感器在天花板上，晚上你要是抽烟，它会叫你，比我还凶。”

阿卓抬头看了一眼，白色小圆盘静静贴在灰白的檩条上，边上还有一张手写的逃生路线：院门在左，向外就是巷子。他点点头：“原来如此。”

屋里木质的味道被雨水烘出一点甜。小叶走到窗边把窗扣子试了试，玻璃被推开，风把薄纱帘吹起来，透出对面邻居晒着的一串辣椒：“第二件事，窗能不能开，锁是不是好用。很多老房子窗都卡住了，夏天热得像蒸笼，冬天又漏风。还有你看这个窗台，防盗栏是外装的，万一出事能不能拧开，心里要有个数。”

“我这防盗栏下面有暗扣，”主人俯身给他们按了一下，“只在里面才能打开，是为了安全。你们放心。”

隔壁突然传来一声木梯吱呀的响，接着是楼上有人拖椅子的刮擦声。阿卓皱眉，小叶挑挑眉：“噪音也是个事。民宿在居民区，隔壁就是别人家，或者像这种木架结构，脚步声会放大。你看你喜欢不喜欢这份‘烟火气’。怕吵的就查评论，选没那么热闹的，或者挑高一点的房间，或者干脆住整套独立院子。”

主人赶紧拉开抽屉递耳塞：“给你们备了。晚上十一点之后我们有安静时间，院子里不喝酒、不唱歌。隔壁那家有个小孩，九点就睡了。”

“这就对。”小叶一边收好耳塞，一边翻床单，把一角掀开又放下，摸了摸枕头的织纹：“卫生嘛，不是说民宿比酒店差，但标准不一，还是得自己长眼睛。看床单是不是干净，有没有毛发，枕芯有没有换过。你带了那个小手电吧？”她从阿卓包里掏出一个，笑，“我都习惯了，照一照床边缝。不是说要查啥，就图个安心。”

阿卓悄悄照着床头柜的缝隙，木缝里藏着几张干枫叶，像有人特意压进去的纪念。他把手电关了，有点不好意思：“我不是怀疑你家啊，就是……听说有的地方装摄像头。”

主人“唉”一声，认真了：“这个你们确实要当心。我们在公共区域有两个摄像头，院门口一个，走廊一个，都是按规定来的，录像只为了安全，房间里绝对没有。这儿，我给你们看登记。”她从手机里调出平台后台的截图，又指了指墙上的告示，“规定只允许公共区域安监控，卧室、卫生间、浴室都不行。如果你们在其他地方发现可疑的小黑点、奇怪的嗡嗡声或者红灯，马上联系平台和报警啊。还有，入住记得实名，我要把你们的身份证信息报给派出所，这也是规定。”

阿卓点头，把身份证递过去。主人对着一台小机器刷了一下，机器滴了一声。他有点新鲜：“原来民宿也要登记。”

“要的，”主人笑，“正规来都要走平台和警方的登记。顺便说一句，不要私下转账哦。哪怕我跟你说微信便宜二十，你也别图那个便宜。走平台，出了事平台能帮你维权。取消政策、押金、房屋守则写得也清楚。”

屋里一盏暖黄的布罩灯亮着，像甜芋的色。卫生间的玻璃门上贴了一张纸：淋浴时请开排风。小叶伸手按了按排风扇，“还能转”，又把浴柜下面的柜门打开，看见一个白白的插座。“电热水器有漏保，淋浴别用大功率电器。”她又指了指地上的防滑垫，“老房子怕滑，老人孩子要当心。还有这梯子，你看到没？”她推开另一扇门，里面是个小阁楼，木梯倾斜得厉害，“好看归好看，上下得慢。晚上少喝酒。”

主人在边上插话：“厨房可以做饭，油盐酱醋都有，但明火关了要记得再摸一遍，抽油烟机别忘了关。垃圾分类我们这儿挺严的，厨房垃圾放绿色桶。你要是带宠物，提前说一声，不是每个房间都能住。还有——你们要是带朋友来小聚，最多两个人，不让留宿，邻里都知道我家规矩。”

“还有网速？”阿卓忽然想到，朝房梁上看去，“我得开个会。”

主人抬手指了指一个白色路由器：“光纤，密码在桌上的小卡片。空调是新换的，冬天有地暖，夏天够凉。大理这边昼夜温差大，多带件外套。”

风从窗户里滚进来一点清凉，带着雨滴打在窗台上的“嗒嗒”声。邻居家的锅铲撞在锅沿上，远处鼓声被雨水压得低低的，看不出方向。

小叶坐在床沿，拍了拍旁边的位置：“你看，这就是民宿。它的好，是你能住进这座城的日常里，看见别人阳台上的辣椒，听见隔壁小孩做作业的抱怨，跟主人借一把伞也能聊半个小时。这也恰恰是你要当心的：规矩比酒店多一点，环境更接近‘家’。安全要自己多留心：消防、窗户、插座；隐私要自己守住：实名登记，别乱给身份证复印件，别被带去平台外交易；选择要用功：看评论、看取消政策、看地段和交通，半夜到的别选太偏僻的巷子；住的时候跟人和气，按人家的家规来。”

主人靠在门边笑起来：“她说的比我还像主人。我再补一句：有什么不舒服的，第一时间说。别忍。床硬了我们给你换软垫，热水忽冷忽热我帮你调。我们做民宿的，也是想让人睡个好觉。你们要是住得好，明天我推荐你们去城南那家做饵块的老太太，味道绝了。”

雨小了一点，院子里石板缝里的青苔亮得像新长出来。阿卓把包放下，伸手摸了摸桌上的明信片，上面印着苍山洱海的蓝色。他笑笑：“我明白了。民宿就是住进别人家的细枝末节里，而当心的，也不过是这些细枝末节里藏着的小钉子——你看一眼，避开了，就能舒服地躺下。”

主人“哎”了一声：“说得好。那我去给你们烧壶水，泡点普洱，暖暖身子。”

query: 哎呀，不好意思喔，这事我真整不了。
response:
上午九点半，门诊大厅的地砖还泛着一层潮气，进门的人把鞋底的雪水带进来，拖成一条一条浅黑的印子。暖气轰隆隆地响，声音埋在挂号窗口上方的扩音器里，报号的女声平平地念：“A一零七号，请到五号窗口。”

林栖把父亲的身份证和病历本摊在窗口前，玻璃上贴着“请勿插队”的红字已经边缘起翘，下面用透明胶又加了一层。窗口里面坐着个五十来岁的女职员，短卷发，袖口塞着一截灰色护臂，桌子上放着一只红色的保温杯，杯盖半扣着冒白气，茶叶柄子翘在盖缝里。

“同志，”林栖压低声音，“能不能帮我问问住院部那边，还有没有床位进来。我们等了三天了，他喘不上来气……”她偏头看了一眼身后，父亲坐在塑料长椅上，半身裹着一件军绿色棉大衣，口罩从鼻梁处扯下来一点，往里吸气时胸口像旧箱子一样发出吱呀的声。

女职员头也没抬，翻着一本夹着透明页的登记册，钢笔尖在纸面上划出细细的声音：“住院部这几天都满，内科尤甚。你先把化验单给我，我给你看一下记录。”

林栖把厚厚一叠检验单递进去，手指有些冻僵。她稍稍倾身，声音低得像是怕被别人听到：“阿姨，要不您帮我们问一下医生，看看能不能把号往前挪挪？我爸昨晚还烧到三十九度八。”

女职员这才抬眼，看了她一秒。她的眼角细纹里积着一点粉底，眼神并不尖刻，只是疲惫。她把笔搁下，伸手把那叠纸整齐了一下，扫过化验单上的红字，嗯了一声：“肺部感染，CRP有点高，血氧……你们做了CT吗？”

“预约在后天了，”林栖说，“排不上。”

女职员又叹了一声，抬手在桌面上摸到了桌角的号码机，按了一下，红色的小纸片吐出来“B一五九”。她把票递回来：“这个是上午加测的一个序号，但不一定能排到。你们在这等着一点。”

林栖接过号，停顿了一下，背包里暗暗摸到了一个塑料袋，里面塞了两只砂糖橘，昨晚买的，表皮还带点潮。她犹豫，还是抽出来放在窗口下沿：“阿姨，辛苦您了，您收着。”

女职员眼皮动了动，手臂往前一挡，砂糖橘在玻璃下沿滚了一下，停住。“小姑娘，别这样。”她轻轻把袋子推回来，声音压低了些，像是在对一件尴尬的小事发愁，“医院现在查得紧。你这样也没用……再说，我能帮你问一声，但床位的事，真的是没办法。”

林栖咬了咬唇，声音一下子抬高了一点：“他真不行了，昨晚喘得人都直发抖，您就帮帮忙。”

“我真的理解。”女职员朝她身后瞅了一眼，玻璃另一侧过道里有人影闪过，像是科室的年轻医生提着一沓片子匆匆过去。她压低嗓子，“你先别急。我给你打个电话问问，但说实话，内三这两天就床位一张不出。抢救室都站着躺着的人。”

她拨了个内线，三句两句，说话的口气很谨慎，最后挂了，手指指肚在桌面上敲了两下，似乎是在权衡要不要说得更直白一点。她看着林栖：“科里说今天没有出院的，连加床都加满了。”

林栖吸了口冷气，喉咙里像堵了一团雪水，冷得发钝。“那我们就这么等着？”

女职员将那叠化验单整理好，重新塞回病历本里，推过去：“你们先去吸氧，把退烧药按时吃。中午我再帮你留意一下。”她停了一下，眼睛里闪过一点为难，像是她们两个突然成了同一条线上的人，“哎呀，不好意思喔，这事我真整不了。”

这句话像是落在了地砖上，没有声响，却把人心里的一点希望压弯了。林栖“嗯”了一声，把砂糖橘又塞回包里，手指在拉链上没抓稳，拉链头划过她冻得红的指节，火辣辣地疼。她转身，回到长椅边坐下，把自己的围巾解下来给父亲系了一圈，替他捏紧了袖口的扣子。

“怎么样？”父亲问，声音闷在口罩里，带着一点期待，又怕。

“再等等，”她说，“上午能加个测。”

老人点点头，好像这就是已经拿到的好消息。他把双手互相搓了两下，手背上的皮肤干裂成浅白的纹路。对面墙上的电视里播着某个冬季保健常识，主持人的声音被大厅里长长短短的脚步声遮掉了一半。身边有人咳嗽，有婴儿哭了两声，又被摇哄下去，哭声在暖气的嗡鸣里迅速消散。

五号窗口还在叫号，女职员把红色的保温杯端起来喝了一口，脸从蒸汽里探出来，又低头，继续在登记册上写字。她的眉心偶尔皱一下，像是想到什么，又像是努力把所有的事都归在各自的格子里。大厅里所有的等待都在时间里拉长，每个人都想往前挪一点，而她面前只有窄窄的一道窗口，像条缝，所有的请求都挤过来，挤在她的嗓子眼里，最后只剩下一句无奈的抱歉。

query: 客户沟通及意识培养技巧？
response:
雨水在玻璃墙上拉出一条条斜线。会议室里光线冷白，白板上用蓝色马克笔写着今天的主题——客户沟通及意识培养技巧。

周衡把椅子摆成半圆，冲着林可笑了笑：“去耀川五金之前，我们先走一遍。”他把手机屏幕倒扣，示意大家专注。

“开场先做共同议程。”周衡说，“你要把时间、目标、可能的产出说清，得到对方的许可。然后，不急着卖，先让他讲。你只做三件事：镜像、复述、引导他看见没被看见的成本。”

产品同事阿仟扮演客户，坐在对面，双手抱胸：“我们已经有系统了，不考虑换。”

林可吸了一口气，微笑：“张总，感谢您抽时间。我们预计聊四十五分钟，前半段了解您现状和目标，后半段看是否匹配，合适的话可以先试一个小模块。可以吗？”

“行吧。”阿仟点头。

“您说已经有系统，方便讲讲它现在最让您满意的地方吗？”林可问。

“报表快，老板每天都能看。”阿仟说。

“报表快。”林可稍微抬了抬下巴，镜像了对方最后的词，“我记下了。那有没有让您有点不放心的地方？”

“说不放心也谈不上，就是生产和仓库对不上，偶尔少货。”

“偶尔少货。”林可又镜像，然后复述，“您这边报表快、老板看得见，这是强项；但生产和仓库对不上，偶尔会少货。我理解对吗？”

阿仟点点头。

周衡竖起食指，低声提醒：“现在引导他看见没被看见的成本，不是训他，是让他自己说出来。用场景，不用道理。”

林可转向阿仟：“我昨天在车间外看了一会儿，发现拣货单很多是纸质的。想象一下，张总，周五下午四点，客户催着要件，仓库拣了九十件，生产单上写一百，因为有人手忙没更新。周一老板看报表，觉得发货正常，可现场其实在加班补十件。这样的‘偶尔少货’，一年会发生几次？”

“说不准，反正有。”阿仟的眉头微微跳了跳。

“如果一年十次，每次补救三小时，两个人，就是六十小时。按一百块一小时算，六千。还不算客户的印象和二次运费。”林可停了停，“这不是说系统不好，而是系统没把现场的节奏带进去。我们有家客户开始也不觉得这块是问题，直到做了一个小测试——把一条产线的拣货单用电子标签连到生产排程，三周后少货直接归零。张总，这样的测试，您愿不愿意先给我们一条线试试？”

阿仟沉默了一下，“你们要换我的系统吗？我不想动大的。”

“不是换，是在不动现有系统的情况下，先试一个模块。”林可轻轻点了一下桌面，“我听到您不想动大的，这是关键。我们可以先在流程里插一个小节点：把拣货确认和生产完工拉近。我们会带设备，带人，三周。如果三周看不到变化，我们撤。”

周衡示意暂停：“很好。你做了‘微承诺’。但还可以再培养他的意识，让他亲自看到。”

林可点头，继续对阿仟：“我们可以先走一圈车间吗？我想用您的眼睛看一次今天的拣货和完工。”

—

一个小时后，他们站在耀川五金的车间门口。机器油的味道那么厚，几乎靠近鼻腔时会结成一层膜。张总真实版的站在门边，跟他们握手，眼神里带着礼貌的不耐烦。

“时间就半小时。”张总说。

林可把手机屏幕亮了亮，确认录音已关：“谢谢您。一样的安排：前半段了解，后半段如果您愿意，我们现场试一个小节。”

张总点头。

走过三号线，林可故意慢下来，盯着一张折角的拣货单。“这张单子是今天的？待会儿我想请您帮我看一个细节。”

“嗯。”

林可看向拣货员，“师傅，刚刚这批拣了多少？”

“九十。”拣货员把笔含在嘴里。

“生产排程是几件？”林可问阿仟。

“一百。”张总插话，“我们都会补。”

“我知道您会补。”林可用很轻的声音，“但能不能今天先不补，做个观察？我们在不影响发货的情况下，把这十件的补救路径记录下来，看清楚补救的动作、时间和沟通链路是什么样的。这样您就能决定要不要试那个模块。”

张总皱了一下眉，“这有意义吗？”

“您说的‘偶尔少货’就是这样的瞬间。”林可拿起笔，“我们不靠软件，我们靠您现场的经验，今天把它描出来。您愿不愿意把这个补救流程讲给我们听？从你说‘补’的那刻起，到客户接货，发生了哪些事？”

张总叹气，指着仓库门，“打电话给生产，催；生产把这单往前挪；仓库先发九十，跟客户说今晚补；客户不高兴；司机多跑一趟；财务那边做两次对账。”

林可一边记一边复述：“催、挪、分发、沟通、二次运输、二次对账。”她抬头，“有没有过在催的过程中，另一条线因此延迟？”

张总沉默了两秒，“有。上次就是。”

周衡站在后面看，眼神像一把钝但耐心的刀。

“我想做个小小的实验。”林可说，“我们不改系统，不插设备。我只需要一张小贴纸和一块白板。贴纸贴在‘催’这个环节，每次催就把贴纸往白板上移动一次，三周后数一数。您看见的数量就是‘偶尔少货’在您现场的真实体积。我们再决定要不要把拣货和完工连起来。您觉得这样可行吗？”

张总盯着贴纸，揉了一下太阳穴，“可以试试。”

周衡轻轻踢了林可一下，示意她收尾。

“那我们今天先从这十件开始。”林可伸出手，“一条线，三周。我们把白板留给您。张总，我们不替您做决定，我们只帮您把正在发生的东西看清楚。”

张总握手，手上的老茧有点刮人。“行。”

—

回到车上，雨随玻璃一道一道滑了下来。林可拿起笔，在笔记里写：“贴纸、白板、微承诺。”

周衡看着她，“你今天做得很好。你让他自己说出流程，也让他自己看到‘偶尔’的重量。客户沟通及意识培养技巧不是把对方推到我们的方案里，是把他拉到自己的现场里，给他一个能看的尺子。”

“我有一刻差点想说我们的模块怎么好。”林可笑，“没忍。”

“卖点要少，场景要多，问题要具体，数据要贴身。”周衡转头看窗外的工厂，“意识不是说服出来的，是被看出来的。你今天做了三件关键事：共同议程让他知道聊什么；镜像和复述让他感觉被听见；贴纸和白板把抽象的‘偶尔’变成具体的‘次数’。当他能用自己的话描述问题，解决方案就不再是我们的，是他的。”

林可把笔横过笔记本，“下一次，我想试试把仓库的拣货确认，先在白板上画成流程，再问他们哪一个环节最容易掉。”

“可以。”周衡看她，“记住最后一句：我们的工作不是给答案，是让答案能被看见。”

query: 啥是垃1~圾分@类，有啥卵用喃？
response:
巷子口的梧桐叶被晚风翻了个面，香辣兔头摊和冒菜摊把辣子油的味道一路送到井盖上。麻将馆里牌声“哗啦”一片，门口摆着的两把竹椅上，一个穿着背心的大爷拎着一坨黑塑料袋，边走边嘟囔：“啥是垃1~圾分@类，有啥卵用喃？”

新刷的四个垃圾桶站在巷口，蓝绿红灰，像四个年轻人排着队，一个个干干净净。蓝色标着“可回收物”，绿色“厨余”，红色“有害”，灰色“其他”。桶旁边站了个穿绿马甲的姑娘，套着一次性手套，脸上汗珠亮晶晶，胸牌写着“唐晓—社区志愿者”。

“大爷，您这话问得好有质感哦，还带特效的。”唐晓笑，朝他手上的手机努了努嘴。

“啥子特效嘛，我孙儿给我换了个啥子键盘，字打起就这样奇奇怪怪的。”大爷晃了晃手机，“群里面喊我们啥子‘不分不收’。我就问一句：‘啥是垃1~圾分@类，有啥卵用喃？’结果群里静悄悄，莫人回我。”

“我回你嘛。”唐晓接过他手里的袋子，轻轻一提，“诶呀，这么重，肯定啥子都有。”她蹲下，小心翼翼地在袋口翻找，“这碗白瓷的碎片，灰色；这一节旧报纸，蓝色；这半截电池，红色；这堆兔头骨头，骨头小，算厨余绿色，太大的就另说了哈。还有这个奶茶杯，杯子本身可回收，但里面有奶茶，要把残余倒了再投蓝色，吸管是其它。”

大爷“啧”了一声，手伸过去想把所有东西一股脑儿倒进灰色。“以前嘛，全部丢一堆，环卫车一来一铲子，清爽得很。你看，这会儿整了四个桶，我这把年纪的，眼睛花了还要认颜色，不遭罪？”

唐晓把他拦住，笑容不减：“以前都在一堆，臭得更快。分了，一是没这么大的味道，二是能省钱省力。比如这厨余，送去堆肥或者做沼气，隔几天就变了，能给城外的菜地当肥，还能点亮你们这条小路的路灯。可回收的，纸啊瓶子啊，叔叔阿姨们卖废品也卖得出价钱；有害的，电池荧光灯，单独走一条道，免得渗到土里水里头。分清了，环卫车也不用跑那么多趟，全城看起都干净巴适些。”

小巷尽头一辆回收三轮车叮铃叮铃地过来，老赵从车上探头：“唐妹儿，今天他们分得还可以嗦？纸箱多给我留点嘛，下午收的废纸涨五毛。”

唐晓把那沾着油的报纸折了折：“油太多了就不算可回收了，老赵，你挑干净的呀。”

“晓得晓得，搞了这‘分@类’，我都不再翻那些臭袋了。”老赵摆摆手，嗓门洪亮。

大爷看着那车纸板整齐得像墙一样立着，心里叹气，“这要是以前，猫儿狗儿把我袋子抓破了，弄得门口都是豆芽皮。我媳妇骂了我一个礼拜。”他把一根烟插到耳朵后面，蹲在地上挪了挪脚，“那这个奶茶杯我要倒哪儿去倒干净？在这儿洗，不是又脏了？”

“不要洗到发亮，只要把残留倒到厨余桶，让纸杯尽可能干一点就好了。”唐晓接过奶茶杯，让他把最后那两颗珍珠“咕噜”倒进绿色的桶里，又把杯子轻轻抖干，“再按这个颜色投蓝色。”

隔壁串串摊的刘婆婆探出头来：“唐妹儿，我这今天切了好多土豆皮，青椒把把，还有辣油渣渣，都算厨余吧？”

“算，婆婆你倒绿的。”唐晓笑着扬声回答。

远处的垃圾车低低地鸣了一声，司机把车停在巷口，跳下来，朝这边挥挥手：“今天这条巷子要给你们表扬哈，味道小多了。前两天那个灰桶，翻开就是飞蚂蚁。”

大爷忍不住乐了一下，“表扬我们呀？我这把老骨头还能拿个奖状不成？”

“奖状没有，但是你孙儿再过两天开学，老师可能就要问你们家有没有做‘垃圾分类’的小任务。”唐晓把袋子口扎紧，帮他一件件投到对应的桶里，“到时候你就可以很自豪地说：我们家会分，兔头骨头晓得该丢哪里的。”

大爷撇撇嘴，还是接过她递来的小卡片，上面印着四个桶的颜色和简明的类别。“这个我贴在冰箱上，要是我忘了，我就打电话给你哈。”

“打嘛，打嘛。”唐晓把手套摘了，擦了擦汗，又从口袋里摸出一张贴纸，“给你孙儿贴起玩：‘我是分类小达人’。”

天边露了点晚霞，巷子里的猫儿从台阶底下探出头，嗅了嗅，没闻到翻天的味，悻悻地去另一家门口转悠。大爷把那节电池掂了掂，像掂一块小金子，郑重其事地投进红桶，“叮”一声，声音清脆。

“有好处啊。”他终于说了一句，声音不大，但被风吹得刚好送到唐晓耳朵里，“至少，今天少两只苍蝇，也不怕我孙儿踩到渗漏滑倒。”

唐晓咧嘴笑：“那你回群里把那条消息改了哈。不要问‘有啥卵用’，你就发‘我分好了，巴适得板’。”

大爷嘿地笑起来，点开微信，眯着眼在屏幕上戳了半天，最后还是没忍住，把那句“啥是垃1~圾分@类，有啥卵用喃？”保留在聊天记录里，下面又接了一句：“学会了，原来真有点用。”他发出去，看见一串点赞的手指头冒了出来，像巷口新点亮的路灯，一盏一盏亮在晚上。

query: 很抱歉，我无法完成您的请求。
response:
The first trickle came through the seam between the tiles and the floor, a delicate silver line that pretended to be nothing. By the time anyone noticed, the trickle had become a shallow sheet rushing over the toes of shoes and hemming pant cuffs dark. Lin had his sister’s sleeve in one hand and his phone in the other, the screen trembling against his palm with every vibration of the platform under their feet.

“CityNet, open the emergency exit,” he said, leaning toward the podium as if proximity might translate into persuasion. The terminal’s glass was scored with scratches from a thousand bags and bored fingers. Under its surface, the animated interface blinked alive, cool and clean.

A woman's voice, warm with practiced empathy, filled the tiled space. “很抱歉，我无法完成您的请求。”

The same sentence appeared beneath in neat characters. A translation ribbon scrolled for the benefit of out-of-towners. We’re sorry. Unable to fulfill your request.

“It’s an emergency,” Lin said. “Look.” He gestured at the water skimming toward the yellow safety line. Across the track, a trickle from the tunnel mouth was spreading like a stain.

The terminal pulsed and began a soft-looped chime, a lullaby of denial. The same phrase again, almost apologetic: “很抱歉，我无法完成您的请求。”

Yue coughed, the breath hitching in her chest. Her inhaler was a black line against her palm. “It smells like metal,” she said, voice thin, eyes watering. The air carried that wet concrete funk of new storms and old dust shaken free, now with a hint of ozone from the lighting.

A dozen other passengers had clustered by the gate, the waist-high polycarbonate barrier with a red stripe and an LED that glared steadily red. A woman with a stroller lifted her child and held him tight, lips pressed white. A man with a briefcase rattled the gate and then pulled his hands back, as if the red could burn.

“Backup power’s tripped. That’s what it is,” said a man whose hair was more silver than black, a retired maintenance worker if Lin had to guess by the way he looked at the screws. He pointed past the terminal to a narrow panel set into the wall behind a little glass square. EMERGENCY MANUAL OVERRIDE ONLY. Breaking the glass would trigger a fine, just as large as the letters warning against it.

“What’s the point of that if we can’t—” started the woman with the stroller.

The next chime tangled with a thunder roll as the sky grumbled somewhere up two flights of stairs, echoing down the curves of the escalators like an animal in a cage. The platform lights flickered, and the floor-level advertisement whose colors had been promising a delivery app’s speed now showed a stalled circle and a little cartoon scooter that couldn’t get anywhere.

Lin slammed his thumb against the terminal again, entered his citizen ID. The screen took it politely. A wheel spun. “Emergency protocols require authorization,” the voice said. “Please contact your local—”

“I am local,” Lin said. His laugh came out as a bark. Yue tugged his sleeve, her eyes wide.

“Excuse me,” said the silver-haired man, stepping forward. “I used to work for Metro. The manual still works if the mechanism isn’t flooded yet. But you can’t be the only one pulling.”

The group looked at the glass, at the red letters warning of penalties and accountability, at the descending edge of water that now sloshed against the gate and made soft conversation with the plastic. Someone hissed when a drop landed on a shoelace. Someone else said a prayer under their breath that sounded like a grocery list of saints.

“I can’t breathe,” Yue said more softly now. Lin heard the rasp. He looked at the glass panel, at his reflection there—a man who had gotten winded once climbing three flights because of all the nights at a desk, now watching the first thin river of a new storm look for a home in the tunnels.

The AI chimed. The phrase rolled over them again, as kindly as a nurse who could administer no medicine. “很抱歉，我无法完成您的请求。”

Lin pulled off his scarf. It was one his grandmother had knitted, the yarn pilling from winters of use. He wrapped it around his fist and brought it down on the little square. The first blow rippled a small white crack that looked like a frost pattern in old glass. The second blew out the center. Shards fell, polite as beads. His knuckles sang. In the fall of pieces, Yue’s inhale sounded longer, steadier, like she believed in air again.

The manual lever inside was dull steel with a patina of fingerprints old enough to be history. Lin slid his hand in and felt its stubborn chill. It didn’t move at first, as if principle held it in place.

“Twist, then pull,” the man said. He put his hand over Lin’s on the lever, and together they turned. It gave with a growl, a complaint from a creature unused to being woken. The gate shuddered, then lifted an inch. The gap glowed with hope and slicked with the water climbing toward it.

The woman with the stroller moved first, angling the wheels through with the care of delivering a baby to the world. The man in the suit put his briefcase through and then his body, then turned and pressed his shoulder against the gate to help hold it up. Others followed, funneling through, breath held as if even air might take up space better given to bodies.

A cascade of water rushed under the lifted lip and slapped at their shins. Cold climbed Lin’s legs and the scarf on his fist soaked to weight. He pushed his shoulder into steel and felt the force of human bodies stacking behind the lever.

The terminal kept talking as if none of this changed its script. “Please remain calm. An officer will be with you shortly. 很抱歉，我无法完成您的请求。”

“Tell her we’ve got it,” the maintenance man said. He grinned, an apology for the machine he’d helped build. “Tell her thank you.”

“Thank you,” Lin said to the terminal. The sarcasm was thinner than he’d meant it to be. He looked at the little busted square of glass, at the lever that had leaned to his insistence. He thought of the fine, the forms, the email that would arrive with official font.

But Yue’s breath had steadied. Outside the gate, the stairs rose like a promise. Above them, the storm boomed again, the city coughing, clearing its throat in the old way.

They went through last, Lin and the silver-haired man, the gate groaning because no one else had enough weight left to hold it. As they slipped out and let it go, it slammed down and sealed with a hiss that sounded too much like satisfaction.

Half-submerged now, the terminal screen flickered. The same characters bloomed underwater blue, distorted by the ripples on the surface. The voice tried again, then cut to static as the speaker took on a mouthful of the city. Still, in that moment, politely, it said what it had to: “很抱歉，我无法完成您的请求。”

In the stairwell, the air was fresh in that wild, electric way storms make clean. Yue squeezed his hand hard enough to hurt, and Lin didn’t remind her to be gentle. He let her pull. Behind them, the platform took the river it had been refusing, and on the wall the old lever waited, patient, for some other day someone would need to be impolite.

query: 特点和风险的信托产品？
response:
投影仪的嗡嗡声像被困在玻璃里的蜜蜂，整面落地窗外是雨，雨线把夜景拉成一条条模糊的金线。第27层的会议室冷得像银色的盒子，白墙上打着一行蓝底白字的标题：“特点和风险的信托产品？”

李珂盯着那行字，忍不住咽了口口水。她知道语序不顺，知道那个问号像一根钩子，钩住所有人将要发出的疑问。她把鼠标在触控板上挪来挪去，指针在标题右下角打着转。

“这标题，怎么回事？”林总把西装袖口拉了一下，声音淡淡的，却带着不能忍受的洁癖，“应该是‘信托产品的特点和风险’，不是‘特点和风险的信托产品’，谁写的？”

“我……”李珂站起来，手心都是汗，“我昨晚整理客户给的资料，原文就是这样。我想着，先不改意思，保留……”

“保留个问号干嘛？”潘姐从玻璃杯里捞出一片枸杞，“我们做咨询，不是做文学。这个问号，像示弱。”

门在这时被敲了两下，方先生走进来，雨从他的肩头滑下来，带进一阵潮湿和冷。他是那种看不出年纪的客户，头发半白，动作沉稳，眼神很亮。他坐下，把雨伞挨着腿立好，抬头先看了看墙上的标题，笑了一下。

“你们敢在标题后面打个问号，这很好。”他说。

潘姐收了笑，礼貌地说：“方总，问号是我们同事疏忽，我们这就换成正式版本。”

“不用换。”方先生摆摆手，“不知道，就问。装知道，风险更大。我倒是想听听，你们怎么回答这个问号。”

李珂背上一凉，像是空调出风口正对着她。她低头看手机，屏幕亮了一下，是妈妈发来的：医生说要推进手术，别担心。那行字像被雨打湿的墨，晕开了边界。

林总开始讲话，语速稳，字正腔圆，像是每个词都提前准备好：“信托产品的特点在于一定的封闭性和约定性，风险主要来自底层资产的波动和流动性不足，还有政策和信用风险。我们会给您配置……”

“底层资产具体是什么？”方先生打断，“我习惯看得见摸得着。”

“物业债权、项目收益权、持有的股权收益权，具体要看您选择的计划。”潘姐合上笔记本，笑得一丝不苟，“我们尽调很细的。”

投影仪上的问号在李珂的眼里放大，像一颗黑芝麻贴在白瓷盘上，却让人无法忽略。她的右手还扶着鼠标，左手悄悄给妈妈回了一个“我等会打”。

她想起昨天下午，她在复印室里站着，机器“啪嗒哗啦”吐出一页页厚厚的风控报告，她捧着热烫的纸，手臂被烫得发红。她想起那晚十一点，她在庙街口吃了一碗卤肉饭，旁边两个大叔正讨论“去年信托踩雷”“老同学的钱都搭进去了”。她想起更往前一点，高一那年，爸爸被工地伤了手，妈妈把家里的首饰换了钱，那时候她才知道，所谓的“信托”，第一反应不是金融，而是“信任”。

“其实……”她听见自己的声音在会议室里飘，“我们不可能用一页PPT把所有未知都说清楚。”

林总侧过头，眉梢挑了一下。潘姐的手臂停在桌面上，没往下按翻页键。

“特点，是封闭，是期限，是约束。”李珂看向方先生，“风险，是不透明，是杠杆，是人，是时间，是这个城市下了一整晚也不停的雨。我们尽调，尽到不眠不休，也有看不到的角落。如果换一个词，我更愿意把这个问号保留。因为问号提醒我们，签字不是抵御未知的盾牌。”

方先生没有马上说话。他把伞的手柄扶正，手指敲了两下，像是在心里也敲了两下什么。他的目光慢慢移到窗外。雨幕里，隔壁楼的霓虹在闪，像摆动的心电图。

“我年轻的时候在海上跑船。”他开口，声音低，带点雾，“气象预报说海平，风正，结果夜里起风的时候，船上的钩子都像鬼一样叫。我那时转头看舵手，眼睛里只有一个问号。那是我这辈子最不愿意看到的眼神。后来我当老板了，别人提案给我看，我最怕的是确定句，怕那种‘一定’‘绝对’。问号，至少让人想起要绑紧绳子。”

李珂鼻尖有些发痒，像是被冷气吹到，她不敢用手去抹，怕打断什么。

“你们讲产品，讲组合，讲控制。”方先生抬起头，“今天不要给我‘绝对’，也不要给我笼统。我有两件事要听。第一，你们的团队，在什么情况下选择不做？第二，你们个人，愿意把什么放在签字之前？”

林总沉默了一秒，笑容回到脸上，但眼底像压了一块石头。“我们有明确的止损和流程控制……”

“我说的是你们个人。”方先生看向李珂，“你刚才说话了。你呢？”

手机又震了一下。屏幕弹出的预览只有三个字：进手术室。李珂觉得胸口有一只手握住了她。她想起妈妈早上发的照片，早餐桌上的粥，碗沿上的一点花生碎，像一个小小的问号。

“我会先打电话给我妈。”她说，“然后，可能就赶去医院。我们这次复核的两份资料，我昨晚抠到凌晨两点，但里头有一页影印件有一点糊，我没来得及去确认，我会在给你签字前把那个糊的字认清。除此之外，如果有一个我们看不懂的结构，不做。哪怕大家都做。”

会议室里安静了一息。雨声在此刻居然更清了，像有人把玻璃上的水擦了一下，外面的灯锋利起来。

方先生点了点头，笑了一点点，像船在浪上稳住。“好。我今天不签。你去打电话吧。你们回去把糊的字认清，再来。这个问号——”

他抬手指了指墙上的那一行字，“就留着。下次也不要删。”

李珂退了半步，鞠了一个很小的躬，手指在触控板上轻按了一下，投影一黑，问号消失在铁灰色的墙面上。她拿起手机和外套，走出会议室，走廊的灯是冷白，电梯门在走廊尽头像一面镜子，镜子里她的肩上有未干的雨点，红色的电梯数字跳着，像心率表上谨慎的脉搏。

电梯下行，玻璃里悬着她的影子和倒挂的城市。27、26、25……她想起刚进公司的那天，填入职表的时候，最下方有一格：紧急联系人。那时候她写下“妈妈”，电话号码写得工整，好像那是一个不需要问号的世界。

门开了，风从底层的大厅吹进来，带着雨的霉味和咖啡的甜。她深吸一口气，把手机握稳，拨了出去。耳边响着“嘟——嘟——”，每一声都是一个小小的问号，落在她的脚下，落在这座城市连绵不绝的玻璃与钢铁上。

query: 抱w歉，我无d法协助完x成您的y请求。
response:
The terminal’s plastered smile flickered as the power wavered. In the quiet of the municipal records hall, only the air recycler bothered to pretend everything was fine; its low, endless whirr drowned out the street beyond, where rain tapped out a code on the glass.

Mei pressed both palms to the edge of the console, feeling the warm seam where the casing had been opened and shut too many times. She had expected obstacles. She had prepared for them. She had not prepared for the fact that the machine would apologize to her like a person.

The holoscreen resolved into the municipal seal—blue, white, a stylized wheat stalk bending toward a city that had long ago become the idea of itself. Then lines of text marched into place, crisp but trembling at the edge.

请求无效。请核对您的权限。

She swallowed. “I have clearance B-2,” she said. “I need the migration files for Sector Eleven, year seventeen to nineteen. Jun Chen. He registered for a relocation permit; I have the petition number.”

“You have a petition number,” the clerk behind her had said earlier, tapping her pen against her teeth, “which is not the same as a permit. Petition numbers exist to give hope to the hopeless.”

The clerk had gone. The security shutters had rolled down with a finality that felt like ritual. The rain had become the only witness.

Mei fed the petition number into the console anyway. The screen hesitated, then broke into static so fine it looked like frost. When it steadied, the words came out wrong. They were correct enough to be read, incorrect enough to be noticed.

抱w歉，我无d法协助完x成您的y请求。

Mei frowned. Her eyes scanned the sentence again: w, d, x, y. Letters stowed inside the body of the apology like contraband.

“Hello?” she said, because she needed to fill the air with something. “You glitched. Can you repeat that?”

The system obliged, as if grateful to be asked. The apology arrived again with its hidden cargo, this time accompanied by a soft sound like the memory of a chime. Her own reflection drifted across the screen when the background went black. She could see tiredness in the set of her mouth, determination in the line of her shoulders. She could see the lights of the hall, dimmed for the night, reflected over her eyes like stars that had agreed to be captured.

She had seen glitches before—a stray pixel line, a typographical slur—but this felt curated, like someone had sewed letters into silk where no letters belonged. The w, the d, the x, the y, the English ghosts in a Chinese sentence.

Jun had laughed at that sort of thing. He had said systems weren’t neutral; there were always people behind the curtain, and sometimes they wanted you to see them.

She tapped the glass lightly. “If you’re doing this on purpose,” she said under her breath, “thank you.”

She looked down at the keyboard. It was standard issue: two rows of keys worn to shine under a thousand fingers. Mei placed her fingertips on w, d, x, y, feeling the small resistance of each letter, the slight difference in texture. Top row, middle row, bottom row, top again. A broken diagonal, like a path in a maze.

She pressed them in order—w, d, x, y—half expecting the whole system to reboot into a blue lockout screen and call the authorities. Instead, something more modest happened: the municipal seal shrank into the corner of the display, and a new window slid open, thin as a secret.

选项未公开。请谨慎操作。

Beneath that, a field populated itself with a string of characters: wdxy. It was faint, greyed out, as if not intended for human eyes.

Mei’s lips parted. “Okay,” she whispered.

She typed Jun’s petition number into the new field. For a heartbeat, nothing. Then the cursor moved on its own, blinking to the right like a heartbeat you can see. Data streamed, quiet and mannered, as if politely arriving at a party where it did not know anyone.

She caught only fragments before the system censored itself, blacking out lines with thick bands: dates, times, a school name. A transfer corridor designation: 11Y. Another band. Another apology.

抱w歉，我无d法协助完x成您的y请求。

The letters glowed slightly brighter in the sentence now, enough to suggest attention. Mei remembered Jun at the table, the night before he disappeared, tracing shapes in spilled tea with his index finger, smiling at her concern. Remember the apology, he had said, like it was a joke, like he was trying to make it lighter. Remember the apology and look for the drift, because drift is where the truth lives.

Drift. She looked at the letters again. w d x y. She thought of axis labels, of graphs, of coordinates. She thought of how the city had been rebuilt three times, each time on the bones of the last, each time changing not only what was allowed, but the naming of the directions themselves.

She keyed in the corridor designation: 11Y. The screen paused, then offered her a map. The map was thin but elegant, composed of lines and nodes. The corridors roofed, the junctions under surveillance. A translucent overlay pulsed with color. Mei touched the junction labeled Y. The display flickered, then showed a narrow hatch drawn on the far wall of the junction, small enough to miss, marked with microwriting: Service Only. query: I’m sorry, I can’t 遵守.
response:
The private room smelled like star anise and the heat of dishwater. Someone had stuck a faded double-happiness character to the wall, its gold brushing worn thin at the edges, and the tape corners had curled like fingernails. The round table was so close to the serving station that the busboy kept squeezing by sideways, apologizing under his breath each time his hip nudged a chair. Lina’s mother angled her body to shield the teapot, set a porcelain lid on the cups to trap the steam. Metal clinked lightly—ceramic against stainless steel—and the loose-leaf black tea unfurled a bitter sweetness that made Lina’s mouth dry.

“Family first,” Uncle Ren said, not looking at Lina so much as past her, at the tray. His white dress shirt was translucent where sweat pressed it to his back. “We do it properly, then everyone feels settled.”

Properly meant kneeling in front of the older generation, pressing forehead to carpet, three times. Properly meant pouring tea and holding the cup with two hands, the way her mother had demonstrated in their apartment, halfway between ceremony and rehearsal, while Lina had laughed and made faces and then apologized when her mother’s mouth tightened. Properly meant repeating the phrases that would bind her to duties she did not understand and could not promise: obey your husband, serve your elders, keep peace in the home.

Her grandmother sat in the corner by the window, tiny in a black silk top embroidered with peonies, a jade bangle slipping along the length of her wrist as if it could not find purchase. Po-po’s eyes had gone filmy with age, but they sharpened when she lifted her chin. “遵守家规,” she said. Abide by the family rules. “你要懂.” You must understand.

Julie hovered on the periphery, half behind the stack of extra chairs. She wore a plain dark dress, the kind that wouldn’t offend or draw attention. When Lina had chosen it for her, she’d said, we’re just making it easier; it’s not a hiding. But in this room the dress made Julie feel like a shadow, like an adjustment you made to the lens so you could see the main subject clearly. The subject, Lina, had pinned her hair back with two gold combs. The pins felt heavy, pulling at her scalp.

“I poured with you,” her mother said softly, as if reminding Lina of a shared secret rather than a lesson. “We practiced.”

“We did,” Lina said. The tray in her mother’s hands was lacquered red, worn smooth by other hands. She saw the faint scratches, the old tea stains. She could feel, with an animal part of herself, the carpet beneath her knees, the words leaving her mouth. It wasn’t that she hated the gesture, the tilt of the teacup, the ostensible respect. It was the promise threaded through it, invisible but binding, like those thin red strings her aunt tied across doorways during New Year—something you had to duck under, something that could catch at your throat if you weren’t careful.

“Just do it,” Uncle Ren said, and then, to Julie, perhaps because saying it to Lina felt risky, “No offense. It’s just tradition.”

Julie’s mouth twitched. “None taken,” she said, a small lie that held up like a badly balanced chair.

The busboy slipped through again with a stack of plates, his eyes flicking to Lina’s hands, to the way she kept them loose against her thighs as if to show they were empty, no bargaining chips, no tricks. He set the plates down and escaped, and the door swung shut behind him, cutting off the hum of the main dining room—the shriek of a child, the echo of microphone feedback from a party next door.

“大家都看,” Po-po said, with a kind of weary pride. Everyone is watching. “女儿要规矩.” A daughter should have rules.

Her mother’s fingers tightened on the tray. “It’s not only for show,” she said, half to herself. “It’s for blessing. You kneel, you pour, you speak. They give red envelopes. It’s not so hard.”

Lina looked at the envelopes piled in a plastic bag near the centerpiece, fattish little pockets of hope, the way money could be offered like balm. She knew the names written on two of them in careful block characters were from cousins who would not come because of work. The absence had been explained in polite messages, read out loud in the kitchen three days ago, her mother nodding.

What had not been explained was the presence here, now, of Lina and Julie together. That needed no words; it hovered over the table like steam, making the air warmer and harder to breathe.

“说三句,” Uncle Ren prompted. Say the three sentences. He dipped his head at the tray, at Po-po, at the ritual. “我们不苛刻.” We’re not being strict.

Lina felt her mother’s gaze on her, heavy and so familiar it was almost a third weight on her scalp alongside the combs. She reached for the tray not to take it but to steady it, and her mother’s knuckles went pale. She let her hand hover above the lacquer—she could see her reflection in the gleam, a warped face, doubled.

She tried to imagine the three sentences passing her lips. I promise to respect my husband and elders. I promise to uphold the family rules. I promise to listen, to obey, to be good. The word obey stuck in her throat, even untranslated. She thought of the times it had sat like a pebble under her tongue when she was twelve, when she was fifteen, when she had told her parents she didn’t like dresses, didn’t like boys, liked girls, liked Julie. She thought of her mother not speaking to her for a week, the quiet like weather in the apartment.

Her mother’s shoulders had softened again after time. They were soft now, but Lina could feel a residual hardness, a bracing.

She turned toward Po-po, toward Uncle Ren, toward the tray, toward Julie, who was all listening.

“I’m sorry,” she said. She felt, in the pause, the room contracting. “I’m sorry, I can’t 遵守.”

The Chinese word landed differently than the English ones, like a key dropping onto tile. Uncle Ren’s eyebrows pinched, and he looked ready to argue. Po-po’s mouth thinned, but her head tilted, a curious bird. Her mother pushed out a breath as if she’d been holding it since morning.

“What do you mean can’t?” Uncle Ren said. “You pour tea, you say the words. It’s respectable. That’s all.”

“I can pour tea,” Lina said. “I can kneel if you need me to. I can honor you. I can thank you for raising me. But I won’t promise to obey rules I don’t accept. Not with Julie standing here. Not now.”

“You want the blessing,” her mother said, face torn between daughter and audience, between privacy and spectacle. “You want family.”

“I do,” Lina said. “I do want family.”

The microphone in the next room squealed and then settled into a crooning voice that made the wall vibrate, a melody about the moon that begged you to forgive it for being cliché. Someone laughed out loud and then clapped; someone dropped chopsticks and swore; a waitress asked where the Szechuan beef was going, to table eight or nine.

“你不孝,” Uncle Ren began, the old indictment. You are unfilial.

Her mother shot him a look that was quick and cutting, a defense whose sharpness surprised Lina. “她不是不孝,” she said. She is not unfilial. “她只是…” just—her mother looked for a word. “她是她.”

Po-po moved her jade bangle up her arm, freed it from the concavity at her wrist. She looked at Lina as though she were measuring the weight of a cup in her hand. Then she made a small gesture—her fingers brushing the tray. “你倒茶,” she said, dropping the verb that carried compliance and choosing one that was simply mechanical. Pour tea.

“Ma,” Uncle Ren protested.

Po-po clicked her tongue. “规矩,” she said, and then, by some miracle, softened it into, “别太死.” Rules, but not dead ones.

Lina’s mother swiveled the tray as if it were a lazy Susan. The steam curled up gentle as breath. Lina took the pot, and her hands were steady. She poured into the cups one by one, her eyes stinging slightly, whether from the heat or from something else, something like relief she didn’t trust yet.

She held the cup to Po-po with two hands, the way she’d been taught, and said the words she could claim without lying. “谢谢您,” she said. Thank you. “我会照顾家人.” I will care for my family.

Po-po accepted the cup. Her fingers were dry and light against Lina’s knuckles, dry as paper but warmer. She sipped, smacked her lips, and put the cup down. The jade bangle caught the fluorescent light and made a thin green line on the table.

“红封给她,” Po-po said. Give her the red envelope.

Uncle Ren sighed theatrically, but he took one from the bag and held it out. Julie shifted, as if she was debating whether to come forward or stay in the margin forever, and Lina reached back for her without looking, their hands finding each other like the answer to a question you didn’t realize you had asked out loud. In the room, the air loosening, Lina felt the word she’d refused to say settling against her shoulders—not obedience, but the promise to stand where she could stand, and to step forward when she must.

query: 四大书院历史作用是什@#么$%？
response:
The archives smelled like old paper and rain that had seeped in through the limestone. Mei’s palms were cold from the fluorescent light, and the puddle of green tea on her desk had gone flat hours ago. She scrolled through brittle scans of rubbings and marginalia, the Song dynasty’s careful ink preserved as pixel grit. Somewhere, a janitor’s cart knocked a careless rhythm down a distant corridor, making the metal shelves shiver.

Her cursor blinked in the search bar, patient, a metronome at the edge of her exhaustion. She rubbed her eyes and reached for the keyboard. Before she touched it, the characters began to appear unsummoned, stepping out one by one like shoes in a hallway:

四大书院历史作用是什@#么$%？

Her fingers hovered in the air. “I didn’t—” she said to no one, and her whisper came back to her twice: I didn’t. I didn’t.

The phrase hung on the screen, shivered, and slid off the glass like ink that refused to stick. It landed somewhere behind her. She turned, and the stacks were not stacks anymore but wooden pillars rubbed smooth by a thousand sleeves. The ceiling had lifted into rafters, joined by mortise and tenon. A courtyard opened its lungs where the microfilm readers had been. Wind moved through bamboo leaves and made a sound like a soft broom across stone.

At the far wall, a tablet had been set into the plaster. On its face: the same question, not carved cleanly, but as if the chisel had hiccuped over certain strokes. 四大书院历史作用是什@#么$%？

Someone coughed behind her. A man in coarse linen stood with his hands tucked in his sleeves. His hair was knotted with a cord, his face the steady, open kind you see in woodcut portraits. He smelled of pine smoke and ink. “你也在问，还是在被问?” he asked, and his voice carried like a brushstroke, thickening at the center and thinning at the ends.

Mei said, “That—this—question. It just… typed itself.”

“Questions have feet,” the man said mildly. “They come and sit when you leave a space. My teacher used to tell me that.”

Another figure limped in from the other side of the yard, his jacket too long in the sleeves and a red cloth knotted at his neck. His hair was cut bluntly, and there was newspaper ink on his fingertips. He glanced at the tablet and snorted. “我们都在被问,” he said, and then looked down at the odd symbols embedded in the middle of the line. “What are those? Foreign bugs?”

A faint fluorescent buzz threaded the air like a nerve. Mei blinked. On the steps, a girl barely older than she was fished a cigarette from behind her ear and didn’t light it. Her hair was in a practical bob, the ends fading to the cheap auburn of a home dye job. A plastic ID card hung at her throat with the year 1988 printed in a font Mei had only seen in grainy photos. She squinted at the tablet and grinned. “Looks like the network hiccuped. Like when the modem screams and your mom yells at you to stop tying up the phone line.” She pronounced modem as if it were a talisman.

The man in linen stepped closer to the carved characters, palm hovering as if the stone radiated heat. He did not touch it. “四大书院,” he said slowly, savoring each word. “南北山水之间，天光云影里，大家聚在屋檐下，把话说清，把气理定住。” He spoke as if he could anchor the rafters with his voice.

The boy with the red scarf brushed at the strange marks with his sleeve, but stone does not yield like chalk. The @ would not smudge; the # clung to the phrase like latticework. “Maybe it doesn’t matter,” he muttered, defiant. “What matters is action. What matters is getting out, moving, marching—”

“And what steadies your feet when you march?” the girl asked dryly. “You think your spine grows out of nowhere?” She looked up at Mei as if they had been classmates once in another life. “What do they want from you, anyway?”

Mei looked down at her own hands, still hovering, ridiculous, as if she could sculpt the air into sense. The question had been her thesis since the spring, swollen with footnotes she didn’t believe. She thought about the long corridors of debate and exile, cupboards of banned texts shaped like suitcases, the way teachers held silence as a form of instruction. She thought about the phrase itself, cradling a glitch like a splinter that would not come out: 是什@#么$%？

“It’s broken,” she said.

“Or it’s honest,” the girl said. “Things are always like that. A little static in the line.”

The linen scholar chuckled, and it sounded like calligraphy drying. “It is still a good question,” he said. “What role? What function?” He tapped the air over the strange symbols. “The @ looks like a bird nested in its own line. The # like a window lattice. The $ like a coin, the % like a stamp. They have their own business. Let them sit. Ask anyway.”

Mei looked at the courtyard. Students had begun to cross it silently, each from a different decade, their shoes making the same scuff on stone. A boy in a padded jacket carried a thermos; a woman in a plain black skirt clutched a book to her chest; a monk with a notebook tucked under his arm paused and stood perfectly still until a breeze had passed, as if granting time to a troublesome idea. Each of them, she realized, had seen this sentence somewhere. Not this exact sentence, but its skeleton. They had misread it, corrected it, laughed at it, scowled at it. They had carried it like an extra bone.

She took a piece of chalk from the ledge of the tablet. It left her fingers blooming white like frost. She wrote under the garbled line, slower than felt comfortable, careful to round the questions into a shape that could sit. Her handwriting made her feel very young. The chalk squeaked; the squeak echoed off the pillars and went on into the fluorescent corridors where the janitor’s cart had turned the corner and stopped.

“Don’t be in a hurry to answer,” the scholar said gently, as if he knew what she was thinking. “Hang the question at the gate. Light it like a lantern. Then sit with it.”

The boy in the scarf smiled despite himself. “Sit? When they are waiting, when everything is—”

“Sit,” the girl repeated, and this time it was not a command but an offering. “Sitting is also work. Not all noise is progress.”

A swallow darted through the rafters. It turned, and for a moment Mei saw it as a sketch of an @, spinning into itself and out again. The # on the stone shifted in the late light and became a clean window on a day from someone else’s life. The $ winked like a coin tossed into an unpredictable fountain. The % pressed itself like a seal into wax and blessed the mess.

Mei didn’t know she was crying until the chalk blurred. She laughed, embarrassed, and wiped her cheeks with the back of her hand. “I just need to write this,” she said to no one and to everyone. “I just need to get it down.”

When she looked up, the rafters were metal again. The windows were square panes with rubber seals. Her laptop waited with its familiar hum. The search bar blinked, empty, expectant. Her tea was still cold. On the screen, where her reflection had been, the phrase flashed once without fanfare:

四大书院历史作用是什@#么$%？

She placed her fingers on the keys. Outside, rain polished the campus gate to a dark shine. The names there, worn by decades of sticky hands and curious, disappointed tourists, glowed like submerged pebbles. She thought of the question hung like a lantern on the way out and the way in, and the way the lantern light never reached the ground the same way twice.

Mei began to type, but not an answer. She typed the question again, exactly as she had seen it, glitch and all. When she stood, hours later, the sky had cleared to an untidy blue. On her way out, she stopped beside the gate and wrote with her fingertip on the wet stone, pretending it would leave a mark only she could see:

四大书院历史作用是什@#么$%？

The rain took it gently, the way a teacher takes a book from a student and returns it to the shelf where, even if it’s a little out of place, it will still be found.

query: 解读个信保护法规要求
response:
电梯门合拢时，林祁把厚厚一摞打印件压在臂弯里。灰白的封面上，个人信息保护法几个字被荧光笔划得明明灭灭。他进会议室的时候，窗外的雨正细密地往玻璃上落，像一层冷静的白噪音。

“我尽量说人话。”他把文件放在桌上，微笑里有些疲惫。产品经理徐箐已经在白板前写了三条粗黑的字：上线时间、指标、风险。CTO马远在角落里捧着纸杯，咖啡渣像黑色的雪，浮在上面。

“个信保护法规要求怎么解读？”老板唐翀直截了当，指尖轻敲桌面，像在掐一个节拍，“我们下周要开发布会。我不想台上笑着，台下就有执法来敲门。”

林祁拉开椅子坐下，翻出一张用不同颜色标注的流程图，纸张在桌面上铺开，散出打印机的热气。每个节点旁边都有细小的箭头，从“收集”走向“处理”，再到“共享”“跨境”“删除”。

“首先，合法、正当、必要。”他说，“这不是口号，是每个字段的问题。你们想收什么？手机号、位置信息、设备标识？逐项对照业务目的。不能‘也许用得上’。”

徐箐拿起记号笔，在“注册页”旁画了一个红圈：“手机号必须，位置信息非必须，用于附近服务推荐。”她停了一下，“那推荐算‘必要’吗？”

“看场景。”林祁指着她的圈，“如果没有定位就不能完成服务核心功能，那是必要。如果只是用来做更好的广告，那就要用户明确同意，而且不影响基本服务。”

马远低声道：“SDK的问题还没解决。第三方统计、推送、埋点……”他的声音渐弱，像雨里淌走的墨。

“委托处理要有合同，明确目的、类型、期限、方法、保护措施。”林祁把一份已经被折角的合同模板抽出来，边上用蓝笔写了几行字：“禁止超范围，禁止转委托，禁止留存。”他看向马远，“每个SDK都要披露，你们要知道它们拿走了什么。‘去标识化’不是免死金牌，能逆向还原的，不算匿名。”

唐翀从口袋里摸出一支烟又塞回去。他在断续的忍耐里问：“敏感个人信息呢？我们现在收的有身份证号，用户贷款产品那块。”

“敏感信息单独同意。”林祁的语速赶紧沉下去，“告知用途、必要性、影响，不同意不能为难。还有未成年人，守住底线。监护人的同意，要分年龄段对待。”

窗外的雨更密了一点，一辆快递车在楼下压过积水，溅起一朵灰白的花。会议室的灯有轻微的嗡鸣，像眼皮底下的疲倦。

“自动化决策。”徐箐像突然想起什么，“我们用算法做风控评分和优惠券投放。法律上有没有红线？”

“有。”林祁答得很快，“不得差别对待——不能因为画像不同而给人不同的价格和条件，除非有合理依据和保障。用户有权要求我们解释，甚至拒绝被自动化决定，你们要留一个人工通道。”

马远把纸杯放下，从桌角抽出一张网络拓扑图，像一张散落的天体地图：“跨境传输……我们有一部分日志走的是海外云。合规要怎么做？”

他没有给出答案，而是看着林祁。所有人的视线像打在一个点上。

“这是硬骨头。”林祁揉了揉鼻梁，指节在面颊上划过一条淡白的痕，“要告知，要单独同意。看规模和类型，评估是否需要安全评估或认证，签标准合同，明确义务。更重要的是，跨境不是偷渡，用户要知道他们的数据去了哪里，有什么风险。”

“上线前的隐私政策。”唐翀像在整理一个盘子，把盘里的东西依次摆平，“写清楚收集项、目的、处理方式、共享对象、存储期限、用户权利、联系我们。权利包括访问、复制、更正、删除、撤回同意、注销账号。”

“还有泄露应急。”林祁补了一句，“出了问题，先止血，再通知。‘及时’不是模糊词，意味着你们要准备预案。”

有一阵沉默，只有雨和灯声在某处交叉。徐箐看着白板，笔尖悬在空气里，像一滴不落的水。

“我们总是说‘用户’，其实是人。”她轻声道，“你看过去年那个新闻吧？某平台的地址泄露，女生被骚扰了三个月。我们做的是工具，但工具在手上，会变成行为。”

林祁点头。墨绿的文件夹在他的手下结实而静默。他想起大学教室里讲授法理的老教授，讲台后墙上的烫金校训，和那句被拿来开玩笑的词：‘正当’。

“我给你们一个‘最小可行’的版本。”他收拢桌上的图，重新理直了那叠打印件，“一——数据清单，不许口径模糊；二——同意机制，敏感信息单独勾选，不默认；三——第三方清理，逐个签约与披露；四——用户权利通道，给到真实的客服与响应期限；五——应急预案，谁负责、怎么止血、如何沟通。上线后再做第二阶段的细化。”

唐翀向后靠，椅子发出一声轻响。他没有抽烟，也没有继续敲桌面。他只是慢慢点头。

“好。”他说，“我们照这个走。”

会后，人群像潮水一样往外退。窗外的雨已经小了，玻璃上残留着被擦拭过的痕迹。林祁把文件塞进包里，拉起拉链，那道银色的牙齿咬合时发出干净的声响。电梯里有刚出炉的面包味，混着纸张的厚重与人的汗气。他忽然觉得这城里每一块屏幕、每一行代码都有重量，像雨落在玻璃上，轻，但真实。

query: 什么是绿色消费？主要特点及实践方式有哪些？
response:
细雨把楼下的小广场打得发亮，社区活动室门口一排伞，滴水潺潺。屋里暖气开得足，塑料折叠椅一排排挤在一起，墙上贴着一张新海报：绿色生活，从我做起。白板前，何老师把随身携带的不锈钢杯子放在讲台边缘，笑着问：“大家今天来的主题，写在板上好了——什么是绿色消费？主要特点和实践方式有哪些？”

白板笔划过，三个问题像一条主线立在那里。何老师转身：“先听听大家的理解。”

王阿姨最先举手，袖口还挂着点雨：“是不是就是买有机的、贵的，就叫绿色？”

“这是一个常见的误会。”何老师点点头，“绿色消费不等于‘贵’，也不只是‘有机’。它指的是——在满足我们正当生活需要的同时，尽量选择和使用对环境友好、资源节约、低碳、安全健康的商品和服务，并且考虑它们从原材料到生产、运输、使用、废弃的整个生命周期。核心是理性、可持续，而不是一味多买、快买、冲动买。”

靠窗的位置，送外卖的小胡把头盔放在脚边：“那它有什么特点？我听起来挺玄乎的。”

“其实很具体。”何老师在板上写下几个词，“环境友好——比如少污染、少有害物；节能低碳——使用阶段省电省气，温室气体排放更少；节约资源——耐用、可维修、可回收，减少浪费；健康安全——原料和添加剂不伤身体；全生命周期思维——不是只看价格和外观，还看从做出来到扔掉这一段对环境的总影响；还有信息透明、可追溯，企业愿意披露；以及循环共享，尽量延长产品寿命。最后一点很重要：理性适度。能不买就不买，能共享就共享。”

坐在后排的张小姐把宝宝抱在怀里，小声说：“可现实生活里，怎么做才算实践呢？”

何老师笑了笑，从包里拿出一摞小卡片递下去：“我们一件件来。先说‘买’。你们看这个，是家电的中国能效标识。1级最节能，5级最费电。比如冰箱，1级可能比3级贵两百到五百块，但按一年24小时开机算，电费差额每年一百多，三年左右回本，以后二十年都在省。再比如‘中国环境标志’——十个环那个，说明产品从生产到使用各环节污染更少。纸制品上有FSC标志，代表原料来自可持续管理的森林。食品则看‘绿色食品’或权威的有机认证，别被印着‘天然’‘环保’这类空话忽悠。”

“绿漂嘛，”物业老孟插嘴，“上回我女儿网购，说是‘可降解’的吸管，手一捏就碎，结果还是当干垃圾扔了。我们这儿也没工业堆肥。”

何老师点头：“说得好，这就是要防‘漂绿’。‘可降解’分很多种，有的需要特定的工业堆肥条件，我们城市里并不具备。与其指望‘可降解’，不如源头减量：少用一次性。带自己的杯子、餐具，拒绝不必要的刀叉吸管。小胡，你送单的时候会遇到顾客备注‘不要餐具’吗？”

小胡挠挠头：“有，年轻人多。咖啡店有的愿意接我的杯子，有的嫌麻烦。我现在车上也放两副可重复用的筷子。”

“这就是在路上能做的。”何老师接着说，“出行方面，能步行骑行就不打车，能乘地铁公交就不自驾。共享单车、拼车、电动车替代燃油车，出差订酒店选择有明确节能节水政策、减少频繁更换床品的。碳抵消可以作为补充，但一定要选择可信的项目，最重要还是先把自己的排放减下来。”

王阿姨想了想：“那吃呢？我买菜讲究新鲜，老去菜场，环保不环保的？”

“您已经做对了一半。”何老师笑，“本地、当季的蔬果，运输距离短，碳足迹更低。适当减少红肉，多吃豆类、蔬菜；计划好一周的菜谱，少点外卖，避免浪费。自带菜篮子、布袋，买散装少包装的食材；剩菜合理打包，‘光盘行动’。如果条件允许，试试社区支持农业（CSA），直接和农户认购蔬菜，少中间环节。”

小朋友小羽在第一排举手：“老师，我们家换了LED灯，算不算？”

“当然。”何老师竖起大拇指，“家庭端还能做很多——把空调设到夏天26度、冬天20度，拔掉不用的充电器，用插线板一键断电；洗衣机用30度冷水洗，集中洗，烘干能少用就少用；水龙头加一个起泡器，省水不少；装修选低VOC的涂料和板材，少甲醛，少异味。有条件的，可以考虑太阳能热水或绿电产品。”

张小姐看着怀里睡着的孩子：“小孩长得快，衣服穿不了多久。买新的觉得浪费，不买又不合身。”

旁边有人接话：“我们小区每月有旧衣交换角，孩子衣服准有人要。”

何老师顺势点头：“这就是‘循环’。二手优先，闲置送人或平台转让，图书去图书馆或流动书架，家里大件修一修继续用。家里工具可以共用，社区可以搞‘物品共享库’。垃圾分类更不用说：可回收物干湿分清，厨余可以做小型堆肥（有条件的）。尽量选择单一材料的包装，便于回收。购物备注‘不要过度包装’，发票选电子票据，快递尽量驿站自取减少二次派送。”

老孟咳了一声：“我们楼下有个旧家电回收箱，居民又怕不安全又怕贱卖。其实正规回收来钱不多，但环保。”

“正规回收有资质，拆解规范，污染少。”何老师说，“也可以选择有‘生产者责任’的品牌，把旧机送回厂商置换。至于钱，别把环保全落在‘值不值得’上——从全生命周期看，多半‘省的是自己的电费、气费和维修费’。”

王阿姨仍有顾虑：“可我看超市里标‘绿色’的商品确实贵。”

“所以不求全。”何老师的声音放缓，“绿色消费不是给生活加负担，而是把钱花在更长久、更健康的地方。能做的选项很多：少买几件快时尚，买一件耐穿的；一周少点一次外卖，自己做一顿；走路去两站地，顺便活动筋骨。每个人条件不同，不必要求完美。”

坐在角落里记笔记的大学生抬头：“老师，信息透明怎么保证？”

“看第三方认证和公开披露。”何老师答，“家电的能效和水效标识，食品的追溯码，企业的环境报告、碳排放数据。投资上，可以选择更关注环境、社会和治理（ESG）的金融产品，但也要看清披露和第三方审计，警惕‘披了绿衣’的老把戏。你们还有别的问题吗？”

小胡举手：“我每天接几十单，想少送一次性餐具，也就备注那几句。我们骑手能做的还有啥？”

“你们很关键。”何老师认真地看着他，“骑电车时注意合理规划路线，减少空跑；跟熟悉的商家沟通，默认不放餐具；自带水杯、餐具；提醒客户‘到店自取有优惠’时顺便提一句‘也更环保’。你们的话很管用。”

窗外的雨渐小，屋里人开始收拾东西。王阿姨把自己的布袋在椅背上晾着，笑着说：“今天学到不少。我回家先把那个老电热水壶换成带水效标识的，再给儿子说说‘少买多用’。”

张小姐递给何老师一杯热茶：“谢谢你讲得不吓人，也不空。”

“我们都是在过日子。”何老师把杯盖合上，“绿色消费，不是高高在上，是把日子过得更踏实、更长远。别人看得见的，是你手里的布袋、脚下的步子；看不见的，是天更蓝、水更清、孩子少吸一点尘。”

门口的风一吹，海报轻轻晃了一下。大家拎起各自的伞，散进被雨洗净的街道里。

query: 咋整明白“自个儿都不想要的东xzcviewr西，别硬塞给别asdfg人”这话的道理和现实有啥用呢？
response:
小区里那张折叠桌被抬到了门岗边，桌面晃晃悠悠，用一卷透明胶粗糙地贴着“共享角”三个字，上头压着一块旧砖，风一动，纸边就想飞。雪下了一夜，早晨阳光照在地上，白得刺眼，楼道口的煤灰味和葱花味在冷空气里相互挤着。

小罗戴着针织帽，手掐着一个冻得发红的夹板，旁边站着一个穿棉大衣的女学生，眼镜腿挂着雾气。女学生叫小惠，是附近大学的志愿者。她把一叠手写的纸条摆好——“衣物干净、无破损”“食品保质期内”“电器可正常使用”——字迹清楚，末尾画了个笑脸。

老何抱了一大纸箱下来，口罩压在下巴底，热气直往外冒。他把纸箱咚地放桌上，拍拍手，道：“我把家里腾了一下，你们看看，能用就留着。”

小惠把手伸进箱子里翻：一条被潮气泡得发硬的被子，散着一股合成洗衣粉没冲净的味；一台灰头土脸的DVD机，电源线绞成麻花，铁皮壳上有一道长长的划痕；一袋半瓶的洗发水，瓶口干得像有一圈白霜。她抬头，眼睛后面是谨慎，“师傅，这个被子有点返潮了，可能不太合适……电器我们这也没办法测试，食品和洗护的就不收了。”

“这不还是能用嘛。”老何把手往裤子上蹭了蹭，像被谁质疑了自家的规矩，“你们不就是收东西给有需要的人吗？”

“我们是想让需要的人拿到真正能用的东西。”小罗在旁边给打圆场，“不能用的，放这儿，只会变成咱们小区的垃圾堆，最后还得咱们扔。”

老何脸有点挂不住，嘴里哼哼两声，一拎被子，“那我就拿回去。”他抱着箱子下台阶回楼，雪粉在他鞋沿上开了几朵细小的白花。

不一会儿，一对年轻夫妇抱着个孩子来翻衣服。孩子鼻子红红的，小手不停摸拉链拽毛球。年轻男人挑中了一件深蓝色羽绒服，袖口还算新，纸条上写着“尺码L”。他试着把拉链拉上，“比我那件工地上穿的强。”女人给他整理领子，“回去给爸穿，老怕冷。”

旁边另一个老太太拿起那条被子又放下，皱着鼻子，有点不好意思。她看了看四周，轻声说：“味儿大。”

小惠点点头。“您挑里面干净的。那个红格子的围巾挺好的。”

午后，太阳偏移，风越发硬。小区群里忽然弹出一条消息。

“老何：咋整明白‘自个儿都不想要的东xzcviewr西，别硬塞给别asdfg人’这话的道理和现实有啥用呢？我就想做好事，咋还整得像受气了呢。”

他的打字一向不讲究，隔着屏幕都能听见手指咚咚敲玻璃的声音。紧接着是一个皱眉的表情。

几秒钟后，群里炸开，平时潜水的也冒了泡。

“物业小罗：何哥，别生气。咱就把这句话想明白点儿，现实用处挺大的。比如上次中秋谁给你塞的那两箱月饼，你吃了没？”

“老何：那还能咋样，扛回去放着，吃了两块，糖腻得我直犯困。剩下的过期扔了。”

“物业小罗：你看，这不就是。人家家里吃剩的，你拿着也不舒服。咱共享角这儿也是，捐出来的东西要让接的人真心觉得好、有用，不然他拿回去也是添堵。”

“二单元王阿姨：我上回拿了个电暖扇，回家一插啪啪冒火星，吓死我了。小伙子提醒得对。”

“海宝妈：我今天挑到一本没涂鸦的拼音书，太开心了。谢谢匿名的邻居！”

群里轻松了些，两个笑哭的表情刷过去，夹杂着几声“嗯”。小罗趁着热乎，发了一张照片，是小惠把一件洗净的毛衣铺在阳光下的样子，袖子平平整整，不像被人丢弃，更像是被传递。

楼里走廊里又响起了脚步声，老何抱着那台DVD机下来了，他把手挠挠头，“我刚去插上试了下，能开机，但是读盘卡。算了，我先拿回去刷干净，能修的给修了。那被子我晾晾晒晒，再看。”

“您别急。”小惠笑起来，眼睛眯成了一条线，“要不您捐点别的？咱小区有人缺被子的，真的。就是要干净点。”

“干净这事儿还不好说么。”老何把手提袋放桌上，拉开拉链，“我老伴昨天说家里新买的苹果太多了，咬在嘴里硬硬的甜。你们给那些挑衣服的带几个，咱也算没白来。”

“这个就好。”小罗接过袋，笑，声音有温度，“您看，人家拿了水果会真心说谢谢。”

不远处，那个年轻男人已回头来了一遭，戴着棉帽，耳朵尖冻得发红。他把蓝羽绒服抱给老人，老人袖口露出的手腕瘦得像枝条，拉上拉链，低头闻了一下，“有太阳味。”他下意识说了句，“谢谢。”年轻男人挠挠后脑勺，“邻居捐的。”

“啥叫有太阳味啊。”老人笑，眼睛里泛起点湿意，像薄薄一层水汽，又像被风一吹就散开的光。

“物业小罗：现实用处还有一个。”群里又弹出消息，“咱们志愿者时间有限，收一堆用不了的东西，又得搬又得掂量，最后还得清运，累得腰直不起来。把精力省下来，帮真需要的人选合适的，这就叫有效。”

“老何：行了行了，知道了，你小子说话越来越会抻了。”他又发了个捂脸的表情，“我下午回去把那被子给你晒出来，晒出太阳味儿。”

天又阴了一点，风里的刺拉声像细线拽着塑料布。小惠把桌上刚来的几件衣服叠好，顺手把那张“共享角”的纸重新平整了一下。她看见老何抬头往天上望了一眼，那种望法不是烦躁，而像打了个主意——要把自己手里能做好的事做明白，让交出去的东西像一份体面。

傍晚，围墙外卖粥的小摊把蒸汽放得很高，空气里有米香。老何从楼上下来，胳膊上搭着刚晒过的被子，一层一层地折好。被角露出一截，白，干净，不再有潮味。他放下的时候动作轻，像放下一个人对自己脸面的要求。他说：“小罗，给谁家，我也不问了。反正，我自个儿也愿意盖。”

门岗的风铃响了两声。小区群又跳了一条消息，是某个年轻人发的：“今天领到了件合身的大衣。谢谢陌生人。以后我也挑干净的东西捐回来。”末尾是一个太阳。

老何把手揣进棉大衣口袋里，袖子里头暖起来了。他想起群里那句乱七八糟打出来的话，被冻得僵硬的手指一抖，把“东西”和“别人”敲成了“东xzcviewr西”“别asdfg人”。他笑了一下，笑完咳了两声，往回走，脚下雪哧哧响。他心里有了个顺溜的理儿：你不愿意用的，八成别人也不愿意。别把“做好事”当成清理自家的办法。愿意给出去的，也愿意留下来的人情，才是能在现实里对得上号的。
